era-2001.says: Both: a black-red-green tricolour with the national emblem, 2004. Wikipedia: restored 28 January 2002, 2004 version used from 9 October 2004 to 15 August 2021 (2013 latest version). FOTW: 4 January 2004 tricolour, 2:3, bearing 1298 AH.
era-2001.open: The mosque-and-wheat emblem content and the shahada placement on this page are not covered; the two sources differ on the 2004 day (4 January vs 9 October).

era-27.says: Wikipedia: plain white banner 27 September 1996 to 26 October 1997; black shahada on white 26 October 1997 to 13 November 2001. FOTW 'Afghanistan 1996-2001': after the Taliban took Kabul in 1996 the flag was 'at least initially' a plain white banner; the black-on-white shahada flag was adopted 27 October 1997 (Reuters, 26 October 1997, on the change of name to Islamic Emirate; a Taliban source says 25 October) and abolished in 2001; FOTW's historical index lists 'September 1996 - November 2001: white flag, at times with the Shahada in black'.
era-27.open: The black shahada date differs by a day or two (25, 26 or 27 October 1997 across the sources). A Flag Bulletin report of a green shahada is called probably mistaken. The symbolism stated earlier on the page is not covered by either source.

era-28.says: Wikipedia: a provisional flag 27 April to 6 December 1992, then the Rabbani government's flag with the shahada and the year 1298 on the emblem, 7 December 1992 to 27 January 2002, in Northern Alliance areas after 1996. FOTW: a provisional green-white-black flag with white lettering on the green stripe and black on the white (April-December 1992, citing Baert 2001), then from 2 December 1992 'three horizontal stripes of green, white, black with the coat of arms over all in the centre' in gold, used by the Northern Alliance to 2001.
era-28.open: The adoption date of the emblem flag is 2 December 1992 in FOTW and 7 December in Wikipedia; FOTW's note that the emblem carries the date 1371 differs from Wikipedia's mention of 1298 on the later emblem. Neither source says this design is the ancestor of the 2004 flag, and the page's colour symbolism is not covered.

era-27-1.says: Wikipedia: tricolour without seal 27 April to 18 October 1978; a red flag with a yellow seal 19 October 1978 to 21 April 1980; the tricolour returned 22 April 1980 under Babrak Karmal until 29 November 1987. FOTW: the republican flag without emblem after April 1978 (Baert 2001); a red flag with a gold emblem of script, wreath and star, 'October 1978 - April 1980' (decree of 18 October 1978); a black-red-green flag with an emblem released 21 April 1980; the same stripes with a new emblem from 30 November 1987 to 1992.
era-27-1.open: The red flag with the gold emblem drawn on the page was in use only from October 1978 to April 1980; from 1980 to 1992 both sources show a black-red-green tricolour. The official colour meanings and the end date in April 1992 are given by FOTW only in passing.

era-17.says: Wikipedia: the republic's flag was identical to the monarchy flag except for the removed year, 17 July 1973 to 8 May 1974; from 9 May 1974 to 26 April 1978 a new seal with a golden eagle, minbar, wheat and sun rays. FOTW (citing Baert 2001): the 1973 flag was the 1930-73 flag without the date; a Republican flag was introduced on 9 May 1974, three horizontal black-red-green stripes with a yellow eagle-and-wheat arms on the canton.
era-17.open: FOTW describes the 1973 flag as probably still carrying the monarchy emblem minus the date, so the eagle emblem of the page's drawing belongs only to 9 May 1974 to April 1978. The 'continuity of national colours' rationale is not covered.

era-1919.says: Wikipedia: the 1919 flag had no tricolour; the tricolour came about 1928 and the final monarchy flag, with a wheat emblem and the year 1348, is dated 27 March 1931 to 16 July 1973. FOTW: Amanullah's 1919 flag was a black field with the new arms (eight-pointed rays, an oval in 1921); a vertical black-red-green flag followed in 1928; the flag adopted on 31 October 1931 (three stripes, mosque and wheat arms, date 1348) served until 1973.
era-1919.open: The tricolour with the mosque-and-wheat emblem that the page draws belongs to 1931-1973; from 1919 to 1928 the flag was black, and the years 1928-1931 saw several changes. Wikipedia dates the 1931 flag to 27 March, FOTW to 31 October (the constitution). The page's colour meanings are not supported by either source.

era-1747.says: Wikipedia (Flag of Afghanistan): the flags of the Hotak dynasty (early 18th century) are remembered as solid black, sometimes with white shahada inscriptions, and the last solid black flag was used under Abdur Rahman Khan, with a white seal added in 1901. Wikipedia (Emirate of Afghanistan): the first coat of arms on a flag was a solid black banner with a white emblem under Abdur Rahman Khan, and under Dost Mohammad and Sher Ali the military flags were triangular, red and green, with white shahada text. Wikipedia (Durrani Empire): an infobox gives two Durrani flags with dates 1747-1818 but the text gives no design. FOTW: black became the national colour under Abdul Rahman (1880-1901). World Statesmen's flag sequence begins in 1881, and Britannica (Whitney Smith) covers twentieth-century flags only (the old white-emblem-on-black flag restored after 1929).
era-1747.open: A black field with a white central emblem is documented only from Abdur Rahman's reign (1880s) and the 1901-1919 flag, not for the Durrani period 1747-1818 or the red-and-green flags described for the mid-19th century. No text read describes the Durrani flag's design, so the caption's Durrani-era black standard is unsupported.

era-1991.says: Wikipedia says the star was removed on 7 April 1992 after the communist government collapsed, leaving the black double-headed eagle on red, standardised by law on 22 July 2002. FOTW's main page gives the flag as adopted on 7 April 1992, a red flag with a black double-headed eagle, and prescribed by the Constitution (1998) and Law 8926 (2002); its history lists the 1946 star and the 1992 restoration.
era-1991.open: Both publishers date the current design to 1992, not 1991, so the era's start year is unsupported. The caption 'unchanged since 1912' is contradicted by both: they record a crown (1928), fasces (1939) and a star (1946-92) on the eagle flag in between.

era-1946.says: Wikipedia: in early 1946 a gold star was placed above the eagle; Law 5506 of 28 December 1976 describes a red five-pointed star embroidered in gold, designed by Sadik Kaceli. FOTW: in 1946 a red five-pointed star with gold border was placed above the eagle's heads. Both give removal on 7 April 1992.
era-1946.open: Page said the star went 'the moment the single-party state ended'; sources date removal to 1992.

era-1944.says: FOTW says the Democratic Government proclaimed on 10 October 1944 flew the pre-war black-eagle flag with a yellow star in the canton, with some flags carrying a hammer and sickle instead, and that the plain eagle flag was used at the Tirana liberation festivities on 29 November 1944. Wikipedia says the Democratic Government's flag was first published in War Bulletin no. 51 of 28 November 1944, was widely used at public events until 1946, and that a golden star above the eagle was added in early 1946 (7 March 1946 per FOTW).
era-1944.open: Only FOTW describes the star (yellow, in the canton, or a hammer and sickle); Wikipedia's text does not describe the 1944 flag's emblems. The star above the eagle belongs to the 1946 constitutional flag, not to this period.

era-1943.says: Wikipedia: in October 1943 the union with Italy was dissolved, the country reverted to the decrees of September 1928, and pre-Italian flags and symbols were used. Flags of the World's German-occupation page: after the German occupation (26 September 1943) the National Assembly re-established the 1928 monarchical constitution on 20 October 1943; the flags of the earlier regime were readopted and the Savoy crown and the Lieutenant's flag were abolished; the emblem is a black double-headed eagle (Fachinger: shifted toward the hoist). Both are Wikipedia and FOTW, two publishers.
era-1943.open: Neither source gives an exact design: whether the Zog-era crown or Skanderbeg helmet was restored is not stated (FOTW says 'flags of 1939' readopted, which contradicts the Savoy-crown abolition); the page's 'no crown or party symbol' is an inference. FOTW's account rests on Ollé (1996) and an observer.

era-1939.says: Wikipedia: a fascist flag replaced Zog's on 4 December 1939; the 1940 yearbook says the flag is red with the black double-headed eagle and the sign of the lictor's fasces at the centre. Flags of the World: the Italian-union kingdom's flag was adopted 13 April 1939 (constitution of 3 June 1939: red with the double-headed eagle in the centre); Royal Decrees 141-142 of 28 September 1939 added the Skanderbeg helmet, fasces and Savoy ribbons; the state flag was used 3 June 1939 to 25 July 1943.
era-1939.open: The sources put the fasces in the arms or at the centre of the eagle, not a small fasces beneath it as the page's caption says; the two sources also differ on the start date (13 April / 3 June vs 4 December 1939). FOTW notes a May 1942 'flag unrest' that brought back the Zog-era flag in part.

era-1928.says: Wikipedia: the 1928 Fundamental Statute (art. III) describes a red flag with a black double-headed eagle in the centre; versions shown for 1928-1934 and 1934-1939. Flags of the World's Kingdom page: Zogu proclaimed King on 1 September 1928, constitution 22 November 1928, flags approved 3 August 1929 and made official by Royal Legislative Decree no. 178 of 8 August 1929 (a state flag with a black eagle, 1:1 eagle, 2:3 flag; royal standard square with two golden branches below the eagle).
era-1928.open: Crown versus helmet is unresolved: the FOTW main page says the eagle was surmounted by Skanderbeg's gold helmet as a royal crown, Wikipedia mentions a crown only in its introduction, and FOTW's Kingdom sub-pages describe neither (only tagging a helmet). The caption's helmet is therefore not established; the red field with black eagle under Zog is.

era-1925.says: Flags of the World's republic page: 'On 25 January 1925 a national assembly proclaimed a republic and the national flag was not modified'; the flag of the republic dates from a 20 January 1920 statute, a black double-headed eagle on red; a 1926 presidential standard has Skanderbeg's golden helmet on the eagle. Wikipedia: the republic's flag was always shown square and first appears in Teki Selenica's 1927 guidebook; images are labelled 1925-1928.
era-1925.open: FOTW dates the flag's design to 1920 and the republic's proclamation to 25 January 1925; Wikipedia gives no design text for 1925-28 beyond the square shape. The caption's 'without a royal crest' is consistent, but the 1926 presidential standard carried a helmet.

era-1914.says: FOTW describes the red flag with the black double-headed eagle as the Albanian flag throughout the period: the 1914 principality flag was the former flag with a yellow-clawed eagle and a star (Hesmer; Ollé); the 1914-15 Regency used it de facto; the 1917 republic under Italian protection adopted it; the Korce province (1916-18) used the Skanderbeg flag; and the Republic's Constitutional Statute (20 January 1920) kept it. Wikipedia shows the Principality flag (1914), a surviving 1920 Lushnje flag (dark red silk with a black eagle), the Korce flag (1916-1920) and the 1925-1928 Republic flag.
era-1914.open: Several variants are described, not one: Essad Pasha's rival government used a red flag with a white star and no eagle in 1913 and 1915 (both publishers), so the caption that rival governments claimed the same eagle flag is not supported for his; the Wikipedia principality section is uncited and the two publishers differ on the eagle's details.

era-1912.says: Wikipedia says no trace survives of the flag raised at Vlore on 28 November 1912 and that 'no definitive proof' of its look exists, but cites Eqrem Vlora's memoir (a black double-headed eagle on red) and Kristo Floqi's 1937 letter (thin red cloth, black eagle), and shows a Provisional Government flag from a 17 December 1912 New York newspaper cover. FOTW says a national flag was formally adopted on 28 November 1912 and shows a reconstruction (after Vexilloteca, from a 1927 illustration); its Albania page says the red flag with the black double-headed eagle is nicknamed the flag of Skanderbeg, said to be his family's standard, and its 1912 page says a white star was added to the autonomist flag in 1912.
era-1912.open: No original flag survives and the accounts differ on details (the star, the eagle's form); the link to Skanderbeg is stated by FOTW as 'said to be' and rests on the red-and-black eagle of his family arms, not on a 1912 source naming the flag as his banner. The drawing is a reconstruction.

era-1479.says: Wikipedia's article on the Ottoman flag says a red flag with white star and crescent was ordered for the Ottoman navy in 1793 and adopted as the national flag in 1844; before that, war flags often showed the Zulfiqar sword. FOTW's Ottoman page lists an 'Albanian civil ensign' (red with a black stripe, after Smith) among Ottoman civil ensigns, and its Albania page says that in the first quarter of the 19th century Albania's non-Muslims used a red flag with a black stripe and Muslim Albanians a red-blue-red flag with a white crescent. It also says nationalists used a red flag with the black double-headed eagle in the 19th century and in the 1910-1911 revolts. Wikipedia's Albanian flag article says the eagle flag was raised at Deciq on 6 April 1911. Encyclopaedia Britannica (Whitney Smith) independently says there were several Ottoman flags in red or green with crescent and star over the centuries, that the present design was established for the navy in June 1793 with an eight-pointed star, and that the star was reduced to five points about 1844.
era-1479.open: The caption's claim that the vilayets had no flag of their own is contradicted by FOTW's civil ensigns and nationalist flags, and the red crescent-and-star flag it shows is documented only from 1793 (navy) and 1844 (national), not for 1479-1844. No source read describes a flag of the Scutari, Janina or Kosovo vilayets themselves. Britannica gives no date for the Ottoman red crescent flag before 1793, so the card's flag is documented for 1793-1912 only (as the national flag from about 1844).

era-1444.says: Flags of the World: on 28 November 1443 Skanderbeg 'raised the red flag with the black double-headed eagle'; Marin Barleti (c. 1508-1510) described the family emblem as a double-headed eagle on red; the modern flag 'is said to have been the flag of Skanderbeg'; the helmet with a goat's head is tied to Durand-Monti's Albanie (1990). Wikipedia: Skanderbeg adopted a flag like the Eastern Roman flag, a double-headed eagle on red, cited to Mucha, Crampton and Louda (1985); the League of Lezhe used it; Elsie (2010) hedges 'also said to have been'; a 1556 Veronese painting is read as showing him with the flag.
era-1444.open: Both publishers hedge: the attribution rests on tradition, one cited book on Wikipedia, and Barleti's later description; no contemporary banner survives. The date differs (FOTW 28 November 1443 with Free Principality; Wikipedia 1443 after Nis), and the goat-horned helmet crest is FOTW-only, from a 1990 book.

era-1962.says: Both sources give 1962, the year this page starts the current flag. Wikipedia's infobox gives the adoption as 3 July 1962; Flags of the World dates it 3 July 1962.
era-1962.open: Only the year the current flag was adopted was compared; the design and the swatch colours were not checked against a specification.

era-1830.says: Wikipedia (Flag of Algeria): the official flag was the French flag (the invasion began under the white Bourbon flag, then the tricolour was adopted); a striped merchant ensign was used 1848-1910 and green-and-white star-and-crescent nationalist flags from the 1930s and in 1945. FOTW (French Colonial Empire): Algeria was considered integrated French territory, depending on the Minister of the Interior, and the French flag 'seems to have been the only national flag flying there'. Wikipedia (List of Algerian flags): a seven-stripe ensign of French Algeria with the French colours whose exact rules and years of use are unknown.
era-1830.open: FOTW qualifies its statement with 'seems', and both sources show subsidiary flags (the striped ensign, the ensign prescribed in 1875, nationalist flags from the 1920s-30s), so the French flag was the national flag but not literally the only flag.

era-1516.says: Wikipedia (Flag of Algeria), citing Cheurfi, Belhamissi and al-Jilali: an all-red flag was the Regency's primary emblem, 'devoid of any symbol' and unlike the Ottoman flags with crescents and stars; a green-yellow-red flag is reported for 1516 and red-yellow-green striped flags were captured by the French in 1830, and the Dey flew a plain red flag in 1830. Flags of the World (Regency of Algiers): apart from the deys' elaborate personal standards 'the flag in use in the country was the Ottoman flag'; ship flags before 1830 were white over black; a French writer's green standard with a gold crescent may be an error. Hubert de Vries's heraldry survey of Algeria shows an Algerian war ensign and merchant flag of about 1700 and a flag chart of about 1750 (Dutch archive) with the Ottoman merchant flag and a blue war ensign showing an arm swinging a sword, and attributes an all-red flag to Tlemcen from 1488, not to Algiers.
era-1516.open: Three accounts disagree: Wikipedia says the Regency's main flag was plain red and unlike the Ottoman flag, FOTW says the Ottoman flag was in use, and the c.1750 chart in de Vries shows an Ottoman merchant flag beside a blue sword-arm war ensign. Neither design is confirmed by two publishers and none dates a single flag to 1516-1830 as a whole; the card's plain red field rests on Wikipedia alone.

era-1866.says: Wikipedia: the civil vertical tricolour dates from 1866 (reforms adopted 22 April 1866 by Bishop Caixal), arms added to the vertical flag around 1939, standardised by the 1993 Constitution. Flags of the World (historical flags): 'In 1866 Napoleon III obtained the inclusion of the blue'; talocci (1993) says the tricolour replaced the yellow-red flag in 1866; a horizontal blue-yellow-red flag with a coronet in the centre is described in 1898 (Spender) and 1917 (National Geographic) and abolished c. 1934/5; a vertical blue-yellow-red flag with the arms (coronet, no motto) is shown in Flaggenbuch 1939. Wikipedia (Andorra): the New Reform of 1866 is linked to the national symbols such as the tricolour flag.
era-1866.open: The page's arms in 1866 are contradicted: Flags of the World shows a coronet, not arms, on a horizontal tricolour between 1866 and about 1934/5, and vertical stripes with arms only from c. 1939; sources differ on the 1993 constitution date (28 April versus 4 May) and the 1866 date is marked uncertain by Flags of the World.

era-843.open: Whether a flag, banner or standard existed in this period was not checked. The colour shown is not evidence of one.

era-1806.says: Flags of the World and WorldStatesmen give a vertical yellow-red bicolour for 1806-1866 (FOTW citing Herzog and Hannes, Pedersen and Talocci). Lang-Valchs (Papers de recerca historica 8, Societat Andorrana de Ciencies) says that some encyclopedias describe a first Andorran flag of two vertical bands, yellow and red, born of the 1806 Napoleonic decree, but that no document from that context, and no other document, mentions it, and that no old encyclopedia or web page gives a checkable source; he concludes its existence must be doubted until an unequivocal pre-1866 mention appears, and dates the flag's creation to 1866. Wikipedia (Flag of Andorra) gives 1866 as the first flag.
era-1806.open: The yellow-red bicolour rests on compilers (FOTW, WorldStatesmen) that give no document, and the one scholarly article read doubts it. The card's yellow-red caption is therefore not confirmed for 1806-1866, though a plain blue-yellow-red tricolour before 1866 is contradicted by every source.

era-1278.says: Lang-Valchs, 'La bandera andorrana i l'escut d'armes' (Papers de recerca historica 8, Societat Andorrana de Ciencies), a scholarly article, says the colours of the flag were taken from the coat of arms and that no document from 1806 or earlier mentions an Andorran flag, even where the coat of arms is described; it holds that until an unequivocal mention of a pre-1866 flag is found its existence must be doubted. FOTW and WorldStatesmen show the Catalan Quatre Barres for the period before 1806 on one contributor's statement, and Wikipedia gives no flag before 1866.
era-1278.open: The card is openly a stand-in, and no source read describes a flag or a flag-like device of the co-princes in 1278-1806; the Catalan flag is an inference by FOTW and WorldStatesmen, with no documented basis.

era-1975.open: Only the year the current flag was adopted was compared; the design and the swatch colours were not checked against a specification.

era-1575.says: Wikipedia's Flag of Angola: Angola flew the flag of Portugal during the Portuguese colonial period, lowered in Luanda at noon on 10 November 1975; its Portuguese Angola article (1575-1975) shows the Portuguese flag as its infobox flag. Flags of the World (Portuguese colonies): since the 1940s the Portuguese government treated the colonies as parts of the country and made no flags for them other than the national flag, apart from flags for officials and military units and unadopted proposals. Flags of the World's Portugal page dates the national flag to the Republic of 1911.
era-1575.open: The two sources support the Portuguese national flag over Angola in the late colonial period (Flags of the World from the 1940s, Wikipedia without dates); the drawn flag is the post-1911 republican flag, and the monarchy's earlier flags and ensigns from 1575 to 1910 are not described by either source.

era-1981.says: Both sources date the current flag to 1967, before this era begins in 1981, so the flag was already in use at the start. Wikipedia's infobox gives the adoption as 27 February 1967; Flags of the World dates it 16 February 1967.
era-1981.open: Only the year the current flag was adopted was compared; the design and the swatch colours were not checked against a specification.

era-1967.says: Wikipedia: the current flag was adopted 27 February 1967, 11 days after royal assent to the West Indies Act 1967, to mark self-government; over 600 people entered the competition, won by Reginald Samuel; full independence 1 November 1981 with the 1967 flag kept. FOTW: flag adopted 27 February 1967 on associated statehood, competition of over 600 entries won by Reginald Samuel, independence 1 November 1981.
era-1967.open: FOTW says a 1994 decision gave the sun seven full points and the page does not confirm that the 1967 flag was identical to today's; FOTW says the flag was apparently adopted for land use at first.

era-1632.says: FOTW's colonial-flags page says that until 1956 the appropriate Blue Ensign for any government boat in Antigua was the Leeward Islands one, that a flag badge for Antigua was introduced in 1956-57 (a beach, hills, a grey building and an agave on a shield, on a white disc), that arms were granted in 1967, and that the plain red ensign was the civil ensign. Wikipedia's list of historical British flags gives a Blue Ensign with the colonial arms of Antigua on a white disc for 1956-1962 and without the disc for 1962-1967, and Leeward Islands Blue Ensigns from 1871. World Statesmen's captions: United Kingdom flag to 1874, Leeward Islands colony flag 1874-1956, Antigua flag 1956-1958 and 1958-1967.
era-1632.open: Three publishers support a Blue Ensign with an Antigua badge only for 1956-1967, and a Leeward Islands ensign from 1871 (Wikipedia) or 1874 (World Statesmen) to 1956; earlier years show the Union flag (World Statesmen) or nothing. Nothing read gives an Antigua-specific flag for 1632-1871. The 'simplified pineapple' badge is not what FOTW describes for 1956-67 (an agave shield; the pineapple was the crest).

era-1861.says: Wikipedia says the flag was officially recognised on 20 July 1816 at Tucumán, that Pueyrredón established the sun flag on 25 January 1818, that on unification in 1861 the national flag replaced Buenos Aires State's flag, that Roca's decree of 25 April 1884 limited the sun flag to government institutions, that decrees of 1943 and Decree 10,302/1944 regulated it, that Law 23,208 of 1985 let individuals use it, and that Decree 1650/2010 standardised colours and proportions. FOTW (Gregoric) says Congress at Tucumán passed the plain triband in 1816, that the Congress, then in Buenos Aires, created the war flag by adding the sun on 25 February 1818, and that the 1884 decree defined the 1:2 ratio and restricted the sun flag to military and government agencies.
era-1861.open: The sources differ on the sun flag's date (25 January or 25 February 1818). FOTW gives only the year for Tucumán, and does not cover 1861. This page used to say the sun flag became the sole civil and state flag.

era-1816.says: Wikipedia says independence was declared on 9 July 1816 and the flag officially recognised on 20 July 1816, and that Pueyrredón established the flag with the Sun of May on 25 January 1818 (a 1944 decree says 25 February). FOTW (Gregoric) says the Tucumán Congress passed the plain triband in 1816 and that the Congress in Buenos Aires added the sun on 25 February 1818.
era-1816.open: The date of the sun differs between sources.

era-1810.says: Wikipedia says Belgrano wrote on 26 February 1812 proposing a national flag, that it was first raised at Rosario on 27 February 1812, that the First Triumvirate ordered him in early March 1812 to stop using it, that he had it blessed at Jujuy on 25 May 1812 and called it the national flag, and that the origin of the colours cannot be accurately established. FOTW (Gregoric) says there are several theories about the design raised on 27 February 1812 and that triband flags were in use by 1814 without the sun.
era-1810.open: This page's «adopted informally as the flag of the patriot army» is close to Wikipedia's account, which also says the government told him to stop.

era-1776.says: Wikipedia (Flag of Argentina): the last formally used Spanish flag was the red and yellow one set by Charles III in 1785, used mainly for naval and military purposes, and a Spanish flag of that kind flew over the fort at Buenos Aires in 1810. Wikipedia (Cross of Burgundy Flag): the cross served as the flag of the viceroyalties of the New World. FOTW (Spain): the Burgundy saltire an ensign 1506-1670s, then a jack until 1785, and the Spanish military flag on land up to 1843 (es_brgdy).
era-1776.open: Neither publisher mentions the Rio de la Plata viceroyalty (created 1776), so use of the cross there is inferred; as a ship's ensign it was superseded by the red-yellow flag in 1785, and the caption's 'military and naval ensign' fits ships only to 1785. The cross stands for the crown, not for a flag of the viceroyalty.

era-1820.says: Wikipedia (Flag of Argentina): the light blue-and-white flag with the Sun of May is listed for 1818-1819 and 1820-1829; Rosas made the official shade turquoise blue in 1829; a Rosas-era Confederation flag with four Phrygian caps and a red sun is captioned 1836-1852; after Caseros (1852) the inland provinces reverted to light blue with the golden Sun of May; the State of Buenos Aires used its own flag 1852-1861. FOTW (Argentina): on 25 February 1818 the Congress created the war flag by adding the sun to the plain triband. Wikipedia (Argentine Confederation): infobox flag captioned 1836-1852 and the Buenos Aires secession of 11 September 1852.
era-1820.open: The sun flag is attested for 1818-1829 and (inland) from 1852, but not as one flag for the whole 1820s-1861 span: Wikipedia, the only source for 1829-1861, shows Rosas-era variants, dark blue and red-and-white federalist flags and Buenos Aires's own flag, and FOTW's page carries nothing on the Confederation period (it only links Olle's external pages). The drawing fits only part of the era. A second look for official Argentine sources (Casa Rosada, argentina.gob.ar) found no readable page; Wikipedia remains the only source for 1829-1861.

era-1516.says: Wikipedia (Flag of Argentina): the first flags used in the territory of modern Argentina were those associated with the Spanish crown. Wikipedia (Cross of Burgundy Flag): earliest use in Spain 1506, and in the colonisation of the Americas it served as the flag of the viceroyalties of the New World (Bandera de Ultramar). FOTW (Spain, 1506): a Spanish ensign 1506-1670s and jack until 1785, 'a military banner' that was never the official flag of the Spanish Empire; FOTW (es_brgdy): the Spanish military flag from the 16th century up to 1843.
era-1516.open: No source read mentions Peru, Lima or the Rio de la Plata specifically, so the cross is the crown's banner standing in for a territory with no flag of its own, not a documented local flag; the field colour varied between periods and the cross was a military banner rather than an administrative flag. The viceroyalties cited by Wikipedia (New Spain, Peru) are not named for this territory.

era-1991.says: Both sources date the current flag to 1990, before this era begins in 1991, so the flag was already in use at the start. Wikipedia's infobox gives the adoption as 1 August 1918 (re-adopted on 24 August 1990); Flags of the World dates it 1995.
era-1991.open: Only the year the current flag was adopted was compared; the design and the swatch colours were not checked against a specification.

era-1920.says: Wikipedia (Flag of the Armenian SSR): the flag was adopted on 17 December 1952 - like the Soviet flag but with a quarter-width horizontal blue stripe in the middle; the 1922 flag was red with the Cyrillic letters ССРА in the upper left corner and lasted a month before the Transcaucasian SFSR; between 1936 and 1940 red with a gold hammer and sickle and the Armenian letters ՀԽՍՀ beneath; between 1940 and 1952 the letters changed to ՀՍՍՌ. FOTW agrees: Soviet Armenia was proclaimed 29 November 1920; 1922 red with yellow initials; 1937 yellow Armenian initials with a yellow hammer and sickle above; 1952 flag with a dark blue bar in the middle, 1/4 of the width, approved 17 December 1952.
era-1920.open: The drawing on the page is the 1952 flag only; the earlier flags (1922, 1937, 1940s) and the TSFSR years 1922-36 are not drawn. Neither source says the stripe was near the bottom edge.

era-1918.says: Wikipedia: on 1 August 1918 the National Assembly voted a horizontal tricolour of red, blue and orange (a 19 September 1918 instruction asked for yellow in place of orange cloth); parliament reaffirmed it in June 1919; Soviet troops entered Yerevan 29 November 1920. FOTW: the flag was used 1918-1921 and the red-blue-orange tricolour was readopted on 24 August 1990.
era-1918.open: Neither source read gives the meanings of the colours (blood, sky, courage) stated on the page; the end date differs slightly (Wikipedia late 1920, FOTW 1921).

era-1828.says: Wikipedia's Flag of Russia article says Alexander II decreed the black-yellow-white tricolour the official heraldic state flag in 1858, with white-blue-red still used by merchants and private citizens, and the white-blue-red the sole national flag from 1896. FOTW's early-flags page says Russia occupied and abolished the Iravan Khanate in 1827. Wikipedia and FOTW describe Armenian flags of the period only as nationalist designs (1826-28 militia banners; Alishan's 1885 tricolours). Second look: World Statesmen lists the Russian flag for Armenia from 22 Feb 1828 to 22 Apr 1918, without saying which Russian flag.
era-1828.open: World Statesmen supports a Russian flag over Armenia 1828-1918 but does not say which; the black-yellow-white flag is documented only for 1858-1896 (Wikipedia) of the 1828-1915 span, and a different flag was used in the rest. No source read says the imperial flag was flown over the Armenian provinces in particular.

era-1375.says: Wikipedia says that after Armenia was split between the Persian and Ottoman empires 'the idea of an Armenian flag ceased to exist for some time' (it gives no dates). FOTW's early-flags page records only the flag of the Iravan Khanate (1747-1827), nominally Persian, captured by Russian troops about 1827 and held in a museum in Baku: diagonally dark red and white with a yellow device at the upper hoist.
era-1375.open: The card's split of an Ottoman crescent and a Safavid roundel is an acknowledged composite. Neither source describes an Ottoman or Safavid flag for these lands in 1375-1828, and the Iravan flag belongs only to the end of the period.

era-1045.says: Wikipedia's Flag of Armenia article describes flags of the Armenian Kingdom of Cilicia and its ports from maps and manuscripts (Dalorto 1325, Dulcert 1339, the Catalan Atlas 1375, the Book of Knowledge, a 1416 armorial), and the flag of Alexandretta and Lamos. FOTW's early-flags page gives the flag of the Principality of Khachen dated 1214, a golden cross on an apricot field. Neither mentions flags under Byzantine, Seljuk or Mongol overlordship after the fall of Ani in 1045. Second look: the Libro del conoscimiento (Markham translation) names Armenia the Less and its cities but the translated text gives no flag for it (its plate is not in the text), and World Statesmen lists no Armenian flag before the Iravan khanate flag of c.1827.
era-1045.open: The brown field with a ring and dot drawn on the card matches none of these; no source read describes it or a flag for Armenian lands under foreign overlordship in 1045-1375. The Cilician and Khachen flags are known from maps, manuscripts and one dated flag, and are not what the card draws.

era-885.says: Wikipedia's Flag of Armenia article says that when Armenia gained independence in 885 the flag was a dark red canvas with a white leopard and a Christian cross, and that the Ani leopard is in the arms of Gyumri. Wikipedia's Bagratid Armenia article describes a relief on the gate of Ani of a lion or leopard under a checkered cross, which modern scholars take as the symbol of Ani and the Bagratids. FOTW's early-flags page covers neither the Bagratids nor the 885 flag.
era-885.open: The dark red field with leopard and cross is stated only in Wikipedia's flag article, without a medieval source named there; no contemporary image of a Bagratid flag is cited in the sources read. The Ani relief is an emblem, not a flag. The card's caption (blue with gold cross and disc) is in no source.

era-1901.says: Wikipedia says a federal flag competition of April 1901 drew 32,823 entries, the winning design first flew over the Royal Exhibition Building in Melbourne on 3 September 1901 with five near-identical entries sharing the prize, Edward VII's approval was announced on 11 February 1903, the Southern Cross stars were standardised to seven points on 23 February 1903, the Commonwealth Star gained a seventh point on 8 December 1908, and the Flags Act 1953 received royal assent on 14 February 1954. FOTW (Morris) says the competition was announced in the Gazette of 29 April 1901, the flag first flew on 3 September 1901, the King's approval was given in 1902 and confirmed by a proclamation of 20 February 1903, a seventh point was added by the Gazette of 19 December 1908, and the Flags Act 1953 was confirmed in a Gazette of 14 April 1954.
era-1901.open: The sources differ on the 1908 date (8 or 19 December), the 1903 dates, and the 1954 date (14 February assent or 14 April gazette). This page used to say the star was seven-pointed from the start.

era-1788.says: Wikipedia's Flag of Australia (citing the Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet) says Phillip raised the Union Jack on 7 February 1788 when he proclaimed New South Wales, that this was the 1606 Union Jack without St Patrick's cross (the cross was added after the 1801 Acts of Union), and that each colony also had its own flag based on the Blue Ensign with a state badge; it dates the National Colonial Flag to 1823-24. FOTW's Australia page notes that the Flags Act 1953 preserves the right to fly the Union Jack and quotes a contributor arguing it was in effect the national flag before 1954; its Victoria and New South Wales pages date colonial Blue Ensigns to 1867-1877. A report in The Argus of 4 September 1901 reproduces the federal flag competition judges' letter, which refers to the Southern Cross already shown in some of the State flags, such as New Zealand and Victoria.
era-1788.open: No source read says the Union Jack was flown as the formal ensign over each of the six colonies throughout 1788-1901; the sources instead give each colony its own Blue Ensign. The 1788 flag differed from the post-1801 Union Jack the card draws. The Department's own timeline (pmc.gov.au) could not be read in an earlier pass (bot-gate and empty pages) and was not worked around. The 1901 newspaper confirms existing State flags but says nothing on the Union Jack as the formal ensign over each colony in 1788-1901. The AustLII text of the Flags Act 1953 returned HTTP 403 and was not read.

era-1955.says: FOTW says the Flag Act passed by the Austrian parliament on 28 March 1984 put into effect the state flag (red-white-red with the arms) and its 2:3 ratio, and that the plain triband is the national flag and civil ensign. Wikipedia's infobox gives 1 May 1945 for the formal adoption and 28 March 1984 for the state flag, and 1230 for the origin of the design.
era-1955.open: The date a plain red-white-red became Austria's flag again depends on which event is meant: 1945 (restoration), 1955 (this era's start) or 1984 (the Flag Act); the sources read do not give 1955. FOTW also notes the law does not specify the shade of red.

era-1156.says: FOTW quotes Peter Diem: Duke Frederick II (1210-1246), the last Babenberg, adopted the red-white-red arms in 1230, with the first colour document dated 1232; Wikipedia gives a seal on a deed of 30 November 1230 for Lilienfeld Abbey and calls the Leopold V story a legend. The AEIOU Österreich-Lexikon (Austria-Forum, TU Graz) gives the same seal as the first appearance of the Bindenschild as the Austrian duke's arms and notes striped shields in the chronicle of Petrus de Ebulo (1194/97); Diem (2010, Forum Politische Bildung) calls Frederick II 'the creator of red-white-red' and says the flag of the colours played a small part afterwards, mainly signifying belonging to the duchy.
era-1156.open: This is evidence for the arms from 1230, not for a banner and not for the era from 1156: nothing found describes a red-white-red banner before 1230, and the striped shields of the 1190s are not shown to be red-white-red. Whether a banner of this design was flown in the 13th century is not established; the sources describe a shield, a seal and a ceremonial dress.

era-1867.says: Wikipedia says black-yellow was the Habsburg monarchy's national flag, later the Austrian Empire's, until 1918 (citing Preuß, Flaggenlexikon). FOTW says the red-white-red ensign with a shield was adopted as merchant ensign on 20 March 1786, that a dual-monarchy merchant flag was created in 1869 (18 February 1869 decree, in use from 1 August 1869), and that a red-white-red war ensign was used from 1880 until 10 October 1915.
era-1867.open: The image shows an eagle on gold, which is the imperial standard rather than the black-yellow flag the sources describe. This page's statement that red-white-red was «used for the Austrian lands since medieval times» is stronger than the sources: Diem puts the arms in 1230 and FOTW the ensign in 1786.

era-1918.says: Göbl (ADLER, via Austria-Forum): on 31 October 1918, before the First Republic was proclaimed, the State Council, then running the government provisionally, fixed the new state colours on the proposal of the Christian Social deputy Wilhelm Miklas, bypassing Habsburg black-yellow for the older Babenberg red-white-red; when the new flag was to be hoisted (12 November 1918), Red Guards tore the white stripes out so that only red cloth rose. AEIOU: the colours were taken over in 1918 by the Republic from the old Babenberg flag. Wikipedia: German Austria adopted the red-white-red triband after Austria-Hungary dissolved in 1918.
era-1918.open: Neither source calls it 'the first government in centuries to fly it without an eagle or crown' (AEIOU says red-white-red survived as the navy flag); the page's text on seeking union with Germany is not covered here.

era-1938.says: Wikipedia (Flag of Germany): from 15 September 1935 the Nazi swastika flag was Germany's exclusive national flag. Wikipedia (Anschluss): German troops entering Austria on 12 March 1938 were greeted with Nazi flags. Flags of the World (Austria): the Austrian flag was not used after the Anschluss of 1938 and was restored in 1945. Goebl (ADLER, reprinted by Austria-Forum): after the Anschluss in March 1938 the 1934 Austrian state eagle was at once shelved.
era-1938.open: No page read says in so many words that the Reich's swastika flag was the only flag flown in Austria in 1938-1945; that follows from Austria's incorporation into the Reich and the 1935 German flag law. The rep paragraph's claim that no red-white-red flag was flown anywhere in the country is stronger than the sources, which say only that it was not used.

era-1945.says: FOTW (Steven Shea, 1996) says the flag was restored with independence in 1945; Wikipedia's infobox gives 1 May 1945 as the formal adoption, with no law or citation named.
era-1945.open: The Allied occupation (1945–1955) is not described by either source; the page's statements about the four zones were not checked.

era-1934.says: Göbl (ADLER): the Fatherland Front's Kruckenkreuz, taken over from a 1924 decoration, was placed in the middle of the red-white-red flag and from 1936 equated domestically with the state flag; the 1934 arms were a double-headed, haloed black eagle with the red-white-red shield. Diem (2010): the Kruckenkreuz, introduced in September 1933, was soon built into the red-white-red flag; the Kruckenkreuz flag counted as equal to the state flag and could be flown beside it domestically; the 1 May 1934 constitution (art. 3) restored the double-headed eagle with haloes in place of the single-headed eagle.
era-1934.open: The page's caption and drawing ('single-headed eagle and mural crown') describe the 1919 arms, not the 1934 ones; neither source says the state flag itself carried the eagle (page text corrected).

era-1919.says: Göbl (ADLER, via Austria-Forum): the State Council set the red-white-red colours on 31 October 1918, bypassing the Habsburg black-yellow for the older Babenberg colours, which also appear in the Habsburg-Lorraine house arms but were less identified with the dynasty. Diem (2010): despite the First Republic's bitter political camps, red-white-red remained largely uncontested until 1938. AEIOU Österreich-Lexikon: in 1919 the colours red-white-red were taken over for the flag of the Republic of Austria. Wikipedia: the triband adopted in 1918 and formally adopted 1 May 1945.
era-1919.open: The 1919 flag rests on three publishers, with Göbl, Diem and AEIOU as reference works. No source gives a separate 1919 act for the flag, and the page's claim that it was a political break with the Habsburgs is only partly supported (Göbl: they avoided black-yellow, but red-white-red is also in the Habsburg-Lorraine house arms).

era-1804.says: AEIOU Österreich-Lexikon: in 1804 the Austrian imperial state took over, with the arms, the black-yellow flag (black double eagle on a gold ground) of the Holy Roman Empire; red-white-red survived only as the flag of the war and merchant navy and as the house colours of Habsburg-Lothringen. Wikipedia: the black-yellow flag was the national flag of the Habsburg monarchy and the Austrian Empire, with a caption dating the Empire's flag c.1804-1867.
era-1804.open: The Congress of Vienna and the 'Holy Roman title' passages of the page are not covered by these sources; the black-yellow flag's end date (1867 per Wikipedia caption) is not confirmed by AEIOU.

era-1453.says: Diem (2010): the red-white-red flag symbolised belonging to the Duchy of Austria, played a relatively small part once mercenary armies replaced knightly ones, and was displaced by the black-yellow imperial banner in the centuries when Austrian archdukes were emperors; red-white-red appeared at homage ceremonies, processions and triumphal arches, and Joseph II introduced a red-white-red sea flag on 20 March 1786. AEIOU: the Bindenschild stayed the arms image of the lands, with the imperial eagle added from 1433. Wikipedia: Habsburgs took the colours after 1278 (Rheinfelden 1283).
era-1453.open: The page's 'war banner' and the 1453 start are not in the sources; red-white-red here was largely ceremonial and the imperial banner prevailed, so 'continues as the lands' own flag' is too strong (page text corrected).

era-1282.says: Wikipedia: the red-white-red arms are first documented on a deed of 30 November 1230, were adopted by Ottokar II after 1246, and by the Habsburgs after 1278 (Rheinfelden 1283); FOTW: Friedrich II adopted the arms in 1230, first document 1232. AEIOU Österreich-Lexikon: the Bindenschild replaced the imperial eagle on Austrian flags about 1230, the first picture of an Austrian army flag dates from 1254, and for the whole of the lands the Bindenschild soon became the only valid flag image, with the eagle added again from 1433. Diem (2010): the red-white-red colours are the creation of Duke Friedrich II, who gave the duchy a new seal image c.1230.
era-1282.open: Sources differ on the first document (Wikipedia 1230, FOTW 1232). None says the Habsburgs chose these colours over their own ancestral ones; Wikipedia records only that they took them over.

era-1991.says: Flags of the World: the flag was 'readopted 5 February 1991' (the 27 February 1993 date it gives is for the national emblem) and its design was set in Article 23 of the 1995 Constitution, and the page links it to the 1918-1920 flag. Wikipedia: the 1918 flag was banned under Soviet rule from April 1920 and reinstated on 5 February 1991 (Nakhchivan adopted it on 17 November 1990), with slight variations in colours and size; infobox dates 9 November 1918, 5 February 1991 and 22 October 2013 (colours standardised). Vexillographia, quoting the legal texts, says the Supreme Majlis of Nakhchivan set the 1918-1920 tricolour as its flag on 17 November 1990 and asked the republic to adopt it, a presidential decree of 29 November 1990 set the new flag, and the law of 5 February 1991 approved the image: three equal horizontal bands of blue, red and green with a white crescent and eight-pointed star in the middle of the red band, on both sides, ratio 1:2; Article 23 of the 12 November 1995 Constitution repeats the description, and the Pantone colours were fixed by law in 2004, 2013 and 2018. Its index page gives blue for Turkic roots, green for Islam and red for progress.
era-1991.open: The reinstatement date is 17 November 1990 for Nakhchivan and 5 February 1991 for the republic; the exact colour match to 1918 is not stated and the colours were standardised in 2013 and 2018. The 'eight branches of the Turkic peoples' reading of the star was not found in the sources read.

era-4bce.says: This page's own caption calls the image a placeholder: «placeholder maroon field — ancient Caucasian Albania, no flag survives».
era-4bce.open: Whether a flag, banner or standard existed in this period was not checked. The colour shown is not evidence of one.

era-1920.says: Wikipedia: the 1918 flags were banned from April 1920 and the Soviet republic used eight flags, the last issued 7 October 1952: red with a horizontal dark blue band on the bottom fourth (the Caspian), a golden hammer and sickle and a gold-bordered red star in the canton, specified 5 May 1956 and discarded on 5 February 1991. Flags of the World (Azerbaijan SSR): the 1952 flag adopted 7 October 1952, dark blue bar in the base one quarter wide, emblem placement unknown. Vexillographia, quoting the law texts, says the 1952 flag was set by decree of the Presidium on 7 October 1952 (design of K. Kazimzade) and written into Article 152 of the constitution by the law of 18 August 1953: two horizontal stripes, the upper red (three quarters of the width) and the lower blue (one quarter), with a gold sickle and hammer and above them a red five-pointed star with gold border at the upper hoist, ratio 1:2; a decree of 5 May 1956 refined the emblem's size and position. The constitutional articles it quotes show earlier flags: red with gold letters on a green canton (1921), then a gold sickle, hammer, crescent and star with lettering (1925-27), then lettering only (1937).
era-1920.open: Two compiled publishers and a reference page quoting the legal texts agree on the 1952 design and call the band blue (Wikipedia: dark blue), not the 'light blue' of the page's caption. The drawing shows only the 1952 design, in force 1952-1991; seven earlier flags of 1920-1952 differ, and the emblem was resized in 1956.

era-1918.says: Wikipedia: the republic declared independence 28 May 1918 and adopted a first flag (red, white crescent and eight-pointed star) on 21 June 1918; a blue-red-green tricolor with crescent and star on the red band was approved in draft 9 Nov 1918 and raised over parliament 7 Dec 1918; banned after April 1920. FOTW: the flag was used 1918-1920 in a slightly different version from today's, and the star was already on it.
era-1918.open: FOTW does not give the exact 1918 adoption date; the page's colour-meaning gloss is attributed by FOTW to Ali Bey Hussein Zade rather than stated as an official meaning.

era-1813.says: Wikipedia (Flag of Russia) says Alexander II declared the black-yellow-white tricolour the national flag in 1858 and Nicholas II replaced it with white-blue-red in 1896, white-blue-red having been the civil ensign since 1705 and a festive land flag from 1883. Flags of the World (Russian Empire) agrees: the black-gold-white tricolour was adopted in 1858 as the Imperial Russia Civil Flag, and in 1883 white-blue-red became a state flag. Flags of the World (Azeri Khanates) records the Ganja, Shaki, Baku and Nakhchivan khanates annexed to Russia between 1803 and 1828, and Wikipedia (Ganja Khanate) says Ganja was captured in 1804. World Statesmen shows a Russian flag (the image is not described) for Azerbaijan from 6 October 1806 to 22 April 1918. Vexillographia says the flags of Azerbaijani counties and towns under the Russian Empire displayed in the Baku flag museum are decorative reconstructions, not based on real historical flags.
era-1813.open: No source says which Russian flag flew in the Azerbaijani provinces: World Statesmen shows only an unspecified Russian flag for 1806-1918. The black-yellow-white tricolour was the Russian state flag only from 1858 to 1896, so the drawing fits part of the era; no local flag of the provinces is documented.

era-1747.says: Flags of the World (Azeri Khanates) describes captured khanate flags kept in museums: Nakhchivan horizontally green over red with an eight-pointed star in the green stripe, a white swallow-tailed flag with a red central stripe reported for Elisu, and flags of Baku, Ganja and Shaki captured c.1804-1806. Wikipedia (Ganja Khanate) pictures the banner of Ganja captured in 1804 and cites a museum item and an article by P. Gezalov on Ganja banners (not found online). Vexillographia, a specialist site that names its basis, says reports of khanate banners are scarce but several survive in Russian and Azerbaijani museums: several Ganja banners (a standard of Javad Khan with three fish appliqued; silk panels in crimson and greenish tones with Arabic inscriptions), a Nakhchivan banner of green and red stripes with an eight-pointed star on the green, a light-crimson Baku banner with crescents and inscriptions captured in 1806, and a white Russian-eagle banner granted to the Karabakh khan in 1805-07.
era-1747.open: Two publishers now agree that individual khanates had their own banners and none is a teal field with a gold disc and arc; the stand-in on the card corresponds to no flag in the sources. Vexillographia is itself a compilation resting on museum holdings and the Gezalov articles, which could not be read; no Persian suzerain flag for the khanates as a group is described.

era-1538.says: Wikipedia (Safavid Iran) shows a Safavid flag (infobox, 1576-1732). Wikipedia (Flag of Iran) and Wikipedia (Lion and Sun) say banners and alams of various kinds were used by the Safavids and that by Shah Abbas the lion and sun was the recognised emblem of Iran, on coins, banners and artworks; Wikipedia (Flag of Iran) adds that Nader Shah avoided green because it was associated with Shia Islam and the Safavids. Flags of the World (Persia XVI-XVIIIth century) gives a green field with a golden sheep before the rising sun from a 1771 encyclopedia for Shah Tahmasb, and Nader Shah banners in red, yellow, blue and white. Neither Wikipedia's nor Flags of the World's Azerbaijan flag page describes a Safavid flag.
era-1538.open: The sources describe a lion-and-sun emblem and a green association but give no surviving Safavid flag or exact design, so the drawing is a reconstruction. The caption's teal field and gold roundel is not described; the Nader Shah period (1736-1747) used different banners, and no source ties the flag to the Azerbaijani provinces specifically.

era-861.says: Wikipedia (Shirvanshah) covers the dynasty of 861-1538, a vassal of the Safavids from 1500, and has no flag or banner. Flags of the World (Azerbaijan in the 'Book of All Kingdoms', c.1350) shows a white flag with a red crescent and cross-like device for 'Bacu' (Baku), described in the text as the device of the Emperor of Sara, and a yellow flag with a red square for 'Caraol', a place it cannot identify. Neither Wikipedia's nor Flags of the World's Azerbaijan flag page describes a Shirvanshah flag.
era-861.open: No source read describes a Shirvanshah state flag, so the green field and white crescent are an illustration only. The Baku flag in the 'Book of All Kingdoms' is white with a red emblem and is not attributed to the Shirvanshahs.

era-1973.says: Wikipedia's infobox gives the adoption as 10 July 1973 and names Hervis Bain as designer; FOTW gives 'Flag adopted: 10 July 1973', designer Hervis Bain, and the coat of arms 7 December 1971. Wikipedia reads the two aquamarine bands as the surrounding water, the gold band as the sun and land-based resources, and the black triangle as the strength and determination of the people; FOTW quotes Smith (1975) giving the gold as the sands of the islands and the black triangle as unity and the resolve to develop land and sea, and doubts the 'embroidered' meanings.
era-1973.open: The two sources agree on the date and designer; the meanings of the colours are later explanations, differing between them (sun/resources vs sands), not official.

era-1490.open: Whether a flag, banner or standard existed in this period was not checked. The colour shown is not evidence of one.

era-1718.says: Three publishers agree on the badged Blue Ensign from 1869. Wikipedia's Flag of the Bahamas: crown colony from 1717; under colonial rule the British Blue Ensign defaced with the colony's emblem (a British ship chasing two pirate ships, motto 'Expulsis piratis restituta commercia'), dated 1869-1904 in its table, replaced by the national flag in 1973. Flags of the World (colonial flags and badges): the badge was introduced in 1869 and changed little until 1973, on a white disc until 1923; officially there was no Red Ensign. WorldStatesmen lists a badged colonial flag for 1869-1904, 1904-1923, 1923-1953, 1953-1964 and 1964-1973, and a white disc badge on blue in its first image.
era-1718.open: Nothing read documents the badged ensign before 1869. WorldStatesmen lists the Union flag for 1718-1869 and a pirate (Jolly Roger) flag for 1706-1718, which the card does not show; no 'Pirate Republic' flag is described by Wikipedia or FOTW. The badge is a ship scene, not the sun and sailing ship shown by the card's stand-in.

era-2002.says: Both sources give 2002, the year this page starts the current flag. Wikipedia's infobox gives the adoption as 14 February 2002; Flags of the World dates it 14 Feb 2002.
era-2002.open: Only the year the current flag was adopted was compared; the design and the swatch colours were not checked against a specification.

era-1971.says: Wikipedia: the serration originally had 28 white points, reduced to eight in 1972, and to five on 14 February 2002 under Decree-Law 4. FOTW historical page: the 1933 serration had 28 triangles; a 5 October 1950 proclamation specifies eight teeth; the flag was adopted 19 August 1972 per Album des Pavillons, with eight teeth until 2002.
era-1971.open: FOTW's contributor argues the eight-point version dates from 1950, not 1972; neither source mentions 1971 independence or points varying print to print.

era-1783.says: Wikipedia: earliest flags plain red; after the 1820 maritime treaty with Britain a white stripe was added (to signify the treaty and distinguish the flag from pirates'); serrations came in 1932. FOTW historical page: plain red before 1820; a vertical white stripe at the hoist was added in 1820 to symbolise a truce; plain red stayed in de facto use until 1910; serration introduced in 1932/33 to distinguish from Ajman, Dubai and Abu Dhabi.
era-1783.open: Both give the white band after the 1820 treaty and the serration in the 1930s, not gradually over a century; the reason given for the band differs between sources (pirates vs truce), and neither mentions 1783.

era-899.says: Wikipedia's History of Bahrain dates the Qarmatian revolution to around 900 (defeated by the Abbasids in 976), the Uyunid emirate from 1076-1077 (163 years), the Usfurids from 1253 and the Portuguese conquest to 1521, and mentions no flag, banner or seal of these dynasties. Wikipedia's Flag of Bahrain says only that the earliest known flags of Bahrain were plain red, without dates. FOTW's historic-flags page says the pre-1820 flag 'may well have been solid red' and doubts a Kharijite origin for the colour.
era-899.open: No source describes a flag, banner or seal of the Qarmatian, Uyunid, Usfurid or Jarwanid dynasties; the plain red flag is undated and speculative. The card is blank and is not evidence either way.

era-1972.says: Both sources give 1972, the year this page starts the current flag. Wikipedia's infobox gives the adoption as 17 January 1972; Flags of the World dates it 13 January 1972.
era-1972.open: Only the year the current flag was adopted was compared; the design and the swatch colours were not checked against a specification.

era-1971.says: WP: 'Swadheen Bangla' flag first made 6 June 1970 at Dhaka University; raised there 2 March 1971 (or stitched 1 March, map added 2 March); Mujib hoisted it 23 March 1971; wartime flag green with red disc and yellow map; map removed 13 Jan 1972. FOTW: red disc with gold map on bottle-green, first flag hoisted at Dhaka University 3 March 1971, Mujib 23 March 1971, design attributed to Quamrul Hasan.
era-1971.open: Sources differ on 2 vs 3 March 1971. Provisional-government adoption is not stated by either.

era-1947.says: Wikipedia's list for Bangladesh gives Pakistan's flag (green, white crescent and star, white strip) for 1947-1971. Wikipedia's Pakistan article says the Constituent Assembly adopted it on 11 August 1947, that it became the flag of the Dominion and from 1956 of the Republic, and that the design is unchanged; FOTW's Pakistan page gives the flag as adopted in August 1947 (14 August there). FOTW's Bangladesh page notes that the first independent Bangladesh flag omitted Pakistan's crescent and star.
era-1947.open: Neither Pakistan source mentions East Pakistan or East Bengal; that Pakistan's flag flew over the eastern wing is inferred from it being the national flag of the whole state. The colour symbolism given earlier on this page is not covered here.

era-1858.says: Wikipedia lists the Union Flag, a Viceroy's flag (1885-1947), a Red Ensign-based British Raj flag (1880-1947) and a Bengal Presidency blue ensign for British India. FOTW's page on British India says India's flag was the Union Jack bearing the insignia of the Order of the Star of India (with Blue and Red Ensigns too), that the Company's territories passed to the Crown in 1858 and that the Empire of India was created in 1876; its Bengal page shows flags of Bengal from 1862 and 1868 charts.
era-1858.open: FOTW's Star of India Union Jack is a contributor description (Roy Stilling, 1996) that does not name the year it began; the page's schematic composite is a drawing of that description. FOTW's Bengal flags (a scimitar between three barrels) are a different, local flag and are not on this page.

era-1757.says: Wikipedia's article on the East India Company's flag gives horizontal red and white stripes with the Union Jack in the canton, adopted 1801 and relinquished 1858; FOTW's East India Company page, citing Wilson's Flags at Sea, gives the ensign with a Union canton from 1707 and the new Union flag from about 1801, with varying stripe counts. FOTW's Bengal page shows a striped ensign with a Union Jack canton from an 1848/1862 chart 'similar to the ensigns of the British East India Company'. Wikipedia's Bangladesh list gives a Bengal Presidency blue ensign.
era-1757.open: Both sources describe the Company's ensign and jack but neither says it was a territorial flag of Bengal as opposed to a Company and shipping flag; the number of stripes varies between sources (9, 11, 13), so the page's schematic stripe count is a choice. The 1757 start (Plassey) is not stated by these sources.

era-1576.says: Wikipedia (Flags of the Mughal Empire) says the principal imperial standard, the alam, was primarily moss green with a lion and sun facing the hoist; Flags of the World (Mughal Empire) likewise shows imperial flags carrying a lion with the sun behind it. Wikipedia (Bengal Subah) pictures a standard from the Battle of Plassey and a nautical flag for the Subah (1576-1793), and Wikipedia's Bangladesh flag page lists a moss-green alam for 1576-1717 (tagged as failing verification) and a Nawab flag for 1717-1757. Flags of the World (Bengal) shows a white flag with a red scimitar between three red barrels, confirmed from an 1862 chart and in yellow in an 1868 source. Second look: Wikipedia's Flags of the Mughal Empire article rests its imperial alam on Blochmann's Ain-i-Akbari (five alams carried with the qur), Edward Terry's Voyage to East-India (a crouching lion shadowing part of the sun) and Padshahnama paintings in the Royal Library at Windsor (scarlet pennons with green borders bearing a passant lion and rising sun, and green fields with a couchant lion and rising sun); none of those originals was reachable, and none is about Bengal.
era-1576.open: The sources support a green Mughal imperial alam with a lion and sun, not a gold sun alone, and nothing read gives a Bengal flag of the period other than the Plassey standard and the 1860s chart flag. The card's green field with a gold sun is a schematic of the imperial alam, not a documented Bengal flag. The imperial alam is better attested than the Bengal flag, but the sources read are descriptions of the lion-and-sun design, not of a green field with a sun alone.

era-1204.says: Wikipedia (Bengal Sultanate) pictures in its infobox the alam of Alauddin Husain Shah, founder of the Hussain Shahi dynasty, taken from a 1930 book (Progressive Tripura), and gives no flag text. Wikipedia's Bangladesh flag page names the Sultanate only as a link, and Flags of the World's Bangladesh page does not cover it. Second look: the Commons file page for the alam image says it is extracted from a photograph in Bhattacharyya's Progressive Tripura (1930, p. 20) captioned as the banner and gun of Hossein Shah captured by Dhanya Manikya and preserved at Agartala. Banglapedia's pages that could be reached (National Flag, which covers only the modern flag; Flag, Flags, Bengal Sultanate and Sultanate returned not found) give no Sultanate flag.
era-1204.open: The one banner shown is the alam of a single ruler, drawn in a 1930 illustration; no source describes a maroon field with a white crescent or any Sultanate-wide flag across 1204-1576. The one banner shown is thus a photographed trophy said to have been captured from Husain Shah by a Tripura king; the claim rests on a 1930 caption read through Commons, not on a museum record or the Tripura chronicle, which could not be reached.

era-1627.says: Wikipedia (Flag of Barbados) says Barbados became part of the Windward Islands in 1833 with the Union Jack as its official flag, that from 1885 the colony's flag was a Blue Ensign defaced with the colonial seal (pictured as 1885-1962 and 1962-1966), and that the trident of the later national flag comes from the colonial seal showing Britannia holding a trident. Flags of the World (Barbados - Colonial Flag) gives a colonial Blue Ensign with a Britannia badge, from a circular seal on the 1870 flag, for 1870-1966, with the governor's Union Jack carrying the badge.
era-1627.open: The two publishers date the Blue Ensign differently (1870 or 1885) and neither covers 1627-1833; the drawing's badge (a ring around a trident) simplifies the seal with Britannia. The card's caption limits the drawing to the 1870-1966 pattern.

era-1995.says: Wikipedia: red-green flag in Decree No. 214 of 7 June 1995 after the 14 May 1995 referendum (75.1% yes); 10 Feb 2012 thicker ornament. FOTW: adopted 1995 by referendum (75.1%), 2012 amendment published February 2012 changing the ornament from 1/12 to 1/9 of the width.
era-1995.open: Meanings differ from the page's wording (Lukashenko: red freedom/sacrifice, green life; no official interpretation); referendum legitimacy is disputed per Wikipedia.

era-1991.says: Wikipedia lists the white-red-white flag for the Republic of Belarus 1991-1995 (also the BNR 1918 and the BSSR 1990-91). FOTW lists 'Historical Flag (1918, 1991-1995)' by link label.
era-1991.open: FOTW gives only a link label; reasons for adoption and replacement not covered.

era-1922.says: Wikipedia: BSSR flag red with gold ССРБ (1919-1927) then БССР (1927-1937), with hammer, sickle and star from 1937; on 25 December 1951 a flag by Nikolai Gusev, red with a green lower band and a hoist ornament designed in 1917 by Matrona Markevich. Flags of the World: red with yellow initials in 1919 and yellow BSSR lettering with a star, hammer and sickle in 1937 and the 1940s; the decree of 25 December 1951 gives a red upper stripe (two thirds) and green lower stripe (one third), a gold hammer and sickle with a gold-bordered red star in the hoist canton, and a white ornament on red along the hoist; the SSR emblem was used until 10 December 1991. Second look: the State Archives of Belarus says the BSSR Supreme Soviet commissioned a new republic flag in 1951, that the Markevich "Rising Sun" towel pattern was found in the pre-war archives, and that artist Mikhail Gusev's design was approved in December 1951. Vexillographia (Russian Centre of Vexillology) lists BSSR flags of 1920, 1927, 1937 and 25 Dec 1951 (green 1/3, red 2/3, ornament by Matrena Markevich, 1917) and a flag law of 27 March 1952. World Statesmen lists BSSR flags only to 1922 and then the USSR flag.
era-1922.open: The 1951 flag is shown by an official archive, two compiled references and Wikipedia/FOTW; it ran from December 1951 to 1991. The page starts the era in 1922 while sources date BSSR flags from 1919/1920, the earlier red lettered flags and the 1937 flag are not what the card draws, and the designer is Nikolai Gusev in Wikipedia but Mikhail Gusev in the Archives and Vexillographia.

era-1919.says: Wikipedia: plain red flag of the Lithuanian-Byelorussian SSR (1919-1920); BSSR flag with gold ССРБ letters 1919-1927. Flags of the World (early flags): Byelorussia merged into the Lithuanian-Byelorussian SSR on 27 February 1919 and was re-established in August 1919; a pure red flag was used in early 1919; the 1919 Byelorussian SSR flag was red with yellow SSRB initials in the upper hoist (Dunin-Borkovsky, 1923).
era-1919.open: The Lithuanian-Byelorussian SSR is dated 1919-1920 on Wikipedia and February to August 1919 on FOTW; neither source mentions a hammer-and-sickle emblem on the 1919-1922 flag; the war-split framing is not covered.

era-1918.says: Wikipedia lists the white-red-white flag as that of the Belarusian People's Republic, 1918. FOTW labels it 'Historical Flag (1918, 1991-1995)' and lists the BNR in exile 1919-1925 by label.
era-1918.open: FOTW gives only link labels; the origin of the colours (Grand Duchy heraldry) is not covered.

era-1795.says: Wikipedia (Flag of Russia): Peter the Great decreed the white-blue-red tricolour as the commercial maritime flag in 1705; the black-yellow-white tricolour became the official state flag in 1858, government buildings flying it while merchant ships and citizens kept white-blue-red; white-blue-red was allowed on land for festivities in 1883 and named the sole national flag in 1896. Flags of the World (Russia): the white-blue-red tricolour was the civil ensign since 1799 and was recognised for use on land in 1883, and the black-orange-white flag was never formally abolished, so Russia had two civil flags from 1883 to 1914.
era-1795.open: Neither source speaks of Belarus or a flag flown over the Northwest Region; the black-yellow-white state flag of 1858-1896 is not shown on the card; the page's 'no regional variant' remark is not covered.

era-1392.says: Wikipedia (Coat of arms of Lithuania / Vytis): the mounted rider became the coat of arms of the Grand Duchy of Lithuania under Vytautas and remained its principal emblem until 1795; at Grunwald in 1410 Vytautas's regiments carried red banners, thirty of them bearing an armoured horseman with a raised sword; in 1578 Guagnini described the state flag as red silk with a white mounted knight on its principal side. FOTW (Belarus arms): Pahonia, 'at first territorial, later a national and state emblem', in written documents from the late 13th century, on Vytautas's seal of 1407 and on the Statutes of 1529, 1566 and 1588.
era-1392.open: The red banner with a white mounted knight rests on Wikipedia's accounts of 1410 and 1578; FOTW describes the emblem, not a banner. The page's 1392 start is tied to Vytautas's rule, not to a flag date, and the drawing reduces the knight to an outline.
