era-1830.says: Wikipedia says insurgents replaced the French flag on Brussels city hall on 27 August 1830 with a horizontal red-yellow-black tricolour, and that on 23 January 1831 the National Congress enshrined the tricolour without setting the stripe order, the stripes changing from horizontal to vertical that day, with the modern form (black at the hoist) reached on 12 October 1831. FOTW says the first true national flag in 1830 was horizontal red-yellow-black, that the Provisional Government decreed on 23 January 1831 that the colours be placed vertically, that the Navy set black at the hoist on 15 September 1831 and the Interior Department on 12 October 1831, that horizontal and vertical flags coexisted until 24 September 1838, and that the colours come from the arms of Brabant. A 2024 FIAV congress paper (Lupant) agrees on the substance: after the revolution began on 26 August 1830 a flag in the Brabant colours was hoisted on Brussels city hall in place of a French flag, the first Belgian flag was a horizontal red-yellow-black tricolour, the Provisional Government adopted a vertical flag on 23 January 1831, and the Navy (15 September 1831) and Interior (12 October 1831) put black at the hoist; it also notes horizontal flags of honour presented in 1832.
era-1830.open: Sources differ on who acted on 23 January 1831 (Wikipedia: the National Congress; FOTW and the FIAV paper: the Provisional Government) and Wikipedia dates the city-hall hoisting 27 August where the FIAV paper gives only the revolution start, 26 August. Nothing read covers changes between 1838 and 1914. The drawing shows the later vertical form, not the horizontal flag of 1830. This page used to say vertical black-yellow-red was adopted within days of the uprising; none of the sources says so (the FIAV paper dates it to 23 January 1831 and offers recalling the French stripes only as one possible reason, among others).

era-1384.says: Flags of the World (Belgium plate) says the Cross of Burgundy was 'adopted by most of the provinces of the Lower Countries in the 15th century', most sources crediting John the Fearless, first confirmed use 1411 as a livery element. Wikipedia (Cross of Burgundy): the banner dates to the early 15th century; the Habsburgs inherited the Burgundian Low Countries in 1477 'and adopted the flag'; a similar flag was used by the Seventeen Provinces in the 15th and 16th centuries. Wikipedia (Burgundian Netherlands) places the Burgundian state at 1384-1482 and links its infobox flag to the Cross of Burgundy.
era-1384.open: Both sources date the cross to the early 15th century (1411), not 1384; the page's 'common banner of their whole domain' with provincial arms kept beneath it is not stated by either. Flags of the World calls its plate 'alleged' in places.

era-1581.says: Wikipedia (Spanish Netherlands) gives the Cross of Burgundy as the flag of the territory (infobox, 1556-1714) with a civil ensign; Wikipedia (List of Belgian flags, tagged citation needed) lists a white flag with the Cross of Burgundy and a red-white-yellow civil ensign with the cross. Flags of the World (Belgium plate) captions a simplified Cross of Burgundy '15th-18th centuries' and a yellow-white-red flag of the Spanish Netherlands '16th-18th centuries', with the cross in the white stripe in a variant.
era-1581.open: Sources differ on the span (Wikipedia 1556-1714 or 1482-1714); the red-white-yellow stripes, which both sources also show, are not on this page's drawing. Wikipedia's list entry is uncited and Flags of the World calls its own plate 'alleged'.

era-1714.says: FOTW (Austrian Netherlands, citing Flag Bulletin 32, 1993): the civil ensign of the Austrian Netherlands from 24 September 1781 to 31 December 1786 was red-white-yellow with the imperial Austrian eagle in front of the Cross of Burgundy. Wikipedia (List of Belgian flags): a red-white-gold tricolour with the arms of Austria for 1781-1786 (marked 'citation needed'); its Austrian Netherlands article (1714-1797) shows a civil ensign in the infobox. Wikipedia (Flag of Belgium): during Austrian rule several flags were tried and the emperor eventually imposed the Austrian flag, which Brussels opposed. A 2024 FIAV congress paper (Lupant) says an Imperial Edict of 28 August 1787 forbade the Brabant tricolour cockade and gives no flag for the Austrian Netherlands. A Marine Info record of Parmentier (1997) shows an imperial flag in Ostend shipping in 1781-83 without describing it.
era-1714.open: Looked for institutional or archival descriptions of an Austrian Netherlands flag (Belgian and Flemish maritime and museum pages, FIAV papers); none found. The eagle and Austrian arms are shown only on the civil ensign of 1781-1786 (FOTW, citing Flag Bulletin 32, 1993), not as a flag of the whole of 1714-1795; no page read describes a flag for 1714-1781 or 1787-1795, and none states a plain gold flag with a black eagle.

era-1940.says: Wikipedia (Military Administration in Belgium and Northern France): the 1940-1944 German administration under the Wehrmacht; its infobox shows a German flag and its text says nothing on Belgian flags. FOTW (Belgium: Military Governor): the square black-white-red flag of the Militaerbefehlshaber with the Nazi eagle and swastika, for Falkenhausen (28 May 1940 to 20 July 1944). Flags of the World's Third Reich page covers the swastika flag as a German national flag. The Liberation Route Europe page on Eupen town hall says local Nazi supporters hoisted a swastika flag there on 10 May 1940, in the German-speaking area that Germany then annexed.
era-1940.open: The Eupen record is the only page read that shows a swastika flag in Belgium, and Eupen was annexed rather than under the Military Administration. The two earlier sources show different German flags (a war ensign in Wikipedia's infobox, the commander's flag in FOTW), and none says the swastika national flag was flown over the rest of Belgium or that the Belgian tricolour was suppressed. Searches for a page on flags at Brussels in 1940 found none.

era-1918.says: Wikipedia: the National Congress enshrined the red, yellow and black tricolour in January 1831 and the modern form (black at the hoist) was reached on 12 October. FOTW: 23 January 1831 decree, vertical stripes with black at the hoist (navy decree 15 September 1831), national flag confirmed 28 January 1936. Two publishers therefore give the same design in force through 1918-1940, with an explicit confirmation in 1936.
era-1918.open: Neither source describes the interwar years in detail or says the flag was 'restored' after 1918; the page's 'restored' wording is unconfirmed.

era-1914.says: Wikipedia (German occupation of Belgium in WWI): the occupation was run by a Governor-General and, from 1915, a General Government; patriotic badges in the royal family's or national colours were banned and replaced by ivy leaves; in November 1918 mutineers flew the red flag over the Brussels Kommandantur. Wikipedia (Flag of Germany) and FOTW (German Empire): the black-white-red tricolour was the German Empire's flag from 1871 to 1918. Neither occupation page nor FOTW's Belgian pages say what flag flew over occupied Belgium. Hugh Gibson, a US legation secretary, records in his diary for 18 September 1914 the notice of the military governor von Luettwitz asking Brussels householders to take down Belgian flags (he had not yet forbidden them), and the arrest of Burgomaster Max over his reply; the diary mentions no German flag over the city.
era-1914.open: The German imperial flag is attested for the Empire but no page read says it flew over the occupied territory or the General Government. The diary shows only that Belgian flags were ordered down in Brussels in September 1914; the ban on Belgian colours is otherwise reported only for badges. A Whitlock memoir was not available in a readable form.

era-1815.says: Flags of the World (Belgium plate) captions the red-white-blue flag '1814-1830' as the flag of the Kingdom of the Netherlands, which then ruled Belgium; Wikipedia (United Kingdom of the Netherlands) shows the Dutch tricolour as the infobox flag for 1815-1839 and says Belgium was declared independent on 4 October 1830. Flags of the World (1830 Revolution) adds that before 26 August 1830 Brussels displayed the orange Dutch cockade or the French flag.
era-1815.open: Neither source says in words that no distinct Belgian flag existed in 1815-1830; the page's 'erasure of separate identity' reading is interpretation.

era-1795.says: Wikipedia (Flag of France): the blue-white-red tricolour was adopted on 15 February 1794, replaced by the Bourbon white flag on the Restoration of 1815. FOTW (France): the tricolour adopted by decree of 27 Pluviose Year II (15 February 1794). Wikipedia (Austrian Netherlands): Revolutionary France annexed the territory after Sprimont (1794) and the Peace of Basel (1795). FOTW (Belgium historical flags) notes the French flag for 1794-1814 is left out of its plate of Belgian flags.
era-1795.open: No page read states that the tricolour was flown over the annexed departments; it is the flag of the French state to which the territory belonged. The sources do not give Belgian departmental or local flags for 1795-1815.

era-1981.says: Wikipedia: adopted 21 September 1981, independence day (standardised 28 August 2019): a royal blue field with red stripes at top and bottom and a white disc holding the 1907 coat of arms, which recalls the logging industry with tools and mahogany trees, with the motto Sub Umbra Floreo and 50 leaves recalling 1950. FOTW: adopted 21 September 1981; blue field with red stripes added in 1981, a white disc with 50 olive leaves and the coat of arms (oar, sledgehammer, saw, axe, ship, tree), the motto glossed 'I flourish in the shadow'; standardised in 2019 at 3:5.
era-1981.open: The sources agree on date and design. They differ on the leaves (Wikipedia: for 1950 and the PUP; FOTW: the year 1950) and FOTW does not call the tree a mahogany; the page's 'laurel ring' simplifies the 50-leaf wreath.

era-1950.says: Wikipedia: from 1950 onward an unofficial national flag was in use, blue with the coat of arms on a white disc, tied to the PUP (50 leaves recalling 1950), and the 1981 flag added red stripes top and bottom. FOTW: the blue flag with a white disk, without stripes, was adopted on 2 February 1950, the PUP proposed a blue flag with the coat of arms in a white circle, and the two red stripes were added on 21 September 1981.
era-1950.open: Neither source mentions a 1964 self-government flag; Wikipedia notes the UDP, founded 1973, objected to the blue-and-white design.

era-1862.says: Wikipedia (Flag of Belize): a British Honduras flag 1870-1919, a flag 1919-1981, a governor's standard 1884-1981; the 1907 arms formed the basis of the badge. Wikipedia (British Honduras): declared a colony in 1862, crown colony 1871. FOTW (bz-bhond): the badge was approved in 1870 and used until 1981, apparently shown on a white disc until about 1920, with the disc ordered removed in 1919; the Blue Ensign continued probably until 1981; the badge has a Union Jack, mahogany-logging tools and a ship flying a red ensign; Lieutenant Governors served 1862-1884.
era-1862.open: Both sources give 1870, not 1862, as the start of the badge ensign, and no flag is dated 1862-1870; the era's start and its end at 1950 are the page's. Wikipedia text read to 100,000 of 125,584 characters.

era-1638.says: Wikipedia (British Honduras): the first English logging settlement is generally attributed to Peter Wallace's landing of 1638, though clear primary sources are lacking; the Treaty of Versailles (1783) and Convention of London (1786) gave British logging rights, and the settlement was declared a colony in 1862. Encyclopaedia Britannica (1911, on Wikisource): the settlement dates from 1638, the colonists were independent and elected their own magistrates until 1786, then a superintendent served until 1862. Flags of the World: the later flag was a Union Flag with the badge.
era-1638.open: No source read describes a flag flown by the settlers or privateers, or the British ensign of the day over the settlement; the 1911 Britannica and Wikipedia date the settlement but are silent on flags. The page's statements on Spanish and Guatemalan claims are not backed by anything read beyond the treaty dates.

era-pre-contact.open: Whether a flag, banner or standard existed in this period was not checked. The colour shown is not evidence of one.

era-1975.says: Wikipedia: after the 1972 coup brought a Marxist-Leninist government, a green flag with a red five-pointed star in the top-left canton was introduced in 1975 and the old flag was reinstated on 1 Aug 1990. FOTW: 1975-1990 the flag was green with a red star in the canton under the People's Republic of Benin; the 1959 flag was re-established at the National Conference of 19-28 Feb 1990 and reintroduced 1 Aug 1990 (the page also says 1991 elsewhere, unresolved).
era-1975.open: Wikipedia says the green flag was never adopted by law (de facto only); the page's claim of deliberate alignment with other Marxist-Leninist states' iconography is not covered by either source.

era-1960.says: Wikipedia: Dahomey became independent on 1 Aug 1960 with the 1959 flag unchanged. FOTW: the flag was first hoisted 1 Aug 1960 and was the same as the current one up to 1975.
era-1960.open: The page's phrase 'a decade of coups' is not covered by either source.

era-1958.says: Wikipedia: Dahomey got limited self-government in the French Community on 4 Dec 1958 and chose its flag (a yellow and red flag with a green hoist band) on 16 Nov 1959 to replace the French tricolour. FOTW: adopted 16 Nov 1959, first hoisted 1 Aug 1960.
era-1958.open: Neither source says the territorial assembly made the choice; the 1959 flag is the same as the one the page labels the 'tricolor'.

era-1894.says: Wikipedia's list of historical flags gives the French tricolour as the official flag of French Dahomey, 1894-1959. FOTW's page on the French colonial empire says the French Tricolore was the common and specific flag of French West Africa, a federation that lists Dahomey among its colonies, and that only some territories hoisted flags of their own in 1958-59 (Dahomey is not named among them); the use of the French flag was the rule and local flags the exception.
era-1894.open: FOTW does not name Dahomey as flying the tricolour; it says so for the federation. Wikipedia ends the period in 1959 and the page in 1958; the 1894 start (French conquest and protectorate) is not dated by FOTW's colonial page.

era-1625.says: Wikipedia (Flag of Benin) lists King Ghezo's royal flag (1818-1859) as white with a red border and an African war elephant, says King Glele (1859-c.1890) is not known to have used any royal flags or banners, and lists King Behanzin's banner (c.1890-1894) as light blue with a coat of arms. Flags of the World (Kingdom of Dahomey) agrees on Behanzin (light blue field, yellow shield with a dark grey shark, egg and tusks, green palm, snakes; a flag captured at Abomey on 18 November 1892 and kept in Paris) and, citing an engraving of Ghezo receiving a French mission under a different flag, suggests that each king may have had his own flag. Second look: UNESCO's listing of the Royal Palaces of Abomey speaks of twelve kings of Dahomey succeeding from 1625 to 1900 (it names no flag).
era-1625.open: No single national flag is established, as the card's caption says, but the card's dark red field with a gold disc and shield matches neither of the flags the sources describe (Ghezo's white and red elephant flag, Behanzin's light blue shark flag). The appliqué praise-symbol banners (ship for Agaja, buffalo for Ghezo) and the c. 1625 start are not covered: Wikipedia's Ghezo flag shows an elephant, and FOTW does not describe Ghezo's design in the text. UNESCO supports the c. 1625 start of the royal succession, not any flag; the dark red and gold design remains an invented stand-in.

era-1969.says: Both sources give 1969, the year this page starts the current flag. Wikipedia's infobox gives the adoption as 1969; Flags of the World dates it 1969.
era-1969.open: Only the year the current flag was adopted was compared; the design and the swatch colours were not checked against a specification.

era-1949.says: Wikipedia: a first flag credited to Mayum Choying Wangmo Dorji in 1947 and introduced in 1949 at the Indo-Bhutan Treaty signing, square, yellow above and red below the diagonal with a green Druk per an official document, though photographs suggest about 4:5 and a pale green; a 1956 version made the dragon white; the red changed to orange in 1968 or 1969. Flags of the World (two history pages, drawing on the on-line book 'The Origin and Description of the National Flag and Anthem of the Kingdom of Bhutan' and Kinga's Polity, Kingship and Democracy): the first flag appeared at the 1949 treaty, square, yellow over red on the rising diagonal with a green dragon; a 1956 royal tour flag with a white dragon; a late-1950s 2:3 redesign; and in 1968 or 1969 the red recoloured orange.
era-1949.open: The two sources differ on who designed the 1949 flag (Wikipedia credits Mayum Choying Wangmo Dorji, FOTW's sources the king, embroidered by Lharip Taw Taw) and on proportions; the dragon's colour changed from green to white during the span, so the drawing's approximate colours fit only part of it. FOTW says the orange-with-green-dragon image once shown 'doesn't seem to have existed'.

era-1616.says: Wikipedia's Flag of Bhutan says the flag features the Druk, a dragon alluding to the country's name Druk Yul, and that the first national flag was introduced in 1949 (design credited to Mayum Choying Wangmo Dorji in 1947); its History of Bhutan article dates the theocratic Druk Desi government to 1616-1907 and describes no flag or banner. Flags of the World (quoting DK Pocket Book 1997) says a monastery called Druk was set up c.1200 and that the name and the emblem of the dragon have been associated with Bhutan ever since.
era-1616.open: No source read describes a banner of the Druk Desi state in 1616-1907, or the dragon's use as that state's emblem on a flag or seal in those years; the association is stated only from c.1200 on, by one publisher, without evidence. The field colour and the line-drawn dragon on the card are a reconstruction. The card itself says it is not an attested state flag.

era-1825.says: Wikipedia: 31 October 1851 tricolor adopted under Belzu; 1888 decree on the colors' meaning; 19 July 2004 Decree 27630 proportions 15:22; 5 August 2009 Decree 241 and wiphala. FOTW: late 1851 decree under Belzu; 14 July 1888 decree; 2004 decree with 7.5:11 ratio; 2009 constitution.
era-1825.open: The proportions are from 2004, not 1888 as the page said.

era-1776.says: Wikipedia (Flag of Bolivia): the gallery captions the colonial flag as the Spanish Empire flag (1506-1825 in Peru and Bolivia, 1821 in Peru; 1506-1785 or 1701 in other colonies), with the image file named Cross of Burgundy. FOTW (Burgundy Cross Flag): the red saltire raguly on white was Spain's ensign from 1506 and its military flag to 1843. U.S. National Park Service: this white flag with the red Burgundian saltire was carried by Spanish ships and flown over the fortresses guarding Spain's New World possessions until the red-and-gold ensign of 1785.
era-1776.open: No source names the Viceroyalty of the Río de la Plata or Upper Peru's own use of the cross; the Wikipedia caption gives the Spanish flag in Bolivia to 1825 but is not discussed in its text, and from 1785 the red-yellow-red flag replaced the cross at sea. The 1776 start comes from none of the sources read.

era-1559.says: Wikipedia (Flag of Bolivia): the colonial Spanish Empire flag in Bolivia is captioned 1506-1825, with the image file named Cross of Burgundy. FOTW (Burgundy Cross Flag): the cross was Spain's ensign from 1506 and military flag to 1843. U.S. National Park Service: it was the flag flown by ships and over fortresses in Spain's New World possessions.
era-1559.open: No source mentions the Audiencia of Charcas or its 1559 founding; the Spanish flag is attested for the empire and for Bolivia in general, not for the Audiencia, and the schematic simplified saltire on the page is a drawing, not a surveyed flag.

era-1998.says: FOTW (Engene, quoting Bullivant, 5 February 1998) says that on 4 February 1998, parliament not having agreed, the High Representative chose among three designs offered by an expert commission, that the colours were changed to match the Council of Europe's, and that the triangle represents the three constituent peoples. Wikipedia says High Representative Carlos Westendorp proclaimed the flag on 4 February 1998 and that the triangle approximates the country's shape.
era-1998.open: FOTW says it was not chosen through a public competition. Wikipedia names Mladen Kolobarić as designer but tags it citation-needed. This page's reason for the colours («neither side claimed them») was not found in either source; FOTW gives the yellow as a sun and symbol of hope and the blue and stars as Europe.

era-1992.says: Wikipedia says the white flag with the Kotromanic lily arms was adopted on 20 May 1992 and used until 3 February 1998. FOTW gives the decree of 27 March 1992 (flag: the arms in the middle on a white field), temporary adoption on 6 April and permanent on 20 May 1992, and says the arms are those of the Kotromanic family; it adds that the committee chose white over blue because of the resemblance to the UN flag. RSE calls it the official flag of the Republic from recognition in 1992 to 1998.
era-1992.open: How the lilies were chosen is told only by FOTW (the committee's four steps, via Safet Halilovic); Serb and Croat objections are reported in general terms only by RSE (Republika Srpska views it as a Bosniak war flag).

era-1945.says: Wikipedia: red flag with the federal Yugoslav tricolour in the canton, officially adopted 31 December 1946, lasting until 6 April 1992. FOTW: adopted 31 December 1946, red with the Yugoslav tricolour and a yellow-edged red star in the canton, retained in the 1974 Constitution; people favoured red because the national tricolours of Serbs and Croats were seen as later imports.
era-1945.open: The era is dated from 1945 but both sources date the flag from 31 December 1946; FOTW gives no end date (Wikipedia: 1992); the page's explanation of why Bosnia had no historic flag to revive is not in either source.

era-1878.says: FOTW says the Austro-Hungarian authorities adopted a horizontal red-yellow flag with the Bosnian arms in the middle for the occupied corpus separatum (1878-1908), and a red-yellow horizontal flag on annexation (1908-1918). Wikipedia's flag article likewise describes a red-and-yellow horizontal bicolour for Bosnia under Austro-Hungarian rule, changed after the annexation.
era-1878.open: The two sources differ over the Herzegovina flag: Wikipedia says Herzegovina used the same colours reversed (citation needed), while FOTW cites Meyers (1897) that Herzegovina had no provincial colours. They also differ on which Hrvatinic noble the arms were modelled on (Stjepan, FOTW; Hrvoje, Wikipedia's arms article).

era-1463.says: Wikipedia says the 1831-1832 revolt of Husein Gradascevic used a green flag with a yellow crescent and star, and that a green flag with a white crescent and eight-pointed star was used by Herzegovinian border landlords and by Bosnian troops at the second siege of Hotin. FOTW's Ottoman-era page independently describes a swallow-tailed Herzegovinian war flag and a flag used by Gradascevic in the uprising for autonomy, and its keywords list a yellow crescent and a yellow star for the latter.
era-1463.open: Colours of the field (green) rest on Wikipedia, whose section carries a citation-needed note; FOTW says the exact date of use of the 1831-32 flag is unknown. Neither source says the general Ottoman flag over Bosnia was plain red, so that part of the caption is unsourced.

era-1377.says: Wikipedia's flag article says the flag of the medieval Kingdom of Bosnia (1377-1463) was white with the Kotromanic arms in the middle (blue shield, six gold lilies around a white bend); the Kingdom article shows a royal banner of Tvrtko I and describes the arms. FOTW's account of the arms says Tvrtko's seals (from 1377) and those of his successors bear the bend between six lilies.
era-1377.open: No flag survives and no source read shows a contemporary banner: FOTW records that the 1991-92 expert committee 'could not reconstruct the color of the medieval Bosnian flag' and supposed it was white, so the white field is a modern supposition. The arms themselves rest on seals and coins.

era-1941.says: Wikipedia's Independent State of Croatia article says the NDH (1941-1945) consisted mostly of present-day Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina, and shows its flag. FOTW says the NDH state flag (red-white-blue with the chequered arms and the Ustasa U) was fixed by law-decree of 28 April 1941, to be used everywhere in the state except by naval forces, and that the state ended on 8 May 1945.
era-1941.open: Neither source names Bosnia in connection with the flag, so its use there is inferred from the territory; the Greater-Croatia intent is not covered.

era-1918.says: Wikipedia's Bosnia flag article says that in the Kingdom of Yugoslavia, Bosnia and Herzegovina had neither a status within it nor a flag. Wikipedia's Flag of Yugoslavia article and FOTW's Royal Yugoslavia page both give the Kingdom's flag as a blue-white-red horizontal tricolour, in use from 1918 (FOTW: used before the 1922 law and prescribed as the national flag by it).
era-1918.open: Neither Wikipedia's Yugoslavia article nor FOTW's Royal Yugoslavia page mentions Bosnia: the absence of a Bosnian flag rests on one Wikipedia sentence, and the tricolour's use in Bosnia is inferred from Bosnia being part of the Kingdom.

era-1154.says: Wikipedia's flag and Banate of Bosnia articles show a banner credited to Stjepan II Kotromanic (1154-1377) without describing it. Wikipedia and FOTW describe the six-lily arms as those of the kings from Tvrtko I's crowning in 1377. Britannica says the 1992 flag used the six-lily arms of King Stjepan Tomas, attributed to Tvrtko I. Enver Imamovic (Spirit of Bosnia, 2006) says medieval Bosnia had a fleur-de-lis flag and arms, evidenced by Tvrtko I's seals, coins and mantle (14th century), and mentions lilies from the days of Ban Kulin but names no Banate-period flag. The Hrvatska enciklopedija entry on the Kotromanici (Stjepan II ban 1322-53) mentions no flag or arms.
era-1154.open: Nothing read ties the lilies to the Banate period before 1377, or describes any banner of Stjepan II or of a ban; the design of the Banate banner is not described in any text. Imamovic argues for continuity but his dated evidence is the 14th-century royal seals.

era-1885.says: Wikipedia: the Bechuanaland Protectorate was formed in 1885; before independence the territory had no distinctive national emblems and flew the Union Jack; the national flag was adopted 30 September 1966. FOTW (High Commissioner): the High Commissioner for Basutoland, Bechuanaland and Swaziland (1931-68) flew a Union Flag with a crowned H.C. roundel in a laurel garland, and 'no mention is made of distinctive badges or ensigns for Swaziland or the Bechuanaland Protectorate' (only Basutoland, a Crown Colony, had a badge, in 1951).
era-1885.open: The page's Blue Ensign with a Bechuanaland badge is contradicted: the sources show no territorial flag, only the Union Flag and the High Commissioner's flag. The drawing needs replacing.

era-1889.says: Wikipedia says a provisional flag inspired by the US flag flew from 15 to 19 November 1889 until Deodoro da Fonseca vetoed it, that Decree No. 4 of 19 November 1889 legally replaced the monarchy's flag, that Raimundo Teixeira Mendes, Miguel Lemos, Manuel Pereira Reis and Décio Villares designed the new one, that the 1889 flag had 21 stars, that stars were added on 21 April 1960 (Guanabara), 30 May 1968 (Acre) and under Law No. 8,421 of 11 May 1992, and that Law No. 5,700 of 1 September 1971 sets the construction. FOTW says Decree No. 4 of 19 November 1889 established the basic design, that Benjamin Constant prepared the decree, that the sphere depicts Rio's sky on 15 November 1889, that the original had 21 stars, and that Law 5443 of 28 May 1968 modified the flag.
era-1889.open: The sources disagree about Law 8421: FOTW dates it 1972 in one place and 1992 in another, and Wikipedia's body says it added four stars in one section and six in another. FOTW does not cover the 1960 change.

era-1822.says: Britannica (Whitney Smith) says the flag of independent Brazil was a green field with a yellow diamond and the imperial arms in the centre incorporating a star for each state, the colours coming from the House of Braganza (green) and the Habsburgs (yellow), and that the arms were replaced in 1889. Wikipedia says Pedro I's decree of 18 September 1822 marks the flag, that Debret designed the royal standard that became the imperial flag (citation needed), and that Law No. 704 of 29 August 1853 added a 20th star for Parana. FOTW says historians attribute the lozenge to Debret and that the imperial flag carried an armillary sphere. WorldStatesmen lists a first flag of the Empire from 18 Sep to 1 Dec 1822 and a second from 1 Dec 1822 to 15 Nov 1889.
era-1822.open: The flag is attested by a reference source and three compiled ones. Within the era the star count changed (19, then 20 in 1853, and more later) and, per WorldStatesmen, the crown changed from royal to imperial on 1 Dec 1822, so the single drawing cannot be right for all of 1822-1889. Britannica dates independence to 7 September 1822 rather than the 18 September decree.

era-1815.says: Wikipedia: Brazil was raised to a kingdom united with Portugal and the Algarves in 1815, and a charter of 1816 gave Brazil arms of a gold armillary sphere on a blue field. FOTW (Colonial Flags of Brazil): the flag of the United Kingdom of Portugal, Brazil and the Algarves was used 1816-1822; the 1816 law quoted gives the Brazilian Kingdom 'a like ensign, a gold armillary sphere in a blue field', which FOTW calls the Brazilian flag from then, while the united kingdom's flag was a 'union jack' of the Portuguese empire.
era-1815.open: Neither source describes the united kingdom's flag in words here; the page's claim that Brazil had no flag of its own is contradicted - an armillary-sphere ensign for Brazil was decreed in 1816.

era-1500.says: Wikipedia: Portuguese merchant ships to Brazil before 1692 used a green-and-white maritime flag linked to the House of Braganza (citing the Cruzeiros National Association), and a new merchant flag of 1692 had a white field and a golden armillary sphere (citation needed). FOTW (Colonial Flags of Brazil): the Order of Christ banner (a cross, usually red) was the banner hoisted in the Portuguese territories from the first landing; the Iberian Union 1580-1640; the Dutch West India Company's flag used as the local flag of Dutch Brazil (1630-54, ended 1661); the Principality of Brazil's flag after 1645, which a contributor says was the heir's personal flag and probably never flew there.
era-1500.open: Neither source gives one colonial banner for the whole 1500-1815 span; the page's statement that none exists is consistent with them, but 'variants of the Portuguese royal arms' is not what they list (Order of Christ cross, a green-and-white maritime flag, the 1692 armillary flag, and the Dutch company flag).

era-1959.says: Both: flag adopted 29 September 1959 with the constitution, the crest added to the striped flag (Wikipedia: designer Pengiran Muhammad Yusuf; FOTW: crest superimposed after the 1959 constitution).
era-1959.open: FOTW also gives 1932 for the coat of arms, unreconciled; the self-government framing is uncovered.

era-1945.says: Both: the yellow flag with white and black diagonals dates from 1906 and was used to 1959 (Wikipedia caption 1906-1959; FOTW 1906-1959 flag, 17:15 per Crampton).
era-1945.open: Neither source treats 1945 as a boundary; the colour meanings differ between sources.

era-1942.says: Wikipedia (Japanese occupation of British Borneo): the infobox flag, captioned 'Flag of Japanese-occupied British Borneo', is the Japanese flag, with 'Kimigayo' as anthem; the text says students bowed to the Japanese flag each morning; Brunei Town was captured on 22 December 1941 and the sultan was retained. FOTW (Brunei, historical flags): a British Resident until the Japanese occupation in 1941, no flag given for the occupation years. Wikipedia's Flag of Brunei has no occupation-period flag.
era-1942.open: The Japanese flag over occupied Brunei rests on Wikipedia alone (one publisher), and its text about bowing to the flag concerns schooling in the occupied territory as a whole; neither source describes a Japanese military-administration ensign, or says that no Bruneian flag flew. FOTW gives no flag or end date for the occupation. Britannica's flag of Brunei page was read and does not mention the occupation; the rbvex.it page failed on a certificate fault and was not read.

era-1906.says: Wikipedia and Flags of the World both say the flag was solid yellow until 1906, and from 1906 to 29 September 1959 yellow with white and black diagonal stripes (FOTW cites Flaggenbuch 1939 and Dorling-Kindersley 1997).
era-1906.open: Neither source says whether the stripes were flown continuously to 1942, and the 1888 start of the protectorate is dated 1886 on FOTW.

era-1888.says: Wikipedia and Flags of the World both describe a plain yellow flag, the sultan's colour, before 1906, and the protectorate from 1888 (1886 on FOTW).
era-1888.open: The sources give 'until about 1906' for the plain yellow flag and do not date its first use; 1886 versus 1888 for the protectorate differs between publishers.

era-15.says: Wikipedia: before 1906 the sultans and officials such as the wazirs used personal standards as Brunei's only flags, and yellow is traditionally the royal colour in Southeast Asia. Flags of the World (Brunei historical flags): 'Yellow was the royal colour of Borneo' (W. J. Chater, Sarawak Long Ago, 1969, quoted by C. C. Teo 1998) and 'the plain yellow flag was used in Brunei which represents Brunei's Sultan' before 1906 (Kariyasu 2000).
era-15.open: Both publishers support yellow as the sultan's colour, but neither describes any 15th-century flag, and the plain yellow flag is attested only for the years before 1906 by a single contributor; the drawing is a representative colour, not a documented banner.

era-1989.says: Wikipedia says the Zhivkov Constitution was amended so the pre-communist flag could return, readopted on 27 November 1990, and that the 1991 Constitution (Art. 166) describes a horizontal white, green and red tricolour. FOTW says the 27 November 1990 amendment removed the coat of arms from the description, that the fourth Constitution took effect on 13 July 1991 with no coat of arms, and that the current coat of arms was adopted on 21 July 1997.
era-1989.open: Neither source says the 1991 text 'keeps the coat of arms as a separate state symbol'; the 1997 arms law is FOTW's.

era-1946.says: Wikipedia says the Dimitrov Constitution kept the colours and put the People's Republic emblem at the hoist of the white stripe; a version valid from 27 January 1948, a slightly redesigned emblem from 5 January 1967, and a ribbon split into 681 and 1944 first hoisted on 21 May 1971. FOTW dates the second Constitution to 6 December 1947 and the third to 18 May 1971.
era-1946.open: The emblem's parts (wheat wreath, star, dam and factory) are not described in either source; the 1946 date of the republic is not in them.

era-1878.says: Wikipedia says the flag was first adopted in 1879 after the 1877–78 war, in Article 23 of the Tarnovo Constitution, as three horizontal colours white, green and red. FOTW gives 16 April 1879 and notes a white-green-red banner with a lion and 'BULGARIA' presented at Braila in 1877, and a view that a 1878 constitution confirmed the tricolour without a lion.
era-1878.open: No flag for Eastern Rumelia in either source; the earlier 'almost immediately' and green flag claims were not found.

era-1885.says: Wikipedia and the FOTW main page give the white-green-red tricolour from 1879. FOTW's page on the principality (1878-1908) quotes the first constitution of 16 April 1879 (article 23: three horizontal colours, white, green, red), shows the merchant ensign as the plain tricolour and the naval ensign as the tricolour with a red canton bearing a golden crowned lion, and gives a prince's standard with a crowned lion.
era-1885.open: The lion is on the naval ensign's canton and the prince's standard, not on the national flag as these sources describe it, so the lion drawn on this page's flag is not shown by them to belong to the national flag. The union with Eastern Rumelia (1885) is not covered by FOTW's page or the flag articles.

era-1908.says: Wikipedia and FOTW's main page give the same tricolour from 1879 to 1947. FOTW's pages on the kingdom (1908-1944) describe the royal standards and a naval ensign that keeps the principality's pattern, a tricolour with a red canton bearing a crowned lion, 'the shape of the crown ... established' (Bogoslovski 1912, Flaggenbuch 1939).
era-1908.open: A crown appears on the lion of the naval ensign's canton and on the royal standards in FOTW; neither source puts a crown on the plain national flag, so the crown drawn on this page's flag is not shown to belong to it. The 1908 independence date is not stated by Wikipedia's flag article or by FOTW's main page.

era-1944.says: Wikipedia dates the coup to 9 September 1944 and gives the national flag with no crown and no lion until the emblem of 1947. FOTW's page on 1944-1946 says the kingdom's flags became obsolete on 9 September 1944, that navy commanders chose designs at will, and (from a 1955 atlas, contributor note) that a tricolour with the letters 'OF' (Fatherland Front) on the green stripe was used 1944-1947.
era-1944.open: The OF-lettered tricolour rests on a single FOTW contributor's report from a 1955 atlas and is not on this page; the page's plain tricolour is what Wikipedia and FOTW's main page give. The page's 1946 end date and the 'Soviet-occupied transition' wording are not stated by these sources, which put the next change at the 1947 constitution.

era-1941.says: FOTW treats 1908 to 9 September 1944 as one period of kingdom flags, all abandoned on that date, and its section on changes in 1937-1944 lists only a division commander's flag (1937) and colours given to naval units (December 1937). Wikipedia and FOTW's main page give the plain tricolour as the national flag from 1879 until the 1947 constitution.
era-1941.open: Neither the flag articles nor FOTW's pages discuss the Axis alliance or 1941 as such, so the row rests on the tricolour being in force throughout the kingdom's period, not on a source describing 1941-1944 flags specifically.

era-1396.says: WorldStatesmen lists the Ottoman flag for Bulgaria to 16 Apr 1879 (de jure to 5 Oct 1908) and a separate nationalist flag, 'Freedom or Death', for 1868-1877. The TDV Islam Ansiklopedisi (BAYRAK) says Ottoman provincial governors carried red standards in the 16th century, that the sultan's standards included white and red, and that the red flag with crescent and star was the national flag by the first half of the 19th century. Wikipedia (Flag of the Ottoman Empire) dates plain crescent flags to c. 1480-1780, the crescent and star to 1793 and the official flag to 1844. FOTW's page on 19th-century Bulgarian flags shows insurgent banners (the 'Freedom or Death' flag, the 1876 April Uprising flag).
era-1396.open: Ottoman flags over Bulgarian lands are attested in general terms, but no source describes flags specific to Bulgaria or says which design flew in a given decade: the plain crescent drawn fits roughly c. 1480-1780, and the star came later. The card's claim that no distinct Bulgarian flag existed is not supported, because insurgent banners are documented for 1868-1877.

era-1185.says: Wikipedia (Flag of Bulgaria) says portolan maps of the 14th and 15th centuries show Bulgarian flags with white or golden grounds bearing either the insignia of the House of Shishman or unknown symbols in red, and shows charts of Vesconte (1321), Dalorto (1325-1340), Soler (c. 1385) and Beccario (1426). Wikipedia (Second Bulgarian Empire) captions two infobox flags as after Dulcert's portolan (c. 1325) and Soler's (c. 1380). Flags of the World says only that the lion was known from coins of Tsar Ivan Shishman in the late 14th century and that the 1997 arms use crowns modelled on those of Second State rulers. Looking for a Bulgarian museum or academic study of the medieval banners turned up only a 2025 paper on heraldic lion medallions from Veliko Tarnovo (N. Markov, National History Museum), which treats them (in its abstract, the only part read) as horse-harness pendants and says nothing of banners.
era-1185.open: No source ties a gold lion on dark red to the Asen dynasty or to a banner of the empire; the flags the sources describe have white or golden grounds with red insignia, no lion. The portolan flags themselves rest on one publisher (Wikipedia). No Bulgarian reference on the medieval banners was found or read.

era-1018.says: Wikipedia (Flag of Bulgaria) discusses red banners of Krum and Simeon from late manuscripts of the First Empire (whose historicity it calls impossible to verify) and portolan flags from the Second Empire, and nothing in between. Wikipedia (Theme of Bulgaria) covers the Byzantine province set up after 1018 and describes no flag. Flags of the World's Bulgaria pages (main, 1878-1908, 1908-1944, 19th century) describe no flag for Bulgarian lands under Byzantine rule.
era-1018.open: No source read gives a flag for Bulgarian lands under Byzantine rule, 1018-1185. The card's schematic imperial device is a placeholder; its Byzantine imperial basis was not checked in a Byzantine flag source.

era-1984.says: Wikipedia's infobox gives the adoption as 4 August 1984. FOTW's Burkina Faso page says the flag was adopted 4 August 1984 after the August coup, in the pan-African colours with a yellow star over the red and green stripes (red for the revolution, green for abundance, the star as the revolution's guiding light).
era-1984.open: Design and swatch colours not checked against a specification.

era-1960.says: Wikipedia: the Upper Volta flag was introduced on independence, 5 August 1960, listed for 1960-1984, its bands standing for the Black, White and Red Volta. FOTW's Upper Volta page: the flag was horizontal black-white-red for the same three rivers and was in use until the 1984 change.
era-1960.open: The adoption date differs: FOTW says 9 December 1959 (citing Smith 1975), Wikipedia 5 August 1960.

era-1958.says: Flags of the World (Upper Volta page, citing Smith 1975): the black-white-red horizontal flag, for the Black, White and Red Volta, was officially adopted on 9 December 1959, within the autonomous republic's term. World Statesmen's captions agree: France's flag from 20 Feb 1895 to 9 Dec 1959 and the Upper Volta flag from 9 Dec 1959 to 4 Aug 1984. Wikipedia (Flag of Burkina Faso): the French tricolour was the official flag of French Upper Volta, and the national flag of the Republic of Upper Volta, black, white and red, was introduced on gaining independence on 5 August 1960.
era-1958.open: FOTW and World Statesmen date the tricolour to 9 December 1959 and Wikipedia to August 1960, so the tricolour is established for at most the last eight months of the 1958-1960 span; for 1958 to late 1959 the French tricolour is the flag these sources give. The tricolour is not established for the whole era, nor 'a year before independence'.

era-1904.says: Wikipedia says the French tricolour was the official flag of French Upper Volta and lists its periods 1904-1919, 1919-1932, 1932-1947 and 1947-1958; its French Upper Volta infobox shows the French flag. FOTW's French colonial empire page says that use of the French flag was the rule in all French colonies, local flags the exception, and lists Upper Volta among the French West Africa colonies.
era-1904.open: FOTW also notes governors' flags; whether a distinct local ensign existed for Upper Volta is not addressed by either source.

era-1967.says: Wikipedia: the flag that became the current design was adopted 28 June 1967 (ratio 2:3 changed to 3:5 on 27 September 1982); white saltire for peace, green for hope, red for the nation's suffering in the freedom struggle; three red six-pointed stars for Hutu, Twa and Tutsi and for Unity, Work, Progress. FOTW: current flag adopted 28 June 1967; ratio 3:5 set 27 September 1982; red the independence struggle, green hope, white peace; stars for the motto and said to represent Hutu, Tutsi and Twa.
era-1967.open: The page's era label gives 1966 for the republic, which neither source dates; the 1967 date shown for the flag is 28 June 1967.

era-1962.says: Wikipedia's Flag of Burundi: the first national flag was adopted on 1 July 1962 and included a karyenda drum as a symbol of the monarchy, replaced by a sorghum plant after the monarchy was abolished in November 1966. FOTW's historical page agrees: a white saltire dividing red and green areas, central disc with the karyenda drum (with a sorghum plant), removed after the republic of 28 November 1966. Wikipedia (Karyenda) repeats the 1962-1966 use on flag and arms.
era-1962.open: Two compiled publishers (Wikipedia, FOTW) agree on the design and the 1962-1966 span; no encyclopedia or government source on the 1962 flag could be opened (Britannica's page is cited by Wikipedia but was not read). FOTW records variants (a red drum; a version the king reportedly had changed) and its 1966 dates differ internally. The card's caption names the saltire, quarters and drum as the sources do.

era-1916.says: Wikipedia's Ruanda-Urundi article (Belgian occupation from 1916, mandate 1922, UN trust territory 1946-1960) uses the plain Flag of Belgium as its infobox flag and has no flag text. FOTW's Burundi history page dates the mandate to 1922 in one passage and 1924 in another and describes no Ruanda-Urundi flag. Heraldry of the World (Ruanda-Urundi) says unofficial colonial arms - a shield with a crane over a lion's head - were used until 1962, and mentions no flag. UN trusteeship documents were not readable (PDF text not extractable).
era-1916.open: No source read describes a flag or flag badge for Ruanda-Urundi in words; the Belgian flag is shown only by a Wikipedia infobox image. The colonial arms are documented by Heraldry of the World, but nothing says they appeared on a flag; the card's colonial badge is not supported. FOTW's mandate dates conflict.

era-1897.says: Flags of the World's German East Africa page says the German colonies had no flags of their own and used the imperial German flags throughout the empire, and that the flag of the governors of German East Africa was the national flag with the uncrowned imperial eagle in the white stripe (adopted 1898); it says German East Africa comprised Tanganyika, Burundi and Rwanda by 1890, and its Burundi page dates German control to 1903. Wikipedia's German East Africa article (1885-1918) shows the service flag of the Colonial Office as its infobox flag and says the 1914 colonial flag drafts were never used.
era-1897.open: No source says which imperial flag was flown over Burundi itself, or what status the mwami's court had in flag terms; the German start date differs (FOTW's Burundi page gives 1903, the card c. 1897). The card's black field with a black-white-red canton is not what the sources describe: they give the black-white-red national flag, with an eagle for the governors.

era-1993.says: Wikipedia says the present flag was first adopted in 1948 and readopted on 24 September 1993 after the Constituent Assembly election and the restoration of the monarchy. Flags of the World's history page says the 1948-1970 flag, a blue-red-blue triband with a white Angkor Wat, was reestablished on 30 June 1993 (the main page gives 29 October 1948, the history page 20 October 1948, for the original adoption); in 1993 the temple is usually outlined black rather than red.
era-1993.open: The sources differ on the 1993 day (24 September per Wikipedia, 30 June per FOTW) and on the October 1948 day. The design and the swatch colours were not checked against a specification.

era-802.open: Whether a flag, banner or standard existed in this period was not checked. The colour shown is not evidence of one.

era-1ce.open: Whether a flag, banner or standard existed in this period was not checked. The colour shown is not evidence of one.

era-1970.says: Three publishers agree. Wikipedia (Flag of the Khmer Republic) gives adoption on 9 October 1970 and relinquishment on 17 April 1975 and describes a blue field with a red canton bearing a white Angkor Wat and three white stars in the upper fly; it cites Article 4 of the Constitutional Law voted on 7 October 1970 for the meaning of the stars. Flags of the World (Cambodian flag history) gives the same design for 9 October 1970 to April 1975. WorldStatesmen lists the Khmer Republic flag for 9 October 1970 - 17 April 1975 and its image shows a red canton with a white temple and three white stars on blue.
era-1970.open: The constitutional law text itself could not be read. The earlier note that the card showed a red border and no stars is now out of date for the caption, which matches these sources; the drawing was not re-examined here.

era-1975.says: Wikipedia gives adoption in 1976 and relinquishment in 1979. Flags of the World's history page says the January 1976 constitution of Democratic Kampuchea set a red field with a three-towered yellow stylised temple (called only a 'monument' in the constitution), used until January 1979 and afterwards by Khmer Rouge forces and at the UN.
era-1975.open: The era starts in 1975, but FOTW says that from April 1975 to January 1976 plain red flags seem to have been used inside the country and the 1948-1970 flag stood at the UN; the page's 'plain red field' fits 1975 only if that is meant. A contributor adds that a plain red flag may have flown beside the national flag.

era-1979.says: Three publishers agree on the People's Republic of Kampuchea flag. Wikipedia: in 1979 the FUNSK revived the Khmer Issarak flag, with the colour pattern of the Democratic Kampuchea flag and a yellow five-towered Angkor Wat silhouette, dated 1979-1989. Flags of the World: a flag based on the 1976-1979 one with five towers instead of three, used 1979-1989. WorldStatesmen lists the PRK flag for 7 January 1979 - 1 May 1989 (its image is a yellow five-tower silhouette on red) and a separate State of Cambodia flag for 1989-1992 and the UNTAC flag for 1992-1993.
era-1979.open: The plain red flag with the emblem is documented only for 1979-1989; the 1989-1991 State of Cambodia flag (red over blue, per Wikipedia and Flags of the World) and the UNTAC flag fall within the card's 1979-1993 span. The sources call the emblem yellow, not gold.

era-1953.says: Wikipedia: the blue-red-blue design with Angkor Wat was adopted in 1948 and used 1948-1953 under the protectorate and 1953-1970 after independence; the Khmer Republic flag replaced it on 9 October 1970. FOTW: the present horizontal-band flag was officially adopted on 29 October 1948 and used until October 1970; the present flag returned on 24 September 1993.
era-1953.open: Neither source mentions a separate 1953 flag; the colour of the silhouette (white) and the number of towers are not described in the sources read.

era-1863.says: WorldStatesmen lists a Cambodian flag (red field, blue border and a white pavilion) for c.1863 - June 1940, the French flag for 1887 - 9 March 1945 and 8 October 1945 - 29 October 1948 (the Indochinese Union years), and a Cambodian flag from 1948. Wikipedia (Flag of Cambodia) lists protectorate flags for 1863-1940 and 1940-1948 and says Angkor Wat has appeared since around 1875. Flags of the World (Cambodian flag history) says the first Cambodian flag dates from about 1863 and was used, with variations, until 1948.
era-1863.open: WorldStatesmen alone gives the French tricolour for Cambodia (from the 1887 Union), with no basis; neither Wikipedia nor Flags of the World says it was the protectorate's flag. Nothing read covers 1863-1887 for the tricolour or the 1948-1953 end of the card's span, and whether the tricolour flew beside the Cambodian flag is not stated.

era-1975.says: Both sources give 1975, the year this page starts the current flag. Wikipedia's infobox gives the adoption as 26 October 1957; Flags of the World dates it 20 May 1975.
era-1975.open: Only the year the current flag was adopted was compared; the design and the swatch colours were not checked against a specification.

era-1961.says: WP: 1961-1975 Federal Republic flag had two gold stars in the upper half of the green band for East and West Cameroon. FOTW: in 1961, when Southern Cameroon joined, two yellow stars were added to the upper green stripe (citing Cannon).
era-1961.open: Both sources read are compiled; WP's stars paragraph is uncited.

era-1957.says: WP: tricolour (green, red, yellow) adopted 26 Oct 1957 by Law 46, confirmed by the 21 Feb 1960 constitution; pan-African colours, Cameroon 'second state to adopt'. FOTW: first flag adopted 29 Oct 1957 (law 57/46), vertical green-red-yellow.
era-1957.open: Sources differ on 26 vs 29 October. Whether the 1957 flag had no star, and any Ethiopian link, are not stated.

era-1916.says: Wikipedia's page shows a French Cameroon flag (1916-1960) and a British Cameroons flag (1922-1961). FOTW's French colonial page lists Cameroon as a mandate of French Equatorial Africa whose common flag was the French Tricolore; its Cameroon history page says the territory was divided on 28 June 1919 between a French mandate (Cameroun) and British mandates (Northern and Southern Cameroons) administered from Nigeria, that the British territories 'did not have distinctive flags or badges' (a 1922 badge was proposed and probably never used) and that the Union Flag was lowered over Buea in 1961.
era-1916.open: Neither publisher gives the design of the Wikipedia captions, and FOTW does not explicitly say the Tricolore flew in Cameroun itself or the Union Jack in the British Cameroons before 1961; the page's 'no unified flag existed' is the only part left unsupported. FOTW dates the split to 1919, Wikipedia's French flag to 1916.

era-1884.says: FOTW's Cameroon history page says German colonies and protectorates had no flags of their own and used Imperial German arms and flags throughout the Empire, and that Wilhelm Solf's 1914 colonial arms and flags (for Kamerun, an elephant head) were never implemented because of the war; FOTW's colonial flags page lists Kamerun 1884-February 1916. Wikipedia's page shows a German Colonial Office flag and a 'proposed flag of German Cameroon' that was never adopted.
era-1884.open: The page's black-white-red ensign with a Kamerun badge is contradicted by both: the badge flag was only a 1914 proposal. Which German flag (the black-white-red national flag or the imperial naval ensign) flew over Kamerun is not stated, so the row's claim holds only as 'imperial German flags, no colony flag'.

era-1965.says: Wikipedia says the House of Commons passed the design 163 to 78 on 15 December 1964, the Senate approved it two days later, Queen Elizabeth II signed the royal proclamation on 28 January 1965, and the flag was inaugurated on Parliament Hill on 15 February 1965; its all-party committee voted 15 to 0 for George Stanley's single-leaf design. FOTW says Parliament adopted the National Flag on 22 October 1964, certified it on 28 January 1965, and that it was proclaimed by the Queen and took effect on 15 February 1965, after a «33-day debate».
era-1965.open: The sources disagree on the parliamentary date (15 December or 22 October 1964). Wikipedia credits Stanley's design.

era-1000.says: This page's own caption calls the image a placeholder: «placeholder — no banner recorded for this brief Norse outpost».
era-1000.open: Whether a flag, banner or standard existed in this period was not checked. The colour shown is not evidence of one.

era-1921.says: Wikipedia says the Royal Arms proclaimed in 1921 made red and white the official colours, that the coat of arms replaced the composite shield on the Red Ensign, that an Order in Council of 1924 approved it for government buildings abroad, and that a 1945 Order in Council approved it wherever a distinctive Canadian flag was desirable. FOTW says the Red Ensign was used from 1870 and authorised by the British Admiralty for use at sea in 1892, that red and white are the official colours King George V designated in 1921, and that the 1921 arms showed three maple leaves.
era-1921.open: This page used to call it «semi-official»; both sources describe formal approvals. A 1946 parliamentary committee recommended a red ensign with a golden maple leaf and the prime minister declined to act (Wikipedia).

era-1957.says: Flags of the World (Canada, Prothero): the maple leaves in the arms were green in 1921 and not changed to red until 1957; (the 1957 Red Ensign page) on 8 October 1957 the government announced that the maple leaves would be red, with the Irish harp changed. Wikipedia (Canadian Red Ensign): the 1957 version has red and gold leaves where the 1922-1957 version had green leaves. The Canadian Heraldic Authority's register blazons the ensign as the Royal Union Flag in the canton with the shield of the Dominion's arms in the fly, in use until the national flag of 1965.
era-1957.open: The register entry does not mention the leaf colour; the ensign's date is given as 1957-1965 by FOTW and Wikipedia treats 1957 as a revision of the 1922 design.

era-1867.says: Wikipedia says the first Canadian flag after Confederation was the governor general's flag, a Union Flag with a shield (1867); that no official national flag was adopted in 1867–1965 and the Union Flag was the de facto flag in Canada; and that the Red Ensign with a Canadian composite shield was used unofficially from 1870 and approved by the British Admiralty in 1892. FOTW (Palac) says the Red Ensign, created in 1707 as the Merchant Navy ensign, was used on sea and land from 1870 and authorised at sea as the Red Canadian Ensign in 1892.
era-1867.open: FOTW describes a parliamentary resolution of 18 December 1964 approving continued use of the Union flag as a Commonwealth symbol. This page's «only fully official flag» is stronger than Wikipedia's «de facto».

era-1534.says: Wikipedia's Flag of Canada says Cartier planted a cross bearing the French royal arms at Gaspe in 1534 and that the Royal Banner of France held prominence in New France with evolving French military flags; its footnotes (quoting the Canadian Encyclopedia and another history) say the blue banner with three gold fleurs-de-lis was flown above fortifications and that the completely white flag of the French Royal Navy was flown from ships and forts and sometimes at land-claiming ceremonies. FOTW (French Canada) says that from 1534 to 1763 the royal banner of France was the most commonly used flag in New France and that French military flags, including the white flag of the royal navy, were also flown. The Government of Canada's history of the national flag says that from the first days of European presence the flags of homelands such as France were displayed, and describes the historic royal banner of France as a blue field with three golden fleurs-de-lis.
era-1534.open: Both publishers make the blue Royal Banner the main flag and the white naval flag a secondary one, so the caption's white flag is attested only as a secondary flag; the card's drawing now shows the blue banner. Neither dates the white flag within 1534-1763. The Canadian Encyclopedia article cited by Wikipedia returned HTTP 403 and was not read. The Government of Canada page does not date the banner within 1534-1763 or say it was the flag of New France; the Canadian Encyclopedia article cited by Wikipedia was not retried after the first reader's HTTP 403.

era-1763.says: Flags of the World (Canada 1763-1865): after the Treaty of Paris the Royal Union Flag was flown over British North America, the 1606 version until the 1801 version with the Irish cross. Wikipedia: the Union Flag was the de facto British national flag in Canada from British settlement in Nova Scotia after 1621, the Red Ensign in unofficial use from the 1860s, and a United Empire Loyalist flag used by Loyalists (undated).
era-1763.open: Neither source says the Union Flag was the sole flag or gives it a legal status in the separate colonies; the colonies' own flags and the Loyalist flag are not described.

era-1992.says: Both sources give 1992, the year this page starts the current flag. Wikipedia's infobox gives the adoption as 25 September 1992; Flags of the World dates it 22 Sep 1992.
era-1992.open: Only the year the current flag was adopted was compared; the design and the swatch colours were not checked against a specification.

era-1975.says: Wikipedia: first national flag hoisted 5 July 1975, official by law on 19 April 1976; yellow and green horizontal bands with a red hoist band bearing a black star framed by corn and a shell; based on the PAIGC flag like Guinea-Bissau's; replaced 25 September 1992. FOTW (cv_1975): very similar to Guinea-Bissau's flag but 2:3 instead of 1:2, with a black star, maize wreath and golden scallop shell; both flags derive from the PAIGC flag; Cape Verde changed it in 1992 (22 September per cv.html) after the 1980 coup in Guinea-Bissau ended the planned union.
era-1975.open: FOTW gives no adoption dates for 1975-76 and does not state the band order in the text read; Wikipedia and FOTW differ by three days on the 1992 change (25 vs 22 September). The page's 'PAICV' attribution: Wikipedia says the PAICV succeeded the PAIGC in 1980.

era-1910.says: Wikipedia (Portuguese Cape Verde): the infobox shows the Portuguese flag dated 1910-1975 for the colony, with the colony's arms dated 1951-1975 and 1932 and 1965 flag proposals shown as proposals only. Wikipedia (Flag of Portugal): the green (hoist, 2/5) and red (fly, 3/5) flag with the armillary sphere and arms was presented on 1 December 1910 and made official by decree of 19 June 1911. Flags of the World (Portuguese colonies): from the 1940s the government treated the colonies as part of Portugal and officialised no flag other than the national flag; the 1960s colonial flag proposals (Cape Verde 1967) never took effect. World Statesmen: Portugal's flag for Cape Verde to 5 Jul 1975 (caption), with the 1967 colonial flag proposal.
era-1910.open: FOTW dates the no-colonial-flag policy only from the 1940s, so 1910-1940 rests on Wikipedia's infobox and World Statesmen. 'Without change' is not stated by any source, though the 1911 design is the present Portuguese flag; the 1910-11 interim and the proposals of 1932 and 1965-67 (never adopted) are outside the drawing. The arms on the drawing are simplified.

era-1830.says: Wikipedia (Flag of Portugal): in 1830 the liberal government on Terceira decreed a flag of equal blue (hoist) and white (fly) with the arms centred on the boundary, in use from Maria II's return in 1834 until 1910. Flags of the World (Portugal, historical): 1830-1910 a vertical blue-white bicolour with the arms, approved in 1830 and hoisted in Lisbon only in 1833. Wikipedia (Portuguese Cape Verde) shows no flag for this period, only the anthem Hino da Carta (1826-1910).
era-1830.open: Portugal's flag is established by two publishers; its use over Cape Verde in 1830-1910 is not stated by any source read. Wikipedia and FOTW differ on the hoisting date (1834 against 1833).

era-1495.says: Wikipedia (Flag of Portugal): in 1495 Manuel I changed the national flag to a white 2:3 rectangle with the coat of arms in the centre (the earlier square banner of arms having ended with John II's of 1485); the arms became seven castles on a round shield in 1521. Flags of the World (Portugal, historical): from 1495 to 1830 the national arms on a white field, in three variations, with a green Order of Christ flag in 1640-56. Wikipedia (Portuguese Cape Verde) dates the colony from 1462 and shows no flag for this period.
era-1495.open: Portugal's flag in 1495-1830 is established by two publishers; its use over Cape Verde is not stated by any source read. The page's 'five small blue shields' quinas-only banner simplifies the arms described.

era-1460.says: Wikipedia (Portuguese Cape Verde): Portuguese settlers founded Ribeira Grande in 1462, the first recorded inhabitation, and the colony's span is given as 1462-1975. Wikipedia (Flag of Portugal): before 1495 the national flag was a square banner of the royal arms, John I's version with a green Aviz cross lasting 1385-1485 and John II's of 1485 being the last. Flags of the World (Portugal, historical): five heraldic banners from 1143 to 1495, usually drawn square, the 1385-1485 one red with castles and the green Aviz cross, the first three not sure to have been used as flags. World Statesmen's Cabo Verde page shows only a Portugal flag and no pre-1975 detail.
era-1460.open: No source states what flag the first settlers carried or flew over the new colony. A white field bearing the quinas shield is the post-1495 type, not the square banner of arms the sources describe; the islands were found in 1460 and settled in 1462.

era-1958.says: Both sources give 1958, the year this page starts the current flag. Wikipedia's infobox gives the adoption as 1 December 1958; Flags of the World dates it 1 December 1958.
era-1958.open: Only the year the current flag was adopted was compared; the design and the swatch colours were not checked against a specification.

era-1894-1.open: Whether a flag, banner or standard existed in this period was not checked. The colour shown is not evidence of one.

era-1894.says: Wikipedia: the flag of France was used during colonial Ubangi-Shari from 1903 until 1960 (it does not date 1894). FOTW: there was 'no distinctive colonial flag' and the French tricolour was used before independence; French Equatorial Africa ran 1910-1958 and no AEF flag is described.
era-1894.open: Start date differs: Wikipedia 1903, the page 1894, FOTW gives none; whether the tricolour was used until 1958 or 1960 is not settled.

era-1959.says: Both sources give 1959, the year this page starts the current flag. Wikipedia's infobox gives the adoption as 6 November 1959; Flags of the World dates it 6 November 1959.
era-1959.open: Only the year the current flag was adopted was compared; the design and the swatch colours were not checked against a specification.

era-1900-1.open: Whether a flag, banner or standard existed in this period was not checked. The colour shown is not evidence of one.

era-1900.says: FOTW's page on the French colonial empire says the French Tricolore was the common flag of French Equatorial Africa and that Chad adopted its current flag on 6 November 1959 and 'had previously no other flag than the French Tricolore', while a special governor's flag (ochre with a red circle and a blue bird?) was reported but seems older (Second World War?). Wikipedia captions the French flag as used in French Equatorial Africa (1900-1959) and shows a Free French government of Chad flag and a personal flag of Pierre-Olivier Lapie (both 1940-1942); FOTW's Chad page dates the protectorate 1900, the colony 1920 and the province of French Equatorial Africa 1946.
era-1900.open: The Free French government of Chad flag (1940-1942) and the governor's flag are exceptions to 'no distinct territorial flag'; the governor's flag description in FOTW is a query ('blue bird?') and may belong to the Second World War period.

era-1990.says: Both sources date the current flag to 1817, before this era begins in 1990, so the flag was already in use at the start. Wikipedia's infobox gives the adoption as 18 October 1817; Flags of the World dates it 17 October 1817.
era-1990.open: Only the year the current flag was adopted was compared; the design and the swatch colours were not checked against a specification.

era-1818.says: Wikipedia: 18 October 1817 official by decree; 1854 square canton and 2:3 ratio; 1912 star diameter; 1967 Decree 1534. FOTW: 17–18 October 1817 decree by O'Higgins; the original carried a coat of arms; 1854 legislation; 1912 Law 2597; 1967 Decree 1534.
era-1818.open: The decree day differs (17 vs 18 October); the designer is disputed.

era-1817.says: Wikipedia: Patria Vieja flag reportedly raised 4 July 1812, formally adopted 1813; Reconquista 1814–17; a transitional blue-white-red flag in 1817 dropped within months; current flag 18 October 1817. FOTW: independence declared 1810 with the blue-white-yellow Patria Vieja; 1817 transitional blue-white-red horizontal tricolour; decree 17–18 October 1817.
era-1817.open: The sources date the Patria Vieja flag differently (1810 vs 1812).

era-1541.says: Wikipedia (Flag of Chile): in colonial times Chile had no flag of its own and Spanish royal symbols were used, the Cross of Burgundy among the most frequent, and in 1785 Carlos III set a red-and-yellow ensign for Armada ships. Wikipedia (Captaincy General of Chile): the infobox shows the flag of Spain and the Cross of Burgundy as a military flag. Wikipedia (Cross of Burgundy Flag): it served as the flag of the Viceroyalties of the New World and remained in use in Spain's overseas empire. Flags of the World (Burgundy Cross Flag): a red saltire on a usually white field was the Spanish military flag from the 16th century up to 1843.
era-1541.open: Only Wikipedia ties the Cross of Burgundy to colonial Chile specifically; Flags of the World's Burgundy pages speak of Spain generally. The drawing is a simplified, straight-barred saltire, and the captaincy is not shown to have had a flag of its own. Searches for a Chilean institutional page (Biblioteca del Congreso Nacional, Memoria Chilena) on the colonial flag found none that could be read, so the support is unchanged.

era-1973.says: Wikipedia: the construction of the flag is defined, at present, by Supreme Decree No. 1,534 of the Ministry of the Interior of 1967 (adopted 18 October 1817); it mentions Decree No. 890 of 1975 making public mistreatment of the flag a felony and the 1980 theft of the 1818 original flag by MIR members. Flags of the World quotes an official publication, 'About our Flag': the layout was fixed by legislation of 4 July 1854, the star size in 1912, and 'the flag was last regulated in a law of 18 October 1967'; a contributor adds that subsequent legislation has only specified the design without altering anything.
era-1973.open: No source describes the flag in use under the military government as such: the unchanged flag for 1973-1990 follows from both sources giving the 1967 decree as the current definition, and from neither recording a change. Wikipedia's note on the 1975 decree and the 1980 theft is not about design.

era-1928.says: Wikipedia: Lu Haodong's design 21 February 1895; red field added by Sun in winter 1906; 17 December 1928 act; the 12 rays mean the twelve months and traditional hours. FOTW: twelve points mean the twelve traditional Chinese hours; Decree No. 47 dated 19 December 1928 cited by a contributor.
era-1928.open: The adoption day differs (9, 17 or 19 December 1928); the 'Wholly Red Earth' motto is not in either source.

era-1912.says: Wikipedia: the provisional Senate chose the Five-color flag in 1912; red Han, yellow Manchu, blue Mongol, white Hui, black Tibetan. FOTW (reader comment): five horizontal stripes red, yellow, blue, white and black for the Han and four other groups.
era-1912.open: FOTW is only a reader comment; the exact 1912 date is not given.

era-1644.says: Wikipedia: yellow dragon flag adopted 1862 (originally triangular), used as a makeshift national flag in 1868, rectangular version adopted 1889, used until the 1911 Revolution; azure dragon on yellow with a flaming red pearl; not originally meant as a national flag, used on official occasions and on official vessels. FOTW: dragon flag was state flag and naval ensign from 1872, Zhang Yinhuan proposed it as a national flag in May 1889 and the court adopted it; yellow stands for the Manchu and the dragon for the emperor; five claws for the emperor.
era-1644.open: The page's claim that the dragon was an imperial emblem used for centuries before the flag is not covered by the sources read; neither gives a day-level adoption date.

era-1368.says: Wikipedia (Flag of the Qing dynasty) says yellow has been the royal colour of Chinese emperors since the Ming. Flags of the World (early Chinese flags) shows modern 'Ming flags' (a white disc with the character Ming on fields of yellow, green, red or black), unsure whether they replicate historical flags, and notes that five-colour sets were always shown together. Wikipedia (Flag of China) calls the Qing dragon flag the first national flag of China; Wikipedia (Ming dynasty) mentions no flag. Second look: a page of the 1621 Ming military handbook Wubei zhi (vol. 32, machine-translated scan) governs army movements by the commander-in-chief's five-direction signal flags, which shows Ming armies used coloured signal flags but not a state flag.
era-1368.open: No source describes a Ming state flag or documents red-and-gold or dragon-embroidered banners; the sources point to yellow as the imperial colour and to flags in several colours of uncertain authenticity. The Wubei zhi page read does not name colours. No Ming institutional flag reference was found.

era-1271.says: Wikipedia (Yuan dynasty) says the dynasty chose white as its imperial colour, corresponding to the Metal element, and mentions a flag with three red crescent moons on the Catalan Atlas (1375). Wikipedia (Flag of China) calls the Qing dragon flag the first national flag of China. Flags of the World (early Chinese flags) names the Yuan only as the Mongol dynasty overthrown in 1356 and shows no Yuan flag. Second look: Wikipedia (Tug) reports from the Japanese scroll Moko Shurai Ekotoba that the Yuan fleet's banner was black and that the Mongols flew a white tug in peacetime and a black one in war; Wikipedia (Yuan) quotes the Yuan shi for Genghis Khan's nine-tailed white banner of 1206.
era-1271.open: The card's black as a Yuan or Mongol imperial colour is only partly supported (a black war banner on one scroll; white as the imperial colour); no source read describes a Yuan state flag. The Chen Yuan article behind the white-colour claim (J. Song-Yuan Studies 44, 2014) is paywalled on Project MUSE and Academia.edu returned 403, so it was not read.

era-960.says: Wikipedia (Flag of China) calls the Qing dragon flag the first national flag. Wikipedia (Yuan dynasty) calls Fire the Song's dynastic element, and Wikipedia (Wuxing) lists red as the ritual colour of Fire. Flags of the World (early Chinese flags) describes twelfth-century Song paintings of the Cai Wenji story with five plain flags in cardinal colours, and suggests a multicoloured one may be a Song flag shown anachronistically.
era-960.open: No source describes a Song state flag or banner, or states that red was the Song's flag colour; red appears only as the colour matched to Fire and as one of five direction colours in later paintings.

era-618.says: Flags of the World (early Chinese flags) describes plain red flags with long tails in paintings of Imperial Guards in Princess Changle's tomb (621-643) at the Zhao Mausoleum, and, in a Late Tang mural at Dunhuang (Cave 156, commemorating an 851 victory), yellow sun-and-moon flags and dark flags with four or seven tails. Wikipedia (Flag of China) calls the Qing dragon flag the first national flag; Wikipedia (Tang dynasty) mentions no flag. Second look: Dong Haipeng (Tang shi luncong 2023), a study of Tang army flags from documents and murals, finds six standard types, gate flags, five-colour flags and others, mainly red and yellow with green, white, black and crimson, and patterns including falcon, phoenix, dragon, tiger and sun and moon.
era-618.open: These are army and guard flags, not a Tang state flag. Dong's abstract says yellow was one of the two main army colours, but nothing read calls gold the Tang's colour or shows a single state flag; the full article was not read (abstract page only).

era-206bce.says: Wikipedia (Flag of China) calls the Qing dragon flag the first national flag of China. Flags of the World (early Chinese flags) tells of five cardinal-colour flags in Song-to-Ming paintings of the Han-era Cai Wenji story (captured 194-195, returned 207), but doubts they were used jointly so early. Wikipedia (Han dynasty) mentions a silk banner from Mawangdui (d. 168 BC) and Dong Zhongshu's five-phase cosmology but no state flag or dynastic colour.
era-206bce.open: No source read gives the Han a state flag or says red was its colour. The five-colour flags are shown in much later paintings.

era-221bce.says: Wikipedia (Flag of China) calls the Qing dragon flag the first national flag of China. Wikipedia (Wuxing) says Zou Yan paired ritual colours with elements (black with water) and that from the Qin onward most dynasties invoked the theory, but it names no element or colour for the Qin. Wikipedia (Qin dynasty) has no flag or dynastic colour. Flags of the World (early Chinese flags) has no Qin flag.
era-221bce.open: The Qin's black or water association and any Qin banner are not stated by any source read.

era-1046bce.says: Wikipedia (Flag of China) calls the Qing dragon flag the first national flag of China. Flags of the World (early Chinese flags) reproduces Mencius on call signals (a plain red silk standard for ordinary men, a two-dragon standard for scholars, a feather standard for senior officials) and a reconstruction of a c.1500 BC flag in which twelve red ribbons marked the emperor. Wikipedia (Wuxing) says Zou Yan matched ritual colours to the elements for dynasties but names no colour for the Zhou; Wikipedia (Zhou dynasty) mentions no flag or colour.
era-1046bce.open: These are rank standards and a reconstruction from before the Zhou, not a Zhou state flag. No source read says red was the Zhou's dynastic colour or that later cosmologists assigned it.

era-1861.says: Wikipedia: current arrangement adopted 26 November 1861; Decree 861 of 17 May 1924 and Decree 62 of 11 January 1934. FOTW: 26 November 1861 as the flag-adoption date.
era-1861.open: The double-width yellow is from Wikipedia's description only; the 'unique among Gran Colombian states' claim is unsourced and dropped.
