era-100.open: Whether a flag, banner or standard existed in this period was not checked. The colour shown is not evidence of one.

era-1918.says: Wikipedia: the student society adopted blue, black and white in 1881; the first tricolour was consecrated at Otepää on 4 June 1884; the Provisional Government made it the national flag on 21 November 1918; first raised on Pikk Hermann 12 December 1918; law of 16 July 1922. FOTW: adopted 21 November 1918, used until 1940.

era-1940.says: Wikipedia: tricolour banned on Soviet occupation in June 1940 and replaced on Pikk Hermann on 27 July 1940; widely used 1941–44 under German occupation; removed again 22 September 1944; permitted October 1988; formally re-adopted August 1990. FOTW: re-adopted 7 August 1990.
era-1940.open: Neither source describes the Estonian SSR flag, so the 1953 wavy stripe is unconfirmed.

era-1721.says: Wikipedia's Flag of Estonia pictures the Romanov tricolour for the Emperor of Russia and Prince of Estonia (1721-1917), with a note that the Russian Empire's national flag ran 1858-1896. Wikipedia's Flag of Russia article: the white-blue-red tricolour was a civil ensign from 1705, the black-yellow-white tricolour was decreed the state flag in 1858, the tricolour was authorised on land in 1883 and became the sole national flag in 1896. Flags of the World (Russia) dates the merchant flag to 1705 and recognition for use on land to 7 May 1883; its Estonia history says nationalists rallied around the blue-black-white flag in 1900-14. Second look: Britannica's 'flag of Russia' (Whitney Smith) gives the white-blue-red merchant flag as chosen in 1699, widely popular, with the black-orange-white tricolour that the tsars tried to impose on land failing in the 19th century; it does not mention Estland.
era-1721.open: No source read says which flag flew over the Governorate of Estland, and none supports the statement that no distinct Estland flag existed. The sources show the state flag as black-yellow-white from 1858 to 1896, so the tricolour as the flag of the governorate for the whole span is not confirmed; it is documented as a civil ensign. No reference source ties the Russian tricolour to the Governorate of Estland.

era-1561.says: Wikipedia's Flag of Estonia pictures the flag of the Kingdom of Sweden and its Duchy of Estonia for 1561-1721. Wikipedia's Flag of Sweden article gives the first legal description of the blue flag with a yellow cross in the royal warrant of 19 April 1562, and Flags of the World (Sweden) dates it to a warrant of 1569 and a triple-tailed state flag to the warrant of 1663. Second look: Flaggenlexikon's Sweden page lists the conquest of Estonia in 1561 in its timeline and says King John III expressed the wish in 1569 that the cross of the great state arms be adopted for all banners and flags in his realm.
era-1561.open: No source read says that the Swedish crown flag was flown in Estonia: the Wikipedia Estonia article only pictures it in a caption, Flaggenlexikon's note is about the realm in general, and Flags of the World's Estonia history begins in 1881. The link between the realm's flag and the province is an inference, and 1561-1569 precedes the 1569 wish. The row was labelled attested on the strength of that caption; on a closer read it is not positively shown.

era-1227.says: Flags of the World (Teutonic Order page, after Smith 1975): the Teutonic Order's flag is a black Scandinavian cross on a white field, often with the fly cut into three tails, with a 1464 chart for the Order in Prussia. Wikipedia's Flag of Estonia shows the war flag of the State of the Teutonic Order for 1226-1561. Wikipedia's Livonian Order article calls it an autonomous branch of the Teutonic Order (1237-1561), with the Teutonic Knights' coat of arms in its infobox (marked citation needed).
era-1227.open: No source read shows a flag of the Livonian Order itself or its use across the bishoprics and towns of Estonia; the black cross on white is the Teutonic Order's device, which the Livonian branch is said to have shared. The card's centred cross differs from the offset Scandinavian cross in the sources, and Flags of the World's Estonia pages begin their story in 1881.

era-1903.says: FOTW (Swaziland colonial flags): the protectorate did not have a distinctive flag of its own and the Union Jack was used; the High Commissioner's flag was a Union Flag with a white roundel lettered S.A.H.C. (from 1907) and then H.C. (from 1931). FOTW (Swaziland): the Union flag used during the colonial period was hauled down on 25 April 1967. Wikipedia (Flag of Eswatini): its 'Flag of Swaziland Protectorate (1902-1968)' is the flag of the United Kingdom.
era-1903.open: The protectorate had no flag of its own; the Union Flag stands in. No source describes a Blue Ensign with a Swaziland badge, so the caption's badge is unsupported, and Wikipedia dates the flag from 1902, not 1903.

era-1991.says: Wikipedia (Flag of Ethiopia): the flag is a green-yellow-red tricolour with the national emblem, a golden pentagram on a blue disc, at the centre; the plain tricolour was the commonly used civil flag before 1996, and the current flag was adopted on 31 October 1996, with a darker blue disc specified in 2009. FOTW (Ethiopia): flag and emblem adopted on 6 February 1996, a light blue disc about half the hoist in diameter with a yellow pentagram standing for the unity of the people and nationalities; Proclamation 48/1996 set the emblem to two thirds of the flag width.
era-1991.open: The 1996 adoption date is 31 October on Wikipedia and 6 February on FOTW, and the flag without an emblem in 1991-96 rests on Wikipedia alone. The drawing's disc is smaller than the proportions the sources give.

era-1974.says: Wikipedia (Flag of Ethiopia): the 1974-75 flag lost the lion's crown and the cross tip became a spear point; a blank civil flag was used 1975-1987; 'a number of different emblems were used by the government since 1974'; the 1987-91 flag was 1:2. FOTW (Ethiopia, PDRE and Derg): the plain tricolour continued as the national flag; an emblem with sun, cogwheel and plough in a wreath may have been used (Whitney Smith), and the 1987-91 emblem is a blue shield with an Axum obelisk, cogwheel, lion's head and spear under a yellow star. Britannica (Whitney Smith): in 1975 a revolutionary government established a new coat of arms with socialist symbols, and the 1987 flag had a red star at the top. World Statesmen's captions: imperial flag to 1 Jan 1975, a state flag 1 Jan - 12 Sep 1975, another state flag 12 Sep 1975 - 12 Sep 1987, and a civil flag from 1 Jan 1975.
era-1974.open: The green-yellow-red tricolour is supported, and three different Derg-period state flags are dated by World Statesmen, but their designs are not described in text; no source describes the card's single gold star over a plough as an emblem of the Derg, and FOTW says it is unclear which emblem flew on the state flag when. The dates for the end of the imperial flag differ (1974 on Wikipedia, 1 Jan 1975 on World Statesmen). The card's emblem is openly a placeholder.

era-1270.says: Wikipedia: pennants of 1270-1897 in traditional colours; Menelik II ordered a tricolour on 11 October 1897 (6 October elsewhere), red on top; the imperial lion flag is dated 1897, 1914-1936 and 1941-1974. Flags of the World (Ethiopia and Imperial Ethiopia): a rectangular tricolour with red on top adopted on 6 October 1897; before the 19th century three pennants served together as the national flag (Whitney Smith, 1975); green moved to the top after liberation in 1941; the lion of Judah was added to the centre as the state flag with St George on the reverse (Smith, 1975).
era-1270.open: The change to green on top is 1914 on Wikipedia and 1941 on FOTW; neither source says Haile Selassie formalised the lion flag.

era-100.says: Wikipedia (Kingdom of Aksum) describes the stelae as the most identifiable part of the Aksumite architectural legacy, marking graves and representing multi-storied palaces, and describes no flag, banner or standard. Wikipedia (Flag of Ethiopia) begins with the royal flag and medieval symbols (war drums, red umbrellas, a golden globus cruciger) and FOTW (Imperial Ethiopia) with three pennants before the 19th century (Whitney Smith, 1975) and the tricolour of 6 October 1897; neither mentions Aksum.
era-100.open: The card openly shows the stelae in place of a flag. None of the pages read describes an Aksumite flag or says that none is known, so this records an absence in our sources, not a finding that Aksum had no flag.

era-1874.says: Wikipedia: the plain Union Flag was Fiji's only flag from first raising on 10 October 1874 to 1877; from 1877 a blue ensign with a white-disc badge (foliage, war clubs and a shield with a mermaid), from 1883 a disc with a crowned lion and FIJI, and from 1908 the colony's arms, with the full arms in the fly from 1924. FOTW (British Fiji Islands): the same badge sequence (1877 circular foliage badge with a mermaid shield; 1883 white disc with the lion crest and FIJI approved by the Admiralty; 1908 arms granted on 4 July on a white disc; 1924 the white circle removed on a governor's instruction, noted in the Admiralty Flag Book 1930).
era-1874.open: Both sources date the Blue Ensign from 1877, not 1874, and show that the badge changed four times and the white disc was dropped in 1924; the page's 'roundel with a local landscape motif' matches none of these.

era-1871.says: Wikipedia (Flag of Fiji): before ceding the country in 1874 the government of Fiji adopted a national flag of vertical blue and white stripes with a red shield bearing a white dove in the centre, dropped when the colonial era began. Flags of the World (Historical flags): on 5 June 1871 Cakobau proclaimed the United Kingdom of Fiji, which used a white and blue flag with a dove on a red shield until 10 October 1874, after R.A. Derrick in Vexilla Nostra; a 2015 Fiji Sun article says it did not last long.
era-1871.open: The caption and drawing, a blue field with a Union Jack canton, are contradicted by both sources and need replacing; the order of the stripes and the crown over the shield are shown only in images.

era-1917.says: Wikipedia says a design competition followed the declaration of independence in late 1917, Eero Snellman and Bruno Tuukkanen set the final form, a temporary de facto flag was used from December 1917 to May 1918, the cross flag was adopted in May 1918 (28 May in the infobox), the blue was darkened and the arms made rectangular in 1920, and Law 380/1978 defined the rectangular state flag and swallow-tailed national flag. FOTW says the swallow-tailed state flag is listed as adopted on 26 May 1978 (citing Album des pavillons, 2000) and gives the proportions and the blue as PMS 294.
era-1917.open: The 1918 date is Wikipedia's alone and differs from this page's 29 May by a day; FOTW's page covers only the current flags. Neither source mentions the colours' origin in the 19th century beyond Wikipedia's Topelius tradition (citing Inglefield, 1978).

era-1809.says: Wikipedia: the first known 'Flag of Finland', presented in 1848, showed the coat of arms in laurel on white; captured Finnish merchant ships flew the St George flag in 1853-56; a blue-cross flag was made official in 1861 for private vessels; in 1910 the Russian authorities decreed a Russian flag in the canton, which Finns resisted. FOTW (Grand Duchy of Finland): a Finnish merchant flag of 1809-21 (blue ensign with the Russian tricolour in the canton) was prescribed but soon revoked in favour of the Russian merchant ensign; the unofficial flag of the Grand Duchy raised by students on 13 May 1848 was white with the Duchy's arms and a laurel wreath; yacht club flags from 1861/1882 are the root of the national flag.
era-1809.open: 'Never adopted its own official flag' is too absolute: a merchant flag was prescribed in 1809 and a blue-cross flag made official for private vessels in 1861; the dark-field arms flag drawn on the page is not what the sources describe (white).

era-1150.says: Wikipedia (Finland under Swedish rule): Finland was part of Sweden from the Middle Ages until 1809, Swedish rule over most of it ending on 17 September 1809 (Treaty of Hamina). Wikipedia (Flag of Sweden): the oldest recorded pictures of a blue cloth with a yellow cross date from the early 16th century, a legend places the golden cross on blue at King Eric IX's landing in Finland in 1157 (marked citation needed), the first legal description is the royal warrant of 19 April 1562, and a coat of arms of Prince John as Duke of Finland (1556-1563) carries the two-pointed Swedish ensign in a quarter. Wikipedia (Flag of Finland) dates the first known Finnish flag to 1848; FOTW (Finland) covers the flags in force since 1978 and no earlier flag. Store norske leksikon (Finland) says that since the Middle Ages Finland was part of Sweden and without a flag of its own, and (Sweden) that the Swedish blue flag with a gold cross is first shown in Gustav Vasa's 1557 letter of arms to Duke John and was probably first used officially in connection with the 1562 mission to England.
era-1150.open: A national encyclopaedia confirms Finland had no flag of its own under Sweden, but no source read says Finland flew the Swedish flag, and the blue-and-yellow cross flag is documented only from 1557-1562, so the card's Swedish flag is a stand-in for the late part of the era only. The c. 1150 start is the traditional crusade date.

era-1959.says: Wikipedia: after the 1958 referendum, Gabon adopted in 1959 a horizontal tricolour with a narrower yellow band and the French Tricolour at the canton; on 9 August 1960 the canton was removed and the yellow widened, eight days before independence on 17 August 1960. FOTW: a flag used in 1959 had a French flag in the canton, taking up the hoist part of the top stripe; the 1960 flag was adopted at independence as a green, yellow and blue horizontal tricolour.
era-1959.open: No exact day for the 1959 adoption (FOTW gives no dates; a 3:4 ratio is only a contributor's speculation); the 1960 date is given as 9 August by Wikipedia and a contributor, 15 August by FOTW elsewhere.

era-1839.says: FOTW (French colonies): 'The use of the French flag is therefore the rule, while the use of local flags is the exception'; for French West and Equatorial Africa the common and specific flag was the French Tricolore, and governors had separate flags. Wikipedia (flag of Gabon): the colony was forbidden its own distinctive flag; Wikipedia (French Equatorial Africa): Gabon was one of four colonies of the federation, 1910-1958. FOTW (Gabon): the first Gabonese flag dates from 29 June 1959.
era-1839.open: FOTW's French-colonies page gives no Gabon-specific flag statement or dates, and Wikipedia gives no dates for the ban; the 1839 start is the first French presence rather than a flag event.

era-1970.says: Wikipedia: the flag was adopted on 18 February 1965, first hoisted at midnight on independence day; three bands of red, blue and green separated by thin white stripes (designer Louis Thomasi); it remained unchanged throughout the 1982-89 Senegambia confederation; blue is the river, red the sun and savanna, green forests and agricultural goods, the white stripes unity and peace. FOTW: adopted 18 February 1965 (Dorling Kindersley; Smith says 'officially hoisted' then), stripes red, white, blue, white, green in 6:1:4:1:6; the page records no change when the republic was proclaimed in 1970 and says the flag and arms were not modified during the Senegambia federation (given as 1981-1989 by FOTW).
era-1970.open: The flag dates from 1965, not 1970; 1970 is the republic. Neither source mentions a change in 1970 (a silence, not an explicit statement of continuity), and the sources date Senegambia differently (1981 vs 1982). White-stripe meaning varies in FOTW (unity and peace, or rice fields).

era-1965.says: Wikipedia: the flag was adopted 18 Feb 1965 and first hoisted at midnight at independence, designed by Louis Thomasi, replacing the Blue Ensign with the colony's arms; blue = Gambia River, red = sun and savanna, green = forest and agricultural goods, white = unity and peace. FOTW: adopted 18 Feb 1965 (Smith says officially hoisted that day, so possibly in use earlier); red, white, blue, white, green in a 6:1:4:1:6 ratio; sources differ on which colour stands for savanna and which for forest/farmland.
era-1965.open: The page's claim that the design deliberately avoided Union Jack and party colours is not covered by either source.

era-1888.says: Wikipedia (Flag of the Gambia): the Gambia became a crown colony in 1888; its flag was a Blue Ensign defaced with the colony's badge, showing an elephant, a palm tree, hills and the letter G, used until independence in 1965. Wikipedia (Gambia Colony and Protectorate): a colony in its own right with a permanently appointed Governor by 1888; its flag image is dated 1889-1965. FOTW (gm_col): Blue Ensign with badge 1889-1965 (David Prothero), the badge a brown elephant in front of a palm tree between green mountains over a red G, without garland on the ensign.
era-1888.open: The sources date the ensign 1888 or 1889, not 1888 exactly; the page's 'palm trees over the river' badge drawing does not match the descriptions (page text corrected).

era-1816.says: Wikipedia's Gambia Colony and Protectorate article says British presence at Fort James and Bathurst was established in 1815 and 1816, that the colony was for various periods subordinate to the Sierra Leone Colony, and that by 1888 it was a colony in its own right. Wikipedia's Flag of the Gambia says colonies were permitted to deface the British Blue Ensign with their arms under the Colonial Naval Defence Act 1865 and that Gambia's own distinctive colonial flag came with its crown-colony status. Flags of the World's colonial page covers only the Blue Ensign with the 'G' badge in use 1889-1965. NZ History (a government heritage site) explains that colonial-government ships were required to fly the Blue Ensign with the colony's badge only under the Colonial Naval Defence Act of 1865, and does not mention the Gambia.
era-1816.open: No source read describes a flag for Bathurst or the Gambia settlements in 1816-1888; a plain undefaced Blue Ensign for those years is not documented, and both publishers begin the colonial flag with the badged ensign of 1888-1889. No institutional page on Bathurst flags before 1865 was found.

era-2004.says: Wikipedia and Flags of the World both give 14 January 2004 for adoption of the Five-Cross Flag (a white field, central red cross, four red bolnur-katskhuri crosses), by Parliament; FOTW adds that it replaced the wine-red flag with a black-and-white canton.
era-2004.open: Colours not checked against a specification; the four small crosses are drawn as plain crosses, not the flared bolnur-katskhuri form.

era-1991.says: Flags of the World's 1990-2004 page says the wine-red flag with a black-and-white canton was readopted in November 1990 and suppressed on 14 January 2004; Wikipedia says the 1918 design was re-established on 8 December 1991 and replaced after the Rose Revolution.
era-1991.open: The readoption date differs between the two publishers (November 1990 versus 8 December 1991), so the card says 1990/1991. The canton's exact proportions are as the Commons file draws them.

era-1921.says: Wikipedia's Flag of the Georgian SSR and Flags of the World both give the flag adopted 11 April 1951 (relinquished 1 November 1990): red with a red hammer and sickle and star in a blue sun in the canton and a blue bar in the upper part. FOTW's early-flags page gives plain red flags with yellow initials in the upper hoist: Cyrillic 1922, Georgian script from 1937 and in the 1940s.
era-1921.open: The caption's gold hammer and sickle and blue-white-blue stripe are not what the sources give (red emblem, blue bar). Neither source describes a 1921-22 flag; 1922-36 was the Transcaucasian federation.

era-1918.says: Wikipedia: dark red field with black and white bands in the canton, designed by Iakob Nikoladze, abolished after the 1921 incorporation into the USSR. FOTW's First Republic page agrees: the flag designed by Jakob Nikoladze (contest winner) was flown from 1918 until the Red Army's conquest in March 1921; it is the 1990 flag with a 1:2 ratio and slightly larger canton.
era-1918.open: Contributors on FOTW date the flag's first acceptance differently (1917, 22 April 1918, 26 May 1918, 22 April 1921). A black-white-red variant was also reported.

era-1801.says: WorldStatesmen lists the Russian flag, shown as the white-blue-red tricolour, for Georgia from 24 April 1802 to 22 April 1918, with no basis given. Wikipedia's Flag of Georgia and Flags of the World's Georgia page say nothing of flags flown in Georgia under Russian rule; Wikipedia's Flag of the Russian Empire only distinguishes the black-yellow-white flag (1858-1896) from the white-blue-red flag (1896-1917), and its article on Georgia within the Russian Empire has no flag text.
era-1801.open: No source read says that the black-yellow-white flag drawn on the card flew over Georgia; the only list that assigns a Russian flag to Georgia shows the white-blue-red tricolour, for the whole 1802-1918 span, without a basis. The black-yellow-white dates cover only part of the span.

era-1490.says: WorldStatesmen lists a black flag with a white cross as the 'Kingdom of Georgia' flag for 19 January 1762 - 14 April 1802 (Kartli-Kakheti) and gives no flag for 1490-1762. The State Council of Heraldry book shows 17th-century arms of Kartli (a flaming mountain speared by two arrows) and Kakheti (a horse between two eight-point stars) from the Russian tsar's title book, but no flags. Wikipedia's Flag of Georgia shows flags for Mingrelia, Samtskhe-Saatabago, Kakheti and Imereti without dates or description for the last two, and Flags of the World, relaying the Parliament of Georgia, gives a plain white flag for Imereti (15th-18th c.).
era-1490.open: No source read gives a single dark-red cross on white for Kartli, a white flag with a red fleur-de-lis for Kakheti, or a maroon field with a gold cross; the one dated flag found for the late period (WorldStatesmen, 1762-1802) is black with a white cross, and it gives no basis. Parliament captions are passed on without their basis.

era-1243.says: The Georgian National Encyclopedia (Dulcert entry) describes two red five-cross flags drawn in association with the Georgian state on Dulcert's 1339 chart (near Sukhumi and over Tbilisi) and a third in Asia Minor, reads them as marking Georgia's borders under George V and a joint Mongol-Georgian campaign, and places Ilkhanate flags to the south. Wikipedia's Flag of Georgia and Kingdom of Georgia show the 1339 Dulcert and 1367 Pizzigano charts giving Georgia a white flag with red crosses. Flags of the World's main Georgia page quotes the Book of All Kingdoms (1345-1350) on a white pennant with five red crosses, calling the link to Georgia disputed.
era-1243.open: The brown field with a white ring drawn on the card is described by no source read; the card itself calls it a generic stand-in. Whether the 14th-century five-cross flag was a state flag under Mongol overlordship (1243 to the 1330s) is not stated, and the encyclopedia entry does not give the field colour.

era-1008.says: Second read with sources the first reader did not use. The State Council of Heraldry's 2023 book 'The Story of Georgian Heraldry' pictures a coin of David IV (1089-1125) with a cross and four roundels and says it resembles the design of the five-cross flag; it describes no 12th-century flag. The Georgian National Encyclopedia (entry on Angelino Dulcert) describes red five-cross flags tied to the Georgian state on his 1339 chart, a century after this period ends. Wikipedia's Flag of Georgia, re-read, says the State Council of Heraldry reads a coin found in 2021 as a 'folded five-cross composition', and gives the Queen Tamar flag only 'according to tradition'.
era-1008.open: No source read shows a five-cross flag, or any flag, in use in 1008-1243: the coin is a resemblance, the earliest chart is 1339 and the Tamar flag rests on tradition. The maroon-and-gold flag the card once showed is described nowhere. The Georgian Journal item that Wikipedia cites for the coin returned no text and could not be read.

era-1990.says: Wikipedia says the German Unity Flag was raised in front of the Reichstag on 3 October 1990 and that the current flag was adopted on reunification. FOTW says the tricolour was re-adopted in 1949 and extended to civil use on 14 August 1950.
era-1990.open: The flag itself is the one adopted in 1949 (Basic Law, Article 22); 1990 is when it became the flag of the reunified country.

era-1949.says: Wikipedia says Article 22 of the Basic Law of 23 May 1949 reads «The federal flag shall be black, red and gold», and that East Germany also used black-red-gold in 1949–59. FOTW (Sensen) says the GDR's tricolour had no coat of arms in 1949–1959 and carried one in 1959–1989.
era-1949.open: The sources differ on the West German date: FOTW gives 8 or 9 May 1949 (about two weeks before the Federal Republic existed), Wikipedia 23 May 1949. The 1 October 1959 GDR emblem law was not found in the part of Wikipedia that was read.

era-1933.says: Wikipedia says a ruling of 12 March 1933 made two flags legal, black-white-red and the Nazi Party flag, and banned black-red-gold, and that on 15 September 1935 the dual arrangement ended with the Nazi flag the sole national flag. FOTW says the Third Reich replaced the tricolour with its own flag on 12 March 1933.
era-1933.open: The image reproduces the 1935 Reich flag: red field, white disc, black swastika turned on its point.

era-1918.says: FOTW (Sensen) says the tricolour was re-adopted as the Weimar Republic's flag on 11 August 1919. Wikipedia says the Weimar constitution designated black-red-gold in 1919, that black-white-red was kept as a civil ensign with the new flag in the canton and as a merchant flag in 1919–1933, and that black-white-red was reintroduced for diplomatic missions abroad in 1922.
era-1918.open: This page used to say black-red-gold became a national flag «for the first time»; Wikipedia says the Frankfurt Parliament declared it official in 1848–49. «11 August» is FOTW's; Wikipedia gives only «August 1919».

era-1871.says: Wikipedia says the North German Confederation's 1867 constitution declared black-white-red the civil and war ensign and that the 1871 constitution kept it. FOTW says the Empire chose a flag based on north German traditions, Bismarck favouring a Kleindeutschland solution, and gives no separate date for the 1871 decision.
era-1871.open: This page's explanation of the colours (Prussian black-white plus Hanseatic red-white) was not found in either source.

era-1866.says: Wikipedia: black-white-red appeared for the first time in 1867 in the constitution of the North German Confederation, which declared it a civil and war ensign. FOTW's North German Confederation page: the flag was adopted on 25 June 1867 (Article 55: 'the flag of the navy and merchant fleet is black-white-red'), was made the merchant flag by ordinance of 25 October 1867, and was extended to the whole of Germany on 16 April 1871; the most common theory is a combination of Prussia's black-white and the white and red of the Hanseatic League.
era-1866.open: FOTW says the significance of the colours is 'not completely clear' (other guesses: Prussia and Hamburg, or Brandenburg) and notes that the same colours were long used by the city of Allenstein, so 'deliberately engineered' is a theory; the sources date the flag to 1867, not 1866, and it was only a civil ensign in 1867-1870 (the war ensign was a different flag).

era-1815.says: Wikipedia says the Bundestag adopted the black-red-gold tricolour on 9 March 1848, that the Frankfurt Parliament declared it the official colours in 1848–49, and that the German Confederation was restored in 1850; its origins are in Jena's Urburschenschaft (1815) and the Lützow Free Corps. FOTW says the Frankfurt Parliament adopted it in 1848 for a proposed united German Empire and that it was abolished in 1852.
era-1815.open: Wikipedia contradicts itself on whether the Confederation had a flag of its own. This page used to say the tricolour «was never the Confederation's official flag»; that is not what the sources say for 1848–52. Prussia's black eagle on white, shown beside it, was not covered by either source.

era-962.says: Wikipedia: the Holy Roman Empire (800/962-1806) had no national flag, black and gold were the emperor's colours and the imperial banner was a black eagle on gold, its claws and beak red after the late 13th or early 14th century and a double-headed eagle from the early 15th century. FOTW's Holy Roman Empire page: the flag was an imperial banner used by the Emperor, not a national flag; the banner was a black eagle armed red, generally on gold (sometimes on white), and in 1401 a double-headed eagle replaced the single-headed one; the Empire's territories increasingly acquired their own flags.
era-962.open: Both sources date the double-headed eagle to about 1401-early 15th century, so the double-headed eagle drawn for 962 onward is correct only for the later period; FOTW starts the Empire at 800 (Charlemagne) while Wikipedia gives 800/962. The red 'armed' detail and the white-field variant differ in dating between the sources.

era-1966.says: Wikipedia: the flag was adopted 6 March 1957, flown until 1962 and reinstated in 1966 after Nkrumah was overthrown in February 1966; its text describes a red-gold-green triband with a black five-pointed star in the gold stripe. FOTW's 1964-66 page says the white-stripe flag ran from 1 January 1964 to 28 February 1966, after which the older flag was restored.
era-1966.open: Wikipedia's text says the original flag flew until 1962, FOTW and the page's other sources give the white-stripe variant 1964-66; the 1962-64 years are not explained. Design and swatch colours not checked against a specification.

era-1295.says: This page's own caption calls the image a placeholder: «placeholder — earliest Akan states, no flag or war banner survives».
era-1295.open: Whether a flag, banner or standard existed in this period was not checked. The colour shown is not evidence of one.

era-1964.says: Wikipedia (Flag of Ghana): after the January 1964 referendum Ghana adopted a variant of the 1957 tricolour with white in place of yellow, after the colours of Nkrumah's Convention People's Party, restored in February 1966. Flags of the World (Ghana 1964-1966): in use from 1 January 1964 to 28 February 1966, described in Smith 1975, the white stripe being a feature of the CPP flag; the page is keyed with a black five-pointed star.
era-1964.open: Both sources agree on a white middle stripe and the period. Neither describes an eagle, so the drawing, which shows a gold stripe with an eagle or arc, must be redrawn; the star is only implied by Wikipedia's 'variant of the 1957 tricolour' and FOTW's keywords.

era-1957.says: Both: red-gold-green with a black star adopted at independence March 1957, designed by Theodosia Okoh; colour meanings red blood, gold minerals, green forest; star tied to Black Star Line (Wikipedia 6 March 1957; FOTW 'lone star of African freedom').
era-1957.open: Wikipedia says this flag ran to 1962 (Union of African States flags in between), the page says 1964; unresolved.

era-1821.says: Wikipedia (Historical flags of the British Empire): the Gold Coast flag of 1877-1957 was a blue ensign defaced with an elephant and the letters GC in a disc. Flags of the World (Gold Coast, after Carr 1961): the badge was a brown elephant before a palm tree among green mountains, marked G.C., shown on the Union Flag (in a garland) and on the Blue Ensign, used 1877-1957. Britannica's Ghana page covers only the 1949 Convention People's Party flag. A keyword scan of the colony article's references found no flag-related citation.
era-1821.open: A plain Union Flag, as drawn, is not the colony's own flag in any source read; nothing read covers 1821-1877 and no primary source (Colonial Office or Admiralty flag book) could be reached.

era-1670.says: Flags of the World's Ashanti page (after McMeekin and the Fachinger collection) shows undated Ashanti flags: a yellow-over-black-over-green tricolour with a yellow device, a fimbriated version with a throne emblem, and uprising flags of yellow with a striped canton. T. E. Bowdich, an eyewitness at Kumasi in 1817, records 'flags and banners' waved among the chiefs' processions, 'the King's banners' at his departure, and British, Dutch and Danish flags on either side of the state umbrella; he describes no Ashanti national design or colours. Neither Wikipedia's Flag of Ghana nor FOTW's Ghana page mentions war banners (frankaa).
era-1670.open: Bowdich shows banners were used at the Asante court in 1817 but not a fixed national flag or any colours; FOTW's flags are undated and may belong to the 19th-20th centuries; the maroon-and-gold drawing is described by no source. Nothing read covers c.1670-1800.

era-1974.says: Wikipedia says Law 48/1975 and Presidential Decree 515/1975 took effect on 7 June 1975 making the former land flag the sole flag, that in 1978 the sea flag returned as the sole flag, that its adoption date is 22 December 1978, and that Law 851/1978 describes it as cyan and white with five cyan and four white stripes (the exact blue left to flagmakers). FOTW (Adams) says the plain cross flag was the only national flag from June 1975 until December 1978, that the striped flag was adopted by law on 22 December 1978, and gives Pantone 286 C as a reference blue.
era-1974.open: The shade of blue is unspecified in law; Pilalis says the lighter blue belongs to the defunct kingdom's arms and the flags use dark blue. This page used to say the nine-stripe flag was unchanged since the 19th century.

era-1204.says: This page's own caption calls the image a placeholder: «placeholder maroon field — a fractured patchwork of Crusader lordships, each with its own banner».
era-1204.open: Whether a flag, banner or standard existed in this period was not checked. The colour shown is not evidence of one.

era-1967.says: Wikipedia says a decree of 18 August 1969 made the sea flag the sole national flag, the ratio changed from 2:3 to 7:12 on 18 August 1970, and the monarchy was abolished on 1 June 1973. Flags of the World (history, parts 2 and 3) says the two national flags, plain cross on land and cross-and-stripes at sea, stayed in use unchanged from 1832 to 1970, that all crown flags were abolished in 1970, and that on 18 August 1970 the 7:12 cross-and-stripes flag became the national flag and ensign.
era-1967.open: The sources differ on whether the sole-flag decree is 1969 (Wikipedia) or 1970 (FOTW). Dark blue becoming common from the late 1960s is 'citation needed' in Wikipedia. The phoenix emblem on seals was not checked.

era-1924.says: Wikipedia says the Second Hellenic Republic removed the crowns from all flags on 25 March 1924, after crowns had replaced the arms in a decree of 28 December 1863, and that the 2:3 ratio was set on 20 February 1930. Flags of the World (part 2), counting the republic of 1924-1935 as the First Republic, says the crown flags were most probably not used in that period, while the two plain national flags continued.
era-1924.open: This page used to say the flag had no crown to remove; both sources show that the royal flags did carry one. FOTW says the adoption date of the crown flags is unknown.

era-1832.says: Wikipedia says the first official naval ensign specifications under Otto were published in 1833, with the royal arms on the cross, that crowns replaced the arms by a decree of 28 December 1863, and that a decree of 26 September 1867 set the shape and use of flags. Flags of the World says the striped flag was approved in 1832, and its part 2 says the cross-and-stripes sea flag and plain cross land flag were used unchanged 1832-1970, with a naval ensign prescribed in 1858 carrying the Wittelsbach arms.
era-1832.open: The sources differ by a year (1832 FOTW, 1833 Wikipedia) and on the date of the arms-bearing naval ensign (1858 FOTW), and neither says the plain striped flag was the Kingdom's state flag throughout, as the page used to say; crown flags were used for official purposes.

era-1821.says: Wikipedia says the First National Assembly at Epidaurus officially adopted the flag on 13 January 1822 and that Provisional Government Decree 540 of 15 March 1822 set the land flag, naval ensign and civil ensign. FOTW (Adams) says the striped flag and the plain white cross on blue both date from 1822, the nine stripes said to stand for the nine syllables of the motto «Freedom or Death».
era-1821.open: The meaning of the colours (blue for sea and sky, white for purity), stated on this page, was not found in either source. The syllable explanation is the one given.

era-1941.says: Wikipedia (Flag of Greece) lists the national flag without the crown (the Epidaurus design) for 1941-1944 among the national flags and says the Greek flag was a forbidden symbol during the Axis occupation and a symbol of resistance. Wikipedia (Greek government-in-exile) captions its infobox flag 'Flag from 1863-1973'. Flags of the World (Greece in the Second World War) tells of the Greek flag on the Acropolis in April 1941 and says that, under an order of 10 April 1943, Greek ships with Greek crews flew an occupation-zone pennant directly under the Greek national flag.
era-1941.open: The sources agree that the Greek national flag remained the flag of Greece, but they pull in different directions on whether it was banned or flown by ships under occupation, and which variant (crowned or not) the exile government used is not clear. Neither describes a distinct flag of the government in exile, which is what the caption implies; the drawing is the ordinary national flag.

era-1944.says: Flags of the World (part 2) says the use of the two national flags, and the crown flags of the Kingdom (1935-1970), remained unchanged until 1970. Wikipedia captions the 1863 flag pattern as used 1944-1969 and notes the 1967 Compulsory Law 198 on regional flag days did not change the flag.
era-1944.open: Neither source covers the restoration of the monarchy, the civil war or the 'unbroken legal continuity' wording. The flag of the Democratic Army of Greece (FOTW gr^dse.html) was not read.

era-1935.says: Wikipedia says Kondylis declared the monarchy restored on 10 October 1935 and a decree of 7 November 1935 reinstated the 31 May 1914 decree on crown flags; a caption dates the 1863 pattern to 1935-1941. Flags of the World (part 2) says the Kingdom's flags, with crown flags, were in use 1935-1970 and the two national flags were unchanged.
era-1935.open: Neither source names Metaxas or describes propaganda symbolism, and neither was read for the claim that the flag was never altered under his regime.

era-1913.says: Wikipedia gives a decree of 31 May 1914 making the crown flag the state flag for ministries and civil services. Flags of the World (part 2) says the two national flags were used unchanged from 1832 to 1970 and lists the Kingdom's crown flags for 1832-1924.
era-1913.open: Neither source covers the Balkan Wars, the wartime split between Athens and Thessaloniki or the 1922 catastrophe as flag history; those parts of the page text rest on no flag source.

era-1460.says: WorldStatesmen lists the Ottoman flag for Greece to 24 Jan 1822. The TDV Islam Ansiklopedisi (BAYRAK) says Ottoman sultanic standards in the 16th century included white and red, that beylerbeyis and sancak beys carried red standards, that the Ottoman navy used mostly red flags in the 15th century, and that the red crescent-and-star flag was the national flag by the early 19th century. Wikipedia (Flag of Greece) says unofficial flags were used by Greeks under Ottoman rule, usually with the double-headed eagle, cross, saints or mottoes, and shows a Rum-millet merchant ensign; Flags of the World says Greek ships had to fly a red flag with a blue central stripe and shows the 1797 flag of Rigas Velestinlis. Wikipedia (Flag of the Ottoman Empire) dates a plain crescent flag to c. 1480-1780 and the official flag to 1844.
era-1460.open: Ottoman flags over Greek lands are attested in general terms by three publishers, but no source says which Ottoman design flew over Greece in a given decade, and the plain crescent drawn fits only c. 1480-1780. Distinct Greek flags (unofficial banners, the red ship flag with a blue stripe) are documented, so the Ottoman banner was not the only flag in use.

era-1261.says: Heraldica.org (F. R. Velde, main source Cernovodeanu 1982) says heraldry appears in Byzantium only after the restoration of 1261, that the tetragrammatic cross (a cross between four B's, read as fire-steels or letters) was in fact the arms of the Byzantine empire, that the Palaiologos arms were a gold cross and four B's on red, and that the double-headed eagle was an emblem of the imperial family rather than the emperor, settling on the double-headed form in the 15th century. Wikipedia (Flag of Greece) calls a 14th-century Palaiologan design the only attested Byzantine flag (a Spanish atlas of the mid-14th century, with Pseudo-Kodinos recording the cross on naval banners); Wikipedia (Byzantine flags) says the eagle appears on a flag only on the ship that carried John VIII to Florence. Flags of the World's black eagle on yellow rests on contributor commentary.
era-1261.open: Two publishers agree on the red field with a gold cross and four fire-steels for the late empire, which is what the card draws. Neither says it flew specifically over the Despotate of the Morea, whose despots shared the eagle emblem; the sources cover 1261-1453 and the Despotate lasted to 1460. The caption's mention of the eagle as dynastic emblem is supported.

era-1974.says: Wikipedia: the flag was adopted on 7 February 1974, independence day, replacing a temporary Associated State design (green, yellow, blue bands with a nutmeg); green for vegetation, yellow for the sun, red for harmony and courage, six stars for the parishes, a central star for Carriacou and Petite Martinique, and a nutmeg. Flags of the World: the flag was 'assigned on December 6, 1973, the same day as the Coat of Arms'; its history page says the present flag replaced the associated-state flag at independence.
era-1974.open: The sources differ on the adoption date (6 December 1973 assignment vs 7 February 1974 in force at independence); the caption's 'unchanged since 1974' was not checked against later amendments.

era-1498.open: Whether a flag, banner or standard existed in this period was not checked. The colour shown is not evidence of one.

era-1783.says: Wikipedia's Flag of Grenada lists a Blue Ensign defaced with the first colonial badge for 1875-1903 and with a second badge for 1903-1967, then the associated-state flag of 1967-1974. Flags of the World's history page agrees: a Blue Ensign with a sugar-mill badge (trapiche, motto HAE TIBI ERUNT ARTES) for 1875-1903 and with a ship badge (motto 'clarior e tenebris') for 1903 to 1967 or 1974 depending on the source.
era-1783.open: Both publishers support a badged Blue Ensign only from 1875; no source read gives a flag for 1783-1875. The card's 'harbor badge' matches neither the sugar mill (1875-1903) nor the ship (1903-) badges, and the 1967-74 associated-state flag is a different design.

era-1763.says: Wikipedia's Grenada article: ceded to Britain in 1763, recaptured by the French in 1779 and restored to Britain in 1783; its Flag of Grenada says sovereignty alternated through the 18th century. Neither Wikipedia nor FOTW (main and history pages) names a flag for 1763-1783; FOTW's earliest entry is the 1875 Blue Ensign. Royal Museums Greenwich (Red Ensign, before 1864): British merchant vessels wore the Red Ensign from the early 17th century, with the Union Flag in the canton after the Act of Union of 1707 and St Patrick's saltire added only in 1801.
era-1763.open: A British Red Ensign over Grenada in 1763-1783 is not documented by any source read: the museum record shows only that the Red Ensign was a merchant ensign of the period, not that it flew over the island, and nothing says which flags the French flew after 1779. The canton drawn (with St Patrick's saltire) is the post-1801 form; the 1707 Union Flag of the period had no saltire of St Patrick.

era-1650.says: Neither Wikipedia's Flag of Grenada nor FOTW names a flag for French Grenada; Wikipedia's Grenada article dates the French colony 1649-1763. The Canadian Military Heritage page says the plain white flag, without fleurs-de-lis, became the French navy's flag by Louis XIV's decree of 1661, to fly over coastal forts and in the colonies. Wikipedia's Flag of France calls a blue shield with gold fleurs-de-lis on white the best-known royal flag. A 1762 Bénard flag chart (Flag Heritage Foundation PDF) was fetched but its text could not be extracted.
era-1650.open: No source read says what flew over Grenada in 1649-1763; the white-flag evidence concerns the French navy and New France. The card's gold fleur-de-lis is at odds with the Canadian page, which describes the colonial flag as plain white, and with Wikipedia, which ties the fleurs-de-lis to the royal arms.

era-1968.says: Wikipedia: scroll dated 15 September 1821; 1968–97 a similar state flag; 1997 current design. FOTW: regulation 12 September 1968 (5:8, ISCC-NBS colours, quetzal 'supreme symbol of liberty'); Decree 104-97 current flag.
era-1968.open: The 1997 date is 26 December or 26 September.

era-1871.says: Wikipedia: 17 August 1871 blue and white restored as vertical stripes with a new coat of arms. FOTW: August 1871 decree (12, 13 or 17); 18 November 1871 decree defines the arms.
era-1871.open: The sources differ on the day.

era-1851.says: Wikipedia: a pro-Spanish faction took over in 1851 and added red and yellow to the flag; the table dates a Guatemala flag to 1843-1851 and the 1871 flag restored blue and white as vertical stripes (17 August 1871). Flags of the World (historical flags page, citing Crampton 1990 and Flagmaster): a flag introduced on 14 March 1851 under President Mariano Paredes, with red and yellow recalling Spanish rule, replaced on 21 May 1858 by another with a central stripe, until the vertical blue-white-blue was introduced in 1871 (17 or 18 August, 12 August in another FOTW page).
era-1851.open: The placement of the red and yellow is not settled: FOTW quotes an 1865 French description of a flag cut into a red-white-yellow part and a blue-white-blue part, and its contributors disagree on the 2:3 and 1:2 proportions; the page's 'hoist side of the top and bottom bands' is not confirmed. The 1858 flag falls inside this page's span and is not drawn.

era-1841.says: Wikipedia (Flag of Guatemala): the flag of the Federal Republic of Central America was used in Guatemala until 1851 (a section the article marks as needing citations), and it lists flags of Guatemala for 1838-1843 and 1843-1851. Flags of the World (historical flags): the 1825 federal flag was used between c. 1838 and 1843 with the 1825 arms in the central white stripe, and flags were adopted on 26 October 1843 (ratio 2:3) and abolished on 14 March 1851.
era-1841.open: Neither source describes the 1843-1851 design in text, and the small arms in the white stripe are omitted from the card's plain blue-white-blue. Wikipedia's statement is uncited; the 1841 start date is not covered.

era-1823.says: Wikipedia: United Provinces of Central America flag 1823-1824; Federal Republic flag 1824-1838 in the table; used in Guatemala until 1851. Flags of the World (Central America and Guatemala pages, contributor posts quoting Crampton 1990): the first flag, made by Colonel Arce in 1822, was adopted for the United Provinces on 21 August 1823, the Central American flags derive from the blue-white-blue tricolour, and Guatemala's flags are shown as a member of the United Provinces (1823-1825) and of the Federal Republic (adopted 22 November 1824, a federal flag from 1 January 1825); its timeline gives Guatemala's exit from the federation in 1839 and the federation's end in 1841.
era-1823.open: The emblem details (five volcanoes, cap of liberty, rainbow) are in FOTW images only, not in the text read. The sources differ on the years (Wikipedia 1823-1824 and 1824-1838; FOTW 1823-1825 and 1825 to about 1838), and Guatemala left the federation in 1839, before this page's 1841.

era-1821.says: Wikipedia (First Mexican Empire): the Central American lands of the Captaincy General of Guatemala were annexed to the Empire shortly after its establishment, until 1 July 1823. Wikipedia (Flag of Mexico): the Empire's flag was decreed in 1821 as a vertical green, white and red tricolour with a crowned eagle in the white stripe; Wikipedia (Flag of Guatemala) lists that flag for Guatemala in 1821-1823. Flags of the World (Central America): independence on 15 September 1821, incorporation into Mexico on 5 January 1822, independence again on 1 July 1823.
era-1821.open: No source read describes the flag actually flown in Guatemala, and the crowned eagle is replaced on the card by a plain disc. Guatemala's own situation from 15 September 1821 to January 1822 is not covered.

era-1524.says: Wikipedia (Captaincy General of Guatemala) shows the Cross of Burgundy in its infobox, Wikipedia (Cross of Burgundy Flag) says it served as the flag of the New World viceroyalties, and Wikipedia (Flag of Guatemala) lists a flag of the Kingdom of Guatemala for 1524-1821. Flags of the World (Spain 1506-1700) calls the cross Spain's ensign from 1506 and its main ship symbol. WorldStatesmen, however, lists the Spanish war ensign of 1785 (red-yellow-red) for Guatemala up to 15 September 1821.
era-1524.open: No source describes a flag flown on land in Guatemala, and the Spanish ensign changed in 1785, so the Cross of Burgundy does not cover the whole 1524-1821 span on the evidence read. The royal arms are not covered.

era-pre-contact.open: Whether a flag, banner or standard existed in this period was not checked. The colour shown is not evidence of one.

era-1973.says: Wikipedia (Flag of Guinea-Bissau): the flag was adopted on 24 September 1973, the day independence was proclaimed; its design is a red hoist band with a black five-pointed star and yellow over green bands, almost identical to the PAIGC flag, which carries the party's initials below the star; the party adopted its flag in 1961 on the Pan-African colours of Ghana and Guinea. Flags of the World: the National Assembly proclaimed independence and the first constitution on 23 September 1973, and its article 2 (quoted from the Boletim Oficial of 4 January 1975, and again in the 1984 constitution) describes the flag; the party flag is the national flag with the party sigla beneath the star.
era-1973.open: The national flag is the PAIGC flag without the initials, not a different design, and the independence date differs by a day (23 or 24 September 1973). Neither source records a later change, but 'unchanged since independence' is the card's own wording.

era-1230.says: This page's own caption calls the image a placeholder: «placeholder field — no surviving territorial banner attributed to Kaabu».
era-1230.open: Whether a flag, banner or standard existed in this period was not checked. The colour shown is not evidence of one.

era-1963.says: Wikipedia (Flag of Guinea-Bissau): the PAIGC adopted its flag in 1961, with the Pan-African colours and a Black Star on a red bar at the hoist, party initials beneath. Wikipedia (Portuguese Guinea): the Liberated Zones appear as a successor state with the PAIGC flag. FOTW: the party flag is the national flag with the sigla below the star; a 1974 PAIGC book photographs the independence assembly at Madina do Boé 'in the bush' with many small flags and a large one; a photograph from the independence war showing the flag with Cabral's image was reported. The Presidency of Guinea-Bissau says only that the national flag dates from 1973.
era-1963.open: Two compiled publishers support a PAIGC flag in the war years, but neither dates first use in the liberated areas to 1963 (Wikipedia gives 1961 for adoption); the black hoist band with a red star drawn earlier is contradicted by both. The liberated zones are named only in Wikipedia's infobox. A search for a Portuguese-language reference on the PAIGC flag (including a Brazilian university repository page) timed out.

era-1911.says: Presidência da República Portuguesa (decree text, Diário do Governo no. 141, 19 June 1911; regulation 30 June 1911) and Store norske leksikon (parliament adopted the flag on 19 June 1911) document the green-and-red republican flag. Wikipedia (Portuguese Guinea) shows the Portuguese flag as the colony's flag for 1910-1974, and FOTW (Portuguese colonies) records the government's position that colonies had no flag other than the national flag, apart from officials' and military flags.
era-1911.open: No source read describes flag practice in the colony between 1911 and the 1940s; FOTW's statement is dated 'almost since the 40ies'. The colony's flag is therefore Portugal's national flag by Wikipedia's infobox (1910-1974) and FOTW's government position, not by a document naming Guinea. The 1963 end is the start of the PAIGC war, not a flag change.

era-1867.says: Presidência da República Portuguesa (essay on the flag) and Store norske leksikon agree that Portugal's national flag under the constitutional monarchy was the blue-and-white flag with the royal arms (introduced by decree of the Terceira junta of 18 October 1830 and the flag of the constitutional monarchy), replaced by the green-and-red republican flag decreed 19 June 1911. Wikipedia (Portuguese Guinea): a dependency of Cape Verde until 1879, a colony from 1879, with an infobox flag only for 1910-1974. None of them says the royal flag flew over the colony.
era-1867.open: The royal blue-and-white flag is well attested as Portugal's national flag in 1834-1910, but no source read shows it over Portuguese Guinea; use over the colony is an inference, and the 1867 start is not matched by Wikipedia's dates (dependency of Cape Verde until 1879). FOTW's Portuguese colonies page speaks only of the 20th century.

era-1958.says: Both sources give 1958, the year this page starts the current flag. Wikipedia's infobox gives the adoption as 10 November 1958; Flags of the World dates it 10 November 1958.
era-1958.open: Only the year the current flag was adopted was compared; the design and the swatch colours were not checked against a specification.

era-1727.says: Wikipedia (Flag of Guinea) shows a flag of the Imamate of Futa Jallon captioned pre-1896, and another used after it became a French protectorate (1896-1912). Flags of the World (Futa Djalon): the state, a Muslim clerical oligarchy, existed from c. 1700 to after 1934, was created by the Fulani c. 1725 under Karamoko, with its capital at Timbo from 1780, and two flag images are shown, one with an Arabic inscription read as the tahmid 'Alhamdu liLlah' and one for the French protectorate with the French flag in a canton; an Encyclopaedia Universalis passage dates the regime from Karamoko Alpha (1725-1750) to the French conquest of 1896.
era-1727.open: Neither source describes the colours in text or dates the flag's use to 1727-1891, and the FOTW images are by a contributor without a stated basis. The card's earlier caption, a green field with crescent and star, is not described by either; the redrawn white pennant with a green inscription follows the Commons file.

era-1966.says: Both sources give 1966, the year this page starts the current flag. Wikipedia's infobox gives the adoption as 26 May 1966; Flags of the World dates it 1966.
era-1966.open: Only the year the current flag was adopted was compared; the design and the swatch colours were not checked against a specification.

era-1814.says: Wikipedia's Flag of Guyana: the colonial Blue Ensign carried the colony's badge in the fly, the first colonial flag was introduced in 1875 and changed in 1906 and 1955, and an unofficial red version existed at sea. Flags of the World's historical page: the Blue Ensign carried a circular badge with a three-masted ship from 1875, an oval badge in a yellow garter from 1906 and the badge from the 1954 arms; the Dutch colonies became British in 1814 and were later united as British Guiana. World Statesmen's captions: United Kingdom flag 1803-1875, then British Guiana flags 1875-1906, 1906-8 Dec 1954 and 8 Dec 1954-1966. Three compiled publishers agree on a Blue Ensign with the colony's badge from 1875.
era-1814.open: All three put the badged Blue Ensign from 1875, so the card's 1814/1831 start is not supported: the earlier years (1814-1875) show the Union Flag on World Statesmen and nothing on the other two. They differ on a defaced red ensign (Wikipedia mentions an unofficial one; FOTW says commercial vessels flew the plain Red Ensign and doubts it). The badge on the drawing is a simplified stand-in.

era-1616.says: Wikipedia's Berbice and Demerara articles describe the colonies as held by the Dutch West India Company (Berbice 1627-1792, Demerara 1745-1792) and then by the Dutch state until 1815 or the British, and show a flag in each infobox (dated 1627-1792) without any text on it. Flags of the World's historical page says only that Dutch Guiana had four colonies, the first three of which became British in 1814. World Statesmen's flag captions give the Netherlands for 1616-1781, 1784-1796 and 1802-1803, and the United Kingdom flag for the British periods to 1875.
era-1616.open: World Statesmen applies the Netherlands national flag and Wikipedia the Company's flag; neither describes a flag specific to Essequibo, Demerara or Berbice, and no source read describes a plain tricolour over them. What flew in 1616-1814, and how it varied between the Company's and the States' periods, is not established.

era-1820.says: Wikipedia: 1806 present design under Pétion; 1820–49 plain blue-and-red; 1964–86 Duvalier black-and-red; 26 February 1986 current design. FOTW: 1964 Duvalier black version; 17 February 1986 restoration; constitution of 29 March 1987 defines blue over red with arms on a white panel.
era-1820.open: The sources differ on the 1986 day; neither describes the 1849 empire.

era-1803.says: Wikipedia: 18 May 1803 Arcahaie flag; 20 May 1805 black and red; 1806 blue-and-red under Pétion; 1808 arms. FOTW: 18 May 1803 Arcahaie, made by removing the white stripe from the French tricolour.

era-1697.says: Wikipedia (Saint-Domingue): the colony ran to 1803 and its infobox shows a 'flag before the French Revolution', not described. Wikipedia (Flag of France): before the tricolour (1790) the royal government used many flags, the best known a blue shield with gold fleurs-de-lis on white, and the navy's ensign was a plain white flag. Flags of the World (France: Colonial Empire): possessions of the first French colonial empire (until 1763) mostly used the White Cross or Fleurdelysé flags, and Saint-Domingue was the largest territory.
era-1697.open: No source read states which of these white flags was flown in Saint-Domingue, or describes the colony's flag after 1763; the card's gold fleurs-de-lis on white is one of several royal designs. The colony's start is given as 1659 or 1697 in different places.

era-1492.says: Wikipedia (Captaincy General of Santo Domingo): the infobox shows the flags of Spain and the Cross of Burgundy (the latter described as a military flag); the entire island was Spanish until 1605, and Spain ceded the western part to France at Ryswick in 1697. Wikipedia (Cross of Burgundy): the flag served the Viceroyalties of the New World. The US National Park Service calls it the Spanish Colonial Flag, flown by ships and over the fortresses of Spain's New World possessions, from the early 1500s. FOTW (Haiti historical flags) gives no Spanish flag.
era-1492.open: No source read ties the cross specifically to the western part of the island or dates its use there; the cross is documented from 1506, not 1492, and French, English and Spanish forces contested the west for much of the 17th century.

era-1949.says: Wikipedia: Decree 29 of 18 January 1949 (26 January per infobox) with turquoise; January 2022 turquoise; 27 January 2026 navy again. FOTW: 1949 decree sets the stars farther apart in an X; 2022 turquoise.
era-1949.open: The January 1949 day differs inside Wikipedia.

era-1823.says: Wikipedia's «Flag of Central America» gives adoption in 1823, 2000 and relinquishment in 1839, within a year of this era's 1823 and 1838. The Flags of the World page that article links also carries 1838, and has 1823 next to a word about adopting.
era-1823.open: Only the dates were compared. The Flags of the World page was matched on the two years appearing in its text and on one of them sitting beside the word adopt, introduce, establish or the like; it was not read for what it says about this flag. The design and the swatch colours were not checked against a specification.

era-1866.says: Wikipedia: Medina, Decree 7, 16 February 1866 (or 7 March) adds five stars. FOTW: 1866 stars added (9 January, 16 February or 19 January); 1933 regulation 194 of 27 September closer stars.
era-1866.open: The 1866 day is uncertain and the X pattern dates from 1949.

era-1838.says: Wikipedia: 1823 flag adopted in the United Provinces, based on Argentina's. FOTW: stars added in 1866.
era-1838.open: FOTW does not cover the 1823 flag.

era-1821.says: Wikipedia's First Mexican Empire article says the Central American lands of the former Captaincy General of Guatemala were annexed to the empire shortly after its establishment, and shows the empire's flag in its infobox; the Captaincy article says the elite joined the empire by annexation after 15 September 1821. FOTW's Central America unions page gives incorporation into Mexico on 5 January 1822 and the federal flag adopted 21 August 1823; its Honduras history page and Wikipedia's Flag of Honduras date Honduras's own flag to the federation from 1823.
era-1821.open: The annexation is stated by both publishers, but no source says the Mexican Empire's green-white-red flag with the eagle was flown over Honduras; the eagle is not described and the card's disc is a simplification. The flag shown is the empire's, standing in for a province with no flag of its own.

era-1524.says: Wikipedia's Captaincy General of Guatemala article (the captaincy included present-day Honduras) shows the Cross of Burgundy as its flag for 1527-1821, and its Cross of Burgundy article says the cross served as the flag of the Viceroyalties of the New World. The U.S. National Park Service calls it the Spanish Colonial Flag, carried by ships and flown over the fortresses guarding Spain's possessions in the New World. Wikipedia's Flag of Honduras and FOTW's Honduras page do not cover the colonial period.
era-1524.open: No source says the cross was flown in Honduras itself or alongside the royal arms. The sources disagree on the end: Wikipedia has it to 1821, the National Park Service has the red-and-gold ensign replacing it at sea in 1785 and in forts in 1793. Wikipedia starts the captaincy in 1527, not 1524.

era-1989.says: Wikipedia says no change to the flag was needed after communism fell in 1989 and that it was reaffirmed on 19 June 1990 (Act XL of 1990); it gives 1848 for the design and 23 May 1957 for its adoption as the state flag. FOTW says the 1949 constitution was modified by Law XL of 1990 and the coat of arms adopted in 1990, and dates the flag to 1957.
era-1989.open: This page starts the era in 1989; the legal acts in the sources are 1957 and 1990. The sources agree that the plain tricolour was the flag throughout 1957–1990.

era-1949.says: FOTW (Molnár, 2001) says the flag bore the Rákosi coat of arms in 1949–1956 and that the tricolour was in use again from 1956. Wikipedia says the Rákosi arms became the badge in 1949, that revolutionaries cut the emblem out in 1956, and that on 23 May 1957 the pure tricolour became the official state flag, the new arms never officially placed on it (Act II of 1957).
era-1949.open: The image shows the 1949–1956 flag, so it is evidence for those years only; for 1957–1989 both sources say the plain tricolour was official. This page used to describe the arms as a «1957 redesign»; that was wrong.

era-1946.says: Wikipedia (Flag of Hungary): in 1946-1949 the badge arms lost their crown and the tricolour carried the Kossuth arms, again in 1956-1957; communist arms with a red star followed in 1949. Wikipedia (Second Hungarian Republic) covers 1 February 1946 to 20 August 1949 and its infobox shows the Hungarian flag. Flags of the World (Hungary) says the red-white-green tricolour was used in 1919-1949 and the Rakosi arms replaced it in 1949-1956, adding that the official flag is the tricolour without arms and that one with arms can be used.
era-1946.open: The caption's 'plain red-white-green' is a side detail the sources split on: Wikipedia has the Kossuth arms on the flag, a FOTW contributor treats the arms-less tricolour as official. The page's drawing without any emblem is therefore not what Wikipedia describes.

era-1920.says: FOTW says the tricolour was in use again in 1919–1949 and, quoting the DK book (Phil Nelson, 1999), that until 1945 the royal crown appeared in the centre of the national flag. Wikipedia says the tricolour appears with minor arms in 1920–1944/45, hedging («it seems») and noting a version without arms was also used.
era-1920.open: Both sources are hedged or second-hand on whether the arms were on the flag; the page's description of the shield is not confirmed.

era-1919.says: FOTW (Molnár, 2001) gives 21 March–31 July 1919 for the Hungarian Soviet Republic's red flag. Wikipedia says it used a solid red banner for about four and a half months.
era-1919.open: Neither source says the republic rejected the tricolour as a bourgeois relic, as this page does.

era-1918.says: FOTW says the tricolour was in use in 1867–1919. Wikipedia captions the Károlyi-era flag of the short-lived Hungarian People's Republic in 1918–1919.
era-1918.open: The page's claim that this was the first time the tricolour was stripped of royal emblems «in Hungary's history» was not checked; Wikipedia says the tricolour was used without arms at other times.

era-1867.says: FOTW says the tricolour was in use in 1867–1919 and that after 1848 it represented the Hungarian state within the Empire (Heimer, 2000). Wikipedia says that after the Compromise of 1867 the tricolour became official again, with the Kossuth minor arms as a badge, until 1918.
era-1867.open: The caption describes a crest; the sources describe the tricolour with a badge.

era-1699.says: Wikipedia says red-white-green colours were visible at Leopold II's coronation in 1790, were formally described in 1806, and were mandated by Act XXI of 1848. FOTW records the official colours of the Kingdom as red, white and green in 1806 and Law XXI of 1848 restoring the national colour and arms; it says Hungary was under Austrian occupation from 1849 to 1867.
era-1699.open: This supports the tricolour from 1790 or 1806 to 1867, not for 1699–1790. Both sources give earlier dates that conflict (1608, with Wikipedia saying there is no evidence).

era-1000.says: Wikipedia (Arpad stripes): the red and silver stripes are a heraldic and flag configuration in constant use since the early 13th century, first depicted on the 1202 seal of King Emeric; a banner with the stripes appears in the Chronicon Pictum of about 1360, and the stripes' use as a flag fell away after the Middle Ages. Wikipedia (Flag of Hungary): they were the flag of the royal House of Arpad and became increasingly common in the later medieval period. Flags of the World (Hungary, historical) lists a red-white Arpad Dynasty flag in a modern church collection of historical flags and its main Hungary page does not mention the stripes.
era-1000.open: No source read shows the stripes flown as the kingdom's flag between 1000 and 1200: the earliest depiction is a 1202 seal and the banner depiction is about 1360. The debated banner on coins of Stephen I is marked citation needed. The drawing is a reconstruction of the design, not a surviving flag.

era-1944.says: Wikipedia (Government of National Unity, 16 October 1944 to 7 May 1945): the infobox shows the Hungarian tricolour as the national flag and the Arrow Cross flag as the party flag. Wikipedia (Flag of Hungary): from 1920 to 1944-45 the tricolour carried the minor arms, a version without them also being used. World Statesmen: the Hungarian state flag (tricolour, with and without arms) is listed from 1919/1920 to 1 Feb 1946 (captions only). FOTW: tricolour in use 1919-1949. A scholarly article in Turul (Hungarian Heraldic Society) quotes decree 23/1945 M.E. of 1 Jan 1945 redefining the small state arms for the state seal, and says nothing of a new state flag. Three compiled publishers agree on the tricolour as the state flag in this period.
era-1944.open: The tricolour is supported as the state flag; the Arrow Cross government's own flag is not documented (the Arrow Cross flag was a party and movement flag). Whether flags carried the arms as redefined by the January 1945 decree (laid on a green arrow cross, for the state seal) or the 1915 small arms is not stated; the crowned arms on the drawing follow Wikipedia's 1920-1944/45 description.

era-1541.says: Wikipedia (Eyalet of Budin) mentions no flag; Wikipedia (Flags of the Ottoman Empire) describes the horse-tail tugh, Zulfiqar war flags in the 16th-17th centuries and a simple crescent flag c.1480-1780. The vexillologist J. Martykan (XVII International Congress of Vexillology, 1999) says provincial governors (beylerbeys) were represented by one flag and two tughs, that only pashas and beylerbeys had a personal flag, that such flags were a monochrome field (green, yellow, blue or red) charged with a gold zulfikar, with only a few bearing crescents, and that simpler red crescent flags were used in the land forces in the 17th-18th centuries.
era-1541.open: No source describes a flag used in Ottoman Buda. Martykan's governors' flags were personal and carried a zulfikar, not a crescent, so a single crescent on red as the 'standard provincial banner' is not supported. The end date is 1686 in the Eyalet infobox and 1699 on this page.

era-1526.says: The Hungarian government's National and Historical Symbols site (NISZ) says the red-and-silver striped flag appeared under Imre as the Arpad kings' family flag and that mixed-house kings always used the family striped flag or the striped part of their arms to show kinship with the Arpads. Wikipedia (Arpad stripes) says the stripes appear on seals of Szapolyai and others but fell out of use as a flag after the Middle Ages, and the Kingdom of Hungary 1526-1867 article shows two crowned kings and arms only. World Statesmen lists one kingdom flag image for 1382-1804 (caption only).
era-1526.open: The publishers disagree on whether the striped flag was still flown as a flag in the sixteenth century, and the NISZ statement is general (all mixed-house kings), not about John I or Ferdinand I in 1526-1541. No flag of either claimant is described, so the card stays a stand-in with an invented dashed border.

era-1944.says: Wikipedia: infobox adoption 17 June 1944. Flags of the World (Iceland historical flags): the blue-white-red cross design was approved by royal decree on 19 June 1915 and adopted by law on 30 November 1918; in 1944 legislation dropped the 'ultramarine' specification and the blue became darker. The design itself therefore continued unchanged into the republic, with only the shade of blue altered. The Prime Minister's Office history says the National Flag Act was passed by Parliament on 15 June 1944 and was the first law signed by the president on 17 June 1944, that its amendments did not concern the design, and that the current Act keeps the 1915 wording except that 'ultramarine' has been omitted; Store norske leksikon says the flag was adopted for use on land on 19 June 1915, at sea in 1918 and as national flag on 17 June 1944.
era-1944.open: The design is unchanged (1915 decree, 1918 and 1944 legislation), but the page's 'unchanged' is exact only for the design: Flags of the World says the 1944 law darkened the blue, and the official history says only that 'ultramarine' is omitted from the current Act without dating the omission.

era-1918.says: Wikipedia: Iceland was granted sovereignty by Denmark in 1918 and the flag was adopted as the national flag; the state flag was first flown 1 December 1918. Flags of the World (historical flags): the king accepted the flag on 30 November 1918 and it was adopted by law that day; first hoisted as state ensign on 1 December 1918 when Iceland became a separate kingdom united with Denmark under one king; the 1915 decree had permitted land use and local waters only.
era-1918.open: The page's claim about merchant and international use is not in either source; Flags of the World dates the first state use to the same day as Wikipedia.

era-1814.says: Wikipedia: the Danish flag was required in Icelandic territorial waters until the decree of 19 June 1915 approved Iceland's flag; a blue-and-white flag was used unofficially from the late 19th century and first displayed publicly in 1897. Flags of the World (historical flags, J. O. Engene): the Danish flag was used by ships and in Iceland through the union; unofficial blue-and-white flags appeared in 1897; the 1915 decree approved the present design.
era-1814.open: The page's 'oldest continuously used national flag', the Greece comparison and 'first time a flag of its own flew' are not supported (Flags of the World says an unofficial 1897 flag was rejected as too like the Greek flag); the Dannebrog claim rests on a contributor note without dates.

era-1523.says: Wikipedia (Denmark-Norway): infobox flag is the Dannebrog (official since 1625); Iceland was a dependency, excluded from the 1814 Kiel cession, and a colony of the Kingdom of Denmark; the Dannebrog became the union's only official merchant flag after 1748, Norway having kept its own royal standard until then. Wikipedia (Iceland): the Danish flag was required in Icelandic waters until 1915. Flags of the World (historical flags): Iceland's arms (crowned stockfish) were part of the Danish arms, ships used the Danish flag, and Iceland's union with Norway and Denmark meant the Danish flag was used there. The Prime Minister's Office history of the flag says the royal decree of 1913 'in no way restricts the right to fly the Dannebrog flag as in the past', that in 1917 Parliament feared Icelandic ships might be barred from the Danish flag, that Jorgen Jorgensen flew a blue flag with three cods in Reykjavik for a few days in 1809, and that a 1752-54 company flag showed a split cod; Store norske leksikon says the stockfish arms of Iceland were part of the Danish-Norwegian royal arms from 1592.
era-1523.open: The Dannebrog as Iceland's flag under the union rests on Flags of the World and Wikipedia plus an official history that speaks of Danish flag use 'as in the past' before 1913; no source read documents specific Dannebrog use in Iceland between 1523 and 1814, and Wikipedia's infobox date for the Dannebrog is 1625. A short-lived blue flag was flown in 1809. The page's governance claims are not covered.

era-1397.says: Flags of the World (Kalmar Union Flag): the only evidence of a union banner is two letters of 1430 describing the 'banner of the realms' as a red cross on a yellow field, with no pictorial evidence or surviving flag. Wikipedia (Kalmar Union): the union (1397-1523) included Norway's maritime colonies, 'then including Iceland', and pictures the 'unofficial flag of the Kalmar Union as described by Erik of Pomerania'. Wikipedia (Flag of Iceland) says only that Denmark flew its cross in the other Nordic countries it ruled, as a legend-based account, and that Iceland's own flag dates from the 19th and 20th centuries.
era-1397.open: The union banner rests on a disputed 1430 description; no source read says it flew over Iceland or that Iceland had a flag of its own, and the three crowns shown on the old drawing are in no source.

era-1262.says: Wikipedia (Flag of Norway): Eirik II used a flag described as a golden lion with axe and crown on red, which became the royal standard of Norway (Kongeflagget) from 1280; its earliest certain depiction is on a seal of 1318. Wikipedia (Kingdom of Norway 872-1397): the infobox shows a 'likely royal banner used since the 13th century' and says Iceland, the Faroe Islands and Greenland remained under Norwegian administration until 1814, describing Iceland among the Norwegian crown dependencies.
era-1262.open: Neither source says the royal banner was flown in Iceland or that Iceland had a flag of its own in 1262-1397; the card shows Norway's royal banner as an emblem of the crown, which Wikipedia's text on Iceland does not describe. The 1262 submission is not covered by the pages read.

era-1947.says: Both sources give 1947, the year this page starts the current flag. Wikipedia's infobox gives the adoption as 22 July 1947; Flags of the World dates it 22 July 1947.
era-1947.open: Only the year the current flag was adopted was compared; the design and the swatch colours were not checked against a specification.
