era-1931.says: A congress paper in the FIAV proceedings (Chakrabarti, ICV27 2017) quotes the Working Committee resolution of 1931 setting up a Flag Committee, says an all-saffron flag with a charkha was not accepted, and says the Congress formally adopted the saffron-over-white-over-green flag with the charkha on the white stripe at its Bombay session on 8 August 1931. Another FIAV paper (Rao, ICV22 2007) says a 1931 resolution adopted the tricolour, with a blue charkha on the white band and the stated colour meanings. Britannica says the flag was recognised as the Congress official flag in August 1931. Wikipedia and Flags of the World agree on 1931.
era-1931.open: Sources conflict on place and date: FOTW's Anand Bhawan board places a Karachi AICC rejection of the saffron flag in March 1931 and a resolution on 1 August, while the congress paper says Bombay, 8 August 1931 and Britannica says August 1931. Wheel colour is blue in Rao and the FOTW description. 1931-1947 use of the flag as the Congress flag is covered; its use after independence is outside this card.

era-1921.says: Wikipedia (Flag of India): Gandhi proposed a flag with a charkha in Young India in April 1921; red for Hindus and green for Muslims at first, white added later; secular meanings given in 1929; endorsed by Congress in July 1923. Flags of the World (historical flags of India): at Bezwada on 31 March 1921 an Andhra youth made a red and green flag for Gandhi, who added a white strip and a charkha; it became popular at Congress sessions but was never officially accepted (a second FOTW page credits Pingali Venkayya's design, modified by Gandhi).
era-1921.open: The two sources differ on the date (April 1921 in Young India vs 31 March at Bezwada) and on the colour order; whether the 1921 wheel was yellow or another colour differs in the pictures FOTW shows.

era-1917.says: Wikipedia (Flag of India) dates the Home Rule flag to 1916, adopted by Besant and Tilak, with the Union Jack canton, a star and crescent, seven stars, five red and four green bands; Wikipedia (Historical Indian flags) lists it as 1917. Flags of the World (two pages) dates it to 1917 (one page labels the illustration 1916), same design, associated with Annie Besant and Tilak.
era-1917.open: The year is 1916 or 1917 depending on the source; the meaning of the Union Jack canton as a dominion-status claim appears only in Wikipedia's Historical Indian flags, unsourced; the Coimbatore ban is from Wikipedia only.

era-1906.says: Wikipedia (Flag of India): a flag linked to the 1905 partition of Bengal with eight lotuses, a sun and crescent, and Vande Mataram on a central band; no designer or launch date. Flags of the World (historical flags of India, citing Singh, Nair and the Congress website): the Calcutta flag with eight lotuses, Vande Mataram in Devanagari and a sun, crescent and star, reportedly first hoisted on 7 August 1906 at Parsee Bagan, Calcutta; designers disputed.
era-1906.open: Band order and colours differ between the sources (FOTW: red, yellow, green; Wikipedia: green, yellow, red); the designer and exact hoisting are disputed; the page's Anandamath link is not in either source.

era-1858.says: Wikipedia (Flag of British India): a Red Ensign with the Union Jack in the canton and the Star of India in the fly, the Civil Ensign of British India 1880-1947; Wikipedia (Historical Indian flags) also lists a Blue Ensign with the Star of India for the Royal Indian Marine, 1863-1947. Flags of the World (British Rule in India): the Blue Ensign with the Star of India badge became the ensign of H.M. Indian Marine in 1879, a Red Ensign with the badge was a semi-official land flag, and the Viceroy flew the Union Flag with the badge from c.1885 to 1947.
era-1858.open: The field colour depends on the use: red for the civil ensign, blue for the marine ensign; the card shows the blue form. Dates for the blue ensign differ (1863 on Wikipedia, 1879 on FOTW). How widely these flags flew on land is not stated.

era-1757.says: Flags of the World (East India Company flags): red and white horizontal stripes, usually thirteen, with a canton that carried the Union flag from about 1707 and the 1801 Union flag afterwards; the Company ceased operations in 1864. Wikipedia (Flag of the British East India Company): red and white stripes with a canton changing from the English flag to the Great Britain flag and, from 1801, the Union Flag; the Company was nationalised in 1858 and its flag lost official status.
era-1757.open: Neither source states use on forts; FOTW says the ensign was restricted to eastern waters from 1676; the claimed link to the US flag has no written evidence per Wikipedia.

era-1707.says: Wikipedia (Flags of the Mughal Empire) describes the green lion-and-sun alam as the Mughal imperial standard and shows a flag in a ca. 1840 illustration, a procession of Emperor Bahadur Shah, and a funeral scene of 1797 captioned as showing the green flag of the Mughal Empire raised higher than the Awadh flag. Flags of the World (India before British rule) gives the imperial standard and emperor's flag, both with a lion and the sun, and a simplified army banner.
era-1707.open: Both sources show a lion with the sun, not the plain gold star on the card, and neither says how the banner was used or whether it faded in 1707-1857; the dating rests on Wikipedia's image captions (1797, ca. 1840), not on running text.

era-1526.says: Abu'l-Fazl's A'in-i Akbari (Blochmann translation, Ain 19) lists the Alam or standard among Akbar's insignia: not fewer than five carried with the Qur when the king rides out, in scarlet bags, unfurled in festivity and battle (no design given). Edward Terry, chaplain at Jahangir's court (1655 account), says the royal standard of the great Mogul is a couchant lion shadowing part of the body of the sun. A V&A record of a c.1840 Delhi court painting shows a standard-bearer with a green standard with a gold sun. Wikipedia (Flags of the Mughal Empire) and Flags of the World (India before British rule) describe a lion-and-sun imperial standard, green on Wikipedia's account.
era-1526.open: The primary texts give a standard (Akbar) and a lion-and-sun (Jahangir's time) but not its colour or a single design for 1526-1707; green comes from Wikipedia and a c.1840 painting. Babur's and Humayun's own banners and the years after Shah Jahan are not covered by any source read. The card's plain gold sun omits the lion the sources describe.

era-1206.says: Wikipedia (Delhi Sultanate) shows in its infobox a grey flag with a black vertical stripe from the Catalan Atlas (c. 1375); a footnote quotes Kadoi (2010) reading a brown or originally silver flag with a vertical black line as the Sultanate's flag. The same footnote cites other authors (Qurashi 1942; Thapliyal 1938) who describe two flags, the black Abbasid flag and the red Ghurid flag, and banners with the new moon, a dragon or a lion, Aibak's standards bearing a new moon. Wikipedia (Historical Indian flags) dates the Catalan Atlas flag 1320-1413, attributes it to the Tughlaqs and adds that there is no evidence it was used by the Delhi Sultanate.
era-1206.open: The sources describe a red standard and new-moon banners, but not a dark red field with a gold crescent-and-blade motif as one flag, and give no date or dynasty for the red flag; the card is a reconstruction. The Catalan Atlas flag differs (grey or brown with a black stripe) and its attribution is doubtful. Only Wikipedia was found to describe these flags (one publisher).

era-322bce.says: Wikipedia (Lion Capital of Ashoka) describes the Sarnath capital of c. 250 BCE with a wheel of 24 spokes carved on its abacus, and a larger surmounting wheel known from fragments; Wikipedia (Maurya Empire) records Nehru's 1947 proposal to take the 24-pointed Buddhist Wheel of Dharma from the capital for the national flag, and Wikipedia (Flag of India) traces the Ashoka Chakra to it. Flags of the World (India) calls the wheel the wheel of the law of the Maurya emperor Ashoka. Wikipedia (Maurya Empire) adds that scholars theorise the peacock may have been the dynasty's emblem.
era-322bce.open: No source read says the Maurya had a flag or banner, or that the wheel was a state emblem of the empire as opposed to a feature of Ashoka's monuments; the card draws a reconstructed 12-spoke wheel on maroon, not the carved 24-spoke wheel.

era-320.says: Wikipedia (Gupta Empire) describes Garuda on Gupta coins (a Kumaragupta I reverse with Garuda; Ramagupta coin types including a Garudadhvaja type) and a footnote speaks of the Garuda emblem of the Guptas; it mentions no Gupta flag or wheel. Flags of the World (India) does not mention a Gupta flag. Britannica's Gupta dynasty page (short text) does not mention a flag or emblem.
era-320.open: No source read ties any flag or wheel to the Gupta; the Garuda the sources show is on coins and seals and is not what is drawn. Inscriptions (for example the Allahabad pillar) and literature on a Garuda standard were not examined, so a Garudadhvaja banner remains unchecked.

era-1949.says: Wikipedia: hoisted 27 December 1949 on transfer of sovereignty; made official 17 August 1950; Law 24/2009. FOTW: Law 24 of 2009 gives RGB values; flag adopted 17 August 1945.

era-1527.open: Whether a flag, banner or standard existed in this period was not checked. The colour shown is not evidence of one.

era-1945.says: Wikipedia: 17 August 1945 flag introduced and hoisted in Jakarta; Bendera Pusaka sewn by Fatmawati; 1920s revival; first flown in Java in 1928 and banned. FOTW: independence proclaimed 17 August 1945 and the flag raised; 1922 Leiden banteng flag; 1928 PNI; 1929 plain flag.

era-1293.says: Wikipedia: colours linked to the Majapahit banner (infobox 11 November 1293). FOTW: based on a Majapahit flag with nine red and white stripes.
era-1293.open: The name 'Gula Kelapa' is in neither source.

era-1942.says: Wikipedia's Japanese occupation of the Dutch East Indies carries the Japanese flag as the flag of Japanese-occupied Dutch East Indies and says the ban on the Indonesian flag was not lifted in 1943 and was relaxed in Java after Koiso's promise of 7 September 1944; Wikipedia's Flag of Indonesia dates the Imperial Japanese flag 8 March 1942 - 17 August 1945. FOTW's Indonesia page says the first Indonesian flag was flown among Japanese occupation forces at the 17 August 1945 proclamation.
era-1942.open: The Japanese flag as the occupation's flag rests on Wikipedia alone; no source read describes a military or naval ensign, and the 'military administration ensign' wording is the card's own.

era-1800.says: FOTW's Netherlands Indies page says the Dutch East Indies never had a flag of their own and that flags for Dutch overseas dependencies were only adopted in the 1950s. Wikipedia's Dutch East Indies infobox shows the Dutch tricolour as its flag, and its Flag of Indonesia dates the use of the Dutch East Indies flag 1 January 1800 - 27 December 1949 and says the red-white flag first flown in Java in 1928 was quickly prohibited.
era-1800.open: The sources agree the colony used the Dutch flag but neither says it was a distinct 'colonial state ensign'; the card's end date of 1942 differs from Wikipedia's 1949 (1942-1945 is the Japanese occupation).

era-1602.says: FOTW's page on the Netherlands East India Company (VOC, 1602-1798) shows the company flag as the Dutch tricolour with the VOC cypher, the top stripe being orange at first and red by 1630-1660, and describes the chambers' own flags carrying the cypher. Wikipedia's Dutch East India Company article captions its infobox flag 'Company flag (1630)' and says the VOC monogram appeared on flags, cannons and coins; Wikipedia's Flag of Indonesia dates the Company flag 20 March 1602 - 1 January 1800.
era-1602.open: The span 1602-1800 is not uniform: the top stripe changed from orange to red, the end date differs between FOTW (1798) and Wikipedia (1800), and chamber flags varied. The card's drawing renders the monogram as typed letters.

era-1979.says: Wikipedia: Interim Government removed the crown from the naval ensign in 1979; older flags stayed in use until 1980; current flag adopted July 1980, designed by Hamid Nadimi, Takbir 11 times on each band, 22 in total. era-1979.open: The sources give only July 1980; the 'tulip' reading of the emblem is not in either.

era-1925.says: Wikipedia: 14 August 1905 first official flag; 7 October 1907 laws describe a green, white and red tricolour with a lion and sun; 1933 colours darkened and sun altered; 1964 ratio 1:3 to 4:7. FOTW: tricolour first designed 1907.

era-1789.says: Wikipedia: late Fath-Ali Shah lion and sun on flags and coins; 14 August 1905; 7 October 1907 tricolour with a lion and sun. FOTW: tricolour first designed in 1907.

era-1501.says: Wikipedia (Flag of Iran): although various alams and banners were used by the Safavids, the lion and sun had become the recognised emblem of Iran by the time of Shah Abbas and was familiar on coins, banners and artworks; it also says Nader Shah avoided green because green was associated with Shia Islam and the Safavid dynasty. Wikipedia (Safavid Iran): the infobox flag is captioned 'Flag (1576-1732)' without a described design, and a footnote quotes a catalogue that the Lion and Sun appeared on the national flag of the Safavids since the 17th century at least. Encyclopaedia Iranica (Flags i. Of Persia) says there is no evidence the lion and sun was the emblem of Persia under Shah Esmail I: his alams captured by the Ottomans at Chaldiran show no such emblem and a chronicler (Qasem Gonabadi) refers to his 'banners of green' with the figure of a moon; a Chehel Sotun fresco of 1647-50 shows his banner plain or red and purple and star-studded; other early Safavid banners lack the lion and sun; after Chaldiran he is said to have used only black banners. By Shah Abbas's time the lion and sun was the recognised emblem of Persia. Chardin describes Safavid banners as triangular pieces of rich fabric of various colours with religious invocations, the sword of Ali or a lion with a rising sun, and the great standard as a swallow-tail pennon; a pennon with a lion and sun is pictured in 1714.
era-1501.open: A plain green field is supported only as 'banners of green' with a moon figure for Esmail I, not as a plain state banner for 1501-1736; Iranica describes varied banners, with the lion and sun established by Abbas's time (1588-1629). The card's plain green is an approximation.

era-1736.says: Wikipedia (Flag of Iran): under Nader Shah (Afsharid) the two imperial standards were striped (red, blue and white; red, blue, white and yellow; later red and yellow, and yellow edged red), the regimental colours were narrow pointed slips of red, white or striped silk, the Admiral's flag was white with a red sword, and Nader Shah avoided green; the state flag of Zand Iran was a white triangular pennant with a green border and a gold lion and sun, with another version in green and red. Wikipedia's Afsharid and Zand dynasty articles carry infobox captions for an imperial flag of Nader Shah and a dynastic flag of Karim Khan Zand but describe neither in the text read. Encyclopaedia Iranica (citing Hanway, 1753) independently gives Nader Shah's two lofty imperial standards as striped red, blue and white and red, blue, white and yellow, 'without any other ornaments', says he avoided green as a Safavid and Shiite colour, gives his admiral's flag in 1737 as white with a red Persian sword (citing Lockhart), and notes his signet carried a lion and sun; it documents the sun and lion on a soldier's tombstone of the Zand period but describes no Zand flag.
era-1736.open: The striped Afsharid standards now rest on two publishers (Wikipedia and Iranica); the white Zand pennant with a green border and a gold lion and sun remains Wikipedia-only and undated. No source read shows a maroon field with a gold sun, so the card's design is an approximation.

era-651.says: Wikipedia (Abbasid Caliphate): the Black Standard was the banner under which Abu Muslim began the Khurasan revolt (747), and the caliphate is dated 750-1258. Wikipedia (Flag of Iran): the Seljuk flag was most probably black like the Abbasid flag. Wikipedia (Umayyad Caliphate): the Umayyad banners were white, after the banner of Mu'awiya; Flags of the World (Pan-Arab Colors, quoting PASSIA) gives white as the Umayyads' (661-750) symbolic colour and black as the Abbasids' (750-1258). Encyclopaedia Iranica (Flags i. Of Persia) says the Umayyad banners were white (Tabari; Balami says green), that Abu Muslim raised two large banners, one black and one white, that the imperial standard of the Abbasid caliphs was black with the legend 'Muhammad is the Apostle of God' in white, that opponents of the Abbasids in Persia raised white banners, and that al-Mamun briefly adopted green, the Alid colour, when he named Ali al-Reza his heir and soon reverted to Abbasid black.
era-651.open: Black is attested as the Abbasid caliphs' standard from the revolt of 747-750 onward (Iranica, Wikipedia, Flags of the World), covering 750-819 apart from al-Mamun's short green episode; it does not fit 651-750, when the sources give the Umayyads white (or green), and no source read describes a banner flown in Iran itself for 651-747. It is the caliphal standard, not a separate banner for Iran.

era-224.says: Wikipedia: Derafsh Kaviani was the official Sasanian standard (224-651); Shapur Shahbazi describes a heavily jewelled purple background, a star emblem and tassels in red, gold and purple; known images are artistic renditions (a 17th-century Safavid miniature, a 1948 painting, a modern illustration); the apron legend is Iranian mythology.
era-224.open: Wikipedia's Flag of Iran article and FOTW do not cover it; Wikipedia does not name the Shahnameh as the legend's source, and does not state that nothing survives.

FOTW: parliament voted on 22 January 2008 for the act that removed the three stars and kept the green Kufic takbir (described as interim for one year).

era-1963.says: Wikipedia: three-star flag adopted 31 July 1963 under Law 28 of 1963 by the government of Abdul Salam Arif. Flags of the World (Iraq evolution page): the 1963-1991 flag is dated 31 July 1963 - 13 January 1991; three red-white-black stripes with three green stars on the white stripe; the stars were meant to remind Iraqis of attempts to unify Arab countries (Egypt, Syria), later reinterpreted as the Baath motto after the 1968 coup (a contributor, citing a site no longer online).
era-1963.open: The two sources name different governments (Wikipedia: Arif's; Flags of the World contributor: the Baathist government); the colour description in FOTW is inferred from the UAR flag rather than stated for 1963.

era-1991.says: Wikipedia: in January 1991, during the Gulf War, Saddam Hussein added the takbir between the stars (the page gives 13 or 14 January from different sources; amending law dated 22 January 1991) and says its form 'was said to be Saddam's own handwriting'. FOTW: takbir added 13 January 1991, with comments saying it was in Saddam's handwriting. Wikipedia also records a transitional Kufic-script version unveiled 28 July 2004 with the three stars retained, so the flag was not unchanged until 2008.
era-1991.open: The exact 1991 day differs between sources; the 2004 Kufic version falls inside this span.

era-1958.says: Wikipedia (Flag of Iraq): following the 14 July 1958 revolution Iraq adopted a new flag (Law 102 of 1959), used 1 January 1959 to 31 July 1963: a black-white-green vertical tricolour with a red eight-pointed star containing a yellow circle at its centre; it also lists the 1958 Arab Federation flag. Flags of the World (Republic of Iraq 1959-1963, citing Alexander & Smith) describes the flag adopted a year after the revolution as vertical black-white-green with an eight-pointed star and a circle in the white band, in use 1959-1963.
era-1958.open: The two sources differ slightly on the star's colours and the circle's detail. Neither describes a distinct flag for July 1958 to 1959 other than the Arab Federation flag Wikipedia lists for 1958.

era-1932.says: Flags of the World (Kingdom of Iraq 1924-1958), quoting Article 4 of the 1925 Constitution, describes a black-white-green horizontal tricolour with a red trapezoid at the hoist carrying two white seven-pointed stars, in use at independence in 1932; it also quotes a contributor that Faisal adopted this design in 1921. Wikipedia (Flag of Iraq) gives the same design with the trapezoid replacing the triangle on 10 July 1924, the stars said to denote the Tigris and Euphrates, in use until 1 January 1959, and reused for the 1958 Arab Federation.
era-1932.open: Flags of the World dates the design to 1921 in one contributor's note and to 1924 elsewhere on the page, and titles the page 1924-1958 while its text says 1924-1959; Wikipedia's 10 July 1924 date is the firmer one.

era-1920.says: Wikipedia (Flag of Iraq): the first flag of Mandatory Iraq, adopted in 1921, was a black-white-green horizontal flag with a red triangle at the hoist, inspired by the Arab Revolt flag, in use from 23 August 1921 to 10 July 1924 and then replaced by a trapezoid version. Flags of the World (Iraq 1920-1924) says sources disagree about the flags of this period: Alexander & Smith give a two-star flag for 1920-21 and the same flag without stars for 1921-24, and Smith (1975) shows a starless black-white-green flag with a red triangle for 1920-24. The two publishers agree on a starless black-white-green flag with a red triangle for 1921-24.
era-1920.open: Flags of the World itself marks these flags with question marks and does not tie the flag to Faisal or to the 1921 date; the 1920-21 flag is given with two stars by one of its sources. The 1924-32 flag in this card's span (red trapezoid with two stars) is shown on the next card.

era-1534.says: Flags of the World's Iraq index lists 'Ottoman Empire c. 1535-1920' (tr-ottom.html) as the historical flag entry for Iraq in that span; Wikipedia (Flag of the Ottoman Empire) describes a simple crescent flag in early centuries, an eight-pointed star decree for naval ships in 1793, and the five-pointed version officially adopted in 1844 (footnote: 1826 under Mahmud II). Flags of the World's Ottoman page gives 1793 and 1844 from Zanamierowski, flagged as unevidenced.
era-1534.open: Neither source describes an Iraq-specific provincial flag; the sultan for 1844 is not named; Ottoman 1844 date is contested (1826); the 1534 start is close to the FOTW 1535 date.

era-762.says: Wikipedia (Abbasid Caliphate): infobox flag captioned 'The Abbasid Black Standard'; Baghdad capital from 762 (to 836 and 892-1258), the caliphate ending with the Mongol sack of 1258. Wikipedia (Black Standard): Abu Muslim's revolt used the black banner, associated with the Abbasid Caliphate, and a quoted passage (Hathaway) says the Abbasids kept black as dynastic colour after 750 for banners, headdresses and garments. Encyclopaedia Iranica (Bosworth): Abu Moslem unfurled the 'ʿAbbasid black banners' in Khorasan in 747. Aramco World (1978): the Abbasids chose black as the colour of the Prophet's banner. Flags of the World (Pan-Arab Colors, quoting PASSIA): the Abbasid dynasty (750-1258), ruling from Baghdad, took black.
era-762.open: A reference work (Iranica) and three compiled sources agree that black was the Abbasid banner colour, but the Iranica entry read dates it to the 747 revolution and none of the texts read spells out the black banner at Baghdad decade by decade to 1258; the continuation after 750 rests on a Hathaway passage quoted in a Wikipedia footnote. The Flags of the World religious-flags page adds nothing independent of Wikipedia.

era-637.says: Wikipedia (Umayyad Caliphate): the Umayyad banners were white, after the banner of Mu'awiya ibn Abi Sufyan. Flags of the World (Pan-Arab Colors, quoting PASSIA) says the Umayyads (661-750) took white as their symbolic colour. Wikipedia (Black Standard): Ali used the Prophet's white liwa at Siffin, and the Abbasid Revolution adopted black, forces loyal to Marwan II adopting red.
era-637.open: The Umayyad statements are about the dynasty's banner and colour in general, not its use in Iraq; Flags of the World describes a symbolic colour rather than a particular flag. The Rashidun banners of 637-661 and the plain white field's exact form are not described, and the Abbasid black takes over from 750.

era-1949.says: Wikipedia quotes Article 7 of the 1937 Constitution: «The national flag is the tricolour of green, white and orange». FOTW says the tricolour was adopted as the national flag in 1937, confirmed on 29 December 1937. Wikipedia gives the Department of the Taoiseach's reading of the colours (green for Catholics, orange for Protestants, white for peace) and Meagher's 1848 explanation.
era-1949.open: The sources date the flag's status to 1937 (and its use to 1922); 1949 is the Republic's start, not a flag event.

era-1171-1.open: Whether a flag, banner or standard existed in this period was not checked. The colour shown is not evidence of one.

era-1922.says: Wikipedia says the Executive Council adopted the tricolour for the Free State without contest and without statute, as a provisional decision (all citation-needed), and that Article 7 of the 1937 Constitution confirmed it. FOTW says the tricolour was used almost entirely within the Free State in 1922–39 and often called the Sinn Féin flag, that the Defence Forces adopted orange as the third colour in 1923, and that a 1928 government document said the government had taken over the «Free State flag» to forestall republican use.
era-1922.open: This page used to say it was formally adopted at independence; the sources say it was taken up without statute and confirmed in 1937.

era-1919.says: Wikipedia says the flag was adopted by the Irish Republic during the War of Independence (citation needed) and, for 1916, that the tricolour was raised over the GPO, that a green harp flag also flew, and that the Irish Republic flag was treated as a banner rather than the national flag. FOTW dates Meagher's unveiling to 7 March 1848 in Waterford, earlier than the 15 April 1848 date formerly given.
era-1919.open: The GPO flags are from 1916, which is before this era. Wikipedia's April 1848 date and FOTW's 7 March 1848 differ.

era-1541.says: Wikipedia (Kingdom of Ireland): although numerous flags of Ireland existed during the period, the Kingdom 'had no official flag or arms'; the infobox shows a royal banner and an alternative flag from 1782, and the kingdom is dated from the Crown of Ireland Act of 18 June 1542. Wikipedia (Flag of Ireland): a green flag with a harp is described as used by Eoghan Ruadh O Neill in 1642 and by the Irish Catholic Confederation in the 1640s. Flags of the World (Ireland): a gold harp on a green field was the traditional Green Flag of Ireland before the tricolour; its Lordship of Ireland page calls the three-crowns banner non-historical. Second look: the Irish Statute Book address tried for the 1542 Crown of Ireland Act returned not found and the gov.ie national flag page returned HTTP 403, so neither was read.
era-1541.open: No source read calls a green harp flag a flag of the Kingdom of Ireland itself, and Wikipedia says the Kingdom had no official flag; the sources date the green harp flag only to the 1640s onward, and the Kingdom's date is 1542 in Wikipedia, not 1541. Henry VIII's replacement of the three-crowns arms is not covered. No Irish institutional reference describing a flag of the Kingdom could be reached.

era-1171.says: Wikipedia says a commission of Edward IV of about 1467–68 blazoned the arms as «Azure, three crowns in pale Or, bordure Argent» (Kennedy, 1991), that their origin may lie with Irish magnates in Edward I's Scottish wars about 1300, and that the Dukedom of Ireland of 1386 may be linked.
era-1171.open: Arms, not a flag; no source says they were flown as one. The reason for abandoning them is called speculative.

era-1801.says: FOTW (United Kingdom): the Union Flag was adopted 1 January 1801, adding St Patrick's saltire for Ireland after the Union with Ireland Act 1800, on top of the 1606 flag combining England and Scotland. Wikipedia (Union Jack): the design dates from 1 January 1801 and was not changed after the Irish Free State was established in December 1922.
era-1801.open: Neither source describes how the flag was used in Ireland between 1801 and 1919, or the 'governed directly from Westminster' framing; the saltire's origin is given by Wikipedia as the FitzGerald arms.

era-1948.says: Both sources give 1948, the year this page starts the current flag. Wikipedia's infobox gives the adoption as 1885; Flags of the World dates it 28 October 1948.
era-1948.open: Only the year the current flag was adopted was compared; the design and the swatch colours were not checked against a specification.

era-1917.says: Wikipedia (Mandatory Palestine): the infobox shows the Union Flag as the flag of Palestine for 1920-1948. Flags of the World (Palestine historical flags): the British took Jerusalem in December 1916 and a Union Flag variant was used for Palestine and Transjordan 1916-1923; the mandate was created 25 April 1920 and approved 24 July 1922. Flags of the World (Mandate of Palestine 1922-1948): a Union Flag is shown and nothing was done about a flag as a special badge was not thought desirable; a defaced Red Ensign was authorised in 1927 and a PALESTINE Blue Ensign in 1929. Flags of the World (history of the national flag): the Zionist flag had no official standing (Karner 2023).
era-1917.open: Neither source describes how the Union Flag was flown in practice; the 1916-1923 'variant' is not described in text; the 15 May 1948 cancellation of departmental flags matches the page's end date.

era-1517.says: Wikipedia (Ottoman Syria): infobox shows the Flag of the Ottoman Empire for 1516-1918 and says Palestine was part of Syria (the mutessarriflik of Jerusalem and parts of the vilayets of Beirut and Syria). Flags of the World (Palestine historical flags, Dotor 2000): Palestine 'was part of the Ottoman Empire and used the Ottoman flag', with the image captioned 'Ottoman Palestine until 1916'. Flags of the World (Jerusalem civil ensign): the Ottomans had authority over the Holy Land until 1918.
era-1517.open: No source describes a provincial flag of Palestine under the Ottomans, and the design of the Ottoman flag before 1793 or 1844 is contested (see the Ottoman Empire page of this atlas); Flags of the World ends Ottoman Palestine at 1916, Wikipedia at 1918, and this page at 1917.

era-1291.says: Wikipedia's Mamluk Sultanate article (Emblems and blazons): the Mamluk sultans followed the Ayyubids in using yellow as the official colour of the sultan, used on sultanic banners; Baybars is said to have noted the yellow of his banners against the red banners of Bohemund VI; after Selim II conquered Damascus in 1516 Ibn Tulun noted that the yellow silk banner of the Mamluks was replaced by the plain red Ottoman banner; red banners are also recorded. It adds that sultans and emirs had personal blazons (Baybars a panther, Qalawun a fleur-de-lis), that a European source of after 1360 gives Cairo a white flag with a blue crescent, and that the Catalan Atlas (1375) shows a yellow flag with a crescent for Babylon and Cairo and a panther flag for Alexandria. Wikipedia's and Flags of the World's pages on Israel's flag do not mention a Mamluk flag.
era-1291.open: Only Wikipedia was read for the Mamluk banners (it cites Grove and other works), so the yellow standard rests on one publisher; no eagle blazon is described for the sultanate, and the sources show blazons varying by sultan and flags in European sources differing from each other. The card's exact design is the page's own reconstruction.

era-1099.says: Flags of the World (Kingdom of Jerusalem 1099-1291) shows a white flag with a yellow cross potent and four crosslets, quoting Fox-Davies's blazon, and says after Smith that Baldwin III used a plain white flag and Amalric I (1162-1173) added the yellow cross. Hubert de Vries's heraldry survey, citing seals, coins, Matthew Paris (1237), a York Minster window and the Wijnbergen and Camden rolls, says one can speak of arms of the king of Jerusalem only in the first half of the 13th century (a silver cross on gold for John of Brienne; a cross potent between crosslets in the later 13th century), and describes no banner of the kingdom; he records Conradin flying a vexillum crucis in 1268. Wikipedia's Kingdom of Jerusalem infobox calls the flag 'Latin Jerusalem' without describing it.
era-1099.open: The Jerusalem cross is evidenced as arms from the 1230s, not as a banner for 1099-1291; de Vries does not mention a plain white banner or the addition of the cross under Amalric, and the crosslet form is disputed (Smith versus Fox-Davies and Neubecker). The earlier 'attested' label did not survive a closer read.

era-636.says: Wikipedia's Umayyad Caliphate article: the Umayyad banners were white, after the banner of Mu'awiya ibn Abi Sufyan (with sources cited, not read here). Wikipedia's Fatimid Caliphate article: white was the dynastic colour of the Fatimids, in opposition to Abbasid black, while red and yellow banners were associated with the caliph's person, and green is also cited as a dynastic colour; it records the Fatimid retaking of Palestine from the 970s and the First Crusade in 1099. Flags of the World's Egypt page cautions that attributing flags to the early Islamic dynasties is probably an 'invented tradition' and anachronistic; its Israel pages describe no Umayyad or Fatimid flag.
era-636.open: Both descriptions come from Wikipedia alone, and neither describes an actual flag of Palestine; the 636-1099 span also includes Abbasid (black), Tulunid, Ikhshidid and Seljuk rule that the card does not draw, and the caption's later green Fatimid flag is not what Wikipedia calls their main colour. A Flags of the World contributor calls such dynastic flags anachronistic.

era-1946.says: FOTW says the plain tricolour, without arms, has been used since 19 June 1946 and officially since 1 January 1948. Wikipedia's infobox lists the flag as adopted with the founding of the Republic (18 June 1946) and says Article 12 of the Constitution defines it as a vertical tricolour of green, white and red; the civil flag variant is dated 9 November 1948.
era-1946.open: The 1946 decree text was not read. The two sources differ by a day on the 1946 date, and by two years on when it became official.

era-1032.open: Whether a flag, banner or standard existed in this period was not checked. The colour shown is not evidence of one.

era-1861.says: Wikipedia says the Kingdom of Italy was proclaimed on 17 March 1861, the tricolour became its national flag, and the 1861–1946 state flag was defaced with the arms of Savoy and a crown. FOTW says the flag with the Savoy arms on the white stripe was the Kingdom of Sardinia's flag and «later (1861)» the Kingdom of Italy's.
era-1861.open: The design of the crowned shield in 1861 is not described by either source beyond this.

era-1848.says: Wikipedia says that about 23 March 1848 Charles Albert said his troops would carry a tricolour with the Savoy arms superimposed on the white. FOTW says the flag with the Savoy arms on the white stripe was the Kingdom of Sardinia's flag from 1848.
era-1848.open: Neither source mentions the Statuto's flag decree that this page cites; a 1999 FOTW discussion says a Sardinian ship could not have displayed the tricolour before 1848, and that it may have been in popular but unofficial use.

era-1814.says: FOTW (Kingdom of Sardinia part 2) says the state flag, with a crown, was adopted by letters patent of 30 December 1814: blue with a red canton bearing layered white and red crosses, and was superseded on 15 April 1848; the merchant version had no crown. Wikipedia's Kingdom of Sardinia article gives a state flag and war ensign for 1816-1848 and says Savoy naval flags included a blue flag with the Savoy cross in one canton.
era-1814.open: The two publishers agree on a blue flag with a canton of crosses, but the details of the canton and of the dates (1814 or 1816) vary in the sources, and another FOTW contributor says only the royal standard was used c. 1814-1848. The caption's 'restored unchanged' is not supported: the 1814 flag's canton carries a triple cross for Sardinia, Savoy and Genoa, unlike the old Savoy cross.

era-1416.says: FOTW: the traditional flag of Savoy is red with a white cross, blazoned 'de gueules a la croix d'argent', in use 'since the Middle Ages'. Wikipedia (Flag of Italy): the Savoy arms are gules a cross argent (later fimbriated azure); Wikipedia (County of Savoy): Savoy was raised to a duchy in 1416 by King Sigismund.
era-1416.open: Neither source gives a 14th-century date or states that the flag was used continuously; the page's later description of this flag as 'blue Savoy-cross' (Kingdom of Sardinia era) is a separate, unconfirmed claim.

era-1945.says: Wikipedia's Flag of Italy article gives the Kingdom's flag as the tricolour with the Savoy arms and crown, 1861 to 1946, ending with the Republic on 18 June 1946. FOTW says the tricolour with the Savoy shield was the Kingdom of Sardinia's flag from 1848 and Italy's from 1861, that the state flag and war ensign included the crown over the shield, that the merchant flag had the shield without the crown, and that the plain tricolour became the flag on 19 June 1946. The Ministry of Defence says the State flag added the royal crown to the arms and that a presidential legislative decree of 19 June 1946 set the provisional form of the new flag. The October 1944 lieutenancy decree removed the fasces from the state arms and seals only.
era-1945.open: No source read describes the flag actually flown in 1945-1946, so the claim rests on the 1925 models staying in force until the 19 June 1946 decree. Neither source mentions a June 1944 decree removing the crown, or a crownless flag for 1945-1946 on land; the crownless shield in FOTW is the merchant variant, used throughout, not a wartime change.

era-1943.says: Wikipedia (Flag of Italy): the Salo national flag was identical to the modern Republic's plain tricolour and its war flag bore a silver or black eagle and fascio littorio. FOTW: the Salo Republic's state flag was the plain tricolour and its war flag a Roman eagle (black in official descriptions) grasping fasces, per Decree No. 141 of 28 January 1944.
era-1943.open: FOTW's decree text also puts a republican fasces on the flagstaff of the state flag, and the colour of the eagle and fasces varies between descriptions; the page's propaganda framing is not covered.

era-1922.says: Wikipedia says that after the March on Rome the tricolour officially became the national flag of the Kingdom of Italy by royal decree no. 2072 of 24 September 1923 and law no. 2264 of 24 December 1925, and that in 1926 an attempt to add the fasces to the national flag was stopped by strong monarchist opposition. It shows a separate Fascist flag bearing the fasces (party use). FOTW's Kingdom of Italy (1848-1946) page describes the flag as green white red with the Savoy arms. The Italian Ministry of Defence says the models of the national flag and State flag were fixed by law only in 1925, the State flag adding the royal crown to the arms. Normattiva lists Law 2264 of 24 December 1925 as converting the decree-law of 24 September 1923 on the use of the national flag. A lieutenancy decree of October 1944 removed the fasces from the state arms and seals and restored them to their form before the decrees of 1926-1929, which concern the arms, not the flag.
era-1922.open: The text of the 1923 decree and the 1925 law was not shown by the pages read, so the Savoy shield on the flag rests on the Ministry of Defence summary, FOTW and Wikipedia. The 1926 attempt to add the fasces to the flag rests on Wikipedia alone; the only primary source read on the fasces concerns the state arms. No source read documents the fasces on the Kingdom's state flag.

era-1798.says: Wikipedia's Kingdom of Sardinia article says Joubert occupied Turin on 6 December 1798, the king left for Sardinia, and the provisional government voted to unite Piedmont with France; the mainland domains were eventually annexed by Napoleonic France. Wikipedia's Napoleonic Italy article says the Subalpine Republic replaced the Savoyard kingdom and was annexed to the French First Republic on 11 September 1802, and that in Napoleonic Italy the French tricolour increasingly replaced the Italian one. FOTW says the Republic of Piedmont adopted a red-blue-gold triband on 9 July 1800 and was incorporated into France in 1801. A paper by Breschi in the proceedings of the 20th International Congress of Vexillology (FIAV, 2003) says the Piedmontese Jacobin republic's red-blue-orange flag was formally adopted on 9 July 1800, that Piedmont was united directly to France in 1801, and that in the territories absorbed into the French empire, Piedmont among them, the old flags were lowered and the French tricolour hoisted.
era-1798.open: The French tricolour over Piedmont is positively stated for the period after incorporation (1801 in Breschi, annexation of 1802 in Wikipedia) up to 1814; for 1798-1801 the sources show occupation, a provisional government and the Piedmontese Republic with its own flag, and give no flag over Piedmont itself. No source read describes a Savoy flag on Sardinia in these years, and the vertical order of the bands drawn is not shown by Breschi's text.

era-1720.says: Wikipedia's Kingdom of Sardinia article says that when Savoy acquired Sicily (1713) and Sardinia the Savoy flag became that of a naval power, modified as a naval ensign by adding the letters FERT in the four cantons, a blue border, or a blue flag with the Savoy cross in one canton; its image captions give a royal standard / 'state flag of the Savoyard states (late 16th-late 18th century)'. FOTW's Duchy of Savoy page says Savoy had used a red flag with a white cross since the Middle Ages, shows an 18th-century version with FERT letters (Britannica, 1771), a flag dated 1785 with a thin blue border, and an undated blue flag with a red canton bearing the white cross.
era-1720.open: Both sources are about the Savoyard states in general, not dated to the Kingdom's title in 1720; which version flew at a given date, and the crown on the cross, are not established. The caption's 'Savoy blue' is not how the sources describe the main flag: it is red with a white cross, and blue appears only as border, canton or ground on naval variants.

era-1962.says: Both sources give 1962, the year this page starts the current flag. Wikipedia's infobox gives the adoption as 6 August 1962; Flags of the World dates it 6 August 1962.
era-1962.open: Only the year the current flag was adopted was compared; the design and the swatch colours were not checked against a specification.

era-1875.says: Three publishers agree on the badged flags. Flags of the World (Jamaica colonial flags, citing Prothero and the 1881 HMSO list of colonial badges): in 1875 the arms became the flag badge on the Blue Ensign and the Union Jack, an oval shield with St George's cross and five gold pineapples; the badge was replaced in 1906 and again by a new grant in 1957, and the flags were discontinued on 6 August 1962. Wikipedia (Flag of Jamaica and List of Jamaican flags) shows the Blue Ensign with the colony's arms in a white circle from 25 August 1875, and WorldStatesmen lists colonial flags for 1875-1906, 1906-1957 and 1957-1962.
era-1875.open: The badge changed in 1906 and 1957 and the card shows a simplified badge; FOTW notes that Red Ensigns of this design were unofficial and undated. Wikipedia gives no description of the 1875 badge. The 1881 HMSO list itself was not read.

era-1655.says: Two compiled lists, from different publishers, give the British flag as Jamaica's colonial flag before the 1875 badge. WorldStatesmen lists the Union flag for Jamaica up to 1875. Wikipedia's List of Jamaican flags gives the flag of Great Britain for 10 April 1655 - 30 December 1800 and the UK flag for 1 January 1801 - 24 August 1875, then a Blue Ensign defaced with the colony's arms in a white circle from 25 August 1875. Flags of the World quotes John McGhie's opinion that the colonial flag was 'of course the Union Jack, in some form', and its colonial-flags page dates the first badge to 1875.
era-1655.open: Both lists are unsourced, and neither describes the earlier Union flags: the Union Flag changed in 1801, and the drawing uses the post-1801 design for the whole span from 1655. The 1655-1660 Commonwealth period and the use of any flag over Jamaica's separate establishments are not covered.

era-1509.says: Wikipedia's List of Jamaican flags gives the royal arms of Castile as the colonial flag from 1510 to 1516 and the Cross of Burgundy from 1516 to 1655, in an unsourced table. It is the same publisher as the Cross of Burgundy article, which says the cross served as the flag of the New World viceroyalties. FOTW calls the cross a Spanish ships' and military banner, never the official flag of the empire. WorldStatesmen's Jamaica page lists no flag before the British one.
era-1509.open: No source read other than that unsourced Wikipedia table places the Cross of Burgundy in Jamaica, and publishers disagree on whether it was an official colonial flag. The card's claim is an inference from general Spanish use; no basis for the table's dates was found.

era-1947.says: Wikipedia: 701 Shoku Nihongi sun flag; Genpei War 1180–85 white flag with red disc; 13 August 1999 Act designating the Hinomaru. FOTW: 1999 legislation sets 2:3 with disc at 3/5 of the hoist; a 1931 bill passed the Commons but not the Peers.

era-1945.says: Wikipedia (Occupation of Japan): flying the Hinomaru was initially severely restricted (individuals and prefectural offices could apply for permission), partially lifted in 1948 and completely lifted the following year; Wikipedia (Flag of Japan): MacArthur lifted some limits in May 1947 and general restrictions ended in January 1949. FOTW: a modified signal flag 'E' replaced the Hinomaru as the Japanese merchant ensign from 2 September 1945 until 31 March 1952.
era-1945.open: Wikipedia's two articles differ on the first easing (May 1947 vs 1948); the occupation lasted to April 1952, beyond this era's 1947 end date on the page.

era-1868.says: Wikipedia: Proclamation 57 of 27 February 1870 for merchant ships; 16-ray rising sun war flag 15 May 1870; Imperial Japanese Navy ensign 1889–1945. FOTW: Proclamation 57 of 27 January 1870; army 16-ray flag gazetted 13 June 1870; Proclamation 651 naval flag with centred disc; 8 October 1889 new set of flags.
era-1868.open: The two sources differ on 27 January or 27 February 1870 and on the naval gazette date.

era-1603.says: FOTW: the shogunate adopted the sun flag for its ships in the early 1600s. Wikipedia: in 1854 ships were ordered to fly the Hinomaru.
era-1603.open: The sources do not mention clan mon.

era-1336.says: Flags of the World (historical flags): in the period of war among the states (1467-1603) each of 68 kuni was ruled by a daimyo, each with colourful flags based on mon (daimyo flags, hata-sashimono). Wikipedia's Flag of Japan: at Nagashino (28 June 1575) Oda Nobunaga and Tokugawa Ieyasu each had flags with family crests but also held the Hinomaru, as did Takeda Katsuyori's side, so that Wikipedia says the Hinomaru was used as a national symbol; the oldest existing flag, at Unpo-ji, is at least older than the 16th century. A nippon.com article says the Japanese government stated in a written answer of June 1999 that records of use of the Hinomaru before the Edo period exist while its origin is unclear, and that a white flag with a red disc is said to date from the Genpei War. A Bungeishunju Online essay by the historian Hando Kazutoshi says it became common in the Nanbokucho period (14th century) according to the established view, without naming a source.
era-1336.open: The card's placeholder says no national flag was attested, which the sources do not state and which Wikipedia's Nagashino account (1575, just after the Ashikaga shogunate ended in 1573) cuts against. Flags of the World supports clan flags only from 1467; the two new pages mention earlier Hinomaru use only in general terms (the essay without a source) and nothing read describes flags for 1336-1467.

era-1185.says: Wikipedia's Flag of Japan: the Genji (Minamoto) formed the samurai government (bakufu) after the Genpei War (1180-1185); their white flag with a red circle and the Taira's red flag with a gold circle are recorded for the war; the priest Nichiren is said to have given the shogun a sun banner during a 13th-century Mongol invasion. Flags of the World (Japan) repeats the Nichiren story with 'it is said' for the invasions of 1274 and 1281. Wikipedia's Genpei War article adds that red and white, the Taira and Minamoto standard colours, became Japan's national colours. None of these describes a flag of the Kamakura shogunate itself.
era-1185.open: The card is an openly labelled placeholder, but the sources read do not say that no flag existed: they record clan sun-disc banners at the start of the span and a legend of a sun banner in the Mongol invasions. No source describes the flags actually flown under the Kamakura shogunate.

era-794.says: Wikipedia's Flag of Japan: the Shoku Nihongi records a sun-motif flag (the golden-sun Nissho) at Emperor Monmu's New Year ceremony in 701; until the Heian period the Nishiki flag, a symbol of the Imperial Court, had a golden sun and a silver moon on red; at the end of the Heian era the Taira used a red flag with a gold circle and the Minamoto a white flag with a red circle in the Genpei War (1180-1185). Wikipedia's Genpei War says red and white, the colours of those standards, became Japan's national colours. Flags of the World's Japan page has nothing on this period. A nippon.com article (citing a book by Ito Shunji) also dates the first sun-motif flag to the New Year ceremony of 701 and says it was not a red disc, says a white flag with a red disc is held by one account to appear in the Genpei War of the late 12th century, and quotes a 1999 government answer that the origin is unclear.
era-794.open: The card's placeholder ('no national flag yet') is not confirmed: the sources record an imperial court flag and clan banners in this era, though none of them calls these a national flag, and nippon.com treats the Genpei-era white-and-red flag as one account only. Beyond Wikipedia, nippon.com is the only other page for the Heian period; no Heian-dated drawing of the Nishiki flag was found to compare with.

era-1946.says: Both sources date the current flag to 1928, before this era begins in 1946, so the flag was already in use at the start. Wikipedia's infobox gives the adoption as 16 April 1928; Flags of the World dates it April 1928.
era-1946.open: Only the year the current flag was adopted was compared; the design and the swatch colours were not checked against a specification.

era-1921.says: Britannica (Whitney Smith) says Abdullah's Transjordan flag modified the Arab Revolt flag by adding a white seven-pointed star on the red triangle, that it was recognised under the Transjordan constitution of 16 April 1928, and that no change was made when Jordan became independent on 22 March 1946. Wikipedia (Flag of the Arab Revolt) says the Emirate used the Hejaz flag 1921-1928 and its own flag from 1928; Flags of the World describes black, white and green stripes with a red hoist triangle and disputes whether the star dates from 1921 or 1928. WorldStatesmen lists an Emirate of Transjordan flag from 30 Mar 1921 to 16 Apr 1928 and the Hashemite Kingdom flag from 16 Apr 1928, and also a British flag for 25 Sep 1918-25 May 1923.
era-1921.open: The flag drawn (black, white and green with a red triangle and white star) is attested from 1928 to 1946 by a reference source and three compiled ones. For 1921-1928 the sources differ: Wikipedia has the Hejaz flag, Flags of the World a variant with the star possibly from 1921, WorldStatesmen a separate Emirate flag with no description; no source read gives the 1921 decree. The British flag listed by WorldStatesmen for 1918-1923 is not explained.

era-1517.says: The TDV Islam Ansiklopedisi (BAYRAK) says the Ottoman sultans' standards numbered four at first and seven in the 16th century (white, red, green and mixed), that provincial governors (beylerbeyis and sancak beys) carried red standards, that Selim I set white and red banners before his tent when he conquered Egypt, that Selim III added an eight-pointed star to the crescent on army and navy flags, and that the red flag with crescent and star was the Ottoman national flag in the first half of the 19th century. Flags of the World says Jordan used the Ottoman flag before 1916; Wikipedia (Flag of the Ottoman Empire) dates plain crescent flags to c. 1480-1780, the red star-and-crescent to 1793 and the official flag to 1844; WorldStatesmen lists the Ottoman flag to 25 Sep 1918.
era-1517.open: Three publishers agree that Ottoman flags flew over the region, but none describes flags specific to the Syrian or Transjordan provinces. The design changed over four centuries, so the single crescent without a star fits only the middle of the era (TDV puts the star on flags from the late 18th century). The end of Ottoman rule is 1916 (FOTW) or 25 Sep 1918 (WorldStatesmen); the card carries the era to 1921.

era-1260.says: The TDV Islam Ansiklopedisi (BAYRAK) says the official Mamluk colour was yellow as under the Ayyubids; the sultan's banner was of yellow silk, embroidered with his name and titles, and Baybars' emblem, a lion (bars), appears on banners as on coins. It adds that a 14th-century Spanish friar's account shows Damascus under a yellow flag with a white crescent and Alexandria under a yellow flag with a black disc holding a lion, and that an old Spanish map at the Topkapi Palace shows a gold-yellow Mamluk banner with a red crescent, though historical sources say nothing of it. Wikipedia (Mamluk Sultanate) likewise reports yellow sultanic banners and personal blazons (a panther for Baybars). Neither Jordan flag page describes a Mamluk flag.
era-1260.open: Described in sources but no Mamluk banner survives, and the sources do not agree on a single device: lions, panthers and crescents are named, never an eagle. The black eagle on the card is in none of them. No banner specific to this region is documented, and blazons changed with each sultan, so the gold field fits the reported colour but no single emblem fits 1260-1517.

era-1189.says: The TDV Islam Ansiklopedisi (BAYRAK), which names its sources, says Ayyubid sources speak of Saladin's sultanic banner, that contemporary sources mention yellow flags in the army at the conquest of Jerusalem, that the ruler's banner was yellow, that yellow and red flags are both known in Ayyubid armies, and that yellow followed the Fatimid tradition. Wikipedia (Mamluk Sultanate) says the Mamluks followed the Ayyubids in using yellow for sultanic banners. Neither Jordan flag page, nor Wikipedia (Ayyubid dynasty), describes an Ayyubid banner for this region.
era-1189.open: Described in sources but no image survives. The reports concern the sultan's banner and the armies in general; no banner specific to Transjordan or to Kerak is documented. The plain dark field on the card is a placeholder and does not match the yellow the sources report. Whether any emblem was borne on the yellow banner is not stated.

era-1115.says: Heraldica.org (F. R. Velde, citing Pinoteau and Schlumberger) says very little evidence survives on the arms of the Crusader states, that the Jerusalem arms (a cross potent between four crosslets) are not known before the 1230s (earliest a seal of 1227), and that the known seals of the kings of Jerusalem bear no arms; it lists nothing for Oultrejordain. Wikipedia (Lordship of Oultrejordain) describes no banner or arms; Wikipedia (Jerusalem cross) says the cross was not used by the Christian rulers of Jerusalem in the 12th century. Neither Jordan flag page mentions the lordship.
era-1115.open: No source read describes any banner, seal arms or flag for the lordship in 1115-1189, and the cross shown is the kingdom's later arms, not attested even for the kingdom before the 1230s, so the card is a stand-in only. The 1115 start is the castle at Montreal; Wikipedia dates the lordship itself to c. 1118. Schlumberger's seal catalogue (1943), Pinoteau's article and the Corpus Inscriptionum Crucesignatorum were cited by Heraldica but not read.

era-636.says: Wikipedia (Umayyad Caliphate): the Umayyad banners were white, after the banner of Mu'awiya ibn Abi Sufyan. Wikipedia (Pan-Arab colors): white was the Umayyad dynastic colour and the Black Standard that of the Rashidun and Abbasids, with a white banner also given for the Fatimids. Wikipedia (Jund al-Urdunn): the district was ruled under the Umayyad, Abbasid and Fatimid caliphates. The Jordan flag pages (Wikipedia, FOTW) use these only as colour symbolism.
era-636.open: Only the Umayyad period (661-750) is directly covered by a white banner; later rulers of the district (Abbasid black, Fatimid white, Seljuk and others) are not shown, and no surviving banner or banner of Jund al-Urdunn itself is documented. The plain white is a reconstruction.

era-1991.says: Wikipedia's infobox gives the adoption of the current flag as 4 June 1992; FOTW's header gives 'Flag adopted 1992-JUNE-4' and cites the law of 4 June 1992 (a later section on the law says 4 July 1992). FOTW also lists a first variant and 1992 proposals.
era-1991.open: The era starts in 1991 but the flag dates from June 1992; Wikipedia says the Soviet-era flag remained in use until after December 1991, so the interval is not covered by this flag. The 32-ray sun and ornament details were not compared against a specification.

era-1936.says: Wikipedia: the 1953 flag, red with a hammer and sickle, a star above and a light blue horizontal stripe, was used until after independence in December 1991 (and a 1937 flag with hammer and sickle and the republic's name preceded it). FOTW: the Kazakh SSR flag was 'adopted in 24 January 1953; blue bar in lower part of flag', with construction proportions 6+2+1; Kazakhstan became a Union Republic in 1936.
era-1936.open: The drawing shows the 1953 flag; the 1936-1953 flags (1937 and 1940 variants) are described only by Wikipedia, without detail. FOTW calls the bar blue, Wikipedia light blue.

era-1920.says: Wikipedia's Flag of Kazakhstan says the Kazakh ASSR was established in 1920 and its first flag had two lines of yellow text in the canton, 'KSSR' and 'R.F.', surrounded by a yellow line; Wikipedia's article on the republic shows a flag image for 1920-1936 and says it was created as the Kirghiz ASSR on 26 August 1920 and renamed in 1925. FOTW's early-flags page shows a 'possible' 1920-1936 flag as an unconfirmed reconstruction made from a badge for members of the government.
era-1920.open: FOTW's author says nobody knows whether the flag existed or was designed for the pin, and no photographs of real flags or documents are known to him; Wikipedia gives no source in the text read. The card's earlier claim that the RSFSR's own flag simply flew is not what either source says.

era-1731.says: Wikipedia's Kazakh Khanate article says Abu'l Khayr of the Junior Juz swore fealty to Anna of Russia on 10 October 1731 and that the oath stayed nominal until the end of the 18th century; FOTW says Russian protection of the Lesser Horde was acknowledged in 1734, the khanate was abolished in 1822-1824 and Kazakhstan became a colony regulated in 1868. Wikipedia's Flag of Russia says white-blue-red was the civil and merchant flag, the black-yellow-white was decreed the state flag in 1858, and white-blue-red became the sole national flag in 1896. WorldStatesmen lists a 'Russian flag' for Kazakhstan from 1824 to December 1917, without describing it, and nothing earlier.
era-1731.open: No source read says which Russian flag flew over the steppe. WorldStatesmen supports a Russian flag only from 1824, not 1731 (1731 was nominal vassalage), and the Russian flag itself changed in 1858 and 1896, so a single white-blue-red tricolour for 1731-1920 is not supported.

era-1465.says: Wikipedia's Kazakh Khanate article dates the khanate from 1465, shows only the tamga of the Tore dynasty as its emblem and describes no flag; Wikipedia's Flag of Kazakhstan article begins its flag history with the 1916 revolt and the Alash proposals, not with the Khanate. FOTW's Kazakh Khanate page shows an 'ancient flag (1456-1822)' taken from a website and the Turkish government's iconography, but its contributors say the flag looks 'suspiciously modern', that no one knows its origin, and that there is no consensus on whether it is real; it also notes flags shown in a 2016 Kazakh film, whose historical basis a contributor doubts.
era-1465.open: No source read documents a flag of the Khanate; the card's tamga-style motif is an acknowledged stand-in, and the only emblem a source names is the Tore dynasty's tamga. Dates differ (1465 in Wikipedia, 1456 in the FOTW heading).

era-1895.says: Wikipedia: IBEA Company flag 1888-1895; East Africa Protectorate flag 1895-1921; Colony and Protectorate of Kenya 1921-1963; designs not described. Flags of the World (historical flags of Kenya): Blue Ensign with a red lion on a white disc 1895-1921 and with the red lion directly on the fly 1921-1963; the Union Jack with the lion on a white disc and garland 1895-1963; the badge a red lion rampant guardant; British East Africa page: a crown and rayed sun badge for the IBEA Company, and by independence a Blue Ensign with a red lion on a white disc (Stilling).

era-1800.says: Wikipedia's Flag of Kenya lists the Imperial British East Africa Company flag of 1888-95 as its earliest flag (image only). FOTW (British East Africa): the company leased the coast from Mombasa from the Sultan of Zanzibar; the first British flag in what became Kenya was that of the Protectorate of Witu, a red Zanzibar flag with a small Union Jack, agreed in 1893. Wikipedia's Flag of Zanzibar: Muscat and Oman flew a plain red flag from 1698 and Zanzibar adopted no new flag in 1856; FOTW (Zanzibar) quotes a 1959 source that Zanzibar's flags are plain red.
era-1800.open: No source read says that a plain red Zanzibari flag was flown at coastal trading posts in what is now Kenya between about 1800 and 1888; the nearest evidence is the 1888 lease and the 1893 Witu flag. Nothing read describes any flag of the interior.

era-1899.says: Wikipedia (Flag of Kuwait) says the Ottoman flag was retained after the 1899 protectorate, that in 1903 Sheikh Mubarak raised a red flag reading 'We trust in God', that after friendly-fire incidents in 1914 Kuwait adopted a red flag with the word Kuwait in Arabic, used to 1921, when the Shahada was added (kept to 1940), with a falcon's claw added in 1940. Flags of the World (Kuwait, historical flags) lists flags for 1899-1909, 1909-1915, 1915-1956 and 1956-1961, quotes a British officer that on 6 November 1914 the Sheikh's boat flew the Turkish flag until it was changed to white Arabic lettering on red, and describes the 1921-1961 flag as red with the white word Kuwait and a vertical shahada.
era-1899.open: The red flag with 'Kuwait' in Arabic is documented from about 1914 only, not for 1899-1914, and the Shahada (1921) and later marks are not on the drawing; the 1899-1914 flags differ, and the card's 'early 20th century' dating is vague.

era-1752.says: Wikipedia (Flag of Kuwait) says Kuwaiti ships flew the Sulaimi flag, red with a serrated white ribbon near the mast, raised under Sheikh Sabah I in 1752 and used to 1871, and that the Ottoman flag was used under Ottoman rule and retained after the 1899 British protectorate. Flags of the World (Kuwait, historical flags) says only that before 1899 the flag is supposed to have been plain red (Jaume Olle, 1997). The heraldic scholar Hubert de Vries says that in the Ottoman era and the first years of the British protectorate Kuwait was symbolised by the flag of an Ottoman military commander, green with a white crescent and star, to which the Ottoman national flag was added in 1871, and that red flags with white inscriptions date from 1903 and 1906. World Statesmen lists an Ottoman flag to 1914 and a 'Flag of Kuwait before 1899' (caption only).
era-1752.open: Three accounts conflict: a red Sulaimi flag with a serrated ribbon to 1871 (Wikipedia alone), a supposed plain red flag (FOTW), and an Ottoman commander's green flag then the Ottoman national flag (de Vries). None is dated by a contemporary document, and no source documents a Kuwaiti flag for 1871-1899 other than the Ottoman one.

era-1991.says: Wikipedia's infobox gives adoption on 3 March 1992 and Flags of the World states 'Flag Adopted 1992-MAR-3', by decision of the Supreme Soviet, as a red flag with a golden sun of 40 rays surrounding a stylised tunduk (the roof of a yurt), the rays standing for the forty tribes or Manas's forty soldiers.
era-1991.open: Both sources say the flag was modified on 22 December 2023 (the sun and tunduk redrawn), so the design described here is the 1992-2023 flag; the page's 1991 start precedes the 1992 adoption (FOTW treats 1990-1992 as a Soviet-flag period and calls a flag without the hammer and sickle 'erroneous'). The tunduk's colour (red) is not stated by the sources.

era-1924.says: Flags of the World (Kyrgyz SSR) gives the 1952 flag, with official proportions from the 1978 constitution: blue, white and blue stripes taking a third of the flag's height with the white stripe one twentieth, and a star, hammer and sickle on the obverse only. Wikipedia (Flag of Kyrgyzstan) describes the 1952-1991 flag as red with a gold-bordered red star, hammer and sickle in the canton and two navy blue bars with a white stripe in the middle, kept to 1992, and dates the Soviet-era flag's adoption to 1953 in its text. Flags of the World (early flags) says no Kyrgyz flags existed in 1926-1936, gives a possible 1929 flag of unknown use, and describes 1937 and 1940s flags as red with the republic's name at the hoist.
era-1924.open: The flag drawn is documented only for 1952-1991. For 1924-1952 the two publishers describe different flags (red with the name in lettering) or none, and neither mentions a light-blue stripe near the base as in the caption.

era-1876.says: Wikipedia (Flag of Russia) and Flags of the World (Russian Empire) say white-blue-red was the civil flag, a land flag from 1883 and the sole national flag by an 1896 order, while black-yellow-white was the state flag from 1858. Wikipedia (Russian Turkestan) dates the Governorate-General 1867-1918 and says a Turkestan ASSR followed; Wikipedia (Turkestan ASSR) pictures Turkestan ASSR flags of 1919-1920 and 1921-1924 (the latter marked citation needed). Flags of the World (Central Asian Khanates) describes other Turkestan flags of 1917-1924: Kokand, Bukhara, Alash Orda, an all-Turkestani flag and a Basmachi flag. Wikipedia's Kyrgyzstan flag page mentions white rebel banners in the 1898 and 1916 risings. Vexillographia (Turkestan) says the Turkestan Governor-Generalship was created from the conquered khanates, that an autonomous Turkestan government of December 1917 adopted a red-and-blue horizontal flag with a white crescent and star, and that the autonomous Turkestan SSR had no official coat of arms or flag (a red flag appears on some badges, with no document for it); it also describes a 1921 flag of the Jami'at after Trembicky.
era-1876.open: No source says which flag flew over Russian Turkestan in 1876-1917. The tricolour was the sole national flag only from 1896 to 1917, and Vexillographia contradicts the Turkestan ASSR flags pictured by Wikipedia for 1919-1924 by saying no official flag existed.

era-1876-1.says: Wikipedia's Yenisei Kyrgyz, Kyrgyz Khaganate and History of Kyrgyzstan articles describe no flag, banner or tribal emblem. Wikipedia (Kokand Khanate), the power over the Tian Shan Kyrgyz in the 19th century, shows a Flag of Kokand image in its infobox without text. Neither Wikipedia's nor Flags of the World's Kyrgyzstan flag page, nor Flags of the World's Central Asian Khanates page, describes a pre-Russian Kyrgyz flag.
era-1876-1.open: No source read documents a flag or tribal emblem for the Yenisei Kyrgyz or the Tian Shan confederations. The dark field with a gold diamond outline is the page's own reconstruction, as its caption says.

era-1975.says: Wikipedia: red-blue-red with white disc re-adopted 2 December 1975; designed by Maha Sila Viravong for the Lao Issara (1945); used by Pathet Lao; blue band double the height of each red band. FOTW: the Pathet Lao flag was adopted in 1975 and replaced the flag used since 1952; red blood, blue Mekong/wealth, white full moon and unity.
era-1975.open: Meanings vary between the two sources; whether the Lao Issara ever officially adopted the design is unclear in FOTW.

era-1953.says: Wikipedia: red flag with a white three-headed elephant under a nine-fold umbrella on a five-tier pedestal, used 1952-1975 (caption says 1947-1975), adopted by the Luang Prabang monarchy early in the 20th century. FOTW: the 1952-1975 flag originated as the flag of the Kingdom of Luang Phabang.
era-1953.open: Start date 1952 (not 1953); Lan Xang origin not covered by either source.

era-1893.says: FOTW (Laos, French Protectorate): French rule was established in 1893 and the flag of one of the three kingdoms (Luang Prabang) was adopted with the French tricolour in the canton (Jaume Olle, 1996); another contributor says Laos 'had the Tricolore in its flag' under the protectorate. Wikipedia (Flag of Laos): lists a flag of the French protectorate for 1893-1947, shows an 'image of the French protectorate flag of Laos (Kingdom of Luang Prabang)', and says the Luang Prabang monarchy adopted a red flag with a white elephant under French rule.
era-1893.open: Neither source gives the year or a decree for the elephant flag with the tricolour canton, and FOTW does not know whether Vientiane and Champasak had flags of their own. A plain French tricolour, as the caption says, is not what the sources describe as the protectorate's flag; the drawing now shows the Luang Prabang flag with a tricolour canton. Wikipedia dates the flag to 1893-1947.

era-1707.says: Wikipedia (Flag of Laos): infobox captions list flags for the Kingdom of Vientiane (1707-1828), Luang Phrabang (1707-1893) and Champasak (1713-1904) without describing them in the text, and say the Luang Prabang monarchy adopted a red flag with a white elephant under French rule, inspired by a Thai flag. FOTW (Laos, royal flag): the three-headed elephant flag (1952-1975) 'was originally the flag of the Kingdom of Luang Phabang', and the story that its heads stood for the three kingdoms was 'made up much later'.
era-1707.open: No page read puts an elephant banner on Luang Prabang before the 20th century or describes the flag Wikipedia lists for 1707-1893; the card's three-headed elephant is the later royal design, not shown to be the 1707 flag. A scholarly paper cited by Wikipedia (Murashima, Waseda University repository) could not be reached (the server did not answer) and was not read.

era-1990.says: Wikipedia: restored on 27 February 1990 (lead) or 15 February 1990 (Restoration section); carmine red with white stripe, 2:1:2; Pantone 1807 C chosen in 1995, 201 C in 2009. FOTW: flag and arms adopted 27 February 1990; independence declaration 4 May 1990; the 1921–39 flag was revived in the 1990 demonstrations.
era-1990.open: The 15 vs 27 February conflict inside Wikipedia is unresolved.
