era-1905.says: Store norske leksikon (Norges flagg): the national and merchant flag, a white-bordered blue cross on red, was adopted in 1821 and its colours are fixed by the flag law of 1898; the swallow-tailed naval ensign had the union mark from 1844 and was introduced without it on 9 June 1905, and the state flag without the mark dates from 10 December 1898 (a heading elsewhere gives 15 December). Wikipedia (Flag of Norway): the union mark of Sweden-Norway was placed in the flag in 1844 and the Nordic cross flag without it is dated 1899 to the present, with the royal standard adopted on 15 November 1905.
era-1905.open: SNL itself gives the state flag date as 10 December and 15 December 1898 in different places, and the royal standard date rests on Wikipedia alone.

era-1814.says: Store norske leksikon: Dannebrog with the Norwegian lion in the upper hoist field was proclaimed Norway's flag on 27 February 1814 by the regent Christian Frederik; Swedish-pattern union naval flag from 1815; Meltzer's flag laid before the Odelsting on 4 May 1821 and adopted by royal resolution of 13 July 1821; on 20 June 1844 both countries' merchant and naval flags received the common union mark (the 'herring salad') in the canton, until 1905. Wikipedia agrees on 1814, 1821 (13 July approval for civilian use) and 1844.
era-1814.open: The 1821 flag's Storting approval is dated May 1821 by Wikipedia (11 and 16 May) and 4 May presentation by SNL; the page's earlier statement that the plain civil flag never carried the union mark is contradicted by both sources.

era-1523.says: Store norske leksikon: in the 17th and 18th centuries the Danish Dannebrog gradually became the usual flag, also on Norwegian warships and fortresses, and from 1748 it was the only recognised Danish-Norwegian merchant flag; the lion banner was occasionally used as a ship and fortress flag. Wikipedia: Norway used Denmark's flag from 1537 to 1814 (citation needed), the Norwegian lion banner flew over Akershus at least until 1698, was in regimental colours from 1641, and the 1748 decree made Dannebrog the only legal merchant flag.
era-1523.open: Neither source says Dannebrog was the flag from 1523; Wikipedia gives 1537 and SNL describes a gradual change in the 1600s and 1700s. 'No flag of its own for the entire span' is too strong: the lion banner survived on ships and fortresses (page text corrected).

era-995.says: Store norske leksikon: the oldest known form of Norwegian flag is the lion of the realm's arms on a banner, shown on Duchess Ingebjorg's seal of 1318 - a royal flag with the golden lion and silver axe on red, later sometimes used on ships and fortresses. Wikipedia: Eirik II used a golden lion with axe and crown on red, which from 1280 became the royal standard; the earliest certain depiction is the 1318 seal; earlier rulers used other banners (raven, serpent, red lion on gold under Inge I in the 1130s, Sverre's eagle).
era-995.open: Before about 1280 the sources describe other banners, not the lion on red, so the c.995-1280 stretch of this era is not covered; 'St. Olav's axe' is not stated by either source.

era-1940.says: Wikipedia's chronology table shows a break at 1940 with a Nazi Germany flag icon until the national flag returned in 1945. The Storting's own history page reproduces a wartime photograph of the occupied Storting building with a German propaganda poster and a swastika in the flagpole; the building was taken over by the occupiers and later by Reichskommissar Terboven. FOTW covers no historical Norwegian flags.
era-1940.open: Only the Storting building is documented; Reich flags over other Norwegian institutions, the Nasjonal Samling emblem, any domestic ban on the Norwegian flag and its use abroad are not covered by sources read.

era-1397.says: FOTW (Union of Kalmar) and Wikipedia (Emblems of the Kalmar Union) both cite two letters of 1430 in which King Eric of Pomerania orders the priests of Vadstena and Kalmar to wear the 'banner of the realms' on their robes, described as a red cross in a yellow field. FOTW adds that there is no pictorial evidence from the time and no surviving flag, and that a red Scandinavian cross on yellow seen in a museum is a recreation. Wikipedia's emblems article places the Three Crowns in the union's arms, not on the banner.
era-1397.open: The red cross on yellow rests on the two 1430 letters only, which neither page quotes from a primary edition; the cross's shape (Nordic or centred) and any crowns are not described, so the drawing, which now omits the crowns, is a reconstruction. The caption's three crowns are not supported.

era-1970.says: Both sources give 1970, the year this page starts the current flag. Wikipedia's infobox gives the adoption as 22 May 2004; Flags of the World dates it 18 October 1995.
era-1970.open: Only the year the current flag was adopted was compared; the design and the swatch colours were not checked against a specification.

era-1856.says: Wikipedia: until 1970 the Sultanate of Muscat and Oman used the plain red banner (gallery caption dates the Sultanate flag 1856-1970). FOTW: the red of the 1970 flag came from the old Omani flag, which was red.
era-1856.open: The sources read do not support the 'maritime colour' wording or the absence of an emblem in detail; neither dates the start of the red flag beyond Wikipedia's 1856 caption.

era-1744.says: De Vries (Oman History and Heraldry): after the Ya'ariba dynasty died out in 1744 the Abu Sa'id dynasty flew its own flag, red without any other symbol, from 1749. Wikipedia (Flag of Oman): until 1970 the Sultanate of Muscat and Oman used the plain red banner (gallery caption 1856-1970). Flags of the World (Muscat and Oman): a contributor says Oman flew a plain red flag until 17 December 1970, and the red flag was restored in 1871 after the 1868-1871 white imamate flag.
era-1744.open: Only de Vries reaches back before 1856, and he does not cite a basis; FOTW's 'since 750 CE' claim is uncited, and a FOTW contributor's claim that ships used the French maritime ensign about 1844-1910 conflicts with a single red flag. No source read calls the red flag a maritime ensign or covers the African holdings.

era-1624.says: De Vries (Oman History and Heraldry) says the flag of the Ya'rubi dynasty is documented by a mid-18th-century Dutch flag chart as a flag of 13 stripes (red, white, green, yellow ...) with green crescents on the yellow stripes, and that the plain red flag belongs to the Abu Sa'id dynasty from 1749. Wikipedia (Ya'rubid dynasty) shows an 'Ensign of the Ya'rubids' in its infobox, citing de Vries, but describes no flag in its text. Neither Wikipedia's Flag of Oman nor the FOTW Oman pages cover the Ya'ariba period.
era-1624.open: The card shows a plain red field as an informed reconstruction of Ya'ariba maritime colour; the sources read give the Ya'rubi flag as a striped design and the plain red as the later Abu Sa'id flag, so the plain red is not confirmed for this period. The striped description rests on a single Dutch chart as reported by one heraldry site. No second publisher was found for the striped Ya'rubi flag.

era-1507.says: Wikipedia (Portuguese Oman) dates Portuguese rule over the coastal cities from 1507 to 1650/1656 and describes no flag; neither the Wikipedia nor the Flags of the World Oman pages cover the period. De Vries (Oman History and Heraldry) reports that Diogo Homem's 1555 map of the Indian Ocean gives the Portuguese-held Omani settlements a red flag with four blue escutcheons charged with white balls, and gives no Nabhani flag.
era-1507.open: The card is a text panel saying there is no single flag and shows none. The only flag found, the Homem map flag, rests on one heraldry website's account of a map and is not shown on the card; no banner of the interior Nabhani Imamate is documented in any source read.

era-1971.says: Both sources date the current flag to 1947, before this era begins in 1971, so the flag was already in use at the start. Wikipedia's infobox gives the adoption as 11 August 1947; Flags of the World dates it 14 August 1947.
era-1971.open: Only the year the current flag was adopted was compared; the design and the swatch colours were not checked against a specification.

era-14.says: Wikipedia: adopted 11 Aug 1947, official 14 Aug 1947 (Dominion); green for the Muslim majority, white hoist stripe for minorities, crescent and star. FOTW: adopted 14 Aug 1947; white and dark green represent minorities and the Muslim majority.
era-14.open: Muslim League derivation is stated by Wikipedia only; 11 vs 14 Aug differs; FOTW notes disputed designer.

era-1956.says: Wikipedia (Flag of Pakistan): the flag, adopted in 1947, was retained as the flag of the Islamic Republic of Pakistan with the 1956 constitution and remains in use; the design has not changed since 1947. Flags of the World (Pakistan) gives the flag as adopted 14 August 1947 and the coat of arms as adopted 23 March 1956, with no later change to the flag.
era-1956.open: Neither source mentions East Pakistan or its use there; the page's East/West framing is not covered. FOTW does not state in so many words that the flag was unchanged in 1956.

era-1857.says: Wikipedia's Flags of British India lists the Union Jack with the Order of the Star of India (1869-1947), a Red Ensign defaced with the Star of India (1880-1947) and a Blue Ensign (1876-1947); FOTW's British Rule in India page says India's flag was the Union Jack bearing the Star of India insignia, with a Blue Ensign and a Red Ensign, and that East India Company rule passed to the Crown in 1858.
era-1857.open: Neither source ties the ensigns to the future Pakistani territories specifically; the Red Ensign shown was used from 1880 and the flags before 1858 were the East India Company's.

era-1526.says: Wikipedia (Flags of the Mughal Empire): the principal imperial standard, the alam, was primarily moss green with a lion and sun facing the hoist, traced back to Timur; it cites the Ain-i-Akbari (five alams carried with the emperor under Akbar), Edward Terry's Voyage to East-India of 1655 (a royal standard of silk with a crouching lion shadowing the sun) and Padshahnama paintings showing scarlet pennons with green borders, or green fields, with a lion and sun. Neither Wikipedia's Flag of Pakistan nor FOTW's Pakistan page mentions Mughal flags.
era-1526.open: One Wikipedia article, tagged for missing citations, supports the green standard. The plain green placeholder drawn omits the lion and sun, and no source shows a flag specific to the Pakistani territories.

era-1994.says: Both sources date the current flag to 1981, before this era begins in 1994, so the flag was already in use at the start. Wikipedia's infobox gives the adoption as 1 January 1981; Flags of the World dates it 1 January 1981.
era-1994.open: Only the year the current flag was adopted was compared; the design and the swatch colours were not checked against a specification.

era-1947.says: Wikipedia's Flag of Palau lists the UN flag for 1947-1965, the Trust Territory flag for 1965-1981 (flown jointly with the UN and American flags) and the US flag in its 48-, 49- and 50-star forms to 1994. FOTW's Trust Territory page says the territory's flag (blue with six stars for the six districts, official 19 August 1965) was preceded by the US and UN flags, and that Palau was the last district, ending the trust with a free-association agreement.
era-1947.open: The Trust Territory flag (blue with six stars, 1965-81) is not the flag drawn; FOTW dates the end of the trust to 1980 for the flag while Wikipedia's US-flag range runs to 1994. Where exactly each flag flew in Palau is not stated.

era-1914.says: Wikipedia (Flag of Palau) pictures the flag of Japan 'used during the South Seas Mandate, 1914-1944', the Japanese Imperial standard for 1914-1944 and a separate flag of the Governor of the South Seas Mandate. Wikipedia (South Seas Mandate) shows the flag of Japan as the mandate's flag (1919-1947), with the German New Guinea territory as predecessor and a section on the Governor's flag. Flags of the World (Palau) says Japan administered the formerly German islands from Koror through the South Pacific Agency and that no special military or regional flag was made except one service flag, a fishery investigation vessel flag adopted on 18 September 1930.
era-1914.open: The sources agree that Japan's flag, not a local one, served for the mandate, but FOTW does not itself say the Hinomaru flew over Palau; Wikipedia's mandate dates are 1919-1947 (the card has 1914-1947) and a distinct Governor's flag existed, so 'no distinct emblem' holds only for the territory as a whole.

era-1899.says: Three publishers agree that German imperial flags flew over Palau. WorldStatesmen lists the German Empire flag (the black-white-red tricolour) for 12 October 1899 - 8 October 1914. Wikipedia (Flag of Palau) pictures the flag of the German colonial empire for all of the territory in 1899-1914 and the German Emperor's standard for the same years. Flags of the World (German colonies) says that the colonies had no flags of their own, with imperial arms and flags used throughout the empire, and that the Caroline Islands used either the Foreign Office service flag or the Imperial ensign.
era-1899.open: Which imperial flag flew where is not established: FOTW names the service flag or the war ensign, both with an eagle or cross, whereas WorldStatesmen shows the plain tricolour that the card draws. The earlier white field with a canton and Palau badge is described by none of them.

era-1885.says: Wikipedia's Flag of Palau lists the Spanish flag (1785-1899) and its Spanish East Indies article says Palau was ruled from Manila until the remaining islands were sold to Germany under the 1899 treaty, showing the 1785 Spanish flag as the colony's flag. FOTW's Spain page gives the flag as red-yellow-red in the ratio 1:2:1 (the yellow stripe twice the width of each red), originating as the 1785 war ensign and made the state and war flag by Royal Decree of 13 October 1843.
era-1885.open: Neither source states where the flag was actually raised in Palau; Wikipedia also lists the German New Guinea Company flag for 1885-1899, which did not govern Palau.

era-1999.says: Wikipedia: made 1 November 1903 by María de la Ossa de Amador from Manuel E. Amador's sketch; Law 64 of 1904; Law 48 of 25 March 1925; Law 34 of 15 December 1949; Decree 337 of 22 December 2017. FOTW: first hoisted and baptised 20 December 1903; Law 64 of 1904; Law 4 of 1925; designer disputed.
era-1999.open: The 1925 law number and the designer differ between sources.

era-1821.says: Wikipedia's «Flag of Gran Colombia» gives adoption in 1821 and relinquishment in 1830, within a year of this era's 1821 and 1830. The Flags of the World page that article links also carries 1830, and has 1821 next to a word about adopting.
era-1821.open: Only the dates were compared. The Flags of the World page was matched on the two years appearing in its text and on one of them sitting beside the word adopt, introduce, establish or the like; it was not read for what it says about this flag. The design and the swatch colours were not checked against a specification.

era-1903.says: Wikipedia: first flag used from 3 November 1903 to 1904; current design ratified by Law 64 of 1904. FOTW: flag first hoisted 20 December 1903; Law 64 of 1904.
era-1903.open: Neither source covers the Canal Zone.

era-1830.says: Wikipedia: the flag of the United States of Colombia (also the current Colombian flag) was in use from 26 November 1861 to 3 November 1903, a provisional New Granada flag from 1830 to 1834, the New Granada and Grenadine Confederation flag from 1834 to 1861, and Panama had its own Federal State flag (1855-1863) and Sovereign State flag (1863-1886); Wikipedia (Flag of Colombia): New Granada's colours adopted 9 May 1834, Colombia's flag adopted by law 26 November 1861. FOTW (Panama historical flags): flags of the Province of Istmo adopted 1821 and 9 May 1834, a State flag from 1855, flags from 26 November 1861 to 1886, and a provincial flag of 1886 abolished 3 November 1903.
era-1830.open: FOTW's table gives dates only, with no design in its text, and Wikipedia's 1863-1886 Sovereign State dates are not matched by FOTW's single 1861-1886 entry; the designs of the Panama state flags were not compared.

era-1519.says: Wikipedia (Flag of Panama): lists the Cross of Burgundy as the Spanish Empire's flag until 1793, with a Flag of Spain for 1786-1821. Wikipedia (Cross of Burgundy): it remained in use in Spain's overseas empire and as a jack until 1785. Flags of the World (Spain 1506-1700): the red Burgundy cross was a military banner, the Spanish ensign from 1506 to the 1670s and a jack until 1785, with separate ensigns for American waters. Second look: World Statesmen lists the Spanish war ensign (1785-1931) for Panama up to 6 Oct 1821, and a UCM survey of Spanish military flags (Militaria 9, 1997) says the red aspa was on Spanish flags from the early 16th century and the red-yellow-red warship flag was set in 1785 and extended to coastal fortifications in 1793.
era-1519.open: Neither publisher nor the UCM survey mentions Panama specifically; the cross was superseded at sea in 1785 and on forts in 1793, so it cannot be shown as the colony's banner for the whole 1519-1821 span, and World Statesmen puts the red-yellow ensign over Panama from 1785.

era-1975.says: Both sources date the current flag to 1971, before this era begins in 1975, so the flag was already in use at the start. Wikipedia's infobox gives the adoption as 1 July 1971; Flags of the World dates it July 1971.
era-1975.open: Only the year the current flag was adopted was compared; the design and the swatch colours were not checked against a specification.

era-1884-1.open: Whether a flag, banner or standard existed in this period was not checked. The colour shown is not evidence of one.

era-1920.says: Wikipedia's Flag of Papua New Guinea lists the Flag of Australia in the Territory of Papua and New Guinea for 1949-1971 alongside a Territory of Papua flag (1906-1971), a Territory of New Guinea flag (1921-1971) and a 1962 local flag, without designs. Flags of the World's historical page says Papua's flag from 1908 was an Australian Blue Ensign with PAPUA on a white disc, the Mandated Territory of New Guinea used a defaced Blue Ensign with a crown above T.N.G., the customs flag from 1951 to 1975 was the Australian national flag with a disc lettered T.P. & N.G.C., and the undefaced Australian Blue Ensign was reportedly flown for customs after 1942.
era-1920.open: Both publishers show the territories flying defaced territorial ensigns on an Australian Blue Ensign base before 1949, so the card's undefaced Australian ensign is documented only for 1949 onward (and in a customs role), not for the whole 1920-1975 span. The claim that neither territory had its own flag is contradicted by both sources.

era-1884.says: Wikipedia's Flag of Papua New Guinea shows the flag of the German Imperial Colonial Office (1884-1914), a 1914 proposed German New Guinea flag that was never implemented, and a Territory of Papua flag from 1906. Flags of the World's historical page gives British New Guinea a Blue Ensign with a crown above NG on a white disc in 1885-1888 and BNG in 1888-1906, then a Blue Ensign with a crown above PAPUA from 1906 (an Australian version from 1908), and says the Territory of New Guinea was German from 1884-85 until Australian occupation in 1914-15 (mandate 1920-21); its German New Guinea flag pages were not read.
era-1884.open: No source read describes a split flag or a German eagle motif for this period: the card's split design is its own device, openly standing in for the divided rule, and the sources give separate flags for the German and the British/Australian parts. Nothing read describes the German colonial flag actually flown over German New Guinea.

era-1870.says: Wikipedia: on 25 November 1842 Congress unified the flags as a red, white and blue tricolour, 'officially adopted in 1842', the obverse with arms and the reverse with the treasury seal (a lion below a Phrygian cap, 'Paz y Justicia'), last modified by decree of 15 July 2013. Flags of the World: the flag was introduced by the General Congress on 25 November 1842 and its history lists 'flag with the national coat of arms on the obverse and a Treasury Seal on the reverse' for 1842 to 1954(?), with later versions to 2013 (decree of 15 July 2013, proportions 11:20).
era-1870.open: Both publishers date the flag to 1842, so 1870 is only the start of the post-war era, not of the flag; the emblems were simplified in 1988-90 and altered by the 15 July 2013 decree, so the plain triband drawn is a simplification.

era-1864.says: Wikipedia (Flag of Paraguay): on 25 November 1842 Congress unified the flags as a red-white-blue tricolour with the arms on the obverse and the treasury seal on the reverse, the design that is still the national flag. Flags of the World (history and 1842 page): the same version is listed for 1842 to 1954(?), modelled on the 1812 flag, so it was the national flag during 1864-1870.
era-1864.open: No source read mentions the Paraguayan War or says how the flag was worn or flown in it; FOTW's 1842-1954 span is queried. The flag in force is established, not wartime use or variants.

era-1811.says: Wikipedia: a blue flag with a six-pointed star was raised 15 May 1811; blue-yellow-red stripes were used from 17 June 1811; a red-white-blue tricolour was adopted 15 August 1812; Francia restored the blue design in 1826; Congress unified the flag as the red-white-blue tricolour on 25 November 1842. FOTW: the earliest mention of a red-white-blue tricolour in Paraguay is 15 August 1812, and the design was regularised in 1842.
era-1811.open: The page's 'same general colours' for the Francia period is wrong; Wikipedia lists blue and other flags. FOTW does not name Carlos Antonio Lopez, and Wikipedia names him only for 1842.

era-1537.says: Wikipedia (Cross of Burgundy): the flag served as the flag of the Viceroyalties of the New World; the U.S. National Park Service calls it the Spanish Colonial Flag flown by ships and over the fortresses of Spain's possessions. The Spanish Army's Institute of History and Military Culture dates the Cross of Burgundy to 1506, the first Spanish flag in America to 1519, the red-and-gold navy flag to 1785 and the cross on regimental colours to 1802. Wikipedia (Governorate of Paraguay) places Paraguay in the Viceroyalty of Peru from 1617 and in the Río de la Plata from 1782. Wikipedia (Flag of Paraguay) and FOTW give the red-yellow flag of 1785 as the last Spanish flag, FOTW the 1806 troop flags and 1811-1812 flags.
era-1537.open: No source read, including the Spanish Army guide, mentions the Cross of Burgundy in Paraguay itself; the identification rests on its general colonial use, and from 1785 the red-and-gold flag replaced it at sea, in forts and on the navy's ships, so it fits the card's end date of 1811 only loosely. Nothing is said of a flag particular to the Jesuit missions. Downgraded from attested because no source places this flag in Paraguay.

FOTW: flag and arms adopted by law 25 February 1825; Decree 1323 of 31 March 1950 confirmed the plain triband as the pabellón nacional; flag without arms is civil, with arms state and war.

era-1821.says: Paz Soldan (Historia del Peru independiente, 1868) cites the decree of 21 October 1820 (flag 8 by 6 feet, divided diagonally into four, white top and bottom, red sides, with an oval laurel wreath and a sun rising over mountains and sea), the reform of 15 March 1822 (a white stripe between two red ones with a red sun on the white), and the later change to vertical stripes after a column mistook a Spanish flag for the Peruvian one; Congress approved the flag and new arms in February 1825. Britannica gives the same sequence: quartered flag in 1820, horizontal red-white-red on 15 March 1822, vertical on 31 May 1822, and the arms design on 25 February 1825. Wikipedia agrees; FOTW's 'horizontal form in 1823' is the outlier.
era-1821.open: Paz Soldan gives no date for the change to vertical stripes (Britannica and Wikipedia give 31 May 1822). The sun on the white band is red in Paz Soldan and Britannica and gold in Wikipedia, so the card's gold emblem is uncertain. Between 1821 and March 1822 the quartered 1820 flag, not the one drawn, was in force.

era-1542.says: Wikipedia's Flag of Peru says the colonial-era Spanish flag flew over Peru during the Viceroyalty and, citing historian Jorge Fernandez Stoll, that the old viceroyalty flag was the red-and-white cross of Burgundy. FOTW says the Burgundy cross was Spain's ensign from 1506 and its land war flag to 1843. The U.S. National Park Service says Spain's New World ships and fortresses flew the white flag with the red Burgundian saltire until 1785, when the red-and-gold ensign replaced it.
era-1542.open: The sources show the Spanish Cross of Burgundy over Spain's American possessions, not a Peru-specific flag, and none dates the viceroyalty (1542-1821). The NPS puts the change to the red-and-gold ensign at 1785 for ships, so late-colonial Peru would have flown other Spanish flags. The drawing is a simplified saltire.

era-1532.says: FOTW's Spain 1506-1700 page says the Cross of Burgundy was Spain's naval ensign from 1506 and a land war flag to 1843, and 'the flag, if any was, carried by the conquistadors in their conquest of the Americas', adding it was a military banner rather than the official flag of the empire. The U.S. National Park Service says the red-saltire white flag was carried by ships and flown over fortresses guarding Spain's possessions in the New World. Wikipedia's Flag of Peru does not cover the conquest decade.
era-1532.open: No source read names Pizarro's banner or dates a flag for 1532-1542; FOTW itself hedges ('if any was') and notes the Royal Standard as the nearer flag of the Crown. The Burgundy cross shown is a Spanish military emblem, not a flag documented for the conquest of Peru.

era-1946.says: Wikipedia: 1936 E.O. 23 standardised specifications; 4 July 1946 hoisted at independence; RA 8491 of 1998 codified colours; eight-rayed sun for the provinces that rebelled. FOTW: E.O. 23 (25 March 1936); E.O. 321 of 12 June 1950; RA 8491 of 12 February 1998; white triangle for the Katipunan.
era-1946.open: The blue shade changed several times (1955, 1985, 1998).

era-1565-1.open: Whether a flag, banner or standard existed in this period was not checked. The colour shown is not evidence of one.

era-1942.says: Wikipedia: flag banned during the occupation, then used by the Second Republic. FOTW: Second Republic revived it 14 October 1943; upside-down from 8 December 1941; wartime position in 1944.
era-1942.open: The two sources describe the occupation differently.

era-1935.says: Wikipedia: ban repealed 30 October 1919; legally adopted 26 March 1920; E.O. 23 standardised specifications in 1936. FOTW: 1919 Flag Day order; E.O. 23 of 25 March 1936.
era-1935.open: The Commonwealth's start date (1935) is not covered.

era-1898.says: A diary entry for 13 August 1898 records that when Manila was surrendered the Spanish flag was lowered and replaced by the American flag. Act No. 1696 (23 August 1907, a primary text) punishes display of flags used against the authority of the United States and of Katipunan flags, and Act No. 2871 (22 October 1919) repeals it and provides a holiday for the restoration of the use of the Filipino flag. WorldStatesmen lists the United States flag for the Philippines from 14 Aug 1898 to 25 Mar 1936. Wikipedia's Flag of the Philippines lists the United States flag for 1898-1919, with variants for 1908 and 1912, and says from 30 October 1919 both the US and the Philippine flags were flown (FOTW: the same ban and repeal).
era-1898.open: The United States flag is attested by a primary diary, two primary acts that presuppose US authority, and two compiled lists. The star count (45, 46, 48) rests on Wikipedia's table alone, and no source describes a 'US insular ensign' of stripes without a canton, as the old caption said. Wikipedia gives the repeal as 24 October and FOTW as 30 October 1919, while the act itself is dated 22 October 1919.

era-1898-1.says: Wikipedia: unfurled at Kawit on 12 June 1898, first displayed in battle on 28 May 1898. FOTW: conceived by Aguinaldo in Hong Kong in 1897, sewn there; adopted 19 May 1898; Battle of Alapan 28 May 1898; proclaimed 12 June 1898 at Kawit.
era-1898-1.open: The era title says Malolos; the proclamation was at Kawit.

era-1945.says: FOTW (explanation of the flag): the 1936 flag, with the navy blue, was restored upon the return of American forces in 1944 and was hoisted at the recognition of Philippine independence on 4 July 1946; FOTW (flag history) says the Commonwealth flew it upside down from 8 December 1941 to Japan's surrender. Wikipedia: the flag is flown red-side up in wartime and was the national flag of the Commonwealth; its Flag of the Philippines article says the flag was legally adopted in 1920 (Act 2928).
era-1945.open: The orientation flown in 1945-46 is not stated; the page's 'peacetime blue-over-red' is an inference from the 4 July 1946 hoisting.

era-1565.says: Wikipedia's Flag of the Philippines history table lists the Cross of Burgundy (a red saltire of roughly pruned branches on white) for 1565-1762 and 1764-1821 as the flag used when the islands were a colony of New Spain, then Spanish red-yellow-red flags from 1821 to 1898, with a British occupation flag in 1762-1764. The U.S. National Park Service says the Cross of Burgundy was carried by Spanish ships and flown over the fortresses of Spain's possessions in the New World and across the Pacific to the Philippines, until the red-and-gold ensign replaced it from 1785.
era-1565.open: The two publishers support the Cross of Burgundy for the early and middle colonial period only (to 1821 by Wikipedia, 1785 by the National Park Service); from 1821 Wikipedia lists the red-yellow-red Spanish flag, so the card's single cross for 1565-1898 does not cover the later decades. FOTW says it holds no detailed Spanish-era flags.

era-1989.says: Both sources date the current flag to 1919, before this era begins in 1989, so the flag was already in use at the start. Wikipedia's infobox gives the adoption as 1 August 1919; Flags of the World dates it 1 Aug 1919.
era-1989.open: Only the year the current flag was adopted was compared; the design and the swatch colours were not checked against a specification.

era-750.open: Whether a flag, banner or standard existed in this period was not checked. The colour shown is not evidence of one.

era-1947.says: FOTW (Kedzierski) says the flag was unchanged except for the eagle, and that the communists took the crown off it, without a date. Wikipedia has the crown removed in 1944–1990, the crownless emblem used from 1944 and legalised in 1952, a resolution approving the crownless design in 1955, and a decree of 7 December 1955 upholding the 1927 shade of red.
era-1947.open: This page used to say the crown was removed in 1955; the sources put it in practice from 1944. The 1980 Act (31 January 1980) is the flag law in force through the end of this era.

era-1945.says: FOTW says the flag stayed the white-red bicolour under the communists. Wikipedia's coat-of-arms article has the communist-era emblem in use from 1944. Second look at the statutes: the Polish law of 1 August 1919 sets the national colours as white and red in parallel stripes, the upper white and the lower red; the decree of 1955 (Dz.U. 1955 nr 47 poz. 314) again gives the colours of the People's Republic as white and red in two horizontal stripes, upper white, lower red, and its last article repeals the regulations of 13 December 1927 on state arms and colours, which therefore stood until then.
era-1945.open: Nothing read is specific to the Provisional Government of National Unity (1945-47). The continuity of white over red across 1945-47 rests on FOTW's statement and on the 1955 decree repealing the 1927 regulations (their text was not read directly); the 1919 law and 1955 decree bracket the period rather than cover it.

era-1939.says: Wikipedia says Home Army and Peasants' Battalion insurgents wore white-red armbands in 1939-1945, that Polish soldiers raised a flag at Monte Cassino on 18 May 1944 and that a white-red flag was hoisted in Warsaw on 1 August 1944. Flags of the World (General Government page, contributor text) says German swastika flags flew in the major cities of the occupied territory and the Polish flag was forbidden on pain of death; its underground-state page says the legal symbols of the government in exile and its Delegation were those of the Second Republic; its 20th-century page says the government in exile and its troops in WWII kept using the crowned eagle.
era-1939.open: All the FOTW statements are contributor posts without a cited basis. Neither source describes a civil flag of the government in exile in detail (the page's 'white-red civil flag with the crowned eagle' is not itself described), nor the move of the government from Paris to London.

era-1918.says: FOTW (Kedzierski, citing the Encyclopaedia of Poland, 1996) says the question was resolved on 1 August 1919 with white above red; Pierre Gay explains the order heraldically. Wikipedia says the Sejm adopted the white-red bicolour on 1 August 1919, with a coat-of-arms variant for civil ensign use and diplomats abroad, and that a presidential decree of 13 December 1927 set the red as vermilion from 29 March 1928.
era-1918.open: The placement of the eagle at the hoist, as this page describes the state flag, is not confirmed: the 1980 law places the arms in the white stripe.

era-1815.says: Flags of the World says the Sejm formally introduced the national colours, white and red, on 7 February 1831 during the November Uprising. Wikipedia says the white-red cockade was adopted that day and was worn by insurgents in 1830, 1846, 1848 and 1863-1864; FOTW's 19th-century page notes that white-red flags were also used in the January Uprising of 1863-64. The same page (contributor posts) describes an official flag of the autonomous Kingdom of Poland in 1815-1831, white with a blue St Andrew's saltire and a red canton bearing a crowned eagle, replaced by the white-red bicolour in 1831, with only Russian flags legal afterwards.
era-1815.open: The caption's 'no official Polish flag' is contradicted for 1815-1831 by those FOTW contributors, one of whom gives 12 April 1833 for the saltire flag's abolition in Russia, a date no source confirms. Whether each partitioning power banned the white-red colours is stated only in an unsourced FOTW post about Russia; Prussian and Austrian practice is not described.

era-1807.says: Wikipedia (Flag of Poland): the military of the Duchy of Warsaw (1807-1815) used the white cockade; the white-and-red cockade was adopted by the Sejm on 7 February 1831. Wikipedia (Coat of arms of Poland) gives the Duchy's arms as the House of Wettin with the Polish eagle. Flags of the World's 19th-century page has conflicting contributor posts: a horizontal white-amaranth flag, a red flag with the white eagle, and a guess that it used white-over-red. Wikipedia's Duchy of Warsaw article carries a hidden infobox note that the Duchy used no national flag. Second look: a second reading of Wikipedia's Duchy of Warsaw article for flag, banner, cockade and colours found no flag text, and the Polish Ministry of Education platform pages found by search describe only the Duchy's political position.
era-1807.open: The sources give no flag of the Duchy, only a white cockade and arms; they do not show the white-red bicolour drawn here, and the Polish white-and-red colours are dated to 1831. The FOTW posts name no basis and conflict; the Wikipedia remark is an editors' note. No reference or primary source describing a flag of the Duchy was found.

era-1025.says: Wikipedia (Coat of arms of Poland): the eagle first appears on coins of Boleslaw I (reign 992-1025), initially as the arms of the Piast dynasty, and from the 12th century on the shields, ensigns, coins and seals of the Piast dukes; the arms are a white eagle on a red field. A contributor on Flags of the World's 20th-century page says some very early Polish arms and banners had the eagle without a crown, and that a crown came in 1295 or slightly earlier.
era-1025.open: The sources show the eagle as the Piast dynasty's emblem, not a flag of the kingdom in 1025-1138. That a white eagle on red was flown as a banner in this period is not stated; 'royal seals' is not in them (Wikipedia names coins); the uncrowned form rests on one unsourced FOTW post.

era-1795.says: Wikipedia (Flag of Poland): the Commonwealth ends in 1795 and the Duchy of Warsaw's military wore the white cockade from 1807. Flags of the World's royal banners page ends with the banner of Stanislaw August Poniatowski (1764-1795) and its 19th-century page begins with the Duchy of Warsaw (1807); neither has anything for 1795-1807.
era-1795.open: The card is an openly stated placeholder ('no flag documented') and no source read gives a Polish flag for 1795-1807. This records what these sources contain, not that none existed; the Polish Legions of 1797-1807 were not looked up.

era-1569.says: Wikipedia (Flag of Poland): the Commonwealth banner (1569-1795) combined the White Eagle of Poland and the Pursuer of Lithuania, was first plain white, later dominated by red and white, and in the 17th century was often divided into two to four stripes. Wikipedia (Coat of arms of Poland) gives the Commonwealth shield as quarters of the crowned eagle and the Pogon. Flags of the World (Poland): banners of Zygmunt III (red-white-red) and of Wladyslaw IV and Jan Kazimierz (four red and white stripes) bore the official crest of the State; its royal banners page also pictures banners of Zygmunt II August, Zygmunt III, Wladyslaw IV and Stanislaw August.
era-1569.open: The drawing, the eagle beside the Pogon on red alone, is not described by any source read; FOTW does not name the Pogon and its royal banners page gives pictures with little text. The statement rests on Wikipedia for the eagle and Pursuer, with FOTW confirming banners that carried the state's arms.

era-1320.says: Wikipedia (Flag of Poland): under Ladislaus the Short (r. 1320-1333) a red cloth emblazoned with the White Eagle of Poland's arms was established as the Banner of the Kingdom, used at coronations and in battle. Flags of the World (Poland): the Polish flag began as a red banner with a white eagle, such a banner being beside King Wladyslaw Jagiello at Grunwald in 1410; its royal banners page also lists a banner of Wladyslaw Lokietek (1320-1333). A contributor on FOTW's 20th-century page says the eagle gained a crown in 1295 or slightly earlier.
era-1320.open: The crown rests only on that FOTW contributor post, which gives no basis; Wikipedia does not say the eagle was crowned, and neither source says the banner was crowned or standardised from the coronation. A Lokietek banner is shown on FOTW's page with little text.

era-1138.says: Wikipedia (Flag of Poland): early Polish vexilloids (stanice) existed by the 10th century and a royal banner of arms dates to Boleslaus the Generous (r. 1076-1079). Wikipedia (Coat of arms of Poland): from the 12th century the eagle appears on the shields, ensigns, coins and seals of the Piast dukes. A Flags of the World contributor says some very early Polish arms and banners had the eagle without a crown. Second look: a Polish Ministry of Education platform card (zpe.gov.pl) says that from the twelfth century the eagle appeared on the coins, banners and shields of the Piast state; the heraldist Alfred Znamierowski, quoted in Rzeczpospolita, says the eagle went on the royal seal of Przemysł II in 1295, that the oldest known depiction of the arms in colour is a heraldic plaque on the Szczerbiec from the early 14th century, and that the Polish banner was for centuries a red banner with a white eagle.
era-1138.open: Neither source says each duchy flew its own variant of the eagle, or that no single design was shared; nothing read describes a banner of any individual duchy in 1138-1320. The dukes' use of the eagle is stated only in general terms, without a red field or banner design. These add that the eagle was on Piast banners from the 12th century and that a red banner with a white eagle was the Polish banner for centuries, but they speak of the Piast state or the later Kingdom in general: none describes a banner of any individual duchy of 1138-1320, so whether each duchy flew its own variant or a shared eagle on red is not established.

era-1910.says: Wikipedia says the republican revolution of 5 October 1910 was followed by a flag commission on 15 October 1910, the flag's first presentation on 1 December 1910, a decree published in the Diário do Governo on 19 June 1911 after approval by the Constituent Assembly, and official adoption by regulations published on 30 June 1911. FOTW says the flag and arms were adopted on 30 June 1911 and that the Assembly described two vertical bands of dark green and scarlet, green at the hoist. Wikipedia gives green as the nation's hope and red as the blood of those who died; FOTW's contributors give Hope and Sacrifice (Marques) and say the symbolism was added later (Candeias).
era-1910.open: The meanings of the colours are disputed. Neither source covers the Estado Novo era.

era-1640.says: Wikipedia (Flag of Portugal): royal flags had a white field until 1830, when the liberal government decreed blue and white, and the victorious standard became the national flag in 1834. Flags of the World: the national arms on a white rectangular field were the national flag from 1495 to 1830/34, a green Aviz-cross flag was popular but unofficial in 1640, and 'the liberal flag, a vertical bicolor of blue and white charged with the coat of arms' was used for about 80 years (1830-1910). Wikipedia's list: white arms flag 1640-1667, national flag vertical blue-white 1834-1910.
era-1640.open: The card shows only the 1830/34-1910 flag, while the era runs from 1640 and the flag was white with the arms until 1830/34; the sources differ on 1830 (FOTW, decree) versus 1834 (Wikipedia list, national flag), and neither describes a crown on the arms.

era-1580.says: Flags of the World (Portuguese historical flags): from 1495 to 1830 the flags were white charged with the coat of arms, and during the Spanish domination (1580-1640) Portugal, as a separate realm under the same king, was allowed to use its own flags on land and at sea. Wikipedia (List of Portuguese flags): a royal flag for 1578-1640, with an alternative royal flag of white with the arms (1616-1640), and a white sea flag with the arms of Portugal on branches used at sea during the Iberian Union (1616-1640).
era-1580.open: Neither source says the Cross of Burgundy flew in Portugal, and the card's caption that there was 'no separate Portuguese design' is contradicted by both publishers.

era-1139.says: Wikipedia's list of Portuguese flags: royal banner of five blue escutcheons on white from 1185, with a red border bearing yellow castles from 1248 (1248-1385), and a green Aviz cross added 1385; earlier banners (blue cross, 1095/1143) are hypothetical. Flags of the World's history page: 1185 white with five blue escutcheons (11 bezants each), 1248 red with yellow castles (number not fixed), 1385 with the Aviz cross; Wikipedia's Flag of Portugal: the Ourique legend of 1139 is myth, five-shield quinas date from Sancho I (1185, verification needed), the red bordure with castles is linked to the 1249 Algarve conquest by a weak argument, and seven castles were fixed in 1578.
era-1139.open: The card's 1139 start is not supported (the sources date the quinas to 1185 and earlier banners are hypothetical); the flag shown fits only 1248-1385, since the Aviz cross follows in 1385 and white arms flags replace banners from 1495.

era-1926.says: Presidência da República Portuguesa (essay on the national flag): the same symbol stood through 'a Ditadura Militar, o Estado Novo, o 25 de Abril', and the flag is described as bipartite dark green (on the hoist side) and scarlet with the national arms, by the decree of the Constituent Assembly of 19 June 1911, with the detailed regulation of 30 June 1911. Store norske leksikon gives the same adoption by parliament on 19 June 1911. Wikipedia (List of Portuguese flags; Flag of Portugal) and FOTW date the national flag from 1911 to the present.
era-1926.open: A government reference, an encyclopedia and two compiled publishers all cover 1926-1974; the Presidency's essay names the Military Dictatorship and the Estado Novo as periods under the same flag. The card's drawing simplifies the emblem to a disc, and the Wikipedia/FOTW dates differ on the day (19 or 30 June 1911) because the decree and its regulation are separate.

era-1971.open: Only the year the current flag was adopted was compared; the design and the swatch colours were not checked against a specification.

era-1916.says: Wikipedia: 1916 treaty with Britain (the nine points stand for the ninth reconciled emirate); in 1932 the British Navy suggested an official flag and Qatar added the nine-pointed serrated edge, diamonds and the word 'Qatar'; maroon was standardised in 1936; the wording and diamonds were removed in the 1960s; adopted 9 July 1971. FOTW: the distinctive flag emerged in the 1930s and in about 1949 the plain flag came into use with the colour altered from red to maroon.
era-1916.open: The sources disagree on the date maroon was fixed (Wikipedia 1936, FOTW c.1949); neither uses the word 'protectorate' and neither describes the page's intermediate plain white hoist band.

era-1868.says: Wikipedia (Flag of Qatar): the historic plain red flag of the 18th century to 1860 was modified in the 19th century with a white vertical stripe at the hoist to suit a British directive. Flags of the World (Qatar historical flags): about 1860 a narrow serrated white stripe was added at the hoist (some sources say it was not originally serrated), and this flag is dated 1860-1916.
era-1868.open: Both dates are approximate ('about 1860', '19th century'), and the FOTW entry rests on a single contributor; neither source covers the 1868 treaty, the sheikhdom's separate status, or a red flag shared across the coast.

era-1783.says: Wikipedia (Flag of Qatar): Qatar's historic flag was plain red, in correspondence with the banner of the Kharijite leader Qatari ibn al-Fuja'a, and its table of historical flags dates the plain red flag from the 18th century to 1860; in the 19th century a white hoist stripe was added to suit a British directive. Flags of the World (Qatar historical flags): the first flag of Qatar was plain red and used until about 1860, when a narrow serrated white stripe was added at the hoist. Second look: the Qatar government site qatar.qa, Britannica's flag of Bahrain page and the Qatar National Library (Qatar Digital Library) file on 'Anthems and Flags of Various States' that Wikipedia cites (IOR Coll 30/15, 1936) all returned HTTP 403 and were not read; Hukoomi's page returned no flag text.
era-1783.open: The two publishers agree on a plain red flag to about 1860, but neither covers 1783 as a date or Bahrain's Al Khalifa orbit, and nothing read supports the caption's 'Bahrain's shared maritime colour'. The years 1860-1868 of this row fall in the white-striped period. No archival or institutional source for the plain red flag could be reached.

era-1871.says: Flags of the World (Qatar historical flags): the red flag with a narrow serrated white hoist stripe is dated 1860-1916, and a white flag with a red square and a yellow or red crescent in the canton around 1916, seen as short-lived; a contributor summarising 1929 British letters says Qatar's flag was 'exactly like Bahrain's flag but dark red'. Wikipedia (Flag of Qatar): a white hoist stripe was added to the red flag in the 19th century at a British directive, and the Ottomans expanded into eastern Arabia in 1871 and withdrew in 1915 (Wikipedia, History of Qatar). Second look: the Qatar Digital Library file (IOR Coll 30/15) cited by Wikipedia, and the Qatar government site, returned HTTP 403 and were not read.
era-1871.open: The card shows a 'contested / no single flag' placeholder, but the sources read give Qatar a red flag with a white hoist stripe throughout 1860-1916 (dated only as 'about 1860'). No source describes Ottoman garrison banners at Doha or an Al Thani flag specific to 1871-1916, and no source says the flag was contested. No archival or institutional source describing a flag for the Ottoman garrison or Al Thani rule could be reached.

era-1989.says: Wikipedia says protesters in Timișoara on 20 December 1989 waved flags with the Communist arms cut out, and that on 27 December 1989 the National Salvation Front restored the simple tricolour of 1867. FOTW (Heimer) gives 27 December 1989 for the re-establishment of the plain tricolour without naming the instrument, says the flag with a hole became a symbol of the revolution, and gives Article 12 of the Constitution (21 November 1991) and Flag Law 75/1994.
era-1989.open: The instrument of 27 December 1989 is not named by either source.

era-1947.says: FOTW (Neumann) says that after the communist takeover in 1948 the tricolour was charged with a new coat of arms of Soviet inspiration. Wikipedia says Romania became a people's republic on 30 December 1947 and royal symbols were outlawed (citation needed), that a 1948 emblem showed a rising sun, tractor, oil drill and wheat, that a red star was added in 1952 and that the arms changed in 1965 (all citation needed).
era-1947.open: FOTW does not cover 1965. This page used to say the coat of arms formally replaced the royal one in 1965; neither source says so.

era-1918.says: Wikipedia's coat-of-arms article says that after Transylvania joined Romania its arms went in the fourth quarter and Banat's in the third, and that the lesser arms appeared in the Official Gazette no. 92 of 29 July 1921. FOTW says the tricolour was codified in 1872 as a plain tricolour with the arms on military and naval ensigns.
era-1918.open: This page used to date the new arms to 1922; the source gives 1921. Whether the flag was unchanged at the union is not described by either source.

era-1859.says: Wikipedia says the United Principalities used a red-yellow-blue horizontal tricolour in 1859–1866 and that the vertical order, blue at the hoist, yellow, red at the fly, was set on 26 March 1867. FOTW says the tricolour became the national flag in 1859 under Cuza, horizontal with blue on top until 1862 and red on top from 1862 to 1867, and that sources differ on the switch to vertical (Heimer 1866, Neumann 1867).
era-1859.open: The sources disagree on which colour was on top in 1859–62, so the drawing follows Wikipedia. This page used to say a vertical tricolour was adopted in 1861–62, and that it fused Wallachia's blue and yellow with Moldavia's red; neither source says that.

era-1944.says: Wikipedia's Flag of Romania says that the plain tricolour was the civilian flag of the Kingdom, with arms on army and princely flags only, and that when the people's republic was proclaimed on 30 December 1947 the royal arms and the tricolours showing it were outlawed. FOTW's Romania page quotes a Romanian source that the national flag was a plain tricolour until 1948, when it was charged with a new coat of arms; FOTW's 1922-1948 page covers the royal standards used until the monarchy ended.
era-1944.open: Neither source describes 1944-1947 separately; the plain tricolour's continuity through these years rests on the general statements for the Kingdom, and on Wikipedia's gallery entry for the Kingdom. How much power the king held is not flag evidence.

era-1940.says: Wikipedia's Flag of Romania (section 1867-1948) says that the country's arms were placed only on army and princely flags while civilian flags stayed without arms, that this lasted until the people's republic of 30 December 1947; its gallery lists a Kingdom of Romania (1881-1947) flag. FOTW's Romania page quotes a Romanian source that the national flag has been a plain tricolour since 1872 with arms only on military and naval ensigns, and that this usage continued until 1948. FOTW's 1922-1948 page records Marshal Antonescu's personal standard (tricolour with the eagle, Berlin, 23 November 1940) as a standard only.
era-1940.open: Neither source speaks of 1940-1944 separately or of the Iron Guard; the continuity of the plain blue-yellow-red tricolour through those years rests on the general statements for the whole Kingdom.

era-1881.says: Wikipedia (Flag of Romania): the vertical blue-yellow-red tricolour (blue at the hoist) was set on 26 March 1867, the coat of arms placed only on army and princely flags, the civilian flag carrying none. FOTW (ro.html): the flag was codified in 1872 as a plain tricolour, military and naval ensigns carrying the arms. Wikipedia (Kingdom of Romania): the kingdom ran 1881-1947 and the Flag of Romania is its infobox flag; its arms are shown for 1881-1921. FOTW (ro-1922): the 1872 arms were used until 1921.
era-1881.open: The sources date the tricolour differently (Wikipedia 1867, FOTW 1872). Neither describes an 1881 flag change, a crown on a state version or a personal Hohenzollern flag, so the caption's 'first king's own arms' is not confirmed; FOTW says only that military ensigns carried the arms.

era-1600.says: Wikipedia's Flag of Romania says Michael the Brave's Wallachian flag was a damask banner, originally yellow-white and faded to white, with a black eagle on a green juniper branch holding a cross. FOTW gives several different Wallachian flags: a red flag with a black eagle on a mountain peak (1532-35), a white damask flag with a raven and juniper (1593-1602, after Spontoni; one contributor says yellow), a blue naval ensign with the eagle (1640 code), Brancoveanu's striped standard with a blue medallion and black eagle (c. 1700), Ypsilanti's yellow flag with the arms in a blue oval, and from 1834 a yellow civil ensign with the Wallachian eagle and a red canton with three stars. World Statesmen's Romania flag sequence begins in 1859 and Vexilla Mundi's Romania page carries images without text, so neither adds a description.
era-1600.open: No source read describes a Phanariote-era princely flag that was a black eagle on a plain gold field; the black-eagle-on-yellow combination nearest to the card is Michael the Brave's (before 1601) and the 1834-61 civil ensign (eagle in blue, with a canton), neither of which is a Phanariote princely flag.

era-1600-1.says: FOTW describes a red great banner of Moldavia with the arms painted in gold (a Krakow document of 1533) and a red flag of Prince Ieremia Movila captured in 1601 and painted in a Dresden manuscript, with an aurochs head, an eight-pointed star between the horns and two crescents; its arms are given as gules, an aurochs' head Or with a star, a rose and a crescent. Wikipedia's Moldavia article calls the 14th-15th century flag in its infobox a modern reconstruction of a princely standard, whose symbols other than the aurochs vary considerably, and shows a 'flag according to the Organic Regulation (1831-1862)'.
era-1600-1.open: The aurochs head is gold or silver in FOTW's sources, not black (a few 16th-17th century sources show it black on silver); the rose is in FOTW's blazon but not in the 1601 painting. Which of these was the princely flag through 1600-1859 is not settled, and FOTW itself notes that information on ancient Moldavian flags is scarce.

era-82bce.says: Wikipedia (Dacian Draco): the Dacian standard has the form of a dragon with open wolf-like jaws containing metal tongues, carried by Dacian soldiers in about 20 scenes of Trajan's Column (wars of 101-102 and 105-106); it is thought to have been filled by the wind and to have whistled; Rome probably adopted it after conquering Dacia, and the first Roman cavalry depiction dates to Marcus Aurelius (161-180). FOTW (ro.html and ro_legnd.html): the standard on Trajan's Column was a metal wolf's head with coloured cloth bands, Dan Dima agreeing the wolf-head standard existed but saying its colours cannot be reconstructed from marble.
era-82bce.open: Attested only as a Dacian military standard shown on Trajan's Column (101-106), not as a national flag of a kingdom from c.82 BCE; the draco's origin is disputed and its colours are not reconstructable. The page's 82 BCE start and Roman Dacia end (271) are not covered by these sources.

era-1991.says: Wikipedia says the RSFSR Supreme Soviet declared the imperial tricolour the national flag on 22 August 1991, that Decree No. 2126 of 11 December 1993 defined it as three horizontal bands with a 2:3 ratio, and that a federal constitutional law of 25 December 2000 legalised it. FOTW says the flag was raised over the Supreme Soviet building on 21 August 1991 and officially acknowledged on 22 August, that it was used alongside the Soviet flag until a December 1991 decree, that decree No. 2126 changed the ratio from 1:2 to 2:3, and that Flag Day was introduced on 22 August 1994.
era-1991.open: FOTW's contributors place the 1991 adoption steps differently (21 or 22 August). This page used to say the tricolour was the national flag from 1883 to 1917; the sources say it was authorised on land in 1883 and made the sole national flag in 1896.

era-1922.says: Wikipedia says the USSR flag was established on 18 April 1924, that rules of 23 March 1925 required the RSFSR flag on local soviet buildings, and that in January 1954 the RSFSR flag gained a light blue strip near the pole, approved by the law of 2 June 1954. Flags of the World's Soviet Union page (a contributor) says the flag with hammer, sickle and star was adopted in 1923, with a red star bordered yellow; its RSFSR pages say the RSFSR flag was revised in 1954 to add a hoist bar of one eighth of the flag's length, light blue by the 1978 constitution, and that the 1918 RSFSR flag with initials in the canton stayed in use to 1937, with another flag in 1937-1954.
era-1922.open: The sources differ on the year the USSR flag was set (1923 FOTW, 1924 Wikipedia). The page's RSFSR details (the blue stripe from 1954) belong to the republic's own flag, not the all-Union banner drawn, and the 1937-1954 RSFSR flag is not described here.

era-1917.says: Wikipedia says that on 13 April 1918 the All-Russian Central Executive Committee set a red RSFSR banner, the decree not specifying colour, size or proportions, and that the initials appear in the sample of 17 June 1918. Flags of the World (early Soviet Russia page, contributors citing orders and the 1918 constitution): a red flag with the Cyrillic initials in the canton was recommended by Order No 320 of April 1918, and a flag approved on 20 May 1918 had yellow ancient-script initials in the canton with a gold border; the flag of that pattern was readopted as war flag in 1920 and continued to 1954.
era-1917.open: The dates differ among sources for the first lettered flag (April, May and 17 June 1918). Whether plain red improvised flags were official before then is not settled, and the page's 'gold initials' is FOTW's 'yellow'.

era-1917-1.says: Wikipedia says the Provisional Government kept the white-blue-red tricolour until the October Revolution (citation needed). FOTW (Bottasini) says it was used until the fall of Kerensky's government in November 1917.
era-1917-1.open: Neither source says it was flown without a crown or eagle, as this page does.

era-1721.says: Wikipedia says the tricolour was first raised on 6 August 1693 on the yacht Saint Peter, became the commercial maritime flag by decree on 31 January 1705, that the black-yellow-white tricolour was decreed the official heraldic state flag on 23 June 1858, that white-blue-red was authorised on land on 28 April 1883, and made the sole national flag by an imperial order of 29 April 1896. FOTW says it was used as a naval ensign in 1693 without formal adoption, adopted as the merchant flag on 20 January 1705, became the civil ensign in 1799, and was recognised for use on land in 1883 as an alternate civil flag, Russia having two civil flags until 1914.
era-1721.open: FOTW and Wikipedia differ on 1693 (raised vs not formally adopted) and on 1883 (7 May or 28 April). This page used to say the tricolour became the official national flag by decree in 1883.

era-1547.says: Flags of the World (Russia) cites Allard's 1695 flagbook for a white-blue-red triband with a golden double-headed eagle, and its Tsar's personal flags page gives a vessel standard of 1699-1917 as a golden flag with a black coat of arms and eagle (quoting the Russian Navy website), and the Tsar's standard in Moscow in 1693-1699 as the white-blue-red tricolour with a golden eagle; Wikipedia (Russian Imperial Standard) describes the Imperial Standard as the black double-headed eagle on a golden banner, representing the Empire and the Emperor. For the earlier part of the era Wikipedia (Flag of Russia) gives the 1552 banner of the Saviour, Pozharsky's crimson banner of 1612, a white banner with a red border and golden eagle in 1669, a white-blue-red tricolour with a golden eagle in 1693, a red banner with a golden eagle in 1696 and the tricolour as the merchant flag from 1705.
era-1547.open: The gold flag with a black double-headed eagle is documented by FOTW from 1699 and by Wikipedia for the Imperial Standard, so it fits only 1699-1721 of this era; for 1547-1699 the sources show other flags (golden eagles on white, red or tricolour grounds, the Saviour banner). The real standard also carries arms and maps in the eagle's claws; the card's eagle alone is simplified. The 1497 seal and the card's 'Tsar's own standard' wording are not covered, and Wikipedia does not date the Imperial Standard to 1699.

era-2001.open: Only the year the current flag was adopted was compared; the design and the swatch colours were not checked against a specification.

era-1962.says: Wikipedia: the red-yellow-green vertical tricolour of 1961 with a black R added in late September 1961, kept at independence on 1 July 1962 and used to 31 December 2001. FOTW's historical page: the first flag of Rwanda (1962-2001), three vertical bands red-yellow-green with a big black R in the middle of the yellow band, flag adopted 1 July 1962 (the R already in practice from about September 1961 per Whitney Smith); the R was added to tell it apart from Guinea's flag and stands for Rwanda, revolution and referendum.
era-1962.open: The date of the R and of the tricolour differs by source (1961 against 1 July 1962 for formal adoption); the R's exact shape was never prescribed.

era-1916.says: Wikipedia's Flag of Rwanda says Belgium was awarded Rwanda and Burundi as the mandate of Ruanda-Urundi in 1919 (confirmed by the League of Nations in 1922), that the Belgian flag flew in Rwanda from then until the end of Belgian rule on 1 July 1962, and shows the Belgian civil flag; its Ruanda-Urundi article (1916-1962) uses the Flag of Belgium file as its infobox flag. Flags of the World's Burundi history dates the Belgian mandate to 24 October 1924 and a UN trusteeship afterwards, with no flag statement. Encyclopaedia Britannica says Belgium administered Ruanda-Urundi from 1922 to 1962 (mandate from 1924, UN trust territory from 1946) as an integral part of the Belgian Congo with a separate budget; it does not mention a flag.
era-1916.open: No source read documents a colonial badge on the Belgian flag in Ruanda-Urundi, and 1916-1919 (Belgian occupation) is not covered by the flag statement; the card's cream middle band and gold disc have no source. Only Wikipedia states which flag flew; Flags of the World gives dates but no flag. Britannica supports Belgian administration (and the link to the Belgian Congo) but not which flag was flown.

era-1967.says: Flags of the World (kn-ai), Wikipedia and Britannica all describe the associated state's flag, a vertical tricolour with a black three-branched palm adopted on 27 February 1967; Britannica and Wikipedia give green-yellow-blue, FOTW blue-yellow-green.
era-1967.open: The publishers disagree on the order of the colours; the drawing follows the Commons file (green at the hoist). Palm proportions not checked.

era-1882.says: Wikipedia lists the Leeward Islands flag for 1871-1958 (images only) and a Saint Christopher-Nevis-Anguilla flag for 1958-1967 (image only); neither it nor Flags of the World describes either in words.
era-1882.open: No source read describes the Blue Ensign with a colonial badge that the card draws; it resembles the 1958-1967 Commons file, but that is a picture, not a description.

era-1713.says: Wikipedia's Flag of Saint Kitts and Nevis lists the Leeward Islands flag for 1871-1952 and 1952-1958 as images without description. Flags of the World says the flag history starts with the Leeward Islands flags, used until perhaps 1958, and asks the question itself. Wikipedia's Saint Kitts article describes alternating English and French control and British affiliation from 1783 without a flag. Britannica's page dates the united British colony from 1882 and describes no colonial flag.
era-1713.open: No source read describes a flag for 1713-1871, or a Blue Ensign with a Saint Kitts-Nevis badge; the plain Blue Ensign drawn is a stand-in.

era-1623.says: Wikipedia's Saint Kitts article: the first English colony was established in 1623 and a French colony in 1625; the colonists partitioned the island with the English in the middle and the French at both ends; a Spanish force seized it in 1629 and the English settlement was rebuilt after the 1630 peace; control alternated between English (later British) and French through the 17th and 18th centuries. Wikipedia's Flag of Saint Kitts and Nevis and Flags of the World's Saint Kitts and Nevis page describe no flag for this period; Wikipedia's flag history table begins in 1871.
era-1623.open: The card openly uses the English ensign as a stand-in 'flag of record'; no source read states that it, or any other flag, was flown at Saint Kitts or Nevis in 1623-1713. The settlement history is sourced, but Nevis's English status in the period is not covered by the text read.

era-1979.says: Wikipedia: the Pitons flag was adopted on 1 March 1967 (Associated State) and kept at independence in 1979, when 'the blue colour's shade and the triangles' sizes were modified marginally' (1979-2002: yellow triangle enlarged, arrowhead narrower); designed by Dunstan St Omer. Flags of the World (Saint Lucia): the 1967 flag (1 March 1967 - 1979) had a lower golden triangle and a lighter blue; the current flag was adopted 22 February 1979 and designed by Dunstan St Omer.
era-1979.open: The caption 'adopted 1967, unchanged since' is contradicted by both sources, which report a marginal redesign at independence in 1979; the page's description of the meaning of the colours was not checked against either source.

era-1814.says: Flags of the World (Colonial flags, Prothero) describes a Blue Ensign with the colony's seal badge (the island seen from the west, with the Pitons) for c. 1875-1937, a new badge approved 26 October 1937, and the arms granted on 16 August 1939 on a Blue Ensign until 1967. Wikipedia (Flag of Saint Lucia) lists the Union Jack with St Patrick's saltire for 1801-1875, a Union Jack defaced with the 1875 arms for 1875-1939, the Blue Ensign with the colony's arms for 1939-1967 and the Pitons flag from 1 March 1967. WorldStatesmen lists the Union flag to 1875, a colonial flag for 1875-16 Aug 1939 and 16 Aug 1939-1 Mar 1967 (plus an unofficial one), and the Pitons flag for 1 Mar 1967-22 Feb 1979.
era-1814.open: Three publishers agree that a distinct colonial flag with the colony's badge or arms flew from 1875 and, on a Blue Ensign, from 1939 to 1967 (FOTW and Wikipedia). They also agree on the Union flag before 1875 and on the Pitons flag from 1967, so a single Blue Ensign does not describe 1814-1875 or 1967-1979. For 1875-1939 FOTW says Blue Ensign and Wikipedia says Union Jack; WorldStatesmen gives no description. The card's badge is simplified.

era-1660.says: Wikipedia (Flag of Saint Lucia) says France colonised the island in 1635 and signed a treaty with the indigenous people in 1660, that it changed hands frequently until 1814, that French officials adopted the drapeau aux serpents in 1766 as a civil ensign for both Saint Lucia and Martinique, and that the King's Colours were its flag after British annexation (1796-1801). Flags of the World says French rule used the same flag as Martinique. WorldStatesmen gives a dated chronology of the island (French claim 1635, colony 1643, English occupation 1664-1667, French crown colony 1674, British occupations 1762-63, 1778-84, 1794-95 and 1796-1802, return to France 1802-22 Jun 1803, British from 1803, confirmed 30 May 1814) and lists the Union flag for 1781-83, 1794-95, 1796-1802 and from 1803; it shows no French flag.
era-1660.open: The snake flag is documented only for 1766-1796 and by one publisher plus FOTW's remark on Martinique. No source mentions a white ensign with gold fleur-de-lis; WorldStatesmen's list of British and French periods does not itself give the count of fourteen changes of hands. The French settlement date differs (1635 claim, 1643 colony, 1650). British periods flew the Union flag, which the card does not show.

era-1979.says: Wikipedia's infobox gives the adoption of the current flag as 12 October 1985; FOTW says it was introduced on 21 October 1985 when the new government rejected the 1979 independence flag, keeping the colours (blue, larger yellow, green) without white fimbriations and adding three green diamonds in the centre.
era-1979.open: The sources differ on the day (12 or 21 October 1985) but agree on 1985; the era begins at the 27 October 1979 independence, when a different flag (vertical blue-white-yellow-white-green with the arms on a breadfruit leaf) was adopted, so the 1979-1985 flag is not the one drawn. The colour meanings were not compared.

era-1797.says: Wikipedia lists a Blue Ensign defaced with the colony's badge for 1877-1907 and a revised badge for 1907-1979, and says Saint Vincent became an Associated State on 27 October 1969. FOTW (colonial flags): the badge was approved for the Blue Ensign in 1877, a revised badge was used 1907-1979, and St Vincent became an Associated State on 27 October 1969 keeping the Blue Ensign; the arms were granted in 1912.
era-1797.open: FOTW says the Union Jack was the state flag until 1975 and the Blue Ensign was used unofficially ashore; no source gives a flag for 1797-1877, so the Blue Ensign applies to 1877-1979 only.

era-1763.says: Wikipedia (Flag of Saint Vincent and the Grenadines): sovereignty over Saint Vincent switched between the French and the British through the 18th century until the Peace of Paris (1783) gave it to Britain; its colonial flag list begins with the Blue Ensign defaced with the colony's badge for 1877-1907. Flags of the World (colonial flags): the badge was approved in 1877 and the Union Jack was the official state flag until 1975. Neither names a flag for 1763-1797 or mentions the Carib Wars.
era-1763.open: The card's caption says openly that the plain British colours are a representative claimant flag and that no flag is documented; the sources read bear that out. The Blue Ensign shown is not documented before 1877, and the sources are silent on the period rather than saying no flag existed.

era-1997.says: Wikipedia: a red field with a blue canton bearing five white stars forming the Southern Cross, designed with four stars in 1948 and the fifth star added; infobox adopted 24 February 1949; the Official Flag and National Anthem of Samoa Act 1994 regulates it. FOTW: the flag has a red field and blue canton with five stars (construction from the official government site and the 1994 Act); the four-star flag was adopted 26 May 1948 and the five-star flag on 24 February 1949.
era-1997.open: Both sources date the design to 1948-49, not 1997; the page's statement about the fa'amatai system is not covered. FOTW notes that the country was called Western Samoa until 1997, and the name change did not alter the flag.

era-1962.says: Wikipedia: New Zealand approved the flag on 26 May 1948 (four stars), a fifth star was added on 24 February 1949, and the flag was kept at independence on 1 January 1962. FOTW (historical flags): Samoa adopted the flag on 26 May 1948 with four stars like New Zealand's, the fifth star was added on 24 February 1949, and Samoa gained independence in 1962; a Colonial Office letter says the four-star flag was approved on 9 September 1948 and the five-star version was published in the New Zealand Gazette on 24 February 1949.
era-1962.open: The exact 1948 approval date varies (26 May or 9 September 1948 in FOTW); 'adopted 1949' on the page is the date of the five-star flag. Neither source covers the 1997 change of name.

era-1914.says: Two publishers agree for the first years. Wikipedia (Flag of Samoa): New Zealand occupied German Samoa on 29 August 1914 and the flag of New Zealand was the only flag flown until 1920, when a Blue Ensign with three palms was adopted; on 26 May 1948 a new flag was approved. WorldStatesmen lists the New Zealand flag for 29 August 1914 - 25 January 1925, a Western Samoa colonial ensign for 1925-1948 and a Western Samoa flag from 1948. Wikipedia (Occupation of German Samoa) says the Union Flag was raised at the courthouse in Apia on 30 August 1914. FOTW lists defaced Blue and Red Ensigns with three palms and the four-star flag of 1948.
era-1914.open: The New Zealand ensign is documented only for 1914 to 1920 or 1925 (the sources differ on the end year and one says the Union Flag was raised in 1914); from then Samoa had its own defaced ensigns and from 1948 its own flag, so the card's single drawing for 1914-1962 is not confirmed after the mid-1920s.

era-1900.says: Wikipedia (German Samoa): the German colonial period began with the raising of the imperial flag at Mulinu'u on 1 March 1900, and the infobox shows the colonial office's service flag; Wikipedia (Flag of Samoa) describes the flag raised as a Reichsflagge defaced with the imperial eagle. FOTW (German colonies, after Schurdel 1995): colonies without their own arms flew the Reichsdienstflagge or the national flag, and a photograph shows a normal national flag at a beach pavilion in Apia. FOTW (1914 colonial flags): Solf's 1914 design for Samoa, a black-white-red flag with a shield of three palms, was never introduced.
era-1900.open: The sources show the imperial and service flags but no Samoa-specific flag; the eagle motif in the caption belongs to the service flag, and the drawing shows only the black-white-red triband. The three-palm shield is the 1914 proposal that was never used.

era-1862.says: The Government of San Marino (Conoscere San Marino): the flag is white over blue with the national arms at the centre, adopted on 6 April 1862 and slightly modified in 2011, and the arms took their final form on 6 April 1862 after the treaties with the Kingdom of Italy, the colours being drawn from the 14th-century arms of the three peaks of Titano. Flags of the World: flag adopted 6 April 1862 by decree of the Supreme Council (Southworth). WorldStatesmen lists the flag as the state flag from 6 Apr 1862, to 2011. Wikipedia: the decree of 6 April 1862 standardised the coat of arms but did not mention the flag; a white-azure bicolour is first recorded in 1829.
era-1862.open: Wikipedia's infobox gives the flag as early 1800s and says the 1862 decree concerned the arms; the government and two other publishers date the flag to 1862. The card's snow-and-sky meanings are not in the sources, which give peace for white and liberty for light blue (Wikipedia). The 2011 law changed the design slightly.

era-1600.says: The Government of San Marino (reference) says the first flag, adopted in 1465, was an orange, white and violet horizontal tricolour with the arms at the centre, and that a white and blue cockade adopted in 1797 started the change to the colours of 1862. Wikipedia gives the 1465 standard as gold, white and 'alessandrino' with two hypothetical reconstructions (Malagola, Casali), a white-azure bicolour first recorded in 1829, and unstandardised white-blue flags until 2011. Flags of the World says the old flag was used until about 1797, and WorldStatesmen lists an old flag from before 1465 to before 1797 and the later flag from before 1797 (state flag from 6 Apr 1862). Wikipedia (History of San Marino) dates the Statutes of 1600 to 1 September 1600 (WorldStatesmen: 8 Oct 1600) and says nothing of a flag.
era-1600.open: Four publishers describe the 1465 tricolour as the flag to about 1797, but no image survives, so the drawing is a reconstruction. None connects it to the 1600 Statutes, and the white-over-blue colours arrive only in 1797-1829, so for the end of the era (1797-1862) the card's flag is not the one the sources describe. The government says the bands were horizontal with the arms at the centre; the card draws vertical bands without the arms. Casali's article and the rbvex.it history cited by Wikipedia could not be read (TLS certificate errors; not worked around).

era-301.says: Wikipedia: the oldest attested standard of the republic is dated 4 September 1465, commissioned in Florence, a tricolour of gold, white and alessandrino. The Government of San Marino (reference) describes the 1465 flag as an orange, white and violet horizontal tricolour. Flags of the World dates the old republic flag attested in 1465 to about 1797, and WorldStatesmen lists an old flag from before 1465 to before 1797. Wikipedia (History of San Marino) gives the foundation by Saint Marinus in 301 as tradition only and mentions no flag.
era-301.open: No source covers any flag before 1465, and none dates white-over-blue to this era; for 1465-1600 all describe the tricolour, so the card's white-over-blue drawing is contradicted for the later part of the span. The dashed frame already marks the colours as tradition.

era-1975.says: Both sources give 1975, the year this page starts the current flag. Wikipedia's infobox gives the adoption as 12 July 1975; Flags of the World dates it 2003.
era-1975.open: Only the year the current flag was adopted was compared; the design and the swatch colours were not checked against a specification.

era-1471.says: Wikipedia's article on Portuguese Sao Tome and Principe (a colony 1485-1951 and overseas province 1951-1975) shows the flag of Portugal as its infobox flag, and lists colonial flag proposals of 1932 and 1965 as proposals only. Wikipedia's Flag of Sao Tome and Principe says the Portuguese began colonising the then uninhabited islands in the 16th century. FOTW's Sao Tome page lists a '1967 Colonial Flag Proposal' only as a link title.
era-1471.open: The infobox is one publisher and does not date the Portuguese flag it shows; the green-and-red flag is Portugal's from 1911, so it cannot stand for the whole span (earlier Portuguese flags differ). No source read describes a flag flown on the islands, and the 1471 start is not given (Wikipedia: 1485).

era-1973.open: Only the year the current flag was adopted was compared; the design and the swatch colours were not checked against a specification.
