era-1932.says: Wikipedia: flag not standardized before 15 March 1973; essentially present form by 1938 (more curved sword). Flags of the World: basic design in use by 1932, current version adopted 15 March 1973.
era-1932.open: Neither source describes a 1932 unification flag event; 1946 and 1958 dates are cited as uncertain by Flags of the World; Wikipedia's 'by 1938' versus Flags of the World's 'by 1932'.

era-1926.says: Wikipedia says the Nejd state's flag followed today's Saudi pattern very closely and that Abdulaziz added a sword in 1921; the Hejaz flag followed pan-Arab patterns. FOTW's historic-flags page says that in 1925 Abdulaziz became King of Nejd and Hejaz 'with unknown flag alterations', that the second design stage (shahada in thuluth script filling the field) may have been introduced at the unification in February 1927, that E.H. Baxter (1934) described a green flag with a white strip, a motto and a sheathed scimitar, and that a 1932-34 photograph shows the flag with one sword. Second look: Saudipedia (a Saudi reference encyclopedia) says that after the annexation of the Hijaz in 1926 the flag reverted to a rectangle with the Shahada in white in the middle, devoid of swords and other inscriptions, and Al Majalla says the sword was removed in 1926 and the flag stayed green with a white border and the Shahada in the centre until 1932, when a white sword was added beneath. World Statesmen lists a Nejd flag for 1926-1932 and a "possible" Hejaz flag, without describing them in text.
era-1926.open: Two Saudi accounts agree that the 1926-1932 flag had no sword, which fits Wikipedia's sword of 1921 and FOTW's 1932-34 photograph; but both are later summaries, they differ on a white border, and FOTW calls the post-1925 alterations unknown, so exact script, layout and border are not established. The sources read give no contemporary description of the flag of the dual kingdom.

era-1902.says: FOTW's historic-flags page says the base flag, the shahada on solid green, was an old Wahhabi flag and was in use in 1911 (a photograph in Lacey's The Kingdom, cited via the Flag Bulletin); it was the flag of Nejd under Abdulaziz. Wikipedia says the Nejd state's flag followed today's Saudi pattern very closely, that a different Arabic inscription was used from 1902 to 1921, and that Abdulaziz added a sword in 1921. FOTW's Nejd and Hasa page reports a green flag with a white hoist strip and white inscriptions in use 1902-1921. Saudipedia says Abdulaziz adopted the First Saudi State flag with a sword under the shahada.
era-1902.open: The sources conflict on when the sword appeared: 1902 (FOTW's page, one contributor and Crampton) or 1921 (Wikipedia); Saudipedia gives no date. None links the sword to the retaking of Riyadh, as the card's caption does, and FOTW calls the Emirate of Nejd and Hasa flag a Wikipedia reconstruction without proof.

era-1818.says: Saudipedia (a Saudi encyclopedia) says the First Saudi State's flag was green with a white part near the pole and the declaration of faith, and that this flag continued to be used through the Second Saudi State. Wikipedia says the followers of Muhammad ibn Abd al-Wahhab used the shahada on their flags from the 18th century and that the Al Rashid emirate of Jabal Shammar opposed the Saudis until 1921. FOTW's Ha'il page shows two Rashidi flags from Wikipedia (an Ottoman-like flag with a thin gold crescent and eight-pointed star for 1835-1920) and says the source is the Arabic Wikipedia and a dead website.
era-1818.open: The card shows a notice, not a flag. The sources read describe flags only for separate powers (the Saudi state in Saudipedia's one sentence; the Rashidis in FOTW, from Wikipedia), none for Najd as a whole, and nothing for the Ottoman-Egyptian occupation (1818-1840). The Rashidi flags rest on Wikipedia's images and an unreachable website.

era-1744.says: Saudipedia (citing the Saudi Press Agency): the First Saudi State, founded 1727 by Imam Muhammad bin Saud at Diriyah, flew a green flag of silk and wool with a white part by the pole and the shahada in the centre (no sword; the sword was added under King Abdulaziz). Wikipedia: followers of Muhammad ibn Abd al-Wahhab used the shahada on their flags from the 18th century. FOTW: shahada on solid green was an old flag of the Wahhabi reformist movement of the late 18th century.
era-1744.open: Saudipedia dates the state's foundation to 1727, not 1744 as on the page; FOTW notes that the flag's exact age is unclear and that 19th-century accounts (Baxter, 1934) give it as about a century old.

era-1999.says: FOTW's Scotland page says the saltire became much more prominent from the 1970s and that on 1 July 1999, the day the Scottish Parliament opened, the Union Flag and the Saltire were both used but normally only the Saltire is flown (the Union Flag flew at Edinburgh Castle; the General Assembly building, the Parliament's temporary home, flew both). Wikipedia says the Saltire is the correct flag for private individuals and bodies and is flown, where possible, from Scottish Government buildings every day.
era-1999.open: Neither source says the Saltire was flown over a new Parliament building in 1999 as such (the Parliament sat in the General Assembly building); Wikipedia gives no date for the government-buildings practice. FOTW's note that the Union Flag is also used is a 1999 observation. The 1801 date in FOTW's UK page is the Union Flag, not the saltire.

era-1707.says: Wikipedia: James VI's proclamation on the Union flag of 12 April 1606, a design presented to Queen Anne in 1707 with the English cross uppermost, and St Patrick's cross added in 1801. FOTW: James VI/I combined the Scottish and English flags in 1606, Queen Anne continued that design in 1707 (a Scottish version put the saltire over St George's cross), and the modern Union flag was introduced in 1801.
era-1707.open: Neither source says the Union Flag was used 'mainly at sea' after 1707; FOTW says only that the saltire became much more prominent in the 1970s.

era-1603.says: Flags of the World (Union Flag history): when James VI of Scotland became James I of England in 1603, the national flags of England and Scotland on land continued to be respectively the red St George's cross and the white St Andrew's cross, and the 1606 Union Flag was for use at sea only (restricted to the king's ships in 1634). Wikipedia (Flag of Scotland): the blue saltire dates from 1542 and the proclamation of 12 April 1606 had Scots subjects keep the white cross in the fore-top at sea 'as they were accustomed'; the saltire was last used officially by the pre-Union Royal Scots Navy and merchant fleets in the 18th century, and an unofficial Scottish Union Flag was used in the 17th century. Flags of the World (Scotland) dates the saltire on blue to 1542 and a Scottish ship illustrated with three saltires in 1588.
era-1603.open: Neither source gives a continuous record of the plain saltire through every decade of 1603-1707, and the shade of blue is not specified; how it was flown domestically on land is stated only in general terms.

era-1249.says: Wikipedia's Royal Banner article: the earliest recorded use of the lion rampant as a royal emblem was by Alexander II in 1222, the double border set with lilies came under Alexander III (1249-1286), and a royal banner displaying the arms was used by the King of Scots until the Union. FOTW's royal banner page: the 1222 seal of Alexander II as the first known lion coat, and the double tressure first definitely on a seal of Alexander III (d. 1286); the lion on yellow also appears on the Great Michael's flag. The Court of the Lord Lyon (official heraldic authority): gold with a red rampant lion and royal tressure is the Scottish royal banner, its use restricted by the Act of 1672 to a few officers representing the Sovereign.
era-1249.open: The lion rampant is dated to 1222, before this row's 1249 start; the double tressure belongs to the 1249-1286 reign. The Lord Lyon page confirms the design and today's restriction but gives no medieval history, so the use of the banner over 1249-1603 rests on Wikipedia and FOTW (the Scran record of the Lindsay Armorial returned HTTP 403). The 'personal banner' wording is the page's own. The Saltire on blue is first certain in 1542 (FOTW) or 1507 (Wikipedia).

era-843.says: Wikipedia's flag article reports as legend that the Saltire's use as Scotland's flag began on the eve of the Battle of Athelstaneford in 832, and its village article tells the story of Saint Andrew's vision to the Pictish King Oengus II and the white cross in the sky. FOTW's legend page gives the same story from the chronicles of Fordun, Boece, Leslie, Spottiswoode and Bower (the king is 'Hungus', the enemy Athelstan's Angles), notes Nick Groom's report that the tale rests on a lost source of c.1165, and FOTW's main page says the earliest record of the flag (1165) refers to a 9th-century battle with no surviving original.
era-843.open: Both treat it as a legend, not as a documented banner; the date varies (832 in Wikipedia and Groom, 'about the 8th century' in FOTW's account, and about 800 in Spottiswoode), and FOTW dates the oldest surviving record to 1180 (a seal) where the cross is a religious emblem. Neither source mentions the Kingdom of Alba or the 843 start used for this row.

era-1959.says: Wikipedia: on 4 April 1959 Senegal merged with French Sudan to form the Mali Federation, whose new green, yellow and red vertical tricolour bore a stylised kanaga figure on the centre band; on 20 August 1960 Senegal left, kept the colours and replaced the kanaga with a green star. FOTW: Mali Federation formed 4 April 1959, independence 20 June 1960, Senegal seceded 22 August 1960 (also given as 20 August) and replaced the 'kanaga (black man figure)' with a green star.
era-1959.open: Bambara and Dogon origin of the kanaga, and Mali's later retention of it, are not covered; FOTW and Wikipedia differ on the day (20 or 22 August 1960).

era-1659.says: Wikipedia's Flag of Senegal: the French tricolour flew over Senegal until 1960 and, under French colonial rule, the authorities forbade the colony its own distinctive colonial flag (undated), with a green flag with a yellow star used by the Republic of Senegal in 1958-59. Wikipedia's Saint-Louis: the French settled the island in 1659 and nine chartered companies administered Saint-Louis between 1659 and 1779. Wikipedia's Flag of France: the tricolour was adopted in 1790 and modified in 1794, with royal banners earlier. Flags of the World's Senegal pages point to French colonial flags elsewhere and show only the 1958-59 pre-independence flag. Second look: UNESCO's listing for the Island of Saint-Louis calls it the first French chartered-company post on the Atlantic coast of Africa in 1659 and the capital of French West Africa until 1902 and later of Senegal, and describes no flag; Britannica's flag of Senegal page speaks of the tricolour only as inspiration for the 1958 flag.
era-1659.open: The sources support the French tricolour over colonial Senegal only for the period after its adoption in 1790-94 and do not date it; the 1659 start and 'three centuries' on the card are not borne out, no flag of the chartered companies is described, and no source states which flag flew over Saint-Louis or French West Africa. The 1659 start is confirmed by a reference source; no source read says which flag flew over Saint-Louis before the tricolour.

era-2006.says: Wikipedia says an Assembly recommendation of 2004 reintroduced the state and civil flags, the new constitution of 2006 sanctioned them, the Law on National Symbols was enacted in 2009 and the flags were standardised, with colour values, in 2010. FOTW says the Assembly declared Serbia the successor of Yugoslavia on 5 June 2006 and raised the state flag, that a 2009 law fixed 3:2 proportions with the lesser arms toward the hoist, and that the Government fixed the official designs on 11 November 2010.
era-2006.open: The flag's first return was 2004; 2006 is the constitution and independence.

era-279bce.open: Whether a flag, banner or standard existed in this period was not checked. The colour shown is not evidence of one.

era-1992.says: Wikipedia's Flag of Serbia and Montenegro gives adoption in 1992 and relinquishment in 2006. FOTW's page on the union says the flag was adopted 27 April 1992, a horizontal blue-white-red, and describes the UN-building flag as the old Yugoslav flag without the red star; the page runs to the end of the union in 2006.
era-1992.open: Colour shades were not checked against a specification. FOTW's separate Serbia page (1992-2004) shows Serbia's own red-blue-white flag in the same years; this era concerns the federal flag.

era-1882.says: Wikipedia says the Kingdom adopted a state flag with arms and a civil flag without in 1882. FOTW says the kingdom kept the principality's tricolour as its national flag, with a civil ensign and a state flag carrying the royal arms (a crowned double-headed eagle bearing the cross-and-firesteels shield) in the centre, used until 1918.
era-1882.open: The page text and drawing put a plain shield with cross and four letters on the blue band; neither source describes the arms that way. The civil flag's exact form differs between the two sources.

era-1878.says: Wikipedia says the four six-pointed stars were removed after the Congress of Berlin in 1878; FOTW's Principality page agrees (stars removed from the canton in 1878; flag unchanged until the kingdom's new arms in 1882) and says the plain tricolour was the civil flag while the state flag carried the arms.
era-1878.open: The page said the arms were not added until 1882; FOTW says the state flag kept the principality's arms through 1878-82 (only the stars went), so the plain tricolour drawn here is the civil flag.

era-1804.says: FOTW (Principality of Serbia) says the Takovo flag of 1815 was a white flag with a large red Greek cross, known from Paja Jovanović's painting, and dates the tricolour to the autumn 1835 decree and the arms-and-stars version to December 1838, used to 1878. Wikipedia (Flag of Serbia) gives the Sretenje Constitution flag of 15 February 1835, a December 1835 firman for a red-blue-white merchant tricolour and a January 1839 firman for arms and four stars. N1 Srbija agrees with Wikipedia on the 1835 and 1839 firmans (the latter with four stars in the upper-left of the red band and arms on the blue band), names the Sretenje colours as open red, white and a dark steel colour, and says only that Miloš unfurled his old voivodship banner at Takovo in 1815, without colours. Wikipedia (The Takovo Uprising) describes the painting but not a documented flag.
era-1804.open: The Takovo flag as a white flag with a red cross rests on FOTW's reading of a painting and on the painting; N1 confirms a banner at Takovo but gives no colours, so no source independently documents it. The flag documented by Wikipedia, FOTW and N1 for the later part of the era (the 1835-39 tricolour, then arms and four stars, to 1878) is not the one drawn. FOTW and Wikipedia differ by a few months on dates.

era-1944.says: FOTW says Serbia in Socialist Yugoslavia used a red-blue-white flag with a star, officially adopted 17 January 1947 (the coat of arms carried a red star). Wikipedia says the Socialist Republic kept the tricolour with a red star from 1947 to 1991, preceded by a Serbian Partisan flag in 1945-47, and that the star was removed in 1992.
era-1944.open: 1944-47 was a Partisan-flag interlude, not the tricolour with star. Neither source describes the star's gold border.

era-1918.says: FOTW describes the Kingdom's flag as blue-white-red, in use before the law and formally introduced with the 1921 constitution and prescribed by Article 2 of the 1922 law; Wikipedia's «Flag of Yugoslavia» gives the 1922 law. Wikipedia's «Flag of Serbia» says Serbia's tricolour use ended with the creation of the Kingdom in 1918.
era-1918.open: This page's statement that the blue-white-red was «presented as a neutral flag for the whole kingdom» was not found in either source.

era-1166.says: Wikipedia (Flag of Serbia) says medieval Serbia had dynastic banners rather than a state flag, gives the 1281 Dubrovnik inventory item of a flag of red and blue fabric (colour order unknown), says the later kings' flag was a red double-headed eagle on yellow (occasionally white), and dates the oldest known drawing to the 1339 Dulcert chart (white flag, red double-headed eagle). Wikipedia (Nemanjic dynasty) repeats that the eagle is attested for the flag of the medieval kingdom by Dulcert (1339). FOTW (medieval Serbia) reads the same chart as a red two-headed eagle on yellow, and cautions that the common red-blue bicolour reconstruction of the 1281 flag has no evidence.
era-1166.open: The sources describe the eagle flag only from 1339 (a drawing on a portolan chart, no surviving flag); none dates it to 1166-1339. The field colour (white or yellow) differs between Wikipedia and FOTW, and the colour order of the 1281 red-and-blue flag is unknown.

era-1941.says: FOTW (Serbia in the Second World War) says its author found no reference to a flag of the Nedic regime and guessed a version of the Serbian colours continued to fly; it says the Serbian Volunteer Corps flag was the regular Serbian flag with the corps emblem and that Cetniks flew black flags with texts such as 'Freedom or Death'. Wikipedia's Flag of Serbia has nothing on 1941-44.
era-1941.open: No source read establishes a state flag for the Nedic regime; FOTW's remark is the author's guess. The card's ghosted tricolour is a stand-in. Wikipedia's Government of National Salvation text was not found to describe a flag.

era-1459.says: Wikipedia (Flag of Serbia) starts the Ottoman-era tricolour story in 1835; FOTW's uprising page says banners in 1804 were borrowed from churches or haiduk bands; N1 Srbija says there was no single flag in 1804, only various voivodship banners based on medieval heritage and religious symbols, mostly a cross. Wikipedia (Flag of the Ottoman Empire) says armies used horse-tail standards until the 19th century, dates a plain crescent flag to c. 1480-1780 and the star-and-crescent naval flag to 1793. Nacionalna revija states that Belgrade had no coat of arms under Turkish rule. Wikipedia (Sanjak of Smederevo) has no flag.
era-1459.open: No source read says which flag, if any, flew over the Pashalik of Belgrade; the Ottoman red banner with a crescent and star is the card's own choice and the star-and-crescent form is later than most of this era. That no Serbian flag existed is not stated either (Nacionalna revija speaks only of arms).

era-1402.says: Flags of the World (Despotovac page, citing Samardžić 1983 and Spasić et al. 1992): Despot Stefan Lazarević kept the old Serbian arms, a white double-headed eagle on red, and was also given arms of Hungarian-Angevin type (a bend or pale between two fleurs-de-lis) probably as Sigismund's vassal; Đurađ Branković used these and later replaced them. Wikipedia (Serbian eagle): Stefan adopted the double-headed eagle as despot in 1402, and Richental's chronicle of the Council of Constance (1420) shows his arms as a red shield with a gold double-headed eagle. Wikipedia (Flag of Serbia) shows a 1439 portolan flag captioned as Dušan's, no colours in text; Wikipedia (Serbian Despotate) describes no flag.
era-1402.open: These pages describe Stefan Lazarević's arms, not a flag of the Despotate; no source read describes a Despotate banner. The vassal shield is described as silver with red fleurs-de-lis, not blue and gold, and the eagle is white (FOTW) or gold (Richental, via Wikipedia). Both rest on compiled pages (Wikipedia and FOTW) that cite printed works not seen.

era-1371.says: Wikipedia (Flag of Serbia), Wikipedia (Lazar of Serbia, Moravian Serbia) and FOTW (Serbia main page and medieval page) describe no flag or banner of Prince Lazar or of Stefan Lazarevic in this period. Wikipedia's Moravian Serbia infobox carries a flag image and the Lazarevic arms, with no supporting text.
era-1371.open: No source read describes or dates a flag for Moravian Serbia, and none says that no banner survives or that a red-cross 'Lazarica' banner is later legend; those statements on the card are not covered. The card shows a placeholder, not a flag.

era-1346.says: Wikipedia (Flag of Serbia) says Dusan was crowned emperor in 1346 and adopted the Byzantine four-fire-steel motif, shows a 1439 Vallseca chart flag captioned as that of Emperor Dusan, and gives the 1339 Dulcert chart (red double-headed eagle on a white flag). Wikipedia (Serbian Empire) lists the Dulcert eagle as the flag of Dusan's realm, a Hilandar flag alleged to be his (red-white-red triband), an imperial divelion (purple with a golden cross) and a red-and-yellow cavalry flag. FOTW describes the Dulcert eagle as red on yellow and two triangular Hilandar flags (orange, yellow and green silk with an appliqued gold cross) that tradition attributes to Dusan but whose dating is undetermined.
era-1346.open: The red double-headed eagle is dated by the sources to 1339, before the empire, and the colours of the field and of the Hilandar flags differ between Wikipedia and FOTW. Neither source shows the small cross-and-firesteel shield drawn on the card; the drawing is a reconstruction.

era-1996.says: Both sources give 1996, the year this page starts the current flag. Wikipedia's infobox gives the adoption as 8 January 1996; Flags of the World dates it 18 June 1996.
era-1996.open: Only the year the current flag was adopted was compared; the design and the swatch colours were not checked against a specification.

era-1977.says: WP: after Mancham was overthrown by France-Albert René in 1977 a red, white and green flag with a wavy white stripe, based on the SPUP flag, was used for 19 years until 1996. FOTW: a green, white and red wavy flag replaced the 1976 flag after a year following the coup.
era-1977.open: Neither source mentions a palm tree or star or the page's colour meanings. WP is inconsistent on the colours' attribution (SPUP vs United Seychelles).

era-1976.says: WP: independence flag (29 June 1976) with alternating blue and red triangles, used 1976-77. FOTW: white saltire dividing blue (hoist/fly) and red (top/bottom) fields.
era-1976.open: The page's green-white-red banded flag with shield is not supported by either source; meanings of colours not given.

era-1810.says: Wikipedia (Flag of Seychelles) pictures a colonial flag with a badge designed by General Gordon for 1903-1961 and a second badge by Mrs McEwen for 1961-1976, with Governor's flags, and notes that before 1903 Seychelles was administered as a dependency of Mauritius. FOTW (colonial flags page) agrees: Gordon's badge from 1903 to 1961, then a Blue Ensign with a badge approved in April 1961 until 1976. Wikipedia (History of Seychelles): Crown Colony in its own right only from 1903.
era-1810.open: Both publishers support a badged Blue Ensign for 1903-1976 only; nothing read gives a flag for 1810-1903, when Seychelles was a dependency of Mauritius, so more than half the span is unsupported. FOTW dates British sovereignty to 1814 and Wikipedia to 1811, not 1810. The card's badge is a blank white disc, not the pictorial badges. Britannica's flag of Seychelles page returned HTTP 403 and was not read.

era-1756.says: FOTW (colonial flags page, citing a Historia article): Captain Morphey took possession for Louis XV on 1 November 1756; colonies founded in 1770 and 1772 failed; on 30 July 1791 a corvette brought the Tricolor; Governor Quinssy hoisted the Union Jack on capitulating to the British in 1794 and later returned to the Tricolore. Wikipedia (History of Seychelles) gives the 1756 claim and the 1794 capitulation, without any flag; Wikipedia's Flag of Seychelles covers only 1903 onward. The Seychelles Nation article on the 1996 flag designer was read and has no history of earlier flags.
era-1756.open: The Tricolor in 1791 and its later reinstatement rest on FOTW alone, and no source read describes the royal ensign at the 1756 taking of possession, which the caption presents. The card ends French rule in 1810, while Wikipedia has Captain Beaver taking possession for Britain in April 1811 and FOTW dates British sovereignty to 1814.

era-1961.says: Both sources give 1961, the year this page starts the current flag. Wikipedia's infobox gives the adoption as 27 April 1961; Flags of the World dates it 1961.
era-1961.open: Only the year the current flag was adopted was compared; the design and the swatch colours were not checked against a specification.

era-1400.says: This page's own caption calls the image a placeholder: «placeholder maroon field — pre-colonial era, no unifying flag».
era-1400.open: Whether a flag, banner or standard existed in this period was not checked. The colour shown is not evidence of one.

era-1896.says: Wikipedia: the colony and protectorate's flag of 1889-1916 was a Blue Ensign defaced with a circle (elephant, oil palm, mountains, initials S.L.), and from 1916 to 1961 with a badge showing an oil palm and an African person watching a ship arrive; arms were granted in 1914. FOTW's colonial flags page gives the same: the 1889-1914 Blue Ensign with an S.L. badge and the 1916-1961 blue ensign whose badge (after Barraclough, 1965) shows a liberated slave, a ship and a palm tree with the motto 'Auspice Britannia Liber'.
era-1896.open: The sources date the first flag to 1889, not 1896, and neither uses the name 'Lion Mountains' for the badge; the drawn badge is schematic.

era-1808.says: Wikipedia's Flag of Sierra Leone says that under colonial rule the territory used the British Blue Ensign defaced with its arms (an elephant, oil palm and mountains with the letters S.L.), and its colony article covers 1808-1961 without describing a flag. Flags of the World's colonial flags page begins with the 1889-1914 Blue Ensign with a badge and describes nothing earlier. Britannica's Flag of Sierra Leone page, which Wikipedia cites, returned HTTP 403 and was not read.
era-1808.open: A plain, undefaced Blue Ensign for 1808-1889, as drawn, is not described by any source read; both give a badge only from 1889, and no flag is described for the eight decades before.

era-1787.says: Wikipedia's Flag of Sierra Leone starts its colonial account with the Blue Ensign defaced with the territory's arms and gives no flag for the Province of Freedom or the Sierra Leone Company; its Sierra Leone Company article has no flag text. Flags of the World's colonial flags page begins with the 1889 flag and mentions only that the 1916 badge showed the Union Flag as it was before 1801.
era-1787.open: Whether the settlement flew the Union Jack is not covered by any source read. The card openly presents the Union Jack of the period as a stand-in, so no settlement flag is claimed.

era-1965.says: Both sources give 1965, the year this page starts the current flag. Wikipedia's infobox gives the adoption as 1959 |1965 }}; Flags of the World dates it December 1959.
era-1965.open: Only the year the current flag was adopted was compared; the design and the swatch colours were not checked against a specification.

era-1299.says: This page's own caption calls the image a placeholder: «placeholder — Singapura, then Malacca and Johor sultanate rule, no flag survives».
era-1299.open: Whether a flag, banner or standard existed in this period was not checked. The colour shown is not evidence of one.

era-1963.says: Britannica (Whitney Smith) says Singapore acquired its own flag on 3 December 1959 and that there was no change in its flag when it became one of the states of Malaysia in 1963, nor on separation on 9 August 1965. Wikipedia's State of Singapore article shows the 1959 flag in its infobox and its Flag of Singapore article says the 1959 flag remained the national flag at independence. WorldStatesmen lists the 1959 flag from 3 Dec 1959 without a break for the Malaysian years. FOTW raises the question and offers only a presumption that the flag was retained as the constituent state's flag.
era-1963.open: Britannica is the only text that states the flag was unchanged in 1963; it does not say how the state flag was flown beside the Malaysian flag, and the National Library Board's Infopedia entry on the flag, which a search summary said records the federation flag representing Singapore at international events, could not be read (its page renders only through scripts). FOTW leaves the question open.

era-1946.says: Wikipedia: Singapore adopted its own Crown Colony flag after the war, modified from the Straits Settlements flag with one crown instead of three (captions 1946-1952 and 1952-1959); the 1959 flag was adopted on 3 December 1959. Flags of the World's page on the Crown Colony of Singapore 1946-1959 shows a Blue Ensign with a Tudor crown badge for the colony; its main page says the Union Jack flew over Singapore 1819-1959 and that the 1959 flag was adopted on 3 December 1959.
era-1946.open: FOTW's main page conflicts with its own sub-page and with Wikipedia (Union Jack only); its sub-page is a short contributor note without a cited basis, asking itself about the crown change in 1953. The colony flag is established for 1946-1959; for 1959-1963 the 1959 self-government flag applies, as the page says.

era-1942.says: Wikipedia's article on the Japanese occupation of Singapore (Syonan-to) shows the Japanese flag (the 1870 merchant flag design, a red disc on white) as the territory's flag in its infobox and says Japanese Rising Sun flags were raised and hung across many major buildings (the sentence is flagged as needing a citation). Wikipedia's Flag of Singapore and FOTW's Singapore page say nothing about the occupation.
era-1942.open: The Japanese flag rests on one publisher's infobox and an uncited sentence; no source describes a separate Syonan-to flag, the 'military administration ensign' wording is the card's own, and whether any Singaporean flag flew is not covered.

era-1819.says: Wikipedia: Singapore was part of the Straits Settlements, whose flag was a Blue Ensign with a red diamond holding three gold crowns; the city had no separate flag. Flags of the World's Straits Settlements page, citing National Archives files: Singapore (bought 1819 and 1824) was administered with Penang and Malacca as the Straits Settlements from 1826, made a Crown Colony in 1867, with a Blue Ensign and a gold crown badge c.1868-c.1880, then the three-crown lozenge badge; the flag was adopted in 1874 and discontinued in 1942. FOTW's main page says the Union Jack flew over Singapore 1819-1959.
era-1819.open: The ensign is established for about 1868-1942 only; the flag over the 1819-1826 trading post and under the East India Company before 1867 is not described, and FOTW's 'Union Jack 1819-1959' conflicts with its own Straits Settlements page.

era-1993.says: Wikipedia says the flag was adopted on 1 March 1990 as the flag of the Slovak Republic within Czechoslovakia, initially without the arms, that the constitution of 3 September 1992 added the coat of arms on the hoist side, and that a law of February 1993 described the details. FOTW says Slovak legislation of 1 March 1990 laid down the plain tricolour, that the constitution was enacted on 1 September 1992 with the flag in article 9, paragraph 2, that the flag was first hoisted on 3 September 1992 in front of Bratislava Castle, that the arms were added because the plain flag could be mistaken for Russia's, and that a law of 18 February 1993 set the shield's proportions.
era-1993.open: The sources differ on 1 or 3 September 1992 and on the article number. This page used to say the arms were first codified in 1939.

era-907.says: This page's own caption calls the image a placeholder: «placeholder maroon field — tribal conquest era, no flag survives».
era-907.open: Whether a flag, banner or standard existed in this period was not checked. The colour shown is not evidence of one.

era-825.says: This page's own caption calls the image a placeholder: «placeholder maroon field — pre-heraldic era, no flag survives».
era-825.open: Whether a flag, banner or standard existed in this period was not checked. The colour shown is not evidence of one.

era-400bce.says: This page's own caption calls the image a placeholder: «placeholder — Celtic and Roman-frontier tribes, then Samo's Empire, no flag survives».
era-400bce.open: Whether a flag, banner or standard existed in this period was not checked. The colour shown is not evidence of one.

era-1990.says: Both sources say a Slovak flag, the plain white-blue-red tricolour, was adopted on 1 March 1990 within Czechoslovakia (Wikipedia: the interior ministry tasked Čisárik and Vrtel with the design). FOTW (Heimer) adds that the state flag was unchanged by that legislation.
era-1990.open: This page shows the Czechoslovak flag for 1990–93 and does not mention the Slovak flag of 1 March 1990. The «hyphen war» was not covered by either source.

era-1939.says: FOTW (Kravcik) says a law of 23 June 1939 enacted the white-blue-red tricolour as the Slovak State's flag. Wikipedia says the Slovak Republic used the flag during the war and that a war flag existed for its military.
era-1939.open: This page used to say the arms were added to the flag in 1939; neither source says so, and FOTW says they were added by the 1992 constitution. The 1939 constitution was not covered.

era-1938.says: Wikipedia (List of Slovak flags): the white-blue-red flag was the unofficial flag of Slovakia in 1919-1938 and the official flag of the autonomous Slovak land in 1938-1939. FOTW: enacted as the state flag by a law of 23 June 1939; in use since 1848, mostly unofficially. The June 1939 government bill of the Slovak Diet (primary, Czech parliament digital library) says the colours of the Slovak state are to remain white, blue and red, the Slovak tricolour of the Stur and Hurban banners, and that the flag laws then in force were Czechoslovak laws 252/1920 and 269/1936, which the new law replaces. World Statesmen's captions give the Czechoslovak flag for 30 Mar 1920 - 14 Mar 1939 and the Slovak flag for 1848 and 14 Mar 1939 - 1945.
era-1938.open: Only Wikipedia's list calls the tricolour official in the autonomous land in 1938-1939; the 1939 bill and World Statesmen point to the Czechoslovak flag remaining the state flag until March or June 1939, with the tricolour as the Slovak national colours. The text of the autonomy act (299/1938) was not read, so an autonomy-period decree on a flag cannot be ruled out.

era-1918.says: FOTW (Sache) says the white-red flag was first officially hoisted in Washington on 18 October 1918, and Wikipedia says the National Assembly approved the flag with a blue hoist triangle on 30 March 1920 to distinguish it from Poland's.
era-1918.open: These sources are about the Czechoslovak flag, not Slovakia specifically; neither says the blue was chosen to include Slovakia (FOTW: the third Slavic colour from 1848; a Slovak-mountains reading is «late mythology»).

era-1699.says: Wikipedia (Flag of Hungary) pictures a flag of the Kingdom of Hungary as part of the Habsburg monarchy from the 18th century to 1848, says the red-white-green colours were displayed at the 1790 coronation, formally described in 1806 and mandated by Act XXI of 1848, and pictures kingdom flags with the arms for 1867-1915. FOTW: the 1806 chronology and the tricolour with the kingdom's arms for 1867-1918. The Hungarian government's NISZ site says the colours were first prescribed by Act XXI of 1848 and that earlier Habsburg-period flags were regimental and county flags with imperial eagles and kingdom arms; Rakoczi's 1703-11 flags were red and white striped. World Statesmen's image captions give a kingdom flag to 1804, the Austrian imperial flag 1804-1848 and 1849-1867, and a Hungarian flag from 1848.
era-1699.open: The publishers differ on what flew in Hungary in 1699-1848 (a kingdom flag to 1804 or the Austrian imperial flag 1804-48 per World Statesmen; the tricolour displayed in 1790 and described in 1806 per Wikipedia, FOTW and NISZ). The tricolour is legally prescribed from 1848 and shown with arms for 1867-1918, so for the first 90 to 150 years of the era no source supports the card's single flag. Nothing is said about the Slovak-inhabited counties.

era-1000.says: Wikipedia (Arpad stripes): barry of eight gules and argent, four red and four silver stripes, depicted from 1202 on the seal of King Emeric, on a Zurich armorial of about 1340 and in a Chronicon Pictum banner of about 1360; a claim that Stephen I used a striped banner is marked as needing a citation. Wikipedia (Flag of Hungary) adds a dynasty standard in the 13th century. Flags of the World (Kingdom of Hungary): Revnivtsev says the Arpad stripes flag was used by Arpad kings 1000-1301; the stripes appear on royal seals from the early 13th century.
era-1000.open: The 1000 start date rests on one FOTW contributor; Wikipedia's earliest evidence is 1202. Neither source says the banner flew in Slovak-inhabited counties, which the page asserts.

era-1948.says: Wikipedia (Flag of Slovakia): Czechoslovakia used its own flag in 1920-1939 and 1945-1992; Wikipedia (List of Slovak flags): the Czechoslovak flag was used 1920-1992. Flags of the World (Czechoslovakia): Sensen writes that through these periods the state used the same flag, and Heimer that the flag of the state was unchanged by the 1990 laws; the 1960 and 1963 arms, not the flag, added a red shield with a star that Kriżan says represented Communism.
era-1948.open: FOTW's Slovakia page is silent on 1948-90; whether any Communist emblem was ever put on the flag itself is answered only by the contributors' statement that it stayed unchanged.

era-1945.says: Wikipedia: Czechoslovakia used its own flag in 1945-1992 and the 1939-45 government in exile used it too. Flags of the World (Czechoslovakia): Sensen writes the state used the same flag at all these times, and the Czech Republic adopted it; its Slovakia pages say a 1939 law gave the Slovak State its own white-blue-red flag.
era-1945.open: The 1945-48 restoration is not described as a separate event by either source; the page's 'deliberate break' wording is its own comment.

era-1526.says: Wikipedia (Arpad stripes) says rulers including Janos Szapolyai (1526-1540) and Gabor Bethlen used the stripes on seals, but that the stripes fell out of use as a flag after the Middle Ages and were revived by Rakoczi's cavalry in 1703-1711. Wikipedia (Flag of Hungary) and FOTW say red, white and green appear from the fifteenth century and were described in 1806 or tied to 1608. The Hungarian government's NISZ site says red-white-green appears in this period only on seal cords and banner edges, and describes reconstructions of Zrinyi's flag at Szigetvar in 1566 (imperial arms on one side, the kingdom's arms on the other, green ground) and of a flag of the Nyitra (Nitra) county noble levy of 1660; it also says mixed-house kings always used the striped family flag or striped arms.
era-1526.open: These are flags of a commander and of a county, not of Royal Hungary as a state; NISZ's striped family flag contradicts Wikipedia's statement that the stripes fell out of use as a flag. No source describes a single flag of Royal Hungary for 1526-1699, so the tricolour with arms stays a stand-in. Slovakia's own place in it is not covered beyond the Nyitra county flag.

era-1991.says: Both sources give 1991, the year this page starts the current flag. Wikipedia's infobox gives the adoption as 25 June 1991; Flags of the World dates it 27 June 1991.
era-1991.open: Only the year the current flag was adopted was compared; the design and the swatch colours were not checked against a specification.

era-200bce.says: This page's own caption calls the image a placeholder: «placeholder — Celtic Noricum, Roman province, and Slavic migration, no flag survives».
era-200bce.open: Whether a flag, banner or standard existed in this period was not checked. The colour shown is not evidence of one.

era-1945.says: FOTW (Heimer, 1996) describes a white-blue-red flag with a star, officially adopted on 18 January 1947. Wikipedia says a red star was officially placed on the republic's flag in 1945.
era-1945.open: The dates differ: 1945 (Wikipedia) and 1947 (FOTW) for the start; FOTW gives the flag's abandonment as 27 June 1990, Wikipedia the removal of the star and adoption of the new flag as 27 June 1991. This page says 1945–1991. Neither source mentions the gold border on the star that this page describes.

era-1941.says: Wikipedia (Province of Ljubljana): Germany and Hungary occupied and annexed the north, Italy annexed the Ljubljana province (3 May 1941 to 9 May 1945), Germany took over the Italian zone in 1943; no flag described. Wikipedia (Flag of Slovenia): the Slovene national colours were used both by the Partisans (usually with a red star) and by the German-sponsored Home Guard. FOTW (Slovenia during WWII): the Home Guard used a Slovenian tricolour with the Carniola-derived arms, Partisans a flag vaguely like the later Yugoslav one. An online occupation-borders exhibition (okupacijskemeje.si) shows only a photo caption 'Town Hall in Ptuj adorned with German flags'.
era-1941.open: No source read says which national flags flew in each occupation zone or describes them; the caption and layout stay unconfirmed. The Ptuj photo caption shows German flags in the German zone but not their design. Hungarian-zone flags are not covered by any source read.

era-1918.says: The transcribed 1922 law (Sluzbene novine #89/22, 28 Feb 1922, via FOTW) prescribes the naval and merchant ensigns of the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes as three equal horizontal fields blue-white-red (Articles 1 and 2); the 1937 law text (same site) is described there as leaving the merchant ensign unchanged. FOTW says the tricolour was used before the law, was formally introduced as the national flag with the 1921 Vidovdan Constitution, was prescribed by the 1922 law as civil and state ensign, and that the 1929 proclamation of the Kingdom of Yugoslavia brought no change. Wikipedia's Flag of Slovenia says the whole kingdom officially used a blue-white-red flag.
era-1918.open: The two law texts are flag-at-sea laws; their application to the land flag in Slovenia rests on FOTW's statement that the ensign was the national flag and on Wikipedia. 1918-1921 use rests on FOTW's single remark that it was used before the law. Wikipedia's infobox gives 1918 and its text 1922 for adoption. FOTW says the Slovene tricolour itself was soon banned or rarely tolerated.

era-29.says: Wikipedia (State of Slovenes, Croats and Serbs): proclaimed 29 October 1918, united with Serbia and Montenegro on 1 December 1918; the infobox flag is not described in the text. FOTW (si.html): the Slovenes adopted the tricolour when they joined the State in 1918 but it was too short-lived to be made official; no colour order given. FOTW (Royal Yugoslavia): the successor Kingdom's flag was blue-white-red. Keyword searches of a Slovenian history-journal article on the National Government (Prispevki za zgodovino delavskega gibanja, 1985), a Croatian legal-news history piece and archontology.org found no description of the State's flag.
era-29.open: Neither the earlier sources nor the extra Slovenian, Croatian and archive pages read say what flag the State flew or in what order its colours ran; the red-white-blue order on the card is the reverse of the Kingdom's documented blue-white-red and remains unconfirmed. A search of the Croatian Sabor and National Council decisions was not possible with the tools available.

era-1816.says: Wikipedia (Kingdom of Illyria) describes a titular crown land of the Austrian Empire from 1816 to 1849 with Ljubljana as centre and shows an unlabelled flag image, but its text does not describe a flag. Balkan Flag History describes a white-over-red bicolour with the Austrian arms, 1816-1849 (2:3), but lists only Wikipedia pages and World Statesmen as sources, so it is not independent. Flags of the World (Austrian Landesfarben) does not mention Illyria and says the Empire allowed colours only. Two German-language flag-encyclopedia pages (flaggenlexikon.de) that a search surfaced returned HTTP 404 and were not read.
era-1816.open: No primary or reference source read describes a white-and-red flag, an eagle or a shield for the Kingdom of Illyria; the only description found traces back to Wikipedia's image. The claim of imperial colours with a double-headed eagle remains unsupported.

era-1809.says: Wikipedia (Illyrian Provinces) presents the provinces as an autonomous province of the French First Empire (1809-1814/15) with Ljubljana (Laibach) as administrative capital and a French-flag infobox; Flags of the World (France: First Empire) gives the blue-white-red Tricolore as the national flag of the First Empire. A keyword read of the Slovenian scholarly volume 'Zgodovinske dimenzije Ilirskih provinc' (ZRC SAZU, 2012) found no passage on flags raised in Ljubljana in 1809-1813 (it mentions the French tricolour only as the emblem of the French soldiers, and tricolours at 1929 commemorations); the Kamra.si page timed out and was not read.
era-1809.open: No source read says in so many words that the tricolour was flown from Ljubljana or by the Provincial administration; the attribution rests on the provinces being French-ruled and on Wikipedia's infobox. The Slovene-schooling point is a plan that Wikipedia says was not fully realised. Not independently confirmed beyond two compiled publishers.

era-973.says: The Slovenian government (GOV.SI, Ministry of the Interior, 2022) and the Museum of Recent History of Slovenia booklet both say that in 1848 the Slovenes set the national colours white-blue-red on the basis of the colours in the arms of Carniola and proposed them to the Austrian administration; the Ministry of the Interior in Vienna confirmed the Carniolan provincial colours on 23 September 1848, colours Emperor Ferdinand had set in 1836. The flag was first raised in Ljubljana on 7 April 1848 by Lovro Toman and fellow students. FOTW and Wikipedia agree on the 7 April 1848 raising and Carniolan land colours for 1848-1918.
era-973.open: Only 1848-1918 is documented as a Carniolan flag or colours; nothing read shows a Carniolan flag for 973/1364-1848, and the 1836 decree itself was not read (only the government's statement of it). The sources name different designers and different inns for 7 April 1848.

era-1849.says: Wikipedia (Flag of Slovenia): the Austrian government recognised the white-blue-red tricolour as Carniola's official flag after 1848; Wikipedia (Duchy of Carniola) says the colours were confirmed as the crownland's flag colours in 1848. Flags of the World (si.html): in 1848-1918 the tricolour was Carniola's land colours, hardly recognised by the Austrian rulers; FOTW (Rosenfeld 1883 list): Krain white-blue-red, Kaernten red-white, Steiermark green-white. The Slovenian government (GOV.SI, Ministry of the Interior, 2022) says the Ministry of the Interior in Vienna confirmed the Carniolan provincial colours on 23 September 1848, colours Emperor Ferdinand had set in 1836.
era-1849.open: The Slovenian government text supports the Carniola colours but not a shared black-and-gold banner for Carniola, Styria, Carinthia and the Littoral; no source read describes such a banner, so the black-over-gold drawing is a stand-in. Whether Austria flew the colours as a flag or only as provincial colours remains disputed between publishers.

era-1813.says: Wikipedia (Illyrian Provinces): Austria recovered the area in 1813-1814 and annexation was formalised at the Congress of Vienna on 9 June 1815. Wikipedia (Kingdom of Illyria): Feldzeugmeister Lattermann was appointed provisional civil and military governor of the reconquered Illyria in September 1813, and the Kingdom of Illyria was formed in 1816 (patent of 3 August 1816). Neither Wikipedia (Flag of Slovenia) nor Flags of the World (si.html) describes a flag for the interval.
era-1813.open: No source read describes a flag for 1813-1816; the card's red field is a stand-in, and this is not a finding that none existed.

era-828.says: Wikipedia (March of Carniola): Friulian dukes held jurisdiction over Carniola 788-828, governors of Bavaria from 828, East Francia from 843; the march is first explicitly mentioned in an imperial charter of 973 and was separated from Bavaria in 976 as part of the Duchy of Carinthia. The article's infobox carries an image captioned Flag of Carniola but the text describes no flag. Flags of the World (si.html) dates the Carniolan arms to the early 13th century, after this span.
era-828.open: No flag for 828-973 is described in any source read; the infobox image is not evidence of a period flag, and the card's red field is a stand-in. This is not a finding that none existed.

era-658.says: Wikipedia (Carantania) describes the principality (658-828) without any flag or arms. Wikipedia (Black panther (symbol)): the current form of the symbol was first reconstructed by Jozko Savli in the 1980s; there is no direct evidence of it from Carantania; the panther appears first in the arms of the Sponheim family of Carinthia. 24ur.com (2 May 2021): historians Miha Kosi and Andrej Pleterski say heraldry did not exist in 8th-century Carantania and call the panther a modern construct.
era-658.open: The card presents the panther as a reconstruction with no period flag, and the sources agree that no Carantanian flag or heraldic symbol is attested. The panther's use in Carinthian and Styrian arms is later (Kosi dates it to the 11th century and the Spanheims).

era-1978.says: Both sources date the current flag to 1977, before this era begins in 1978, so the flag was already in use at the start. Wikipedia's infobox gives the adoption as 18 November 1977; Flags of the World dates it November 1977.
era-1978.open: Only the year the current flag was adopted was compared; the design and the swatch colours were not checked against a specification.

era-1893-1.says: This page's own caption calls the image a placeholder: «placeholder — pre-contact and early-contact era, no single flag».
era-1893-1.open: Whether a flag, banner or standard existed in this period was not checked. The colour shown is not evidence of one.

era-1893.says: Wikipedia's table: Union Jack 1893-1906; Blue Ensign with the protectorate's name and the Tudor Crown 1906-1947; Blue Ensign with a turtle shield 1947-1956; Blue Ensign with a quarterly shield on a white disk 1956-1966 and without the disk 1966-1977; the present flag ratified 18 November 1977. FOTW's historical pages: Blue Ensign badge 'BRITISH SOLOMON ISLANDS' around a crown c.1906-1947, replaced in 1947 when arms were granted by a red shield with a turtle on a white circle (Gresham Carr 1953), replaced again in 1956, with a 1956-1966 Blue Ensign; the official title was British Solomon Islands Protectorate until 1975.
era-1893.open: The page's single Blue Ensign with a badge disc stands for several different badges across the span, and Wikipedia's Union Jack for 1893-1906 is not in FOTW (which starts c.1906 and a Resident Commissioner's ensign c.1902); the description of the turtle badge is internally inconsistent in Wikipedia (shield vs disc) and the 1966-1977 variant is Wikipedia-only.

era-1969.open: Only the year the current flag was adopted was compared; the design and the swatch colours were not checked against a specification.

era-1960.says: Wikipedia: the flag was adopted 12 Oct 1954 by the Trust Territory council (designer Mohammed Awale Liban), used as co-official flag of the Trust Territory 1954-1960, used by the independent State of Somaliland 26 June-1 July 1960 and later adopted by the Somali Republic. FOTW: adopted 12 Oct 1954; Somalia was created 1 July 1960 and united with British Somaliland to form the Somali Republic; Flag Day is 26 June.
era-1960.open: Neither source gives an adoption date for the Republic's use of the flag; FOTW's text gives both 26 June and 1 July for the first republican hoisting.

era-1884.says: Wikipedia (Flag of Somalia): British Somaliland used the UK flag in 1884-1903 and its own flags in 1903-1950, 1950-1952 and 1952-1960; Italian Somaliland used the Italian flag 1889-1941, a British occupation flag in 1941-1950, then the Italian and UN flags in 1950-1960. Flags of the World (British Somaliland): from 1903 to 1950 the Blue and Red Ensigns carried the protectorate badge, the head and shoulders of a kudu on a white disc, changed in 1950. Flags of the World (Italian Somaliland): the colony had a coat of arms but no distinctive flag, and the flag of the Kingdom of Italy was used.
era-1884.open: Wikipedia's captions describe no designs; the Italian flag in the colony is given by FOTW only in general terms, and the badge on the Italian side of the card is not described by either source.

era-1285.says: Wikipedia (Flag of Somalia) lists flags for the Sultanate of Mogadishu, Ajuran, Adal, Hiraab, Majeerteen and Isaaq sultanates as image captions. The sultanate articles caption their infobox flags as the flag shown beside the Mogadishu area on Lázaro Luis' 1563 map, the Mogadishu-area flag on a 1576 Portuguese map (Ajuran), and the combined three banners used by Ahmad al-Ghazi's forces (Adal); the Adal article also says the army's divisions were symbolised with distinct flags and that emissaries presented Emir Mahfuz with a green standard in 1516. Re-read for any text description of a design: none.
era-1285.open: The card is a text panel saying no flag survives. The sources read describe flags from period maps and war banners, but their text gives no designs and does not say whether any survives, and all rest on Wikipedia alone; FOTW's Somalia page does not mention the sultanates. The infobox images may be modern depictions of map images. No map or museum record of the 1563 or 1576 maps could be read.

era-1994.says: Both sources give 1994, the year this page starts the current flag. Wikipedia's infobox gives the adoption as 27 April 1994; Flags of the World dates it 27 Apr 1994.
era-1994.open: Only the year the current flag was adopted was compared; the design and the swatch colours were not checked against a specification.

era-1652-1.says: This page's own caption calls the image a placeholder: «placeholder maroon field — Khoikhoi and San societies, no flag survives».
era-1652-1.open: Whether a flag, banner or standard existed in this period was not checked. The colour shown is not evidence of one.

era-1928.says: Wikipedia says the 1928 flag was first hoisted on 31 May 1928, based on the Prinsenvlag, with the Union Flag, the Orange Free State flag and the Transvaal Vierkleur in the white band; that the arrangement means each miniature flag enjoys equal precedence; that a brighter version was adopted in 1982; and that the flag was relinquished on 20 April 1994. FOTW says the old national flag was in use in 1928–1994, in blue, white, red and green.
era-1928.open: This page says the three small flags symbolise the union of Britain's and the two defeated Boer republics' domains; Wikipedia describes the arrangement as one of equal precedence. FOTW does not give the 1928 date.

era-1910.says: Wikipedia (Red Ensign article): a Red Ensign with the coat of arms of South Africa on a white disc, authorised by Admiralty warrants of December 1910, the civil ensign 1910-1951 and used on land as a de facto national flag until 1928; Wikipedia's Flag of South Africa article says the same of the Red Ensign from 31 May 1910. Flags of the World: Admiralty warrant of 28 December 1910, amended 25 March 1912 to put the shield on a white roundel; the Union Jack was officially the national flag, the Red Ensign often regarded as the national flag, merchant ensign to 1951.
era-1910.open: The Union Jack was officially the national flag; the Red Ensign's 'de facto' status was popular practice (FOTW calls the perception erroneous). The badge is the Union's arms (FOTW says its quartered shield reportedly carries emblems of the four provinces), not a separate 'Union badge'.

era-1652.says: Wikipedia: the VOC used a version of the Prinsenvlag at the Cape from 1652 to 1795; its list dates the VOC flag 1652-1795 and 1803-1806. Flags of the World: the Dutch and VOC tricolours flew until the first British occupation on 17 September 1795; the flags generally used by Dutch vessels were the Prinzenvlag, an orange-white-blue tricolour (the orange later changed to red), and the Cape flag was either the Netherlands' or the Company's, the Dutch flag bearing the Company's cipher, though the author says no evidence of a Cape cipher on flags exists.
era-1652.open: The card's end date of 1806 spans the British occupation (Union flag 1795-1803) and the Batavian Republic (Dutch tricolour 1803-1806). The VOC monogram flag is FOTW's, not Wikipedia's, and FOTW doubts the Cape cipher.

era-1806.says: FOTW's early-flags and Cape pages say the Cape Colony flew the undefaced British Union Flag from the second British occupation (1806) until it adopted a distinctive badge in 1876: a Blue Ensign with the colony's arms in a white roundel (Royal Warrant 29 May 1876), used until 31 May 1910. Wikipedia's list of South African flags gives a Cape Blue Ensign for 1876-1910 and a Natal flag for 1875-1910, and lists the Orange Free State flag (1857-1902) and the Transvaal's Vierkleur (1857-1902, with interruptions). FOTW's Orange Free State page describes seven alternating white and orange stripes with the Dutch flag in the canton. World Statesmen's South Africa sequence begins on 31 May 1910 and adds nothing for the earlier period.
era-1806.open: The Blue Ensign shown fits only 1876-1910 for the Cape and 1875-1910 for Natal; the Cape flew the plain Union Flag from 1806 to 1876. The caption's statement that the Boer republics flew their own flags is supported, but their designs are not on the card, and the Vierkleur's design is not described in the pages read.

era-1948.says: Wikipedia: 12 July 1948 adopted; 15 October 1949 geometry standardised; 21 February 1984 dimensions codified; 1997 decree fixed colours. FOTW: 25 October 1997 presidential ordinance on standard specification; July 2007 National Flag Law.
era-1948.open: FOTW is silent before 1997; the 1883 and 1948 dates rest on Wikipedia.

era-57bce.open: Whether a flag, banner or standard existed in this period was not checked. The colour shown is not evidence of one.

era-gojoseon.open: Whether a flag, banner or standard existed in this period was not checked. The colour shown is not evidence of one.

era-1945.says: Wikipedia's Flag of South Korea says the taegukgi was widely used again after 1945 and that the US Army Military Government in Korea began using it alongside the US flag on 14 January 1946; its gallery has a taegukgi 'used by the United States Army Military Government in Korea from 1945 to 1948'. FOTW's history page says a South Korean Military Administration was set up by US troops on 15 August 1945 and that the present flag, except for the shape of two trigrams, was used in South Korea.
era-1945.open: Neither source calls the use 'informal'; that word is the card's own. The details of the trigram arrangement differ from today's flag, as FOTW notes.

era-1910.says: FOTW's history page says the Resident General's flag was abolished on 22 August 1910 on annexation and the Japanese national flag (Hinomaru) was used in Korea until 15 August 1945 (contributor note), and that the Governor-General used a light-blue flag with a Hinomaru canton. Wikipedia's Korea under Japanese rule shows the flag of Japan as the flag of Korea for 1910-1945 in its infobox; its Flag of South Korea mentions only the government-in-exile's flag (1919-1942).
era-1910.open: The prohibition of the Taegukgi rests on one FOTW contributor note and Wikipedia does not mention it; the Governor-General's own blue ensign is also only a contributor note.

era-1883.says: Wikipedia: no flag in 1876; Shufeldt urged one in 1882; the Taegukgi was promulgated 27 January 1883. FOTW's history page: Pak Yeong-hyo drew a four-trigram flag aboard ship in September 1882 and King Gojong formally proclaimed it on 6 March 1883 (Korea.net), while another contributor note gives 27 January 1883 as the official adoption; a 1882 US Navy chart and a November 1882 copy in the UK National Archives show the four-trigram design.
era-1883.open: The two sources differ on who designed the flag (Wikipedia: Lee Eung-jun, with Pak Yeong-hyo presenting a model; FOTW: Pak Yeong-hyo, with the Chinese delegate Ma Jianzhong pressing the yin-yang design per a Korea Herald report) and on the proclamation date (27 January vs 6 March 1883). Four trigrams are shown in 1882 sources; the 1893 Herold plate with eight trigrams is a disputed contributor report.

era-1897.says: Wikipedia captions a Korean Empire flag (1897-1910) and says the Taegukgi's predecessors were used by the empire. FOTW's history page shows the Denny Taegeukgi (given by Gojong to the American adviser Owen Denny, taken to the US in 1890, returned 1981 and registered as cultural heritage 2008), a 1899 US Navy chart flag 'which might be' the Korean Empire's national flag, and a 1911 geography showing the old flag before 1905 with four trigrams around a yin-yang disc.
era-1897.open: FOTW's 1899 chart identification is hedged ('might be'), and contributors disagree on the trigram colours and arrangement shown in 1890s sources; neither source describes the imperial standards or the empire's status relative to China.

era-1392.says: Wikipedia's Flag of South Korea says Korea had no national flag before 1876, though the king had his own royal standard (its gallery captions one 1392-1907 without describing it); its Joseon article shows a royal standard and a flag of 1883-1897. FOTW's history page, citing Japanese flag charts of 1856, 1871 and 1876, shows a yellow flag with a black dragon ('Korean National flag') and a blue flag with a yellow dragon ('Korean King Standard').
era-1392.open: No source describes a flag in use across 1392-1883 in Joseon's own sources: the royal standard's design is not given, and the dragon flags come from Japanese charts of the 1850s-1870s and disagree on ground colour. The royal blue shown is a stand-in, not a documented banner.

era-918.says: Wikipedia's Goryeo article shows one ceremonial flag of the Goryeo period (a yellow phoenix flag from the royal procession, footnoted to a 1123 Chinese account and the Encyclopedia of Korean Culture). Its Flag of South Korea has only a caption on an 1883 Qing book showing a 'flag of Goryeo', noting Joseon was sometimes called Goryeo in China. FOTW's main and history pages do not cover Goryeo.
era-918.open: No source read describes a state or national flag of Goryeo; the phoenix flag is a processional flag, not shown on the card. The card's statement that Buddhist and court symbolism substitute for a flag is not found in any source read.

era-676.says: Wikipedia's Flag of South Korea, its Unified Silla article, and FOTW's Korea main and history pages were read; none mentions a flag or standard of Unified Silla.
era-676.open: No source read describes or denies a Silla flag; the card is a placeholder. The card's statement about Buddhist iconography and court symbolism standing in for a flag is not found in any source read.

era-2011.says: Wikipedia: the flag was adopted 9 July 2005 after the Comprehensive Peace Agreement and became the national flag on 9 July 2011 at independence (standardised 25 August 2023); the government's meanings are black the people, red blood shed, green land and agricultural wealth, white peace, blue the Nile, yellow unity of the states, hope and determination; a different version had been the SPLM flag. FOTW: three equal bands of black, red and green, the red edged in white, with a blue hoist triangle holding a yellow five-pointed star; the Transitional Constitution of 6 July 2005 gave the South its own flag; the cabinet approved the flag, the SPLM flag of 2005 used as interim flag by the Government of Southern Sudan, on 22 March 2011 and it became the national flag on 9 July 2011.
era-2011.open: The sources agree on design and on 9 July 2011 as national flag status. They differ on whether the 2005 adoption was Wikipedia's 9 July or FOTW's 6 July constitution date, on whether the 2005 flag was the SPLM flag exactly, and on the meaning of the star (optimism per FOTW, unity per the government).

era-1821-1.says: This page's own caption calls the image a placeholder: «placeholder maroon field — stateless Nilotic peoples, no flag survives».
era-1821-1.open: Whether a flag, banner or standard existed in this period was not checked. The colour shown is not evidence of one.

era-1956.says: Wikipedia (Flag of South Sudan): captions show the national flag of Sudan as used in South Sudan for 1956-1970 and for 1970-2011, followed by SPLM/SPLA flag variants from 1983 and 1995. FOTW (Sudan): the national flag was adopted on 20 May 1970 as three horizontal stripes of red, white and black with a green triangle at the hoist, the black said to stand for the Mahdiya. FOTW (historical flags): the first flag of independent Sudan was a blue-yellow-green tricolour, adopted at independence on 1 January 1956 and in use from 1954, until 1970.
era-1956.open: Wikipedia's captions alone say Sudan's flags were used in the south; neither source describes who controlled the south during the two civil wars. The drawing shows the 1970-2011 flag; for 1956-1970 the flag was the blue-yellow-green tricolour.

era-1899.says: FOTW (Sudan, historical flags): during the Anglo-Egyptian Condominium (1899-1956) there was no individual flag for Sudan; the flags of Egypt and the United Kingdom were flown jointly, with the British flag taking precedence (Whitney Smith 1975, except at Suakin), and the Governor-General's flag was a Union Jack with a white disc and garland lettered GOVERNOR GENERAL OF THE SUDAN. Wikipedia (Anglo-Egyptian Sudan): the infobox shows the flags of the United Kingdom and the Kingdom of Egypt, with a governor-general flag and the provisional flag of April 1955; Wikipedia (Flag of South Sudan) shows Anglo-Egyptian Sudan flags for 1914-1922 and 1922-1955 without description. The text of the Sudan Convention of 19 January 1899, Article II, provides that the British and Egyptian flags shall be used together on land and water throughout the Sudan, except in Suakin, where the Egyptian flag alone is used.
era-1899.open: The convention (a primary text) and Flags of the World agree the Union Flag and the Egyptian flag flew together; the treaty does not give the British flag precedence (that is Flags of the World's statement, after Smith), and the Egyptian flag, which changed in 1914 and 1923, is not drawn. Nothing in the sources is specific to the south.

era-1821.says: Wikipedia (Mahdist State, 1885-1899): the state and its armies had no uniform flags, but used certain designs repeatedly; most carried four lines of Arabic and were usually white with coloured borders, and most units had flags of their own; the infobox flag is one of the movement's flags. FOTW (Sudan, historical flags): reports Mahdist flags in several forms (black banners of the Khalifa's family, blue-and-white banners) from battle accounts. Neither Wikipedia's nor FOTW's page on South Sudan's flag covers the Ottoman-Egyptian or Mahdist periods.
era-1821.open: The card openly shows a text placeholder. No source read describes a flag specific to the south under either regime, and none covers the Ottoman-Egyptian period from c. 1821; the Mahdist flags are described only for the movement as a whole.

era-1975.says: Wikipedia says an eagle change took effect on 21 January 1977, that Article 4.1 of the 1978 Constitution reads «The flag of Spain consists of three horizontal stripes: red, yellow and red», that Royal Decree 441/1981 of 27 February set the colours, and that the current arms date from 1981 (19 December in its text, 5 October in its infobox). FOTW says the Constitution was approved by Congress on 31 October 1978 and ratified on 6 December 1978, that Law 39 of 28 October 1981 allowed the arms on the yellow stripe, and that Royal Decree 2964/1981 (18 December, published 19 December) set the official arms and the flag's construction.
era-1975.open: The sources disagree on the 1981 arms date and on the act number. This page's «flown since 1785» is the naval ensign; the 1843 decree made it the national flag.

era-722.open: Whether a flag, banner or standard existed in this period was not checked. The colour shown is not evidence of one.
