era-218bce.open: Whether a flag, banner or standard existed in this period was not checked. The colour shown is not evidence of one.

era-1939.says: Wikipedia says National Defence Junta Decree No. 77 of 29 August 1936 re-established the red and gold bicolour, that the Eagle of Saint John was added to the shield in 1938, that regulations of 26 July and 11 October 1945 fixed a bicolour with a new eagle in force until 1977. FOTW says a decree of 27 July 1938 set the State and war flag (it does not describe the design).

era-1936.says: La Moncloa (Spanish government): after the uprising rebel troops used many flags, and a decree of 29 August 1936 signed by General Cabanellas stated 'The red and weld bi-colour flag is re-established as the Flag of Spain'. Wikipedia: Decree No. 77 of 29 August 1936 of the National Defence Junta did so and the Eagle of Saint John was added in 1938. Flags of the World: the Republic's tricolour was abolished in parts of the territory on 29 August 1936 and abandoned on 1 April 1939; a decree of 2 February 1938 set the arms with the eagle of St John, and a state flag with the arms in the yellow stripe is shown for about 1938-1977.
era-1936.open: Wikipedia's 1931 article says a military version of the Republic's flag served Republican Army units during the war. La Moncloa dates the restoration to 29 August 1936, not 'immediately' after the July uprising.

era-1931.says: La Moncloa quotes the decree of 27 April 1931: three horizontal strips of equal width, 'the upper being red, the central being yellow and the lower being dark purple'. Flags of the World: decree of 27 April 1931, equal horizontal stripes red-yellow-purple, arms with a mural crown on the central yellow stripe; Wikipedia's Second Republic flag article: the same bands (red, yellow, dark purple), adopted by decree of 27 April 1931, with the arms ensigned by a mural crown between the Pillars of Hercules; purple said to recall Castile's Pendon Morado, which modern historians doubt.
era-1931.open: The page's drawing puts purple on the top and red on the bottom, the reverse of the decree, and the page text gives 14 April (the Republic's proclamation) rather than 27 April 1931 as the flag's date. The Comuneros explanation of the purple is given by Flags of the World as a republican belief and by Wikipedia as an error, so it is not established.

era-1873.says: Wikipedia: the First Republic did not alter the flag's colours but all royal symbols of the monarchy were removed from the coat of arms (flag caption 1873-1874). La Moncloa: plans were drawn up to replace the lower red stripe with purple, but no change was made; the Republic's changes concerned the coat of arms (the mural crown, removal of the Savoy arms).
era-1873.open: Two sources, Wikipedia and a government page, so the colours are corroborated; neither describes the flag's arms beyond the removal of royal symbols. The page's wording that the flag itself lost 'the royal crown' is the arms, not the stripes.

era-1814.says: Wikipedia says a decree of 13 October 1843 from the government of Joaquín María López required Army, Navy and National Militia flags to use the war flag's colours, so that it was adopted by all the Armed Forces. FOTW says a Royal Decree of the same date made it the State and war flag and ensign.
era-1814.open: This page says the decree was under Isabella II, which is the reign; the sources attribute it to the government of the day. The era's claim about the Sexennium arms was not checked.

era-1808.says: Flags of the World (Kingdom of Spain 1808-1813, quoting the Lyon library and a Spanish Navy page): under Joseph Bonaparte the flag returned to white with a shield in six quarters (Castile, Leon, Aragon, Navarre, Granada, the Indies) and the imperial eagle, by decree of 12 July 1808; the page calls its drawing a reconstruction and the Lyon library says it is not certain the Spanish used it much, while red and yellow flags were popularised at Cadiz during the war. La Moncloa gives Joseph's arms as six quarterings with a Bonaparte inescutcheon (an arms entry, not a flag). Wikipedia says the bicolour was used by marine regiments fighting inland and raised by many Spaniards as a symbol of resistance, and does not mention Joseph. A Spanish military-history article (Atenea no. 10) describes red-yellow-red recruiting flags of Fernando VII volunteer battalions in the War of Independence, not flags of Joseph Bonaparte.
era-1808.open: The card's red-yellow-red bicolour with a Bonapartist eagle is not supported: Flags of the World describes a white flag, itself a reconstruction, and La Moncloa gives arms only; the red-yellow flag of 1808-14 appears in the sources as a resistance flag, not Joseph's. A second look found no description of Joseph Bonaparte's flag beyond the Flags of the World reconstruction.

era-1716.says: Wikipedia says a royal decree of 28 May 1785 set a red-yellow-red flag with a double-width yellow centre, to avoid confusion with other nations' flags «at long distances or with calm winds». FOTW says twelve war-ensign proposals were designed at the king's request and that a Royal Decree of 25 May 1785 set the war ensign.
era-1716.open: The decree date differs by three days (28 or 25 May 1785).

era-1516.says: Flags of the World: the red Burgundy saltire on a usually white field was the Spanish ensign 1506 to the 1670s and then a jack to 1785, brought in as the personal badge of Philip the Handsome, used first by the Tercios and the Spanish military flag from the 16th century to 1843; fields varied. Wikipedia: from the reign of Charles I (1516-1556) Spanish armies used flags with the Cross of Burgundy on different fields, and Philip II is said (citation needed) to have ordered a yellow flag with the red cross for each Tercio.
era-1516.open: The field was not always white (yellow, blue and purple are reported); FOTW ties the emblem to Philip the Handsome, whereas the page says it came from Charles's grandmother Mary of Burgundy (not stated in either source). Era dates 1516-1716 do not match the sources' 1506-1785/1843.

era-1874.says: Wikipedia's Flag of Spain pictures the red-yellow-red flag as the national flag of 1785-1808, 1813-1873 and 1874-1931, and says the yacht ensign with the royal crown on the yellow stripe was established by royal decree in 1875. La Moncloa (State Symbols of Spain): the Decree of 13 October 1843 replaced all flags with new red-and-yellow ones, and under Alfonso XII (1874-1885) an Instruction of 10 December 1878 defined the national flag in the same terms as that of 1867; its coat-of-arms section says Alfonso XII and Alfonso XIII re-established the royal crown in the arms. Flags of the World's Spain page lists the state flag and ensign of the 1843 decree.
era-1874.open: No source read states that the crowned arms appeared on the flag itself in 1874-1931; La Moncloa speaks of the coat of arms and Wikipedia of a crown only on the yacht ensign. The bicolour is attested; the crown on the emblem is a detail not established for the flag.

era-1479.says: Flags of the World: the Catholic Kings' royal standard (1492-1506) was white with the joint arms, Castile and Leon counterquartered in the first and fourth quarters and Aragon and Sicily per pale in the second and third, with a pomegranate for Granada added after 1492; the realms stayed distinct (Isabella queen of Castile and Leon, Ferdinand king of Aragon and Sicily) and the earlier ensigns were used until 1517. Wikipedia: a Catholic Monarchs' pennant dated 1475-1492; the Castilian and Aragonese flags and arms merged for the 1475 union [citation needed]; Crown of Aragon flag yellow with four red stripes.
era-1479.open: The two sources agree on a combined arms of the two crowns but not on a date (1475 / 1492-1506) and neither names 1479; FOTW shows the combination in the arms while the realms stay separate, which fits 'side by side' only if the arms themselves are not 'merged'.

era-1230.says: Wikipedia: since the final union of Castile and Leon in 1230 the Crown used a quartered flag alternating the Castilian tower and the Leonese lion. Flags of the World (Castile and Leon): the crowns were definitively united under Ferdinand III in 1230, the quartered castle-and-lion arms were devised then, the flag became the Castilian navy ensign in 1248 and was used until 1516; the 14th-century Book of All Kingdoms describes a pendon with two castles and two lions.
era-1230.open: The sources differ on the early castle form (embattled wall with towers, not the later castle) and FOTW's own page is inconsistent on the end date (early 15th century vs 1516); the first banner in this exact quartered form is later than 1230.

era-1972.says: Wikipedia's infobox gives the adoption as 22 May 1972. Flags of the World's history page says the amended flag, with the stylised corner leaves redrawn as natural bo leaves, was first unfurled at the Republic Day celebrations on 22 May 1972, and that the flag is incorporated in the Second Schedule of the constitution of 9 September 1978; the main FOTW page's 1978 is that constitution date.
era-1972.open: The two FOTW pages differ on the year (1978 on the main page, 1972 on the history page); 1972 is given by Wikipedia and the history page. Only the date and the bo-leaf change were compared; the colours were not checked against a specification, and a further small change to the leaves and background shade in 1978 is mentioned by FOTW contributors.

era-1948.says: Wikipedia: 16 Jan 1948 motion by A. Sinnalebbe to make the Lion Flag national; flag adopted for the Dominion; its gallery dates a version 1951-1972 while its text says changes in 1953 and 1972. FOTW: Lion Flag flew at independence 4 Feb 1948; a committee chaired by S.W.R.D. Bandaranaike designed a gold lion on dark red with yellow border; two stripes (green, yellow/orange, each 1/7) added when Parliament adopted the flag on 2 March 1951 to represent Muslims and Tamils.
era-1948.open: 1951 vs 1953 date conflict inside Wikipedia; FOTW and Wikipedia differ on the 1948 corner motifs.

era-1796.says: Flags of the World (British Ceylon, quoting David Prothero) describes the colonial badge, a brown elephant before a dagoba on dark blue in a red ring, in the fly of the Blue Ensign of government vessels from c.1875 to 1948, and on the governor's Union Jack. Wikipedia's Flag of Sri Lanka says the Union Flag replaced the Kandyan royal standard in 1815 and lists colonial flags for 1815-1875 and 1875-1948. Britannica says Kandy lowered the Lion Flag on 2 March 1815 and that the Union Jack continued to fly over the island until 29 October 1953. A Rootsweb page on the 1815 Kandyan convention cited by Wikipedia returned HTTP 403.
era-1796.open: The badged Blue Ensign is established only for c.1875-1948 as a government-vessel ensign; the island's general flag after 1815 was the Union Jack per Britannica, and nothing read gives a flag for 1796-1815 or a badge before 1875. Its use as the colony's general flag was not read.

era-1658.says: Wikipedia's Dutch Ceylon article calls the territory a governorate of the Dutch East India Company and its infobox shows the company flag, a tricolour with the VOC monogram; its Dutch East India Company article says the monogram appeared on corporate items including flags. Flags of the World's VOC page shows the company flag as a tricolour with the VOC cypher (upper stripe orange at first, red from between 1630 and 1660) and quotes Brownell that the flag flown was either the Netherlands flag or the company's version with the cypher. A vexillology paper on the Dutch orange/red pennant cited by Wikipedia (Poels, ICV24; nava.org PDF) returned HTTP 403 and was not read.
era-1658.open: No source read says which of the two flags was flown in Ceylon, or when; the Ceylon link rests on a Wikipedia infobox image, so the earlier 'attested' label did not hold up. The card's claim that the monogram marked company rather than state territory is not stated anywhere read.

era-1505.says: Flags of the World's Order of Christ page: the red cross with white core was used on the Discovery ships over white, green or green-and-white grounds. Wikipedia (Flag of Portugal) gives the Order of Christ cross over green and white as a naval pennon. P. E. Pieris (Ceylon and the Portuguese, 1920) records the Portuguese army carrying a 'Banner of Christ' at the battle of Mulleriyawa (after Dom Jorge de Meneses took command in May 1559), where the Sinhalese elephant captured it, and the Captain-General handing 'the Royal Standard of Portugal' to Dom Antao at the 1597 Malwana convention; neither design is described.
era-1505.open: Pieris shows Portuguese banners in Ceylon but not that the Order of Christ cross on white was the flag of Portuguese Ceylon, nor over forts; no flag specific to the colony is described anywhere read.

era-1592.says: Wikipedia's Flag of Sri Lanka says the standard of Sri Vikrama Rajasinha served as the Kandyan kingdom's flag (c.1798-1815) and the lion design continued until 1815. Wikipedia's Flags of the Kingdom of Kandy, citing E. W. Perera (1916) and a Malwatte manuscript, describes that flag as a lion passant holding a sword (blazoned gules, a lion or) found at the Royal Hospital Chelsea in 1908, and shows an earlier royal standard carried to the Dutch governor in 1785. Flags of the World (quoting DK Pocket Book 1997) calls the Kandy lion flag the national flag of Ceylon before 1815, with temple finials in the corners.
era-1592.open: The sources give the lion flag only for the late 18th century to 1815; no flag is given for the kingdom in 1592-1785 (Wikipedia shows standards of 17th-century princes, one green with an eagle). A gold frame is not described, and the red field is not called maroon by the sources.

era-1236.says: Wikipedia shows flags for Gampola (c. 1341-1408), Kotte (c. 1412-1597) and Sitawaka (c. 1521-1594) without describing them. FOTW: some older Kotte-era flags showed a whip instead of a sword, undated.
era-1236.open: Dambadeniya not covered; no source states a settled lion-and-sword emblem for the period.

era-1070.says: Wikipedia's Flag of Sri Lanka lists historical flags for the Anuradhapura period (a lion banner on a Dambulla mural), Gampola (c.1341-1408), Kotte (c.1412-1597), Sitawaka and Kandy (c.1798-1815), and none for Polonnaruwa. Its Kingdom of Polonnaruwa article has no flag text, and Flags of the World's Sri Lanka pages (main and history) describe no Polonnaruwa flag.
era-1070.open: Whether Polonnaruwa carried a lion banner, or one in gold on maroon, is not stated by any source read; the silence of these pages is not evidence that none existed. The card's drawing is an openly labelled reconstruction.

era-993.says: Wikipedia's Flag of Chola describes a Tiger Flag used by the Chola dynasty, the tiger being its royal emblem on coins, seals and banners, and cites a mention of the flag in the 12th-century Periya Puranam. Wikipedia's Chola dynasty article shows an Uttama Chola silver coin found in Sri Lanka bearing the tiger emblem. Neither Wikipedia's Flag of Sri Lanka nor Flags of the World's Sri Lanka pages mention a Chola flag.
era-993.open: No source read gives the colours of the Chola banner (the gold field is not described), shows a surviving flag, or describes a banner flown in Ceylon specifically; the Flag of Chola article is a short stub from one publisher.

era-377bce.says: Wikipedia: a Dambulla Cave no. 2 mural shows Dutugemunu (c. 162 BC) under a banner with a lion holding a sword, the only ancient representation of the lion flag (lion defaced in 1957); lion linked to Prince Vijaya in the Mahavamsa. FOTW does not cover this period.
era-377bce.open: Dating of the mural and any flag for 377 BCE-993 CE needs an archaeological source; FOTW silent.

era-1970.says: Both sources give 1970, the year this page starts the current flag. Wikipedia's infobox gives the adoption as 20 May 1970; Flags of the World dates it 20 May 1970.
era-1970.open: Only the year the current flag was adopted was compared; the design and the swatch colours were not checked against a specification.

era-1504.says: This page's own caption calls the image a placeholder: «placeholder maroon field — the Funj Sultanate».
era-1504.open: Whether a flag, banner or standard existed in this period was not checked. The colour shown is not evidence of one.

era-1070.open: Whether a flag, banner or standard existed in this period was not checked. The colour shown is not evidence of one.

era-2500bce.open: Whether a flag, banner or standard existed in this period was not checked. The colour shown is not evidence of one.

era-1956.says: Wikipedia (Flag of Sudan) says Sudan adopted a blue-yellow-green horizontal tricolour at independence on 1 January 1956, designed by the poet Macki Sufi and used until 1970, with blue for the Nile, yellow for the Sahara and green for farmlands. Flags of the World (historical flags) agrees that the first flag of independent Sudan was a blue over yellow over green tricolour, officially adopted on 1 January 1956 though in use since 1954, until 1970, and that the naval ensign was white with the national flag in the canton.
era-1956.open: Macki Sufi and the meanings of the colours rest on Wikipedia alone, and FOTW's 'used since 1954' is not matched by Wikipedia; the page's earlier meanings (peace, the south) are in neither source. FOTW's main page covers the 1970 flag and does not mention the 1956 flag or Macki Sufi.

era-1899.says: Wikipedia (Anglo-Egyptian Sudan): infobox shows the Union Jack and the Egyptian flag (1922-1958) captioned 'Flags of the United Kingdom and the Kingdom of Egypt', 1899-1956; Wikipedia's flag article adds that the British flag took precedence. Flags of the World (historical flags): no individual flag, 'the two flags of Egypt and the United Kingdom were used, with the British flag taking precedence' (Smith 1975: Union Jack always first, except at Suakin where only the Egyptian flag flew); the Governor-General's flag was a Union Jack with a white disc and laurel garland (Prothero 1999); a white 'SUDAN' flag was made for the April 1955 Bandung conference; a so-called Anglo-Egyptian Sudan flag is called 'completely fictitious' (Kelly 2022).
era-1899.open: The Egyptian flag changed in this period (red with crescent and star until 1914; three crescents and stars 1914-1923; green with crescent and three stars 1923-1954 per Heimer citing Smith) and the page does not say which one it draws.

era-1885.says: Wikipedia (Flag of Sudan) says that in 1881 the Mahdi handed Abdallahi ibn Muhammad a black flag, which he used to recruit Baggara and other western tribes, and pictures a black standard used in Mahdist Sudan. Wikipedia (Mahdist State) says the state had no uniform flags, that most flags carried four lines of Arabic text and were usually white with coloured borders, and that the 'Black Flag' army under Abdallahi, later led by his brother Yaqub, became the state's main army. Flags of the World (historical flags) cites G. W. Stevens for the black banner of the Khalifa's brother at Omdurman, and a painting of the Khalifa's black flag held upright by the dead; FOTW's page on the current flag says the black stripe stands for the Mahdiya revolution (the Black Flag); its historical page also lists a black-red-green tricolour with crescent and spear and a green-gold-green banner with white lettering.
era-1885.open: The black flag is attested by both publishers for the Mahdist State, but as the flag of one army and of the Khalifa, not a uniform state flag, and neither describes an inscription on it; the card's black field with an Arabic inscription is a placeholder drawing. Other Mahdist banners were white, red, blue or green.

era-1821.says: WorldStatesmen lists the Ottoman flag (a red flag with a white crescent and star) for Sudan from 1820/22 to 26 January 1885, with no basis given. Wikipedia (Turco-Egyptian Sudan) shows an infobox flag captioned 1867-1881 without describing it; Wikipedia (Flag of Egypt) pictures Egyptian flags of 1793-1844, 1844-1867 and 1867-1881 and says the stars and crescents of Muhammad Ali's flag have been read as symbolising his sovereignty over Egypt, Sudan and the Hejaz. Flags of the World says it has no information on flags of 1821-1885.
era-1821.open: Only one compiled list names a flag for Sudan in this period, and it gives no source; Wikipedia's Egyptian flags (three crescents and stars on red, described only in captions) differ from the single crescent and star drawn on the card. No source read describes a flag actually flown in Sudan.

era-1975.says: Wikipedia: five horizontal bands of green, white, red (quadruple width), white and green with a large yellow five-pointed star, designed in a national competition (winner Jack Pinas) and accepted by parliament in 1975; red represents progress, white freedom and justice, green the fertility of the land, the star unity and a golden future. FOTW: the flag was established by a decree of the Governor dated 25 November 1975, published in the Government Gazette of 24 November 1975, with the colours defined and the same meanings (red progress and love, green hope and fertility, white peace and justice, the star unity of all ethnic groups).
era-1975.open: The sources give the symbolism differently from the page, which says red stands for 'justice and the road to independence'; Wikipedia gives red as progress and white as freedom and justice. FOTW also reports a 'new national flag?' discussion, but no change since 1975.

era-1500.says: This page's own caption calls the image a placeholder: «placeholder maroon field — indigenous and earliest colonial era, no flag survives».
era-1500.open: Whether a flag, banner or standard existed in this period was not checked. The colour shown is not evidence of one.

era-1954.says: Wikipedia: the pre-independence flag, designed by Noni Lichtveld and adopted in 1959 after the Charter for the Kingdom, was a plain white field with five coloured stars (black for Africans, brown for Asian Indians, yellow for Javanese and Chinese, red for Amerindians, white for Europeans) connected by a black ellipse; it was also the governor's flag and was replaced in 1975. FOTW: the National Decree of 8 December 1959 (effective 15 December 1959) defines a white field with five black-bordered stars in black, brown, yellow, red and white linked by an elliptical black band; the flag of the overseas territory was abolished on 25 November 1975.
era-1954.open: The page's red oval is contradicted: both sources give a black ellipse. The flag dates from 1959, not 1954 (the year of the Charter), and FOTW's own headings also give 1966 for the territory flag; FOTW names Frank Essed as designer where Wikipedia names Noni Lichtveld.

era-1667.says: Wikipedia (Flag of Suriname) says that after the Kingdom of the Netherlands was established in 1815 the Dutch tricolour was used in the colony, that a colony flag with the arms was discussed but never used in practice, and that the governor's flag before 1959 was the Dutch flag with white circles in the corner. Flags of the World (Dutch colony) records a flag with the arms as doubtful, and a contributor who found no coat of arms on the white stripe in photographs (1870-1955) or detailed drawings of Fort Zeelandia (dated 16xx-1900), only a plain tricolour.
era-1667.open: Wikipedia covers 1815-1959 only; for 1667-1815 the support is one Flags of the World contributor's reading of drawings, and the flags of the West India Company and the Society of Suriname are not described. The colours of the Dutch flag before the 19th century are not covered.

era-1905.says: Wikipedia: a law of 28 October 1905 removed the union mark from the Swedish flag as of 1 November 1905, and the flag law of 22 June 1906 set the colours as light medium blue and gold-yellow. Store norske leksikon (Roede): the union mark was removed from Swedish flags on 1 November 1905 after the dissolution of the union; the flag law of 22 June 1906 changed the blue to the lighter 'ljust mellanblå' (the earlier blue was dark, much like Norway's); the national, merchant and state flag adopted 22 June 1906 in proportions 5:8. FOTW: flag 'officially re-adopted 22 June 1906', with pictures of a blue cloth with a yellow cross from the 16th century.
era-1905.open: The flag was not 'unchanged since 1905': the blue was lightened in 1906; 'longest unbroken run of any flag in this lineage' is the page's own comparison, not in the sources.

era-900.says: This page's own caption calls the image a placeholder: «placeholder maroon field — pre-unification era, no flag survives».
era-900.open: Whether a flag, banner or standard existed in this period was not checked. The colour shown is not evidence of one.

era-98.says: This page's own caption calls the image a placeholder: «placeholder maroon field — Suiones & Vendel-era Sweden, no flag survives».
era-98.open: Whether a flag, banner or standard existed in this period was not checked. The colour shown is not evidence of one.

era-1814.says: Wikipedia's Flag of Sweden says a common military ensign for Sweden and Norway with a white saltire on red in the canton was introduced on 6 June 1815 and a common civil ensign in 1818, and that a royal resolution of 20 June 1844 gave both countries their national flags with a union mark in the canton combining the colours of both countries. Store norske leksikon (Sveriges flagg og vaapen) says that in 1844-1905 the flag carried the union mark (the 'Sildesalaten') in the upper hoist field, introduced to meet Norwegian demands for equality, that it was used in both countries as the naval jack and as the common flag of diplomatic missions, and that it was removed from Swedish flags on 1 November 1905.
era-1814.open: The card's mark belongs to 1844-1905; from 1815 to 1844 the common ensigns carried a red canton with a white saltire instead. The mark combines the colours of both countries (blue, yellow, red and white), not simply red, white and blue.

era-1523.says: Wikipedia says the oldest recorded pictures of a blue cloth with a yellow cross date from the early 1500s (citation needed), that the first legal description is a royal warrant of 19 April 1562, and that a warrant of 1569 required the yellow cross on battle standards and banners. FOTW, quoting a Swedish Institute leaflet, gives the same early-16th-century pictures, the 1569 warrant, reliable evidence on Swedish vessels from the 1620s under Gustav II Adolf, and the oldest existing flag warrant of 1663 (a triple-tailed flag, merchant ships square-cut).
era-1523.open: Neither source dates the flag to 1523. This page used to say the cross was the settled national banner throughout 1523–1814; the sources give 1562 and 1569 as the first legal steps and the 1620s as reliable evidence at sea. Wikipedia gives 1442 and 1448 for the arms that inspired it, inconsistently.

era-1397.says: FOTW's Kalmar Union page says sources are scant: the evidence is two letters of 1430 in which King Erik orders the priests of Vadstena and Kalmar to wear the 'banner of the realms', described as a red cross on a yellow field; it adds that there is no pictorial evidence and no surviving flag, and that a red Scandinavian cross on yellow seen in a museum is a recreation. Wikipedia's Emblems of the Kalmar Union gives the same two letters and the same description, quoting FOTW's account in its notes.
era-1397.open: The two sources are not independent, since Wikipedia cites FOTW's author for the letters. The banner is known only from the 1430 text, and no source puts the Three Crowns or discs on it; the Three Crowns appear in the union's arms and seal, not the banner.

era-995.says: Wikipedia says the Three Crowns on blue appear since at least 1336 and that blue and yellow are said to have been Swedish colours since Magnus III's arms in 1275 (no citation).
era-995.open: Arms, not a flag. The page's mention of Magnus Eriksson's seals was not found in the source, and the earliest date given there is 1336, not 995.

era-1848.says: Wikipedia says a federal decree of 12 December 1889 set the cross arms at one-sixth longer than wide (7:6), that the Federal Act on the protection of arms of 2013 (in force 2017) defines the flag as a Swiss cross on a square background, and that the cross height was fixed at 5:8 in 2017. FOTW says Federal Order no. 111 of 12 December 1889 set the cross's relative dimensions with arms one sixth longer than wide, that Act no. 232.21 of 2013 defines the flag and colours, and that the margin was not officially fixed before 2017.
era-1848.open: The sources disagree on 1848: Wikipedia says the Federal Constitution did not name a national flag but prescribed the federal flag for federal troops, while FOTW says the flag was enshrined in the Constitution of 1848. This page says the 1889 decree fixed the proportions «for the first time»; FOTW says it replaced a five-square cross.

era-58bce.says: This page's own caption calls the image a placeholder: «placeholder maroon field — Helvetii, Roman Helvetia, and early medieval overlordship, no flag survives».
era-58bce.open: Whether a flag, banner or standard existed in this period was not checked. The colour shown is not evidence of one.

era-1815.says: Wikipedia says the Tagsatzung reintroduced the white cross on red for the federal seal, accepted on 4 July 1815, and that Bachmann's battalion flag of 12 October 1815 had a red square field and a white cross. FOTW says the restored Confederation adopted a seal with a short white cross and that honorary flags were given to returning regiments in 1815.
era-1815.open: Both sources describe the seal and army flags, not a national flag; Wikipedia says the Constitution of 1848 did not name one.

era-1798.says: Wikipedia: the Helvetic Republic replaced the earlier flags with a green, red and yellow tricolour. FOTW (Helvetic Republic 1798-1803): the flag was green-red-yellow horizontally, the colours being adopted as national colours and cockade colours by the General Assembly on 14 April 1798, with the Directorate fixing details on 13 February 1799; the legion regiments carried flags with William Tell. The cantonal government of Basel-Stadt (1998 press release): green-red-yellow was the national flag of the 'one and indivisible Helvetic Republic'. Universität Freiburg: the French chose a green-red-yellow tricolour rather than a Swiss cross, and it vanished after a few years. The HLS dates the republic 12 April 1798 - 10 March 1803 and shows an 1798 flag in the Bundesbriefmuseum.
era-1798.open: The Liberty figure drawn on the page is not confirmed by any source read; the HLS photograph is of the flag but its stripe order was not read as text.

era-1291.says: Wikipedia says the first attested use of a white cross to identify Confederate troops was at Laupen in 1339, as two textile strips on clothing, and that at Arbedo about 1422 a triangular red flag with an elongated white cross was possibly the first flag used for the Confederacy rather than one canton. FOTW (Mills) says the Laupen troops wore a long-armed white linen cross stitched on breasts, sleeves and thighs, that at Arbedo in 1422 Confederate levies carried red triangular guidons with a white cross, and that the assumption that the flag derives from Schwyz's red banner is incorrect.
era-1291.open: The origin is unproven: FOTW mentions a derivation from a Holy Roman Empire banner, a tenuous Theban Legion link and a stitched-stripes theory. 1291 is the Confederacy's traditional founding, not a flag date.

era-1648.says: Wikipedia: white cross a field sign by the late 13th–early 14th century; Laupen 1339; Arbedo 1422 triangular banner; 1540 first mention of a separate Confederate flag. FOTW: 1339 white linen crosses; 1422 red triangular guidons with a white cross; 1540 last battlefield use; the Confederation was flagless in 1798.
era-1648.open: The 1648 recognition date is not in either source.

era-1803.says: Wikipedia (Flag of Switzerland): after the French invasion of 1798 the Helvetic Republic confiscated all earlier flags and replaced them with a green-red-yellow tricolour; General Bachmann used the white cross on red in his campaigns of 1800 and 1815, and the cross had long been carried on cantonal war flags. FOTW (Switzerland): the white cross on red disappeared from use after 1540 until the French invasion of 1798, the Confederation had no flag but a state seal, and an honorary federal flag was granted to regiments returning from France in 1815. Second look: World Statesmen lists a Swiss Confederation war flag c.1470 - 14 Apr 1798 and the Helvetic Republic flag 1798 - 10 Mar 1803, then the Swiss flag only from 1848, with nothing listed for 1803-1848.
era-1803.open: Neither Wikipedia, FOTW nor World Statesmen describes flags in the Mediation years (1803-1815) or says the old cross persisted at cantonal level under French oversight; the sources even disagree on whether the cross was out of use from 1540 to 1798 (FOTW) or the Confederation's war flag from c.1470 (World Statesmen). The card's claim is not confirmed. The Historical Dictionary of Switzerland (hls-dhs-dss.ch) returned HTTP 403 and was not retried or worked around.

era-2024.says: Wikipedia (Flag of Syria): the caretaker government used the green-white-black three-red-star flag de facto from 8 December 2024 and the Constitutional Declaration of 13 March 2025 kept it as the national flag. Flags of the World: the interim constitution of 13 March 2025 defines it in Article 6, and its 'Since 1932' pages list the two-star flag for 1980-2024 and the tricolour again from 2025. The French Vexillological Society journal (Capron, 2024) says that after the rebels entered Damascus in December 2024 the 1932 tricolour became officially the national flag again and flew in ministries beside the HTS flag (its text misnames the colours as green-white-red).
era-2024.open: Three publishers agree the three-star green-white-black flag is the flag of the transitional authorities. The start date is not fixed: Wikipedia says de facto from 8 December 2024, the French journal says from the rebels' entry into Damascus in December 2024, and FOTW dates the flag from 2025 (constitution of 13 March 2025). Star size and colour swatches were not checked against a specification.

era-636-1.says: This page's own caption calls the image a placeholder: «placeholder maroon field — pre-heraldic antiquity».
era-636-1.open: Whether a flag, banner or standard existed in this period was not checked. The colour shown is not evidence of one.

era-1958.says: Wikipedia's «Flag of the United Arab Republic» gives adoption in 1958 and relinquishment in 1961, 1972, within a year of this era's 1958 and 1961. The Flags of the World page that article links also carries 1961, and has 1958 next to a word about adopting.
era-1958.open: Only the dates were compared. The Flags of the World page was matched on the two years appearing in its text and on one of them sitting beside the word adopt, introduce, establish or the like; it was not read for what it says about this flag. The design and the swatch colours were not checked against a specification.

era-1980.says: Wikipedia (Flag of Syria): the 1972 Federation flag was abrogated on 29 March 1980 and replaced by a two-star flag, the 1958-61 United Arab Republic flag readopted to show Syria's commitment to Arab unity. Flags of the World (Historical Flags since 1932): 1980-2024 was a reintroduction of the United Arab Republic flag of 1958-61 (red-white-black horizontal tricolour with two green stars); its overview page lists the flag for 1980-2024.
era-1980.open: The exact 29 March 1980 date is Wikipedia's alone; Flags of the World gives only the years. What the flag is called in Syrian law was not found.

era-1972.says: Wikipedia: the 1963 flag was replaced on 1 January 1972 by the Federation of Arab Republics flag. FOTW 'Historical Flags Since 1932' gives 1972-1980 as the Federation flag with the Hawk of Quraish.
era-1972.open: The hawk is drawn by hand and simplified (the Commons file is a 66 KB drawing too heavy to embed); the shield on its chest is not checked against the Federation's arms.

era-1963.says: Wikipedia: the restored flag was replaced on 1 May 1963 by a flag with three green stars on red-white-black. FOTW 'Historical Flags Since 1932' has a separate entry for 1963-1972 (red-white-black, three green stars).
era-1963.open: Wikipedia gives 1 May 1963 and does not say what flag flew between the coup of 8 March and then; FOTW gives no day.

era-1961.says: Wikipedia: the green-white-black independence flag with three red stars was restored on 28 September 1961 and replaced on 1 May 1963 by a three-green-star flag and on 1 January 1972 by the Federation of Arab Republics flag. FOTW 'Historical Flags Since 1932': Syria left the union on 28 September 1961 and reverted to the 1946-58 flag; separate entries follow for 1963-1972 (red-white-black, three green stars) and 1972-1980 (Federation flag with the Hawk of Quraish).
era-1961.open: FOTW gives 28 September in one note and 29 September in another for the raising; Wikipedia says 28 September 1961.

era-1946.says: Wikipedia: flag defined by decree 3111 of 14 May 1930, ratio 1:2, three red five-pointed stars; adopted for independence on 17 April 1946; replaced by the UAR flag in 1958. FOTW 'Historical Flags Since 1932': green-white-black with three red five-pointed stars, 1:2, for 1946 (independence) to 1958; first hoisted in Aleppo on 1 January 1932 and in Damascus on 11 June 1932. FOTW 'Until 1932' quotes Article 4 of the 14 May 1930 constitution from the League of Nations Official Journal (three equal bands green, white, black, with three red five-pointed stars, length double the height).
era-1946.open: The sources differ on the flag's origin: 14 May 1930 (decree text, Wikipedia) against 1 January and 11 June 1932 (first hoisting, FOTW); FOTW calls a separate 1930-32 flag 'probably erroneous'. The 1946-58 years themselves are stated by FOTW's headings and by Wikipedia.

era-1920.says: Wikipedia (Flag of Syria): Gouraud's blue flag with a white crescent was used 24 July to 1 September 1920; on 22 June 1922 the Federation adopted a green-white-green flag with a French canton, kept by the State of Syria until the republic of 14 May 1930, whose constitution defined the green-white-black flag with three red stars. Flags of the World (Historical Flags until 1932) agrees on the 1922-30 flag and says the 1920 crescent flag 'might have been used'. The French Vexillological Society's journal (Capron, Drapeaux & Pavillons 160, 2024) independently describes Gouraud's flag as azure with a white crescent and a French tricolour canton, the federation (from 28 June 1922) and then the State of Syria flying green-white-green with the French flag in the upper quarter, and the 1930 constitution flag, officially hoisted at Aleppo on 1 January 1932 and at Damascus on 11 June 1932.
era-1920.open: Three publishers agree on the 1922-1930 flag (Wikipedia, Flags of the World, and the French society journal); the 1920 flag rests on the same three but FOTW calls it only possible. The card draws only the 1922-30 flag. The green-white-black flag is dated by the constitution to 1930 but, according to the French journal, was first hoisted in 1932, a detail the card does not give. The federation's date is 22 June (Wikipedia) or 28 June 1922 (French journal).

era-1517.says: Wikipedia (Flag of Syria) and Flags of the World (Historical Flags until 1932) both say Syria used the Ottoman flag until the Ottomans left in September 1918; Wikipedia (Mamluk Sultanate) has a plain red Ottoman banner replacing the yellow Mamluk one at Damascus in 1516; Wikipedia (Flag of the Ottoman Empire) dates the crescent and star on red to the navy decree of 1793 and the national flag of 1844. The Australian War Memorial record (RELAWM04772) shows what Ottoman troops carried near Damascus in October 1918: a crimson silk regimental standard of the 46th Infantry Regiment bearing the sultan's toghra in gold, pole once topped by a crescent and star. Çetin (2021, museum survey) says the Ottoman state used many banners at once and that crescent-and-star depictions exist before Selim III (1789-1807).
era-1517.open: The Ottoman flag as the flag in use in Syria up to 1918 is supported by two compiled publishers and now a museum record from Damascus itself, but its form varied: plain red or Zulfikar war flags and several concurrent banners in the earlier centuries (Çetin), crescent-and-star on red only formalised in 1793/1844, and crimson regimental standards with the toghra in 1918. The card's single-crescent drawing therefore fits only part of the span. Nothing read says how the eyalets of Damascus and Aleppo flew it.

era-1260.says: Wikipedia (Mamluk Sultanate): the Mamluk sultans followed the Ayyubids in using yellow as the official colour of the sultan and of sultanic banners (Baybars is said to have noted the yellow of his banners against Bohemund's red ones); sultans and emirs bore personal blazons on their banners, Baybars a panther or lion, Qalawun a fleur-de-lis; red banners were also used, and in 1516 Ibn Tulun noted the Mamluks' yellow silk banner replaced by the Ottomans' plain red one. Flags of the World (Historical Flags until 1932): the Book of All Kingdoms (late 14th century) gives Damascus a yellow pendon with a white moon. Wikipedia (Zengid dynasty): yellow remained the symbolic colour of the Mamluk rulers.
era-1260.open: Yellow sultanic banners and personal blazons are described, but no source gives one fixed state flag for the Mamluks, and none gives an eagle blazon, so the card's eagle is a reconstruction not found in the sources. No flag survives from the sources read.

era-1174.says: Wikipedia (Zengid dynasty) calls the yellow eagle banner a 'supposed flag of Saladin', 'apparently inherited from the Zengids', and its footnote quotes J. Hathaway (SUNY Press, 2012): Saladin 'supposedly' carried it and Ayyubid and Mamluk sultanic banners were yellow. Wikipedia (Eagle of Saladin) says the eagle is commonly believed to be his emblem but that historical sources do not confirm it, citing Smith (1975) and Rabbat (1995) for the Cairo citadel carving; Wikipedia (Ayyubid dynasty) says the same. Wikipedia (Mamluk Sultanate) has the Mamluks following the Ayyubids in yellow.
era-1174.open: Every statement of the yellow eagle banner traces to Wikipedia or to Hathaway's book as quoted in a Wikipedia footnote, and all of them hedge it ('supposed', 'apparently', 'supposedly'). I could not open Hathaway (the Google Books lookup returned HTTP 429, and the web-search budget for this task ran out), so no independent reference or chronicle passage was read. No source read gives a Syria-wide state flag for 1174-1260.

era-750.says: Wikipedia (Abbasid Caliphate): the infobox shows the Abbasid Black Standard; the text says the Abbasids kept black as their dynastic colour for banners, headdresses and garments, in contrast to the white of the Umayyads. FOTW 'Pan-Arab Colours' (quoting Abdul Hadi 1986): the Abbasid dynasty (750-1258), ruling from Baghdad, took black as a symbol of mourning for the Prophet's relatives and for Karbala.
era-750.open: Both sources give the colour of the dynasty's banners, not a flag of Syria; neither describes banners of the local successor dynasties between 750 and 1174, which the page rightly does not treat as one flag.

era-636.says: Wikipedia (Umayyad Caliphate): the Umayyad banners were white, after the banner of Mu'awiya ibn Abi Sufyan; the infobox deliberately carries no flag. FOTW 'Pan-Arab Colours' (quoting Abdul Hadi 1986): the Umayyads (661-750, Damascus) took white as their symbolic colour, to recall the Battle of Badr and to set themselves apart from the Abbasids' black.
era-636.open: The sources give a dynastic colour, not a documented design beyond a plain field; they date Umayyad rule from 661 (Mu'awiya), not 636, which is the year of the Muslim conquest of Syria.

era-1949.says: Wikipedia's Flag of the Republic of China says the flag was made the national flag by the Nationalist government in 1928 and, after the defeat in the civil war and the 1949 founding of the PRC, has remained in official use in the Taiwan Area. FOTW's Taiwan page dates the flag to 1928 (Decree No. 47, 19 December 1928) and its Chinese Republic history says the Nationalist government took residence in Taiwan from 1949, retaining the flag.
era-1949.open: Design and swatch colours were not checked against a specification. FOTW's contributors stress that Taiwan had been ROC-ruled since 1945, so 1949 marks the government's retreat, not the flag's arrival.

era-1624-1.says: This page's own caption calls the image a placeholder: «placeholder green field — pre-colonial era, no flag survives».
era-1624-1.open: Whether a flag, banner or standard existed in this period was not checked. The colour shown is not evidence of one.

era-1945.says: Wikipedia's infobox gives 25 October 1945 for adoption in Taiwan (flag law of December 1928 on the mainland). FOTW gives 1928 (Decree No. 47, 19 December 1928) and, in a contributor's comment, says Taiwan has been under ROC rule since 1945.
era-1945.open: 'Ordinary province for the first time' is not covered; FOTW's 1945 support is a contributor comment, not the page text.

era-1895.says: Wikipedia (Taiwan under Japanese rule) shows the Japanese sun-disc flag (the 1870 merchant flag) as the colony's infobox flag, with the 1895 Republic of Formosa's yellow tiger flag as its predecessor. Wikipedia (Flag of Japan) says the Hinomaru was decreed the merchant flag in 1870 and was the de facto national flag, including throughout the Second World War; Flags of the World (Japan) gives the 1870 merchant flag design and its later fixing as the national flag. Flags of the World (Taiwan under Japanese control) lists separate Government-General flags for police (1901-1945), post and vessels, and (Democratic Republic of Taiwan, 1895) a yellow tiger on a blue or black field for 25 May-7 June 1895.
era-1895.open: On a closer read the support is thin: neither source's text says the Hinomaru was raised over colonial Taiwan, and the claim rests on Wikipedia's infobox image and on the Hinomaru's status as Japan's de facto national flag (Japan's own page). The Government-General's police, post and ship flags and the 1895 republic's tiger flag are not drawn. Further searches for a Taiwanese or Japanese institutional source could not be completed (the shared search allowance was used up).

era-1683.says: Wikipedia (Taiwan under Qing rule) shows the Qing flag as the infobox flag for 1889-1895 only. Wikipedia (Flag of the Qing dynasty) says the Qing had no official flag at the time of the 1856 Arrow Incident, that a triangular dragon flag was introduced in 1862 for naval and government use and never formally became the national flag, and that the rectangular Yellow Dragon Flag was promulgated in 1888 and adopted in 1889. Flags of the World (Imperial Dragon Flag) shows dragon flags of 1872 and 1890 for China and does not mention Taiwan. Royal Museums Greenwich's catalogue text for a Qing naval ensign says the Qing did not have a national flag of standard design before the second half of the 19th century, that the Zongli Yamen announced a yellow triangular dragon flag in 1866 for ships hired against pirates, and that it was adopted as the state flag and naval ensign in 1872.
era-1683.open: The Yellow Dragon Flag is documented for Taiwan only for 1889-1895. For 1683-1862 the sources describe no Qing state flag, and nothing read says what flew over Taiwan; the dates for the triangular flag differ (Wikipedia 1862, Royal Museums Greenwich 1866 and 1872) and the rectangular form is dated 1888 or 1889.

era-1661.says: Wikipedia (Kingdom of Tungning) calls it a dynastic maritime state of 1662-1683 founded by the Ming loyalist Koxinga, and its infobox pictures a 'Ming Cheng' flag, but no text describes any flag. Wikipedia (Koxinga), (Siege of Fort Zeelandia), (Southern Ming) and (Zheng Jing) mention no Tungning flag or banner, and Flags of the World's Taiwan page does not cover the kingdom.
era-1661.open: No source read describes a Tungning flag in text, so the infobox picture cannot be checked against a description. The Ming red-and-gold reference on the card is not covered by any source.

era-1624.says: Wikipedia (Dutch Formosa) shows the Dutch East India Company flag as the flag of Dutch Formosa in its infobox, and says the governor gave village leaders a Prinsenvlag (Prince's Flag, the flag of William the Silent) to display. Flags of the World (Netherlands East India Company) describes the company flag with a VOC monogram and says its upper stripe was first orange and changed to red between 1630 and 1660; Wikipedia (Dutch East India Company) says the monogram appeared on company flags. Wikipedia (Spanish Formosa) gives a Cross of Burgundy infobox flag for the Spanish north (1626-1642).
era-1624.open: The card's caption calls the flag the Prince's Flag, which was orange-white-blue; the drawing shows the red-white-blue company flag without its monogram. That the company flag flew over Fort Zeelandia is not stated in text, and the Spanish Formosa flag is not drawn.

era-1991.says: Wikipedia: the national flag was adopted on 24 November 1992 (red, white, green in 2:3:2, yellow crown with an arc of seven stars; designer Zuhur Habibullaev), replacing the Tajik SSR flag. FOTW: adopted 24 November 1992 by law; white stripe 1.5 times the width of red and green; independence recognised 9 September 1991; before the new design the former Soviet colours were used without communist symbols (undated).
era-1991.open: The page's era start 1991 is the independence year; the flag itself dates from 1992. 'Unchanged through the civil war' is not covered.

era-8bce.says: This page's own caption calls the image a placeholder: «placeholder maroon field — ancient, Persian-speaking Sogdiana and Bactria».
era-8bce.open: Whether a flag, banner or standard existed in this period was not checked. The colour shown is not evidence of one.

era-bmac.says: This page's own caption calls the image a placeholder: «placeholder maroon field — Bronze Age Oxus civilization, millennia before any flag».
era-bmac.open: Whether a flag, banner or standard existed in this period was not checked. The colour shown is not evidence of one.

era-1929.says: Wikipedia (Flag of Tajikistan): the Tajik SSR flag was approved in 1953, derived from the USSR flag with added white and green stripes, and used until 1992; Wikipedia (Tajik SSR) dates the infobox flag 1953-1991. FOTW (su-tj): adopted 20 March 1953, red with white and green stripes near the bottom, hammer and sickle with star on the obverse. FOTW (tj-ir, reproducing Encyclopaedia Iranica): the Tajik ASSR constitution of 28 April 1929 set a red flag (1:2) with the state arms upper left; February 1931 a plain red flag with a Russian inscription in gold letters; 20 March 1953 the red flag with white and green stripes.
era-1929.open: Attested for the Soviet red flag, the 1929 and 1931 forms and the 1953-91 stripes design. The gold stripe drawn on the page is not in any source. FOTW's Iranica-based text is a copy; the Iranica site itself returned 403 and was not read. The republic's status (ASSR to 1929, SSR from 5 December 1929) comes from Wikipedia's Tajik SSR page.

era-1920.says: Flags of the World (Encyclopaedia Iranica text): the Bukharan People's Republic's constitution of 23 September 1921 set a flag of green over red stripes with a gold star and crescent and the initials BNSR, the upper stripe turning red in October 1923; the republic was abolished in October 1924. Wikipedia (Bukharan People's Soviet Republic, 1920-24) says its flag combined the hammer and sickle with the traditional crescent, and shows a flag for it and for the Tajik ASSR of 1924-29.
era-1920.open: The two sources describe the flag differently (green over red with star and crescent, then red; or hammer and sickle with crescent). No flag is described for 1924-1929 apart from the Tajik ASSR flag adopted on 28 April 1929 (red with arms at the upper left, per the Iranica text). The drawing follows the 1921-23 flag only.

era-1500.says: For the Emirate of Bukhara (1785-1920): Wikipedia (Emirate of Bukhara) shows the Bukhara national flag as published in 1929 by the deposed emir Sayyid Alim Khan in La voix de la Boukharie opprimee. Flags of the World (Encyclopaedia Iranica text) describes that royal standard, taken as the state flag, as light green with gold inscriptions, an open hand, a star and crescent and an orange border; another FOTW page gives the emir's flag and a museum flag as green with a red border and a white hand, crescent and three stars.
era-1500.open: This covers the Emirate (1785-1920) only: no flag of the Khanate of Bukhara (c. 1500-1785) is described by any source read (Wikipedia's Khanate article is silent). The sources differ on the border colour and the charges, and FOTW calls the national flag 'elusive'; the plain green field with crescent is a simplification.

era-1370.says: Wikipedia (Timurid Empire): the 'sign of Timur', three equal circles in a triangle, is described by Clavijo and Ibn Arabshah on seals and appears on Timurid coins; Timur is thought to have generally used red banners, possibly with a crescent, a black banner with a silver dragon is reported for the Indian campaign and golden dragons before the China campaign; 'there is little certainty about the actual flag'. A flag with three circles in the 1375 Catalan Atlas may be associated with the Timurids (Kadoi, 'On the Timurid flag', 2010), while other authors read it as the Yuan flag. Neither Tajikistan page covers the Timurids. Kadoi's article (on academia.edu, HTTP 403) and the Encyclopaedia Iranica entry 'Central Asia v' were tried; the Iranica entry mentions no Timurid banner.
era-1370.open: The three-ring device is documented as a tamgha on coins and seals, and its link to a flag rests on one study of the Catalan Atlas which could not be opened; the sources read describe red or dragon banners, not a standard of three rings, and give no blue field. No second independent source was found.

era-1220.says: Wikipedia (Chagatai Khanate) dates the khanate from 1227 and says the 1375 Catalan Atlas shows the Chagatai ruler's cities with 'the Chagatai flag', without describing it. Neither the Wikipedia nor the Flags of the World Tajikistan page covers the Mongol conquest or any banner of this span.
era-1220.open: No source read describes the Chagatai or Mongol-successor banner, so the dark placeholder shown stands for nothing documented. This is a gap in the sources read, not a finding that no banner existed; the Mongol conquest date (1220) is not in the Wikipedia article read.

era-819.says: Wikipedia and Flags of the World (Tajikistan) tie the crown on the modern flag to the Samanids but describe no Samanid flag. Wikipedia (Black Standard): black was the dynastic colour of the Abbasids after 750. Wikipedia (Samanid Empire): the dynasty's four founders were made governors under Abbasid suzerainty in 819; no banner colour is given.
era-819.open: The plain black stands in for the Abbasid suzerains; no source read states a Samanid or successor-dynasty flag or that the Samanids flew black. Many dynasties ruled between 819 and 1220, none with a documented banner here.

era-819-1.says: Wikipedia (Umayyad Caliphate): the Umayyad banners were white, after the banner of Mu'awiya ibn Abi Sufyan. Wikipedia (Pan-Arab colors): white was the Umayyad dynastic colour. Wikipedia (Black Standard): the Abbasid Revolution against the Umayyads adopted black, and black remained the Abbasid dynastic colour after 750.
era-819-1.open: The sources describe caliphal banners, not any flag of Transoxiana; the plain white is a reconstruction of the Umayyad colour and covers only the period to 750, after which black is the colour reported. No surviving banner is known from these sources.

era-1964.says: Wikipedia's infobox gives the adoption as 30 June 1964. FOTW: Tanganyika and Zanzibar merged on 26 April 1964 and the union flag recombined the two predecessors, the lower green stripe of Tanganyika's flag taking Zanzibar's blue and the stripes rearranged diagonally; the name Tanzania was adopted 29 October 1964; the 1971 Flag Act gives the flag legal validity from 26 April 1964.
era-1964.open: The sources differ on the day (Wikipedia 30 June 1964, FOTW 26 April 1964 for the union and flag), but agree on 1964; the colour meanings and swatch values were not compared.

era-1700-1.says: This page's own caption calls the image a placeholder: «placeholder maroon field — earliest recorded coastal trade era, no flag survives with confidence».
era-1700-1.open: Whether a flag, banner or standard existed in this period was not checked. The colour shown is not evidence of one.

era-1919.says: Wikipedia: Britain administered Tanganyika Territory from about 1919 under a League of Nations mandate, then as a UN trust territory; its flag in 1923-1961 was a British Red Ensign with the territory emblem; the independence flag of 9 December 1961 was green with a gold-edged black band. FOTW: the mandate was formalised 20 July 1922, trust status from 1946; Red and Blue Ensigns carried a giraffe-head badge (approved 1919) until the end of 1961; the 9 December 1961 flag was green-black-green with thin gold stripes, based on TANU's flag.
era-1919.open: The drawing shows only the 1961 independence flag, the last years of the era; the dates of the Red Ensign differ (Wikipedia 1923, FOTW 1919); the page's colour meanings are covered only for FOTW's 'land, people, minerals' reading.

era-1885.says: Wikipedia (Flag of Tanzania) lists the colony's flag for 1891-1918 as a horizontal black-white-red tricolour with the German Reichsadler in a white circle in the middle, and a German East Africa Company flag for 1885-1891. Wikipedia (German East Africa) gives the colony 1885-1918, with the Colonial Office service flag in the infobox and a 1914 proposal that was never used. Flags of the World (German East Africa) gives the governors' flag, adopted 4 May 1891 and abolished in 1919, as the national flag with the uncrowned imperial eagle in the white stripe, says it flew over German East Africa, and says the 1914 colonial flags were never taken into use.
era-1885.open: Both sources describe a tricolour with an eagle, as the drawing now shows, but Flags of the World calls it the governors' flag and puts the eagle in the white stripe, and the years (1891 or 1898 start) differ. The caption's black field with a canton is not described by either, and the 1885-1891 company flag is not described.

era-1700.says: Wikipedia (Flag of Tanzania) lists a plain red flag of Zanzibar under the Omani Empire for 1698-1856 and a striped Sultanate flag from 1856-1896; Wikipedia (Flag of Zanzibar) shows a plain red flag on an 1890s stamp. Flags of the World (Zanzibar to 1890) says Oman flew a plain red flag that continued after the Sultan moved to Zanzibar in 1840. Wikipedia's reference list for the Zanzibar flag cites only FOTW pages; no institutional or primary source was found.
era-1700.open: The publishers disagree on whether the plain red flag lasted to 1885 or gave way in 1856 to a striped flag. No source names a flag of the Swahili towns or the mainland interior, or says the Zanzibar flag flew there; the text on the card is not part of any flag.

era-1932.says: Wikipedia: 1979 Flag Act proportions 6:9 with blue stripe two parts wide; 30 September 2017 CIELAB standard; blue read as monarchy. FOTW: 1979 Act 6:9 with stripes 1-1-2-1-1; 30 September 2017 colour standard; blue for monarchy, white for Theravada Buddhism, red for land.
era-1932.open: The meanings are unofficial in both sources.

era-6c.says: This page's own caption calls the image a placeholder: «placeholder maroon field — Dvaravati and Khmer-influenced era, no flag survives».
era-6c.open: Whether a flag, banner or standard existed in this period was not checked. The colour shown is not evidence of one.

era-1917.says: Wikipedia: 28 September 1917 middle stripe changed to dark blue; explanations include Allied solidarity and the colour of Vajiravudh's birthday. FOTW: 28 September 1917 stripe changed to blue, reportedly for solidarity with the Allies; Flag Act of 1917 made it the national flag.

era-1782.says: Wikipedia: Rama I decreed a red flag with a white chakra around 1782, Rama II added a white elephant inside it around 1817, Rama IV made the white elephant on red the official flag in 1855, and Vajiravudh changed it in 1916-17. FOTW's historical page reports the same sequence from The History of Thai Flags (Fine Arts Department of Thailand, 1977, quoted by a contributor): chakra 1782, elephant in the chakra 1817, chakra removed and elephant enlarged 1855, caparisoned elephant on 2 November 1916, five red and white stripes in early 1917, blue central stripe on 28 September 1917; Crampton and Poels are cited for the chakra and elephant.
era-1782.open: Dates differ slightly in other FOTW-cited sources (a French tourist site gives 1802 for the elephant and 1851 for removing the chakra); the page's 'plain red field with the white elephant' for the whole period 1782-1917 is a simplification, since the chakra was present until 1855 and the design changed in 1916-1917.

era-1238.says: Wikipedia: Siam used a plain red flag from about 1680 to 1782, probably first under King Narai (1656-88). FOTW's historical page: the first known national flag of Thailand seems to have been a plain red flag, listed for Siam c.1656-1782, and The History of Thai Flags (Fine Arts Department, 1977, quoted by a contributor) says a plain red flag became the national flag on 3 September 1680.
era-1238.open: Neither source covers Sukhothai or the period before about 1656, so the row's 1238 start is unsupported; some flag books cited by FOTW say the first flag was red with a chakra. The 'ship ensign' wording on this page is not in the sources.

era-2002.says: Wikipedia's infobox gives adoption as 1975 (de facto) and 2002 (de jure). Flags of the World (Timor-Leste): the constitutional assembly restored all the symbols of the 1975 independence, the constitution was approved in March 2002 and the flag raised at the 20 May 2002 independence celebrations; (East Timor 1975 flag) the 1975 flag was red with a black triangle, yellow arrowhead and white star, proclaimed by Fretilin on 28 November 1975 (David Rogers), and Zrzavy cites a 1978 source that it is exactly the present flag including the 1:2 ratio.
era-2002.open: The meanings differ: Rogers (1975) gives black for four centuries of colonial oppression, while the 2002 constitution as quoted by FOTW gives yellow as traces of colonialism, black as the obscurantism to be overcome, red as the struggle for national liberation and white as peace; Martins says the 1975 flag was mostly shown at 2:3.

era-14c.says: This page's own caption calls the image a placeholder: «placeholder — pre-colonial Timorese kingdoms, no unifying flag survives».
era-14c.open: Whether a flag, banner or standard existed in this period was not checked. The colour shown is not evidence of one.

era-1999.says: Wikipedia (Flag of Timor-Leste): when the United Nations took control in East Timor after the 1999 referendum it used the UN flag; the CNRT flag, chosen at the 1998 Peniche convention as a provisional national flag, was semi-official until 2002, and on 20 May 2002 the UN flag was lowered and the national flag raised. FOTW (UN mandate): no UNTAET flag was found, only the UN flag hoisted at the INTERFET handover and at ceremonies in 2000 and 2001; FOTW's history page gives the CNRT flag quasi-official status.
era-1999.open: No flag specific to UNTAET is described, and the UN flag is attested at ceremonies and handovers rather than as a standing flag of the administration. The card's earlier lettered 'UN UNTAET' placeholder is not a flag in either source; the drawing now shows the UN flag.

era-1975.says: Wikipedia (Flag of Timor-Leste): Indonesian troops took down the Portuguese flag on Atauro and replaced it with the Indonesian flag on 30 December 1975, and during the occupation (1975-1999) the use of flags other than Indonesia's was forbidden. FOTW (Timor Timur under Indonesia): integrationists, militias and other pro-Indonesians used exclusively the undefaced Indonesian flag; a provincial flag with the occupation arms on orange was reported by one contributor, and the editor notes no local source confirms it.
era-1975.open: The flag in use was Indonesia's red-over-white national flag, not a province flag: the provincial flag with arms on orange is reported by a single FOTW contributor without a source, and the caption's 'province flag' is not supported. Fretilin's flag was proclaimed on 28 November 1975 and was a symbol of resistance, not the flag the occupiers used.

era-1702.says: Wikipedia: Portuguese Timor used only the flag of Portugal and had no separate colonial flag, with Portuguese designs dated 1702-07, 1830-1910 and 1910-75; proposals for a Timor flag in 1932 and 1965 were never adopted. Flags of the World (historical flags): Portuguese flags were used in forts and factories, military or Dominican flags may have been used, and Martins knows of no local tribal flags.
era-1702.open: The Portuguese flag changed over the span (WP's dated designs); the card shows only the 1910 Portuguese design, and the page's earlier wording of a territory banner is not supported.

era-1960.says: Both sources give 1960, the year this page starts the current flag. Wikipedia's infobox gives the adoption as 27 April 1960; Flags of the World dates it 27 April 1960.
era-1960.open: Only the year the current flag was adopted was compared; the design and the swatch colours were not checked against a specification.

era-1922.open: Whether a flag, banner or standard existed in this period was not checked. The colour shown is not evidence of one.

era-1884-1.open: Whether a flag, banner or standard existed in this period was not checked. The colour shown is not evidence of one.

era-1884.says: Wikipedia says Germany's flag was used in German Togoland from 1884 to 1914, without distinguishing imperial and colonial flags. Flags of the World says Togo was a German colony until the German administration surrendered on 26 August 1914; its page on German colonies (summarising Schurdel and others) says civil ships and often official buildings flew the black-white-red national flag, the naval ensign was used at hoistings and by troops, and a service flag is visible in a Lome photograph; its page on the 1914 colonial flags says the colonial arms-bearing flags (Togo's shield showed two snakes and a palm tree) were designed in 1914 but never introduced because of the war.
era-1884.open: The national flag was not the only flag: the naval ensign and the Reich service flag were also used, and the page's 'colonial ensign with a territorial badge' was a 1914 design never introduced (so it did not fly). FOTW's list gives Togo as 1884 to August 1914.

era-1970.says: Both sources date the current flag to 1875, before this era begins in 1970, so the flag was already in use at the start. Wikipedia's infobox gives the adoption as 4 November 1875; Flags of the World dates it November 1875.
era-1970.open: Only the year the current flag was adopted was compared; the design and the swatch colours were not checked against a specification.

era-1845-1.says: This page's own caption calls the image a placeholder: «placeholder — a real, long-running dynasty, but no attested flag».
era-1845-1.open: Whether a flag, banner or standard existed in this period was not checked. The colour shown is not evidence of one.

era-1900.says: Flags of the World: Tonga was a British Protected State from 18 May 1900 to 4 June 1970, and its flag, enshrined in the constitution of 4 November 1875, remained in use (Southworth); Prothero is quoted that Protected States did not have Blue Ensigns or defaced Union Jacks. Britannica says the flag was first hoisted in 1866, codified in the constitution of 4 November 1875, and by law may not be altered. Section 47 of the Constitution of Tonga (2013 text) says the flag shall never be altered but shall always be the flag of the Kingdom. WorldStatesmen lists one flag, adopted 1866 and confirmed 4 Nov 1875, with no protected-state flag. Wikipedia (Kingdom of Tonga 1900-1970) shows the Flag of Tonga in its infobox.
era-1900.open: The flag's continuity is supported by a constitutional text and a reference source, but no source read states in words that it flew throughout 1900-1970 except FOTW (Southworth); the constitution read is the 2013 revision, not the 1875 or 1900-era text, and the Treaty of Friendship was not read. The statement about Blue Ensigns is Prothero via FOTW alone, and the later proportion change (2:3 to 1:2) is undated.

era-1845.says: Wikipedia: a 4 November 1875 constitution codified the flag (red field, white canton with a red Greek cross); the early white flag with a red cross resembled the Red Cross emblem (adopted 1863) and was changed to a canton on red. FOTW: 1862 first design a white flag with a red cross, changed to a canton on red after the 1863 Red Cross; the constitution of 4 November 1875 (section 47) says it shall never be altered; one contributor says the present flag was decreed in 1866.
era-1845.open: The two sources read give 1862 and 1866 as earlier dates for the design; the 'contemporary international convention' wording and 'unaltered ever since' (FOTW notes proportions varied) are not in either.

era-1962.says: Both sources give 1962, the year this page starts the current flag. Wikipedia's infobox gives the adoption as 31 August 1962; Flags of the World dates it 1962.
era-1962.open: Only the year the current flag was adopted was compared; the design and the swatch colours were not checked against a specification.

era-5000bce.says: This page's own caption calls the image a placeholder: «placeholder — pre-Columbian Amerindian settlement, no flag survives».
era-5000bce.open: Whether a flag, banner or standard existed in this period was not checked. The colour shown is not evidence of one.

era-1889.says: Wikipedia: before independence in 1962 the colony used a British blue ensign defaced with a badge of a ship arriving in front of a mountain (its captions list a colonial flag and a red ensign for 1889-1958 and 1958-1962), and its history article says the two islands were incorporated into one entity in 1889. FOTW's colonial flags page (David Prothero): the Blue Ensign badge was introduced for Trinidad in 1875, in 1889 Tobago was annexed to Trinidad and the Trinidad badge became the badge of Trinidad and Tobago, used on the Blue Ensign until 1958 and then replaced by the same scene in a shield with a motto scroll.
era-1889.open: FOTW says there was no official Red Ensign with this badge (only an unofficial one reported), whereas Wikipedia's captions list a red ensign; the 1958 shield badge and the 1959 flag are not on this page. Tobago's separate badge (1876-1889) is in FOTW's Tobago page.

era-1797.says: WorldStatesmen lists the Union flag (not an ensign) for Trinidad from 18 February 1797 to 1 January 1889 and a colonial flag from 1889. Wikipedia (History of Trinidad and Tobago): Trinidad was surrendered to the British in 1797, Tobago confirmed British by the 1814 Treaty of Paris, and the islands joined in 1889. Flags of the World (Tobago): occupied by Britain in 1797, a colony from 1814, separate until 1888/89, 'used British ensigns with a badge'; a blue ensign with badge dated 1877, a badge 1870 or 1876. Its colonial page dates the Trinidad Blue Ensign badge to 1875.
era-1797.open: The dates are supported, but badge-defaced ensigns are dated only from the 1870s, and the only source that names a flag for 1797-1870 (WorldStatesmen) gives the plain Union flag, not the plain Blue Ensign drawn on the card, and gives no basis. The plain Blue Ensign for the whole span is a stand-in and is not established.

era-1498.says: Wikipedia (History of Trinidad and Tobago): Columbus claimed Trinidad for Spain in 1498 and it was administered by Spain until 1797. Flags of the World's Spanish pages date the Burgundy cross as a Spanish ensign from 1506 to the 1670s and a jack until 1785, call it a military banner rather than the official flag of the empire, and make royal arms on white the ensign from about 1701. WorldStatesmen's Trinidad page begins with the British flag in 1797 and lists no Spanish flag for Trinidad. Wikipedia's Flag of Trinidad and Tobago covers only the colonial flags from 1889.
era-1498.open: No source read ties the Cross of Burgundy to Trinidad, FOTW's dates for it as an ensign end in the 1670s, and the national list read gives no Spanish-era flag, so 'Spain's standard colonial and maritime banner throughout Spanish rule' is not established. Tobago's contested ownership before 1763 is not covered.

era-1956.says: Wikipedia: the flag was proclaimed the state flag of the Republic of Tunisia on 1 June 1959 under Article 4 of the constitution, and the Organic Law of 30 June 1999 (adopted 3 July) formalised it for the first time in law. Flags of the World: the national flag was legislated in the Constitution on 1 June 1959, and the current version, with a slightly adapted crescent, was set by the flag law of 30 June 1999 (published 6 July 1999). Second look: Article 4 of the Tunisian constitution of 2014 (Constitute Project) states that the flag of the Tunisian Republic is red and bears in its midst a white circle in which is inscribed a five-pointed star surrounded by a red crescent, as provided for by law; World Statesmen lists a flag c.1831 - 1 Jun 1959, another 1959-1999 and the current one from 3 Jul 1999.
era-1956.open: The design is shown by a primary legal text (2014), the 1959 and 1999 laws (Wikipedia, FOTW) and World Statesmen; the 2014 text does not say the star is red. The sources differ on when the design began (Wikipedia 1827 or 1831, FOTW 1835, World Statesmen c.1831), and the crescent was slightly thinner in 1959-1999, so "unchanged since 1831" is not shown. Independence in 1956 predates the 1959 constitution.

era-1831.says: Wikipedia: government dates the flag to 1831 (1835 also cited), created as a fleet flag after Navarino (1827) under Hussein II. FOTW: adopted 1831 per Sache (Hassine I), 1835 per other books, modelled on the Ottoman flag of the time.
era-1831.open: Sources split on 1831/1835 and on which bey; the page's autonomy-from-Istanbul framing is not in either.

era-1881.says: Wikipedia: the flag was not changed during the protectorate and captions the flag of the Beylik (1827-1881) and Tunisia (1881-1959). Flags of the World (page on Tunisia under French administration, quoting Smith in Flag Bulletin no. 195, 2000): Tunisia, a French protectorate, retained its national flag on land and at sea; an unofficial version with a tricolour canton was used for a time, and a formal proposal in 1925 to adopt it was not acted on. Its historical page quotes the same article on the bey's separate state standard of green and red stripes with the sword of Ali.
era-1881.open: The French tricolour was not flown 'alongside' the flag as a rule in these sources, only in an unofficial canton variant. The start (1881 Treaty of Bardo) and end dates, and the bey's status, are not covered.

era-1574.says: Wikipedia (Flag of Tunisia) shows captions for a flag of the Eyalet of Tunis (1574-1705) and of the Husainid dynasty (1705-1827) and says the design of maritime flags in Tunis was unknown until the mid-18th century, after which, until the early 19th century, the flag was composed of horizontal blue, red and green stripes, the Husainid colours, in multi-banded irregular shapes common along the North African coast; it attributes the bey's nine-striped standard with the sword of Ali to Hussein II, though some sources claim it was three centuries older. Flags of the World (historical flags, citing Franciae Vexilla 1999 and the Flag Bulletin): Tunisia was nominally Ottoman from 1574 to 1881, ensigns with six white and red or green and red stripes were reported from 1756, flags with many stripes and irregular shape were common from the mid-18th to the mid-19th century, and 14th-century portolans show crescent flags for Tunis. Second look: World Statesmen lists the Ottoman flag (de jure) to 1881 and a Tunisian flag only from c.1831, with nothing for 1574-1831. The Libro del conoscimiento (Markham translation) gives the king of Tunis a white flag with a black moon, which is a 14th-century device from before the Ottoman regency.
era-1574.open: Neither publisher shows the plain Ottoman red flag with crescent and star as the flag of Tunis for 1574-1831; they describe striped, irregularly shaped ensigns and standards from the mid-18th century, so the caption is not supported. The redrawn blue, red and green bands follow Wikipedia's description of the Husainid flag; what flew from 1574 to 1705 is not described in the sources read, and World Statesmen lists no flag for the period.

era-1923.says: Wikipedia says the Republic kept the last Ottoman flag in 1923, that Turkish Flag Law No. 2994 of 29 May 1936 set the flag's measures, proportions and red tone, and that Law No. 2893 of 22 September 1983 replaced it. FOTW says no design change occurred when the Empire became the Republic, that the 1936 law adopted the 1844 design without alteration, that the law was enacted on 29 May 1936 and published on 5 June 1936 (as No. 2,995), that Law No. 2,893 superseded it in 1983, and that the law gives no colour specification.
era-1923.open: The sources give the 1936 law's number as 2994 or 2,995. FOTW does not describe the 1919–23 war.
