era-7500bce.open: Whether a flag, banner or standard existed in this period was not checked. The colour shown is not evidence of one.

era-1793.says: Wikipedia says the star and crescent on red was introduced as the Ottoman flag in 1844, a late 18th-century design. FOTW, quoting Smith, says the form was set under Selim III in 1793 and the five-pointed star dates from about 1844.
era-1793.open: The firman of 1844 that this page named was not found in either source; the sources differ on 1793 or 1844.

era-1918.says: Wikipedia (Flag of the Ottoman Empire): the red flag with white star and crescent was the Ottoman national flag from 1844, and the last Caliph's standard (1922-1924) carried the star and crescent. Wikipedia (Government of the Grand National Assembly, 1920-1923): the infobox shows the Ottoman flag for the Ankara government, with no text. Wikipedia (Flag of Turkey) and FOTW both say the republic of 1923 kept the last Ottoman flag. KÜRE Encyclopedia (Turkish Flag): the red crescent-and-star flag was the late Ottoman state flag and was inherited and adopted by the Republic of Türkiye.
era-1918.open: The flag of the Istanbul government in 1918-1922 is supported by Wikipedia and FOTW; for the Ankara government and the 1919-1923 nationalists no source read describes the flag in text - Wikipedia's infobox image and the 1923 statements of continuity (Wikipedia, FOTW, KÜRE) are all that is available. The Ottoman army also used regimental standards bearing the Shahada. The Turkish presidency's flag page redirected (HTTP 302) and was not read.

era-1453.says: Wikipedia (Flag of the Ottoman Empire): a simple crescent flag started to appear from the foundation of the empire in 1453 and was reported as late as 1780 (the page labels it 'c. 1480-1780' and illustrates it from sources of 1480 to 1700), alongside tugh horse-tail standards, plain red banners (1574), Zulfiqar flags in the 16th-17th centuries, and two swallow-tailed naval flags of 1613 in the Spanish Navy Museum (one green with a white crescent, one white with a red crescent). Flags of the World: the basic form was apparently established in 1793, when green naval flags became red with a white crescent and star.
era-1453.open: The sources give the crescent flag but not its field colour for the period; the surviving 1613 flags are green or white, not red, and FOTW has green naval flags before 1793. The red field with white crescent on the card is a reconstruction, and no single flag covered the whole era.

era-330.says: Wikipedia (Byzantine flags and insignia): in the Palaiologan period the dynasty's insignia and the closest thing to a Byzantine national flag was the 'tetragrammatic cross', a gold or silver cross with four letters beta (often read as firesteels), which pseudo-Kodinos calls the customary imperial banner and which appears often in the 14th and 15th centuries. Flags of the World (Byzantine Empire): the c. 1350 Book of All Kingdoms shows flags with a yellow cross and four yellow chain links on red for Constantinople and other Byzantine places, which Neubecker reads as the Palaiologan arms (1258-1453); the firesteel reading is disputed by one contributor.
era-330.open: This covers only the Palaiologan period (from 1261) and the card's caption limits the design to the 13th-15th centuries; it is not a flag of the whole 330-1453 span, for which neither source gives a single flag. Whether the corner devices are letters or firesteels is disputed, and FOTW also describes a yellow flag with a black double-headed eagle.

era-1991.says: Wikipedia: the current flag was adopted 19 February 1992; Wikipedia's Turkmen SSR infobox labels the Turkmenistan flag 1991-1992 and gives independence declared 27 October 1991. Flags of the World (Turkmenistan): in 1992 (a year after independence) Turkmenistan adopted a new flag with a green field, white crescent and stars, five carpet guls at the hoist and a dark red hoist stripe (Notholt, 1995); olive branches were added on 29 January 1997; current version dated 24 January 2001; the five guls are reportedly named after five tribes.
era-1991.open: The page's 'adopted in 1992' is supported, but the era starts in 1991 and neither source says what flag flew between October 1991 and 1992; the 1997 and 2001 changes (olive branches, redrawn guls) show the flag was not unchanged after 1992.

era-1040-1.says: This page's own caption calls the image a placeholder: «placeholder maroon field — ancient Turkmen lands and early Merv».
era-1040-1.open: Whether a flag, banner or standard existed in this period was not checked. The colour shown is not evidence of one.

era-1924.says: Wikipedia's Flag of Turkmenistan article: the Turkmen SSR constitution of 6 October 1926 set a red flag with a gold hammer and sickle and a star in the canton, 1937 gold letters T.S.S.R., 1940 Cyrillic letters, then later changes through to the 1974-91 flag. Flags of the World agrees: a 1924-29 commemorative image with TSSC lettering, 1930s star with hammer and sickle, 1937 Latin initials, 1940s Cyrillic initials, and a flag with two blue bars adopted on 1 August 1953 (Heimer 1996).
era-1924.open: The two publishers agree on the chronology but the span 1924-91 held several different flags; the card's drawing is the late Soviet type, and its caption ('turquoise stripe near the base') does not match either source, which describe two blue bars across the middle.

era-1917.says: Flags of the World (Central Asian khanates): the local Bolsheviks created the Soviet Republic of Turkestan on 30 April 1918, dissolved 27 October 1924, with no flag described for it, only insurgent flags of 1921-24. Wikipedia's Turkestan ASSR article has an infobox flag image but no text on the flag. The 30 April 1918 founding regulation of the Turkestan Soviet Federative Republic (Wikisource) prescribes no flag, arms or seal. The Library of Congress study confirms that the Trans-Caspian District formed part of the Turkestan ASSR until the Turkmen SSR was created in October 1924. The Great Russian Encyclopedia article cited by Wikipedia returned HTTP 401 and was not read.
era-1917.open: No source read describes a flag of the Turkestan ASSR in words, so the card's 'Soviet red flag with hammer-and-sickle emblem' is not confirmed (the drawing, a plain red field with a gold mark, is also not a described design). The Turkmen SSR's own first flag is dated by Wikipedia to 1926.

era-1881.says: Flags of the World (Turkmenistan): the Khanate of Merv, annexed in 1884, flew a plain red flag. Wikipedia's Transcaspian Oblast article: an oblast of the Russian Empire established 1881, with a coat of arms in the infobox but no flag. Wikipedia's Flag of Russia: black-yellow-white decreed state flag in 1858, white-blue-red authorised on land in 1883 and sole national flag from 29 April 1896. The Library of Congress study dates the fall of Gokdepe to 1881. The Russian presidential flag-history page (en.flag.kremlin.ru, read over http only, so not declared as a source) says the tricolour's increasing use halted in 1858 when changes to the flag were proposed.
era-1881.open: No source read says which flag flew over the Transcaspian Oblast. The Russian state flag in 1881-96 was black-yellow-white by Wikipedia's account, so the card's white-blue-red tricolour for the whole span is not confirmed. Wikipedia's end date for the oblast (1921 or 1924) also differs from the card's 1917.

era-1500.says: Wikipedia's Flag of Turkmenistan article says the five carpet guls on the modern flag represent the five major tribes (Teke, Yomut, Saryk, Chowdur, Ersari). Flags of the World's Turkmenistan page says the guls are named after five tribes, and gives the Khanate of Merv, annexed in 1884, a plain red flag. Neither these pages nor FOTW's Central Asian khanates page describe tribal banners, tamgas or a confederation flag for c. 1500s-1881.
era-1500.open: The card openly shows a reconstructed tribal-emblem motif (a diamond), which is not any of the five guls the sources name; no source read calls it documented, and none documents tribal banners or tamgas for the period. The sources tie the guls to the tribes only through the modern (1992) flag.

era-1040.says: Wikipedia's Seljuk Empire article discusses the dynasty's public symbolism (the tughra, little of it Turkic) but gives no flag or banner; its Merv article covers Seljuk rule and the Mongol destruction of 1221 with no flag text. Wikipedia's Flag of Turkmenistan and Flags of the World's Turkmenistan page begin their flag histories in the Russian and Soviet periods, and Flags of the World's Central Asian khanates page covers only c. 1917-1924 (apart from the Khanate of Merv's plain red flag in the Turkmenistan page). None of these describes a flag for Seljuk, Mongol or Timurid-successor rule in the region.
era-1040.open: The card is an openly labelled placeholder and our sources describe no flag for c. 1040 to the 1500s, but that is silence in general flag pages, not a finding that none existed; no source on Seljuk, Mongol or Timurid banners specific to Merv or Turkmen lands was read.

era-1978.says: Wikipedia: the flag, a light blue field with the Union Jack in the canton and nine yellow stars on the fly half, was originally adopted on 1 October 1978, the day of independence; the 1995 government introduced a different flag and the 1997 government reverted on 11 April 1997. Flags of the World (last modified 2026): the 1978-95 flag, the 1995-1997 flag, and the reversion on 11 April 1997 to the 1978 flag; the British Blue Ensign became obsolete on 1 October 1978 when the new flag was adopted on independence.
era-1978.open: The flag was different from 1995 to 1997 (Wikipedia: October 1995 under Prime Minister Latasi, reversed by the next government), so the page's 'present' span has a two-year gap. FOTW's own date of 1975 on the main page refers to the separation of the Ellice Islands, not this flag.

era-1975.says: Wikipedia: Colony of Tuvalu from 1 Oct 1975; own arms 3 Dec 1976; own Blue Ensign with the new arms 3 Dec 1976 to 1 Oct 1978. FOTW: new blue ensign with arms adopted 3 Dec 1976, obsolete 1 Oct 1978.
era-1975.open: Page dated the ensign from 1975 and spoke of a badge disc; the sources date the ensign from Dec 1976; 1975-76 flag not covered.

era-1892.says: Wikipedia's Flag of Tuvalu says that from 1937 to 1975 Tuvalu flew the Blue Ensign of the Gilbert and Ellice Islands, which were granted a coat of arms in 1937, with a Blue Ensign defaced with the arms adopted as an unofficial colonial flag and made official in 1969. Flags of the World's Gilbert and Ellice Islands page (Prothero, Admiralty Flag Book) says government vessels flew the Blue Ensign defaced with the shield of the arms, from 1937 to 1976-1979 (the page notes the arms were without the white disc per a 1941 Admiralty Flag Book amendment), with civil sanction on 28 August 1969; it dates the protectorate to 1892 and the joint colony to 1915-1916.
era-1892.open: The joint colony's Blue Ensign is established only from 1937. Neither source describes a flag of the Ellice Islands for 1892-1937: Flags of the World shows a 'B R' crowned Resident Commissioner's flag for the Gilbert Islands alone (1895-1916). The 1892 start on the card is not supported as a Blue Ensign date.

era-1962.says: Both sources give 1962, the year this page starts the current flag. Wikipedia's infobox gives the adoption as 9 October 1962; Flags of the World dates it 09 Oct 1962.
era-1962.open: Only the year the current flag was adopted was compared; the design and the swatch colours were not checked against a specification.

era-1894.says: Wikipedia (Flag of Uganda): the British protectorate flew a Blue Ensign with its colonial badge featuring a crested crane from 1914 to March 1962, the Governor having a standard with the Union Jack and the badge; Wikipedia (Uganda Protectorate): the protectorate ran 18 June 1894 to 9 October 1962 and its infobox flag is dated 1914-1962. FOTW (ug.html): the crested crane was the flag badge of Uganda under British colonial rule and the former flag-badge; FOTW's British East Africa page lists the date of the Blue Ensign badge as unknown.
era-1894.open: Attested for the Blue Ensign with the crested crane badge; both Wikipedia pages date the flag from 1914, so 1894-1914 is not covered, and FOTW gives no dates. Whether the badge is the 'grey' crowned crane is not stated.

era-1700.says: Flags of the World (Buganda): Thomas Pakenham's account has Lugard, arriving in Kampala in 1892, finding the Kabaka flying 'an enormous home-made flag, two lances and a shield on a red ground'; the page also shows undescribed flag images for 1861-1881 onward by a contributor. Wikipedia (Flag of Uganda) says the Kingdom of Buganda had a national flag before colonisation, without a design or dates.
era-1700.open: Only the 1892 flag is described, in one secondhand account; nothing read describes a Buganda flag for c. 1700-1861 or after 1892, so the red-ground drawing is a stand-in reconstruction for the whole span. The FOTW images for 1861-1892 are undescribed and by a contributor, with no stated basis.

era-1922.says: Wikipedia says that on 7 December 1922, asked whether the Garter King of Arms would issue new regulations after the Irish Free State was established, the Home Secretary said no, and that the flag has never been changed; it says no law has made it the national flag, its status resting on precedent and a 1908 ministerial statement. FOTW quotes Graham Bartram on that 1908 statement and Christopher Southworth that there is no UK Flag Act.
era-1922.open: The flag's status is by custom, not statute; both sources say so.

era-927.open: Whether a flag, banner or standard existed in this period was not checked. The colour shown is not evidence of one.

era-800bce.open: Whether a flag, banner or standard existed in this period was not checked. The colour shown is not evidence of one.

era-1707.says: Wikipedia's Union Flag article says that after the Acts of Union 1707 the 1606 flag gained a regularised status as 'the ensign armorial of the Kingdom of Great Britain', and was then adopted by land forces; its infobox dates the national flag 1707 and the St Patrick's saltire to 1801. FOTW's history of the Union Flag (Prothero) says the flag became the 'ensign armorial of the United Kingdom of Great Britain' as one of the provisions of the Act of Union in 1707, describes the 1606 proclamation of 12 April 1606, and dates the modern flag with St Patrick's cross to 1 January 1801. Wikipedia's Kingdom of Great Britain article dates the state 1707 onwards.
era-1707.open: FOTW gives no 1707 proclamation or royal warrant for a separate flag design, and the 17 April 1707 design approval rests on Wikipedia alone. The card's claim that the flag was 'previously just one option among several' is looser than the sources (they say it was a flag for ships).

era-1801.says: Wikipedia says George III's proclamation of 1 January 1801 set the blazon, adding St Patrick's saltire counterchanged with St Andrew's. FOTW quotes the proclamation's «quarterly per saltire, counterchanged argent and gules», and Southworth that the original saltires were of even width, the narrower St Patrick saltire an Admiralty variant soon after.
era-1801.open: The narrow St Patrick saltire seen on the flag today came after the 1801 proclamation, which this page does not mention.

era-1603.says: Wikipedia says a royal decree of 12 April 1606 joined the English and Scottish crosses for use at sea and that subjects of both kingdoms were to fly it. FOTW says it was introduced as a maritime flag, that the 1606 flag placed the red cross of St George over the blue St Andrew's flag with a white X, and, quoting Procter, that a 1634 proclamation reserved it for warships.

era-1200.says: Flags of the World (England): the earliest reference to the cross of St George as an English emblem (not flag) is a 1277 Welsh war account roll (Perrin, 1922); the St George banner flew at Caerlaverock in 1300; the cross became a national flag in the 16th century after the Reformation removed other saints' banners, with the earliest sea record in 1545. Wikipedia (Flag of England): red crosses marked English soldiers from the 1270s, 1277 banners 'of the arms of Saint George', a St George banner beside the royal banner by 1300, Edward III's Order of the Garter in 1348, and the Genoa/1190 origin 'cannot be substantiated'; the 1367 Book of All Kingdoms shows England's flag as solid red. Wikipedia (Kingdom of England): infobox 'Flag (from the 16th century)' and 'Royal Banner (1406-1603)'.
era-1200.open: Both publishers place the St George's cross as an English emblem from the 1270s and as the national flag only from the 16th century, not from c. 1200 or the Crusades; the claim that the design 'has never once been altered' was not checked.

era-1991.says: Wikipedia says the flag was de facto restored on 24 August 1991 and officially adopted again by parliament on 28 January 1992, and that the sky-blue version of 1917–1921 was reintroduced in 1992 and remains in use alongside a darker blue standard (DSTU 4512:2006). FOTW (Grechylo) gives the State Flag decree of 28 January 1992 (No 2067-XII), a Presidium decree of 18 September 1991 allowing ceremonial use, and says the blue-yellow flag first flew at the Supreme Council on 4 September 1991.
era-1991.open: FOTW's own sources disagree: Gutterman gives 21 January 1992 for making it the only flag. The page's remark that the colours were read as sky over wheat was not found in either source.

era-900.open: Whether a flag, banner or standard existed in this period was not checked. The colour shown is not evidence of one.

era-1949.says: Wikipedia (Flag of the Ukrainian SSR): the UN demanded changes to the republic flags in 1949; the lettering was dropped and an azure horizontal stripe (one third of the width) added; decree of the Presidium of the Supreme Soviet of 21 November 1949, de jure adoption 5 July 1950; the decree says the blue symbolises the might and beauty of the people and the blue banner of Bohdan Khmelnytsky. FOTW (Ukraine in the Soviet Union 1949-1991): adopted 21 November 1949, light blue bar in base covering a third of the height; FOTW's flag-history page (citing the Encyclopedia of Ukraine) agrees on 21 November 1949, red upper two thirds, azure lower third, gold hammer, sickle and star above.
era-1949.open: Neither source calls the blue stripe a coded echo of the banned blue-yellow flag; the page's wording about that is unsourced and has been hedged.

era-1944.says: Wikipedia (Flag of the Ukrainian SSR): a flag adopted in 1937 (caption 1937-1950) carried a small gold hammer and sickle above the gold Cyrillic letters УРСР on red, and the republic's flag was changed only in 1949. FOTW (early flags): the 1940s flag was red with yellow Cyrillic initials URSR in the upper hoist and a yellow hammer and sickle below, replaced on 21 November 1949; the 1937 flag had the hammer and sickle above the initials.
era-1944.open: The two sources differ on whether the emblem sat above or below the lettering and neither mentions a star; the drawing and caption on the page still show a plain red field with hammer, sickle and star and need redrawing from these descriptions.

era-1921.says: Wikipedia: the first UkrSSR flag (10 March 1919) was red with gold Cyrillic У.С.С.Р.; a decade later У.С.Р.Р.; a gold border was added in the 1930s; in 1937 a small gold hammer and sickle was added above gold serif УРСР. FOTW (early flags): 1919 red with yellow initials in the upper hoist; 1923 yellow initials with no hammer and sickle; 1927 initials U.S.R.R.; 1930s yellow border round the canton; 1937 little yellow hammer and sickle above URSR.
era-1921.open: The page's gold 'hammer-and-sickle-and-star' is not what either source describes (lettering with, from 1937, a small hammer and sickle); the drawing and caption still need redrawing. The 1921 start date is the page's own: the sources date the first flag to 1919.

era-1917.says: FOTW (Historical Flags 1917-1918, citing the Encyclopedia of Ukraine): the Ukrainian National Republic was proclaimed 20 November 1917, independence declared 22 January 1918, national flag of yellow over light blue adopted 22 March 1918; under the Hetmanate (from 29 April 1918) light blue over yellow; the restored UNR kept light blue over yellow from December 1919. Wikipedia (Flag of Ukraine): blue-yellow flags in Petrograd on 25 March 1917 and Kyiv on 29 March 1917, 22 March 1918 as official adoption in its infobox; the Hetmanate's and Directorate's flag light blue-yellow; Wikipedia's UNR article records blue-and-yellow flags at the Kyiv demonstration of 13 April 1917.
era-1917.open: The sources agree on a blue-and-yellow bicolour but the stripe order changed (yellow over blue in 1918 per FOTW, blue over yellow afterwards); the page's 'blue-over-gold' drawing fits 1918-21 only in part. Neither source says the Central Rada adopted it.

era-1654.says: FOTW (Hetmanate flags page): the Hetmanate existed 1648-1734, a Hetman flag of c.1706 was red and triangular, a Hetman used a red flag with Archangel Michael in 1655, and the 'famous blue flag' is a regimental flag, not a Hetmanate flag; it also distinguishes the Zaporozhian Sich as a separate host. FOTW's history page: the Sich's great banner was red with a white Archangel Michael and a white Greek cross with sun, crescent and stars; kurin flags were usually crimson with Michael or a white cross; 18th-century flags tended to azure. Wikipedia: blue-yellow, red-black, crimson-olive and raspberry Cossack banners of the 16th-18th centuries. Second look: the Internet Encyclopedia of Ukraine (Regalia) lists flags among the insignia of office of the Zaporozhian Sich and the Hetman state and says Cossack banners were usually made of carmine cloth with images of saints, crosses and coats of arms, carried on each side of the hetman or otaman at the head of the army; Russian tsars gave hetmans and the Host various regalia.
era-1654.open: A crimson field with a white cross is described only for Sich or kurin flags (FOTW alone, and the Black Sea Cossack flag of 1792), not for the Hetmanate as a polity; for the Hetmanate the sources give a red Hetman flag with Archangel Michael and blue regimental flags. The card's single crimson white-cross flag as the Hetmanate's colours is not established. A crimson banner bearing a cross is now supported as typical of Cossack banners by a reference work, but the particular charges drawn (star, two crescents, sun) and the Hetmanate as a polity with one flag are still not.

era-1941.says: Wikipedia's Reichskommissariat Ukraine article presents the flag of Nazi Germany (1935-1945) as the territory's flag in its infobox, and its Flag of Germany article describes that swastika flag as the national flag, ensign and naval jack of Nazi Germany 1935-1945. FOTW's history page dates a yellow-over-azure flag to the Ukrainian Liberation Army and Division Galizien in 1943-45.
era-1941.open: Wikipedia gives no text on a flag flown by the occupation administration and no decree; the infobox use of the German flag is an encyclopedic convention for a territory without its own flag. A second source on which flag actually flew over the Reichskommissariat was not found.

era-1795.says: FOTW's history page (after the Encyclopedia of Ukraine) says that in Ukraine within the Russian Empire only the white-blue-red imperial flag and official flags based on it were used, with no territorial flags. Wikipedia's Flag of Russia says the white-blue-red tricolour was the civil ensign from 1705 and continued under the Russian Empire, was the sole national flag from 1896, and that a black-yellow-white flag was the official state flag 1858-1896.
era-1795.open: The tricolour is supported as the civil flag throughout, but the official state flag was black-yellow-white in 1858-1896. 'No distinct Ukrainian flag' is too absolute: Wikipedia's Flag of Ukraine reports blue-yellow flags in Dnieper Ukraine in 1905 and from March 1917. Neither source dates a Ukrainian-lands era from 1795.

era-1569.says: FOTW's history page (after the Encyclopedia of Ukraine) says that within the Grand Duchy of Lithuania and the Polish kingdom the Ukrainian principalities, voivodeships, lands and counties each had their own banners, usually matching their arms. Wikipedia's Flag of Poland says a red cloth with the White Eagle was established under Ladislaus the Short (1320-1333) as the Banner of the Kingdom of Poland, a royal banner used at coronations and in battle; FOTW's royal-banners page lists banners of the period but only as images. Second look: the Internet Encyclopedia of Ukraine (Coat of arms) gives territorial arms for Ukrainian lands in this period's setting (a yellow lion rampant on azure for Lviv and Halych from the 14th century; an armed Cossack for the Zaporozhian Host from the 16th), which fits Flags of the World's remark that the lands had their own banners; it describes no Polish Crown flag over Ukraine.
era-1569.open: A white eagle on red is described for the Polish Crown's banner by Wikipedia alone; no source read says it was the flag of, or flown over, Ukraine in 1569-1654, and FOTW says the Ukrainian lands had their own banners. No reference work read states a Polish Crown flag flew over the Ukrainian lands.

era-1349.says: FOTW's history page (after the Encyclopedia of Ukraine) says the Grand Duchy of Lithuania's flag was red with a golden Gediminas emblem in the 15th century and later red with a white knight on a white horse (the vytis). Wikipedia's Grand Duchy of Lithuania article says the historical Lithuanian state flag, a horseback knight on a red field, has an initial design dating to Grand Duke Vytautas the Great (reigned 1392-1430), citing the Lithuanian presidency.
era-1349.open: Two publishers agree on a red flag with the knight in the Grand Duchy, but both place it from the late 14th or 15th century, not from 1349; FOTW says the 15th-century flag first bore the Gediminas emblem. Neither says this was the flag across the Rus' lands, and the drawing is a simplified emblem.

era-1240.says: FOTW's history page (a passage from ukrainet.org drawing on the Encyclopedia of Ukraine) says the standard of the Rus' kingdom of the Galician-Volhynian period displayed a golden lion on an azure background. Wikipedia's Flag of Ukraine article has a section headed Kingdom of Galicia-Volhynia and a Kingdom of Ruthenia flag caption but no description in its text of that flag.
era-1240.open: Only FOTW states the design, and it gives no date or object (no seal, banner or surviving flag is named); Wikipedia's Galicia-Volhynia article was also read and has no flag text. The card's lion-on-blue is therefore a reconstruction from a described standard, not a documented flag for 1240-1349.

era-1971.says: Both sources give 1971, the year this page starts the current flag. Wikipedia's infobox gives the adoption as 2 December 1971; Flags of the World dates it December 1971.
era-1971.open: Only the year the current flag was adopted was compared; the design and the swatch colours were not checked against a specification.

era-1853.says: Wikipedia (Flag of the UAE): the white segment was imposed on six emirates' flags - Sharjah and Ras Al Khaimah red with a white border, Ajman and Dubai red with a white hoist bar, Abu Dhabi red with a white rectangle at the upper hoist - and only Fujairah kept plain red; its Trucial States article dates the Perpetual Maritime Truce 4 May 1853 and the Council flag 1968-1971. FOTW: the white-bordered flag (No. 2) for Sharjah, Ras al-Khaimah and Kalba, the white hoist stripe flag (No. 1) for Abu Dhabi, Ajman, Dubai and Umm al-Qaiwain, with the stripe dated after 1833 or perhaps 1864, and Fujairah plain red (with lettering 1952-1961); Stelter also says Abu Dhabi kept a plain red flag on land until 1958. A British official note of the 1930s in India Office file IOR/R/15/2/1694 (f. 32r, Qatar Digital Library, machine transcription) says the flag shown on page 31 of 'Flags of All Nations' is used only by the sheikhs of Sharjah and Ras al-Khaimah as the Qawasim tribal flag, and that all the other Trucial sheikhs fly an oblong flag about three times as long as wide, five-sixths red with the sixth nearest the mast white, never seen with lettering.
era-1853.open: An archival note of the 1930s and the two compiled publishers agree that most sheikhdoms flew red with white elements, so the caption's description holds. The archival note does not separate Fujairah (recognised only in 1952), so its plain red rests on Wikipedia and Flags of the World; the note's transcription is garbled and is for the 1930s only. 1853 is a treaty date, and no single flag covers 1853-1971.

era-1820.says: FOTW's 1820 treaty page quotes Article 3 (C. R. Low, via Prothero): the friendly Arabs shall carry a red flag, with or without letters, within a white border of equal breadth, 'White pierced Red'. Wikipedia's Qawasim article quotes the same, and its Flag of the UAE says a white segment was imposed on each emirate's flag; its Trucial States article dates the treaty 8 January 1820. FOTW (Stelter) adds that plain red flags stayed in use in practice, Abu Dhabi readopting plain red in 1833/34 and returning to the white border after 1835. Lorimer's Gazetteer (1915, p. 672) independently says the third article of the General Treaty prescribed for all the Arabs in the treaty the flag known in the British Navy as 'White-pierced-Red', the red centre perpetuating the Qawasim's blood-red flag and the white border a symbol of peace.
era-1820.open: A reference history (Lorimer) and two compiled publishers agree on the red flag with a white border prescribed by the treaty. How widely it was flown is not settled: Flags of the World says plain red stayed in use in places (Abu Dhabi plain red in 1833/34). 1853 is the date of the later truce, not of a flag change.

era-1727.says: Wikipedia's Flag of the UAE says the Hinawi and Ghafiri confederations had a red banner before 1820, but the Qawasim, although Ghafiri, had their own green, white and red banner to mark them as a maritime power; it quotes Sharjah's ruler (1975) that the Qawasim flag had three horizontal bands, green, white and red, with the Quranic inscription 'A victory from Allah and an imminent conquest' on the white. Wikipedia's Qawasim article captions a 'Flag of the Al Qawasim prior to 1820', flown after 1820 in wartime only, and dates the line from 1722. FOTW's 1820 treaty page says other tribes later saw the treaty flag as the Qawasim flag, and that Gulf flags were undifferentiated red until the 19th century. Lorimer's Gazetteer of the Persian Gulf (1915, p. 672), explaining Article 3 of the 1820 treaty, says the red centre of the prescribed flag was understood to perpetuate the blood-red flag of the Qawasim, the emblem even then of most maritime Arabs.
era-1727.open: The sources conflict: Wikipedia quotes a 1975 statement by Sharjah's ruler that the Qawasim flag was green, white and red with lettering, while Lorimer (1915) calls it blood-red. Neither dates a flag to c. 1727 (Wikipedia gives 1722 for the line). The card draws the green-white-red version, which rests on one 1975 recollection.

era-1960.says: Both sources give 1960, the year this page starts the current flag. Wikipedia's infobox gives the adoption as 3 December 1775; Flags of the World dates it 4 July 1960.
era-1960.open: Only the year the current flag was adopted was compared; the design and the swatch colours were not checked against a specification.

era-1959.says: Wikipedia (Flag of the United States): Executive Order 10798 of 3 January 1959 set the 49-star design after Alaska's admission, and the flag became official on 4 July 1959. Flags of the World (49 stars): the flag flew from 4 July 1959 to 3 July 1960, the proclamation was signed on 2 January 1959, Alaska's admission added the 49th star, and the stars were in staggered rows.
era-1959.open: The signing date is 3 January on Wikipedia and 2 January on FOTW; FOTW calls the document a proclamation and does not number an executive order; FOTW's own pages mention Executive Order 10834 for the 50-star flag.

era-1912.says: Wikipedia: the 48-star flag was adopted in 1912, the first flag act to specify an arrangement, six rows of eight stars. Flags of the World (48 stars): the flag flew from 4 July 1912 and followed Arizona and New Mexico joining; the Army Quartermaster describes the 48 stars in six rows of eight; its star-arrangement page says no law specified the arrangement until 1912.
era-1912.open: The order is not agreed: FOTW says Taft approved the arrangement on 14 February 1912 and attributes Executive Order 1556 of 24 June 1912 to flag sizes and proportions, not the star layout; the end date is 1959 on the page title but 3 July 1949 in one FOTW contributor note.

era-1865.says: Wikipedia's table gives 36 stars in 1865-1867, 37 in 1867-1877, 38 in 1877-1890, 43 in 1890-1891, 44 in 1891-1896 and 45 in 1896-1908. Flags of the World's index lists the same counts and years (36 stars 1865-1867, 37 1867-1877, 38 1877-1890, 43 1890-1891, 44 1891-1896, 45 1896-1908, 46 1908-1912) and its 36-star page says one star was added for Nevada in 1865.
era-1865.open: The page stops at 45 stars and 1912, but both sources add a 46-star flag for 1908-1912; FOTW says the Army and Navy had approved patterns from 1865 but no star arrangement was legally fixed.

era-1861.says: Wikipedia gives 34 stars in 1861-1863 (Kansas) and 35 in 1863-1865 (West Virginia). Flags of the World: the 34-star flag added Kansas (admitted 29 January 1861) and flew from 4 July 1861 to 3 July 1863; the 35-star flag added West Virginia in 1863 and flew from 4 July 1863 to 3 July 1865.
era-1861.open: Neither source says that the Union deliberately kept the seceded states' stars; the page's remark that the refusal to remove a star was a political statement is a comment, not a sourced fact.

era-1818.says: Wikipedia: Congress passed a plan on 4 April 1818, suggested by Samuel C. Reid, returning the stripes to 13 and setting 20 stars, with a star added for each new state on the following 4 July, and gives 33 stars in 1859-1861. Flags of the World quotes the act, approved 4 April 1818, requiring thirteen horizontal stripes, alternate red and white, and a star added on the 4 July after each admission, taking effect 4 July 1818; its index lists 20 stars in 1818 through 33 stars in 1859-1861.
era-1818.open: FOTW does not name Reid; the page's claim that period flags show real variation in star layout is supported by FOTW's note that military patterns existed from 1818 but were not binding on the public.

era-1795.says: Wikipedia: the stars and stripes went from 13 to 15 on 1 May 1795 for Vermont and Kentucky. Flags of the World (15 stars): in 1795 two stars were added for Kentucky and Vermont, the only US flag with fifteen stripes, which flew from 4 July 1795 to 4 July 1818 and over Fort McHenry in the War of 1812.
era-1795.open: The start is 1 May 1795 on Wikipedia and 4 July 1795 on FOTW; neither source read mentions the Flag Act of 1794.

era-1777.says: Wikipedia says Congress resolved on 14 June 1777 that the flag be thirteen alternate red and white stripes with thirteen stars on a blue field, that the designer is unknown, and that William Canby first publicly told the Betsy Ross story in 1870 with no evidence in Washington's diaries or Congressional records. FOTW says Canby said he heard it from his grandmother and found nothing to support it in US records, that no record of a 1776 congressional committee on a flag exists, and that Francis Hopkinson was the only person at the time to claim credit.
era-1777.open: FOTW does not cover the 1777 resolution. The star arrangement is not specified by Congress, and the circular arrangement drawn is traditional, not documented.

era-1607.says: Wikipedia: the Continental Union Flag first appeared on 3 December 1775 aboard Alfred, and whether the flag raised at Prospect Hill on 1 January 1776 was the Continental or the British Union Flag is disputed. Flags of the World (Grand Union Flag): first raised in early December 1775 aboard the Continental Navy's flagship; Ansoff holds the Prospect Hill flag was a British Union flag in the canton; used after the Declaration of Independence, with a latest reference in March 1777; a Philadelphia chandler charged for a 'Union Flagg, Green and Red, 13 stripes' on 20 December 1775.
era-1607.open: The British colonial flags of 1607 to 1775 on this card's long span are not covered by Wikipedia or FOTW's pages read; stripe colours of the Continental Colors are questioned by McMillan.

era-1830.says: Wikipedia: statute of 11 July 1830 reduced the stripes from nineteen to nine; 1952 decree formalised the sun's design with sixteen rays. FOTW: nine equal blue and white stripes, white canton over the top five, yellow sun with sixteen alternating straight and wavy rays.
era-1830.open: The departments claim is in neither source; the 1828 date is inconsistent inside Wikipedia (nineteen or nine stripes).

era-1825.says: Wikipedia: in 1825 the Thirty-Three Orientals planted a tricolour marked 'Libertad o Muerte' at Agraciada Beach, and the flag law that followed specified light blue, white and crimson. FOTW: Lavalleja's flag had three horizontal bands of sky-blue, white and deep scarlet with 'Libertad o Muerte' on the middle band, and a contributor notes the flag was defined as celeste by an 1825 law; the Flag Law of 18 December 1828 later replaced it with the striped sun-canton flag.
era-1825.open: FOTW's page for the 33 Orientales flag does not mention the Agraciada landing or the 1825 law (only the uy_hist contributor note does); how the flag was worn is not described.

era-1816.says: Wikipedia (Flag of Uruguay) says that during Brazilian control a provincial flag of a white stripe between two green ones was in force, its white field bearing arms based on Portuguese royal symbols, and pictures a Cisplatina flag for 1820-1828; Wikipedia (Cisplatina) captions its infobox flag as a merchant ensign. Flags of the World (historical page) gives the dates of Portuguese and Brazilian rule without describing a flag in the text. The Uruguayan and Spanish institutional pages cited by the Spanish Wikipedia could not be read (timeouts and 404s).
era-1816.open: Neither publisher describes the Portuguese flag of 1816-22 or a Brazilian Empire banner as the caption presents them; the green-white-green provincial flag rests on Wikipedia alone, and the dates of Brazilian control differ between sources.

era-1680.says: Wikipedia (Flag of Uruguay) begins with Artigas's flag of 1814 and Flags of the World's historical page describes Artigas's red, blue and white flag (1814-1817) but no Spanish colonial or Banda Oriental flag. Wikipedia (Cross of Burgundy) says the ensign was introduced throughout the Spanish Empire after 1506 and reportedly flown as a jack until 1785. The Spanish Army and Navy flag-history pages cited by the Spanish Wikipedia returned HTTP 404 and a Uruguayan municipal page timed out, so no institutional source was read.
era-1680.open: No source read says the Cross of Burgundy flew over the Banda Oriental or was its standard banner; the only support is Wikipedia's general statement about the Spanish overseas empire (one publisher). The Portuguese-held parts (Colonia, 1680-1777) are not covered, and the 1680 start is not a flag event.

era-pre-contact.open: Whether a flag, banner or standard existed in this period was not checked. The colour shown is not evidence of one.

era-1991.says: Wikipedia's infobox gives the adoption as 18 November 1991. FOTW's Uzbekistan page says the flag was adopted 18 November 1991 under the Law on the state flag (Official Gazette no. 141 of 28 November 1991), with the state emblem following in July 1992, and gives the construction sheet.
era-1991.open: Design and swatch colours were not checked against the construction sheet.

era-1924.says: Wikipedia says the Uzbek SSR flag, derived from the Soviet flag, was approved in 1952 with a blue stripe one-fifth of the width and white edges. Flags of the World (Sokolov, Sensen) says the striped flag was adopted by decree of 29 August 1952: red with a light-blue bar fimbriated white across the middle (stripes 20+1+8+1+20), a hammer and sickle and a star in the upper hoist; its early-flags page lists plain red flags with initials in the upper hoist from 22 July 1925, with Latin lettering from 9 January 1926 and changes in 1931 and 1935.
era-1924.open: The 1952 flag covers only 1952-91; the 1925-52 flags were red with lettering. The card's caption ('light-blue stripe near the base') does not match the sources, which put the white-edged stripe across the middle.

era-1917.says: Flags of the World (after Sokolov and Ivanov): the Bukharan People's Soviet Republic flew a red flag with crescent and star in 1920, a green-over-red flag with a yellow crescent and star bearing a hammer and sickle in 1921 (letters BNSR), and a plain red flag from 11 October 1923; the Khorezm People's Soviet Republic flew a red flag with a green canton holding a crescent and star from 1920. Wikipedia says the Bukharan flag combined the hammer and sickle with the crescent. Wikipedia's Turkestan ASSR article (1918-1924) has only an infobox flag image, and Flags of the World's Central Asian khanates page describes no Turkestan ASSR flag. Second look: Wikipedia's Turkestan ASSR article shows flags for 1919-1920 and 1921-1924 (the second marked citation needed), and the Commons file pages for those images name no source beyond a bare 'Туркестан' and 'ЦИК ТССР' (uploaded 2022 as own work) and an own-work SVG (2010).
era-1917.open: No source read describes a flag of the Turkestan ASSR, which is the flag the card draws (red with lettering at the hoist), and the card's caption of a generic Soviet red does not match the crescent-bearing Bukharan and Khorezm flags the sources do describe; only Bukhara's flag from October 1923 was plain red. The image files give no usable basis for the card's red-with-lettering design.

era-1865.says: Wikipedia's Flag of Russia article: the white-blue-red tricolour was a civil ensign from 1705; in 1858 the black-yellow-white tricolour was decreed the state flag, white-blue-red was authorised for use on land in 1883 and made the sole national flag by an order of 29 April 1896. Wikipedia's Russian Turkestan article: the Turkestan Governorate-General was organised in 1867 and excluded the protectorates of Bukhara and Khiva; it describes no flag. Flags of the World gives Bukhara and Khiva flags only from the early 20th century. Second look: Britannica's 'flag of Russia' (Whitney Smith) says Peter I chose the white-blue-red flag for merchant ships in 1699 (Wikipedia has 1705 for the civil ensign) and that during the 19th century the black-orange-white tricolour the tsars tried to impose as a national flag on land 'completely failed' and was abandoned; it says nothing of Turkestan.
era-1865.open: No source read says which flag flew over Russian Turkestan, and the sources date the white-blue-red tricolour as sole national flag only from 1896 (authorised on land from 1883), with black-yellow-white as the state flag from 1858, so the card's tricolour for the whole span from 1865 is not confirmed. Britannica supports the tricolour as the popular Russian flag in the 19th century but not as a flag specific to the Turkestan Governorate-General, and it dates the merchant flag to 1699 where Wikipedia gives 1705.

era-1500.says: Flags of the World: for the Emirate of Bukhara the national flag 'remains elusive', and only the emir's flag of the early 20th century and an undated museum flag (green with a red border, left hand of Fatima, crescent and three stars) are shown; for Khiva nothing was known before 1917-22, when the museum flag of the khanate during the civil war is the earliest. Its Central Asian khanates page covers only c. 1917-1924 and the Kokand Autonomous State flag of 1917-18. Wikipedia's Flag of Uzbekistan article gives no flag for the khanates. Second look: Wikipedia's Khanate of Khiva article carries a footnote quoting David Straub on Flags of the World that the Khivan flag of the pre-Soviet period is unknown, and dates its flag image to 1917-1922 (after the museum flag at Khiva, via Franciae Vexilla); its Khanate of Bukhara and Khanate of Kokand articles show a flag image in the infobox with no flag text (same publisher, and Khiva's note rests on Flags of the World, so this is not independent confirmation).
era-1500.open: A plain green field with a white crescent as the flag of the Bukhara, Khiva or Kokand khanates between about 1500 and 1865 is not stated by any source read; the nearest evidence is early 20th century, and the one green flag described (the museum flag) has a red border and other charges. No specialist or institutional reference describing a flag of any of these khanates before the 20th century was found.

era-1370.says: Wikipedia's Timurid Empire article: the main symbol of the Timurids is thought to be the 'sign of Timur', three equal circles in a triangle, described by Clavijo (1403) and Ibn Arabshah on the Amir's seal and on coins; Timur's armies are thought to have used red banners topped with a crescent; and a brown or silver flag with three circles in the Catalan Atlas may relate to Timurid lands, though Kadoi calls the evidence scant and ambiguous and the article says there is little certainty about the empire's actual flag. Flags of the World, citing Znamierowski, says blue was Tamerlane's colour.
era-1370.open: The three-ring sign is positively described as an emblem (seal, coins), but no source gives a Timurid state flag, and the sources disagree on colour (red, brown or silver against blue). The blue field with three gold rings drawn on the card is a reconstruction that neither source states.

era-1220.says: Wikipedia's Black Standard article: the Abbasid Revolution adopted black banners and black stayed the Abbasid dynastic colour after 750. Wikipedia's Samanid Empire article: the Samanid brothers were made governors under Abbasid suzerainty in 819, and from 892 under Ismail the dynasty became effectively independent; it has no flag text. Neither Wikipedia's Flag of Uzbekistan nor Flags of the World's Uzbekistan page gives any flag for the region before the Timurids. Second look: the Encyclopaedia Iranica article 'Flags i. Of Persia' says the imperial standard of the Abbasid caliphs was black with a white legend, and that rulers of Abbasid client states received black banners as a sign of legitimacy and carried them along with their own dynastic standards; it adds that Ghaznavid banners were usually red (from an illustrated manuscript, with literary evidence for figures of the homay or a lion) and that the Saljuq monarchs used green, yellow and red.
era-1220.open: Iranica does not name the Samanids or Transoxiana, and it gives no plain black flag as the banner of any ruler of this territory: black is the Abbasid colour carried by client rulers beside their own standards. Iranica's Ghaznavid (red) and Saljuq (green, yellow, red) notes show that black did not remain the colour of the later rulers before 1220. Nothing read describes a Samanid, Karakhanid or Khwarazmian banner, so the plain black field remains a stand-in.

era-1906.says: Wikipedia's flag table lists a British New Hebrides Blue Ensign with the territory emblem (Tudor Crown 1906-1953, St Edward's Crown 1953-1980), a British resident commissioner's flag, a French vertical tricolour (1906-1940, 1944-1980), a Free French version with the Cross of Lorraine (1940-1944), and the 1963 and 1966/1971 Games flags; Wikipedia (New Hebrides) describes the 1906 Protocol as joint sovereignty with two parallel administrations, one British and one French, and no condominium flag. Flags of the World (New Hebrides flags): the British Blue Ensign had a white disc lettered NEW HEBRIDES around a crown (Tudor to 1953, St Edward's after), the Resident Commissioner flew a Union Flag with the same disc; the French-side flag was probably the tricolour (Stilling, unconfirmed); the Free French used a tricolour with the Cross of Lorraine (1940-1945); 'no official joint condominium flag is documented' after the 1889-1906 Commission flag.
era-1906.open: The French-side flag is confirmed only by Wikipedia's table (Flags of the World calls it a probable tricolour); the absence of an official joint flag is Flags of the World's finding for the documents it knows, not proof; the page's single drawing does not show both flags.

era-1929.says: Holy See Press Office (vatican.va): the Lateran Treaty of 11 February 1929 led to the flag's present form, and the modern flag was first raised on 8 June 1929, yellow and white with the crossed keys surmounted by the tiara at the centre. Flags of the World: flag adopted 8 June 1929 (introduced 1825) and arms adopted 7 June 1929; the modern flag first officially hoisted on 8 June 1929. Wikipedia's infobox gives 7 June 1929.
era-1929.open: The adoption day is 7 June on Wikipedia and 8 June on the Holy See and FOTW pages; the page's remark that the 1929 flag is almost unchanged from the last Papal States flag is not stated by the sources, which date the yellow-white colours to 1808.

era-1870.says: Wikipedia's Flag of Vatican City says the Papal States were conquered by Italy on 20 September 1870 and that in 1929 papal authorities chose the 1825-1870 merchant flag as the state flag of the new Vatican City. Flags of the World says the yellow-white flag was used until 1870, when the state was integrated into Italy, and taken again in 1929. The Holy See Press Office history says the flag took its present form after the Lateran Treaty of 1929, first raised on 8 June 1929. Treccani's Enciclopedia Italiana (1930) says the white-and-yellow flag was adopted some years after 1814 for troops and state, and that in the nineteenth century the popes used a white cloth with their personal arms as royal flag; it does not mention flag use after 1870. World Statesmen dates the Vatican City flag from 7 Jun 1929.
era-1870.open: No source read describes papal use of the yellow-white flag, ceremonial or otherwise, between 1870 and 1929; the sources imply the flag lapsed in 1870 and was taken up again in 1929. The Papal Navy ensign FOTW mentions is a different flag, and the Treccani section on the papal flag was read for the pre-1870 flag only.

era-1825.says: Wikipedia: 17 September 1825 yellow-and-white bicolor replaces the earlier flag, colours from the metals of the keys. Flags of the World: yellow-and-white flag recorded as introduced 1825 (Smith: gold and silver accepted 1825); 1808 as origin of the colours.
era-1825.open: Wikipedia and Flags of the World disagree on 1808 versus 1825 origin; neither dates the keys and tiara on the flag; 'unbroken' from 1825 not stated.

era-756.says: The Holy See Press Office history says the old flag of the papal state was red and amaranth/yellow ('giallorossa'), derived from the colours of the Holy See's arms and the traditional colours of the Senate and People of Rome, replaced by white and yellow in 1808, with the oldest surviving yellow-white papal flag dating from 1824. Wikipedia agrees that before 1808 the Papal States commonly used a yellow-red bicolour with the same derivation, and dates the yellow-white merchant flag to 17 September 1825. Flags of the World reports the earliest attested papal flag as red with a white cross (probably c.1195) and yellow-red mostly as cockades in the 1700s.
era-756.open: The sources support the yellow-red colours only for the centuries before 1808 and earlier red flags; none documents a gold and red gonfalone from 756, or calls it a gonfalone. They describe a vertical bicolour (Holy See), not the horizontal gold over red once drawn.

era-1830.says: Wikipedia: 20 November 1817 eighth star decreed; 1930–54 seven-star flag; 17 February 1954 coat of arms on the state flag; 2006 current flag. FOTW: eight stars adopted March 2006; seven-star flag used before 2006.
era-1830.open: The sources give no dates for the 1836, 1859 and 1863 star changes.

era-1810.says: Wikipedia: Miranda's flag first flown 12 March 1806 (Jacmel) and 3 August 1806 (La Vela de Coro); Congress adopted it in 1811. FOTW: Congress recognised it in July 1811.

era-1819.says: FOTW (Great Colombia): the yellow-blue-red tricolour designed by Miranda was provisionally adopted on 17 December 1819 and prescribed by the law of 4 October 1821, with the arms of Cundinamarca; FOTW (Colombia history) gives yellow-blue-red horizontal stripes at 3:2:1. Wikipedia (Flag of Colombia): Miranda created the yellow, blue and red flag, adopted by the Gran Colombia congresses on 17 December 1819; Wikipedia and FOTW on Venezuela say Miranda's tricolour inspired the flags of Colombia and Ecuador.
era-1819.open: A central star is not established: FOTW says Bolivar's variant with an added blue star for Angostura is disputed and that arms sat in the canton or centre in 1820-21; neither source describes a fixed central emblem on the 1819 flag.

era-1777.says: Wikipedia (Cross of Burgundy Flag): after 1506 the ensign was introduced across the Spanish Empire including the Americas, it served as the flag of the Viceroyalties of the New World, remained in use in Spain's overseas empire, and was flown as a jack until Charles III's red-yellow-red naval ensign of 1785. Flags of the World (Burgundy Cross Flag): a red saltire on a usually white field was the Spanish military flag from the 16th century up to 1843, an ensign 1506-1670s and a jack until 1785.
era-1777.open: Neither publisher mentions Venezuela or the Captaincy General of 1777-1810; the Cross of Burgundy is shown as the Spanish colonial and military banner generally, and the naval ensign changed in 1785, so its use as a Venezuelan banner is not documented. The card itself presents it schematically.

era-1976.says: Both sources date the current flag to 1955, before this era begins in 1976, so the flag was already in use at the start. Wikipedia's infobox gives the adoption as 23 November 1940; Flags of the World dates it Adopted 1955.
era-1976.open: Only the year the current flag was adopted was compared; the design and the swatch colours were not checked against a specification.

era-1954.says: Wikipedia: gold-star flag first seen 23 November 1940; modified 30 November 1955 (smaller star, straighter rays); State of Vietnam yellow flag by ordinance 2 June 1948, Bảo Đại 1949; NLF flag 20 December 1960; unified 2 July 1976. FOTW: current design modified from a 1945 flag in 1955 (30 September or 30 November); 2 July 1976 unified hoisting.
era-1954.open: FOTW does not cover the South's flag.

era-1945.says: Wikipedia: Viet Minh proclaimed the gold-star-on-red flag at Tan Trao on 17 August 1945, the Democratic Republic was proclaimed 2 September 1945, a decree of 5 September adopted the flag, the Assembly voted for it on 2 March 1946, and the State of Vietnam's yellow flag with three red bands followed by ordinance on 2 June 1948. FOTW: the Democratic Republic (2 September 1945) flag was set by the Presidential Decree of 5 September 1945 with a construction annex; the Tran Trong Kim government under Japanese rule used a yellow flag with three red stripes; the State of Vietnam was recognised by France on 8 March 1949.
era-1945.open: FOTW's State of Vietnam page has no flag description and copies Wikipedia. The drawing's three red stripes touch each other; the sources describe stripes on yellow. The date of the State of Vietnam's flag differs (June 1948 against the March 1949 recognition).

era-1802.says: Wikipedia (Long tinh flag): the yellow flag with a vertical red stripe was designed by Emperor Khai Dinh, first recorded as a ceremonial flag of the court around 1924, and designated the national flag in the early 1940s, from print sources of 1918, 1941-42 and 1945 (Bulletin des Amis du Vieux Hue, Dong Phap, Tin Moi). Wikipedia (Flag of Vietnam): flags representing the state were only introduced in the later Nguyen period. Flags of the World repeats a Worldstatesmen chronology placing a yellow Long Tinh Ky flag with a red circle in 1802-1885, and WorldStatesmen's own flag strip labels a 'Long Tinh' emperor's flag for 1802-1878/c.1885 (to 1863) with images but no description or basis. A government portal and a Vietnamese-language study cited by Wikipedia were not readable here (one link dead).
era-1802.open: The sources conflict on design (stripe or circle) and date (1920s-1940s or 1802); the 1802-1885 chronology comes from one site and is cited by the other, so it is not independent, and no document of an 1802 flag was found. The card's yellow flag with a red bar for the Nguyen empire in 1802-1887 remains unsupported.

era-1887.says: Wikipedia (Indochinese Union): the infobox flag for 1887-1945 and 1946-1954 is the French flag. Wikipedia (Flag of Vietnam): the French, who gradually gained control in the late 19th century, flew the French flag; in Annam and Tonkin the French flag, a yellow protectorate flag with the tricolour in the canton, and the Long tinh flag were all flown. Flags of the World (French colonies): the flag common to all French possessions was the Tricolore, the use of the French flag being the rule and local flags the exception; FOTW (Indochina) dates the Union Indochinoise to 1887 and a protectorate flag of Annam to 1923-1945.
era-1887.open: Neither publisher describes a separate flag for the Union itself; local protectorate flags of the 1920s-1945 and the Japanese interlude of 1945 are not shown on the card.

era-938-1.says: Wikipedia (Flag of Vietnam): traditional images show the Trung sisters wearing yellow turbans in their AD 40 revolt against Chinese rule, which it describes as royal standards rather than national flags, and says state flags were introduced only in the Nguyen period. Flags of the World (Military History Museum page) shows Vietnamese battle flags of 938 and 1077 and Song, Yuan and Ming flags, but no flag of the Chinese commanderies. No further source on Han-to-Tang banners in Jiaozhi could be reached in this pass.
era-938-1.open: No source read describes a flag or banner flown over the Chinese commanderies of 111 BCE-938, and none mentions a yellow dragon standard; the card's yellow dragon panel is a placeholder, as its caption says.

era-1959.says: Flags of the World: 'The Welsh flag was granted official status in 1959'; in February 1959 the Queen directed that only the red dragon on a green and white field be flown on government buildings in Wales and London; the white-and-green field is 'in the livery colours of the Tudors'. Wikipedia: officially recognised as the national flag in 1959 (cited to a 1959 Hansard written answer by Henry Brooke), government use of the earlier badge-based flag dropped that year at the Gorsedd of Bards' urging; the Tudor livery was added to the flag later.
era-1959.open: The page's 'in informal use for generations' is not stated by either source for this exact green-and-white design: Wikipedia says the Tudor colours came after Henry VII's standard and a badge-based white flag (1953) was used until 1959. Flags of the World's 1 January 1801 date for this row's earlier reading was the Union Flag, not the Welsh flag.

era-1536.says: Flags of the World (Wales): Wales, treated as part of England, never had a portion of the Union Flag; the dragon appears in the royal arms until the union of the crowns in 1605; the Welsh flag was flown with the Union Flag on certain official buildings on St David's Day (Baxter, 1934); the red dragon on a mound became the King's badge for Wales in 1807 and an augmented badge flag was set in 1953 until 1959. Wikipedia's Flag of Wales: in 1910-16 and 1932 Caernarfon town council and Plaid Cymru asked for the Welsh flag to replace the Union Jack on Caernarfon Castle's Eagle tower, and in 1916 the authorities said there was no such thing as a Welsh flag. The Flag Institute quotes the proclamations of 1606 (the Union Flag of the crosses of St George and St Andrew joined) and 1634 (Union Flag reserved for royal ships, other English ships to carry the Red Cross), says the Treaty of Union of 1707 left the design as it was and that the College of Arms designed the new flag of 1 January 1801 adding St Patrick's saltire. Store norske leksikon says Wales is not represented in the Union Flag because it was already united with England when England and Scotland united in 1707.
era-1536.open: The Union Flag of 1801 can stand for the flag of the union Wales belonged to only from 1801; for 1536-1707 the Flag Institute's quotations give the English Red Cross and a royal-ships-only Union Flag, and 1707-1801 had the earlier Union Flag. The sources show the Union Flag flying in Wales only in the early 20th century (Wikipedia); the card's whole-span claim is an assumption.

era-1283.says: Flags of the World (Wales): Edward I defeated Llywelyn and included Wales in an amalgamated kingdom, the Statute of Wales dated 19 February 1284 and Wales treated as a principality within England; the dragon was used in the royal arms in the 15th century; its history page notes Llywelyn the Last probably fought under the Lions of Gwynedd and that Glyndwr unfurled a golden dragon on white on 2 November 1401. Wikipedia's Flag of Wales: Henry Tudor's red dragon standard at Bosworth in 1485. Neither source mentions St George's cross over Wales. Store norske leksikon says Wales was divided in the Middle Ages into small kingdoms, of which Gwynedd and Deheubarth were the main ones, that Llywelyn the Great was recognised as prince of Wales in 1228, and gives the Gwynedd four-lions arms and the dragon banners of Glyndwr and Henry Tudor; it describes no flag of English rule in Wales.
era-1283.open: No page read says that St George's cross or any English flag was flown in Wales in 1283-1536, so the card's caption is not confirmed; the sources document only the Welsh dragon and lion banners of the revolts and of Henry Tudor. A possible source on Edward I's armies and St George's banner (History Today) returned HTTP 403 and was not read.

era-850.says: Flags of the World's history page: the Historia Brittonum gives the dragon as the British symbol, but 'we do not have any clear evidence' of a Welsh dragon banner before the fifteenth century (no unambiguous reference before 1401); Matthew Paris sketched the arms of Gruffudd ap Llywelyn Fawr as quarterly gold and red with four lions, there is no dragon in the arms of Gwynedd, and Llywelyn probably fought under the Lions of Gwynedd. Its Glyndwr page has contributors attributing a four-lions banner to him. Wikipedia's Kingdom of Gwynedd shows an infobox flag of the 13th-century arms and Wikipedia's Flag of Wales gives the Historia Brittonum (c. 828) as the first red dragon. Store norske leksikon (national encyclopedia) says the princes of Gwynedd bore a quartered gold-and-red shield with four lions in the Middle Ages and that Llywelyn the Great (recognised as prince of Wales in 1228) bore the same arms as his father Iorwerth Drwyndwn. A translation of the Chronicle of Adam of Usk has Owain Glyndwr unfurling a golden dragon on a white field at Caernarfon on 2 November (1401). The Flag Institute links the red dragon to the Britons and says Henry Tudor added green and white after Bosworth.
era-850.open: The sources support a lions banner for 13th-century Gwynedd only as a probability (arms are not banners), and give no banner for c. 850-1200 or for Powys and Deheubarth; the earliest dragon banner they document is Glyndwr's of 1401. The lions-and-dragon combination on the card is not described by any source, and the sources state that the arms of Gwynedd have no dragon. The Flag Institute's remark that a dragon has represented Wales since 830 is stated without a source.

era-1990.says: Wikipedia's infobox and FOTW's main page both give 22 May 1990 for the flag, the date Yemen was formed by the union of North and South; FOTW's North Yemen page adds that the new flag removed the star of the Yemen Arab Republic's flag. Both describe a red-white-black tricolour without an emblem.
era-1990.open: Only the adoption date and the removal of the star were compared; whether the flag was neutral 'deliberately', as this page says, and the swatch colours are not stated by these sources.

era-1967.says: Wikipedia: Yemen Arab Republic flag adopted 1 November 1962 (red-white-black tricolour with one green star), relinquished 22 May 1990; PDRY flag adopted 30 November 1967 with a light blue triangle and red star near the hoist. FOTW's North Yemen page: the same tricolour with a green five-pointed star in the white stripe, hoisted 1 November 1962 (the UAR flag with one star removed); FOTW's South Yemen page: red-white-black tricolour with a light blue hoist triangle containing a red five-pointed star, introduced about 30 November 1967.
era-1967.open: The two publishers agree on design and dates; FOTW's date for the southern flag is 'about 30 November 1967'. Wikipedia's wording on the symbolism (triangle for the people, star for the NLF) is not in FOTW.

era-1918.says: Wikipedia's Flag of the Kingdom of Yemen article says the kingdom's flag was plain red from 1918 to 1923, gained the shahada in white in 1923, and from 1927 had a sabre and five stars; it cites the UN Yearbook 1951. FOTW's Kingdom of Yemen page says the flag adopted in 1927 was red with a white sabre and five stars (drawn from National Geographic, February 1951), in use until 1962 and by the royalists until 1970; it also describes the imam's own flag as red with the shahada. For the south, FOTW and Wikipedia give the Aden Colony Blue Ensign with a dhow badge from 1937 to 1963.
era-1918.open: Wikipedia's article and FOTW agree closely and may share wording, so they are not fully independent; the designs for 1918-1927 rest on Wikipedia's gallery and the imam's flag on FOTW alone. Aden did not have 'colonial ensigns throughout' 1918-67: it was part of British India until 1937 (FOTW).

era-1839.says: FOTW's British-rule pages say Aden was first a dependency and later a Chief Commissioner's province of British India up to 1937, when it became a Crown colony; the Chief Commissioner had flown the 'Viceroy's Union', and the Governor of the new colony needed a Union Jack and a Blue Ensign with a dhow badge. Wikipedia and FOTW's Kingdom of Yemen page say North Yemen was nominally part of the Ottoman Empire until 1918. Neither describes a flag for Aden in 1839-1937 beyond the Viceroy's Union, or any Ottoman provincial flag for northern Yemen.
era-1839.open: The plain red field is the page's own placeholder and matches nothing in the sources read; the Aden colonial ensign is documented only from 1937. Ottoman provincial banners for the north are not described by any source read.

era-897.says: Neither Wikipedia's Flag of Yemen article nor FOTW's Kingdom of Yemen page mentions any flag of the Zaidi Imamate before the 20th century or for 897-1839. A search of Wikipedia's articles on the Imams of Yemen and the Qasimid state for flag or colour mentions found none. FOTW notes only the 20th-century imam's flag, red with the shahada.
era-897.open: Green as the Zaidi colour, and any flags of Ayyubid, Rasulid or Ottoman interludes, are in no source read; the plain green field is a stand-in.

era-1964.says: Britannica (flag of Zambia): at independence on 24 October 1964 the new flag was based on the UNIP flag; the green background remains and red, black and orange appear as stripes at the fly end (red for the freedom struggle, black for the African people, orange for copper), with an orange fish eagle flying over them. Wikipedia: green field with an orange fish eagle in flight over red, black and orange stripes in the fly, adopted 24 October 1964 and modified in 1996 (lighter green, adjusted eagle). FOTW: same colour meanings and date, modified in 1996; Whitney Smith cited that the flag is based on the UNIP flag.
era-1964.open: A reference source and two compiled publishers agree on the design and date. The 1996 modification is a design change within the era; the sources do not say the design was a deliberate break from the Blue Ensign tradition, and the green's meaning is given slightly differently (agriculture or vegetation). The National Flag and Armorial Ensigns Act on the Zambian parliament's site timed out and was not read.

era-1953.says: Wikipedia: a blue ensign with the Federation emblem for the Federation of Rhodesia and Nyasaland (1953-1964), and separately a Blue Ensign with the territory's emblem for Northern Rhodesia (1939-1964). FOTW (Northern Rhodesia): Northern Rhodesia joined the Federation on 3 September 1953; the Federation flew a blue ensign with the shield of the Federal Arms in the fly, with the palets wavy taken from the Northern Rhodesia arms; the Federation was dissolved on 31 December 1963; the Governor's flag, a Union Jack with the arms on a white roundel in a green laurel garland, continued through the Federation.
era-1953.open: The Federation's ensign is the flag of the union, and the sources do not say whether the territory's own Blue Ensign (Wikipedia, 1939-1964) was flown alongside it. The Federation ended on 31 December 1963, ten months before independence, so the page's end date of 1964 is approximate.

era-1924.says: Wikipedia (Flag of Zambia) lists the Union Flag for 1924-1964 and a Blue Ensign with the emblem of Northern Rhodesia, and a Governor's Union Jack with the emblem, for 1939-1964. FOTW (Northern Rhodesia): in 1938 the Colonial Office was told the 1928 badge had never been used on any flag; the arms were granted on 16 August 1939; governors were presumed to fly the badge after 1943. Britannica (flag of Zambia): a shield was approved in 1930 (black-and-white wavy stripes for Victoria Falls, blue chief with a gold fish eagle holding a silver fish), first used on the British Blue Ensign as a colonial badge, and approved as arms on 16 August 1939; it does not date the Blue Ensign use.
era-1924.open: The Blue Ensign with the territory's badge is dated by Wikipedia from 1939; Britannica says the badge was first used on the Blue Ensign without a date, and FOTW says it had never been flown by 1938, so the sources conflict over 1924-1939, half the span shown. FOTW's account of 1939-1953 is partly presumption. The badge on the card (a white disc) does not match the arms described.

era-1891.says: Wikipedia (Flag of Zambia) lists for 1891-1924 the flag of the British South Africa Company, a Union Jack defaced with the company emblem in the centre. Flags of the World (British South Africa Company): the company's flag, raised at Bulawayo on 4 November 1893, was a Union Jack with the company badge (a yellow lion holding an elephant's tusk), with or without a red ring, and the company's Blue and Red Ensigns 'in all probability' never flew. FOTW (Northern Rhodesia): the badge was the company crest, which the territory used before 1924, with scant visual evidence of a shield on a blue ensign.
era-1891.open: The sources do not describe the flag specifically over North-Western or North-Eastern Rhodesia; FOTW's Bulawayo hoisting was in the south. FOTW gives the company's rule as 1890 to 1923, against Wikipedia's 1891-1924. The card's drawing was redrawn to the Union Jack form.

era-1980.says: Both sources give 1980, the year this page starts the current flag. Wikipedia's infobox gives the adoption as April 18th, 1980; Flags of the World dates it 18 April 1980.
era-1980.open: Only the year the current flag was adopted was compared; the design and the swatch colours were not checked against a specification.

era-1979.says: Wikipedia: the Zimbabwe Rhodesia flag was adopted 4 Sept 1979; in Dec 1979 Britain took interim control and the Union Jack became the official flag, though the Zimbabwe Rhodesia flag continued to be flown de facto. FOTW Rhodesia: Dec 1979-Apr 1980 the Union Flag was used de facto while the Zimbabwe-Rhodesia flag was in common use. FOTW Zimbabwe: the country returned to British colony status in this period; no new flag described.
era-1979.open: FOTW's Rhodesia page dates the Zimbabwe-Rhodesia flag 1 Sept 1979 / June-Dec 1979, Wikipedia 4 Sept 1979; the Lancaster House stage is not covered.

era-1965.says: Wikipedia: green-white-green vertical triband charged with the coat of arms adopted 11 Nov 1968, the first national flag to contain the Zimbabwe Bird; the 1964 light blue ensign continued three years after UDI. FOTW Rhodesia: UDI 11 Nov 1965; Flag of Rhodesia Act 1968, flag adopted and first raised 11 Nov 1968, three equal vertical stripes with the arms on the white stripe; republic declared 2 March 1970 with the flag unchanged; replaced in 1979.
era-1965.open: The page's claim that the flag was adopted as Rhodesia moved to become a republic is not covered (republic came in 1970); 'plain shield rather than gold relief' is not covered.

era-1923.says: Wikipedia: from 1923 Southern Rhodesia's flag was a Blue Ensign with the shield from its coat of arms (arms granted 11 Aug 1924); Federation of Rhodesia and Nyasaland flag 1953-63; a light blue ensign introduced April 1964. FOTW Rhodesia: dark blue ensign 1923-1953 in two variants (with and without a white disc), Federation ensign 1953-63, Southern Rhodesian light blue ensign 1964-68 flown alongside the Union Flag.
era-1923.open: Both sources have the ensign changing to light blue in 1964 and in use to 1968, not 'until 1965'; they differ on the badge (arms shield vs white disc).

era-1890.says: Flags of the World (BSAC page): the Company's flag was a Union Jack with the Company badge (a yellow lion holding an elephant's tusk on a red and yellow wreath, letters B.S.A.C. beneath) at the centre, with several variants; the first flag of sovereignty was a plain Union Jack raised at Fort Salisbury on 13 September 1890, the first Company flag reached Fort Salisbury in 1892 and was raised at Bulawayo on 4 November 1893; Blue and Red Ensigns with the badge were designed but in all probability never used. Wikipedia's British South Africa Company and Flag of Zimbabwe articles show a 'Flag of the British South Africa Company (1890-1923)' image and say the Company administered the territory until 1923, without describing the design.
era-1890.open: The design rests on Flags of the World alone (Wikipedia gives the flag and dates as an image caption only); the Blue Ensign with a Company badge that the card's caption and paragraph suggest is not confirmed and was probably never used.
