era-1949.says: Flags of the World (colonial flags): sixty-five colonial badges were in use in 1949, declining as colonies became independent, and colonial flags date from 1869. Wikipedia (Historical flags): remaining territories have flags of their own (British Virgin Islands 1960, British Antarctic Territory 1963, British Indian Ocean Territory 1990) and Akrotiri and Dhekelia use the Union Jack. Wikipedia (Flag of the Commonwealth of Nations): the Commonwealth has its own flag, a gold globe on blue adopted on 26 March 1976 and modified in 2013. The Commonwealth Secretariat's history page dates the modern Commonwealth to the London Declaration of 26 April 1949 (a meeting of Prime Ministers in 1949 agreed that republics could be members) and mentions no flag.
era-1949.open: The 1949 date is now supported as the start of the modern Commonwealth, but no source says the Union Flag is used by the Commonwealth of Nations, which has a flag of its own; the 1997 date is not given by any source read, and only Akrotiri and Dhekelia are said to use the Union Jack alone.

era-1947.says: FOTW coflg: 1865 Blue Ensign with colony badge in the fly; 1869 governors' Union Jack with badge; 1882-1927 defaced Red Ensigns; 1941 governor's flag in all circumstances; 65 badges in 1949; badges declined as colonies became independent. WP: colonies adopted own badges from the early 19th century, Colonial Naval Defence Act 1865 required emblems.
era-1947.open: Page said 'badge in the canton'; FOTW says in the fly for ensigns. Dates 1947-1980s as a wave are not stated by either source.

era-1919.says: FOTW (colonial flags): a plain Red Ensign was the proper ensign of any vessel registered in a British colony, and the Admiralty authorised defaced Red Ensigns for overseas territories by warrant between 1882 and 1927 (North Borneo 1882, Kenya 1890, Canada 1892, Palestine 1927). Wikipedia (Red Ensign): the flag flown by British merchant ships since 1707, plain or defaced with a badge, allocated to merchantmen by an order in council of 1864.
era-1919.open: Neither source treats 1919 or the post-war mandates as a turning point (Palestine's 1927 warrant is the only mandate named); the 'informal' territorial use stated on the page is not in them.

era-1783.says: Flags of the World (colonial flags): in 1865 the Admiralty ruled that vessels maintained by a colony under the Colonial Naval Defence Act should wear a Blue Ensign with the colony's seal or badge in the fly; its overview says the official flag of a colony was the Union Jack, with a Blue Ensign for government vessels, and colonial flags and governors' flags date from 1869. Wikipedia (Colonial Naval Defence Act 1865): in 1866 the Admiralty advised that such vessels fly the Royal Navy Blue Ensign with the colony's badge; Wikipedia's historical-flags list adds that colonies began adopting badges in the first half of the 19th century. NZ History (Ministry for Culture and Heritage) says the Colonial Naval Defence Act of 1865 ruled that all ships owned by a colonial government must fly the Blue Ensign with the colony's badge, that New Zealand's government steamers were reprimanded in 1866 for flying it without a badge, and that the Union Jack remained the legal flag of New Zealand.
era-1783.open: The Blue Ensign with a colonial badge is documented only from 1865-69 and for government vessels, so 1783-1865 is not covered and 'standard government/colonial-administration flag' is not stated; FOTW and NZ History both give the Union Jack as the colony's official flag. The drawing shows no badge, whereas the Act required one (New Zealand's plain Blue Ensign was reprimanded).

era-1583.says: Wikipedia (Historical flags of the British Empire): early flags across the Empire, including the Thirteen Colonies, were variations of the Red and Blue Ensigns without colonial badges, and its list shows British America with a Red Ensign bearing the first Union Jack in the canton, also called the Queen Anne Flag and amended into the Continental Colours of 1775, until 1776 (de facto) or 1783 (de jure) in the US. Wikipedia (Red Ensign): an English red ensign with the Cross of St George in the canton from the 1620s, used by Massachusetts from its founding, with a 1674 proclamation of Charles II confirming it for English merchant ships. Flags of the World (United Kingdom): the first Union Flag dates to 1606 and St Patrick's cross was added on 1 January 1801. The Flag Institute quotes the proclamation of 12 April 1606 (subjects of Great Britain to wear the St George and St Andrew crosses joined in the maintop) and the proclamation of 5 May 1634, which forbids subjects to carry the Union Flag, reserves it for the King's own ships and orders other English ships to carry the Red Cross; it adds that the Treaty of Union of 1707 kept the design.
era-1583.open: Both colonial-flag statements are Wikipedia only. The Flag Institute's quoted proclamations speak of ships and give the Union Flag only to royal ships from 1634, so a Union canton on merchant or colonial ensigns before 1707 is not shown by it. 'King's Colours' and 'Grand Union pattern' appear in no source read, FOTW's pages read give nothing on colonial use before 1865, and the c.1583 start is the page's own.

era-1795-1.open: Whether a flag, banner or standard existed in this period was not checked. The colour shown is not evidence of one.

era-1959.says: Wikipedia: the eight-stripe design was kept after statehood in 1959, and Hawaii Revised Statutes 5-19 (2024) define its specifications. Flags of the World: the Hawaii Revised Statutes describe the flag as eight horizontal stripes, alternately white, red, blue; its historical page's chronology (summarising Quaife et al., 1961) has the State of Hawaii using the Hawaiian flag, confirmed in 1959.
era-1959.open: Neither source gives the year the flag was first codified in state law (the FOTW chronology says 'confirmed 1959'), nor the meaning of the eight stripes beyond the contributor's 'eight principal islands'.

era-1898.says: Wikipedia: the design was kept after US annexation in 1898; the governor's flag in territorial years carried 'TH'. Flags of the World's historical page: the Territory of Hawaii used the Hawaiian flag, confirmed in 1903, and it shows a territorial governor's flag, a blue-over-red bicolour with eight white stars. Wikipedia's Republic of Hawaii article records that at the transfer of 12 August 1898 the Flag of Hawaii was lowered over Iolani Palace and the US flag raised.
era-1898.open: The use of the Hawaiian flag as a flag of the Territory rests on one FOTW chronology (summarising a 1961 book) and Wikipedia's 'kept'; whether a separate territorial banner was designed beyond the governor's flag is not covered. The territory's incorporation date is not given in the sources used.

era-1894.says: Wikipedia: the design was kept after the 1893 overthrow of the monarchy. Flags of the World: on 8 April 1896 the Republic's government issued a diagram with flag regulations (a fimbriated Cross of St George one stripe wide, 1/6 border); its historical page's chronology says the Republic of Hawaii readopted the Hawaiian flag in 1894.
era-1894.open: Neither source describes why the flag was kept or its effect on the Republic's legitimacy, which the page's caption asserts.

era-1893.says: Wikipedia's Flag of Hawaii says the Hawaiian flag design (eight stripes and a Union Jack canton) was retained through the overthrow of the monarchy in 1893, the Republic and annexation; its Provisional Government of Hawaii article carries the same flag in its infobox. FOTW's Hawaii page has a chronology giving the U.S. flag flown in Hawaii from 1 February to 1 April 1893 and the Republic of Hawaii readopting the Hawaiian flag in 1894. Second look: no further source could be read; World Statesmen has no page for Hawaii at the addresses tried, and the Hawaii State Archives and Iolani Palace addresses tried returned 404. Wikipedia's Provisional Government article only repeats the Hawaiian flag in its infobox.
era-1893.open: No source describes a flag specific to the Provisional Government (1893-1894) or says what flew over it day to day; FOTW's chronology suggests the US flag flew for part of 1893 and a readoption in 1894, while Wikipedia says only that the design was retained. The caption's 'flown over a government installed at gunpoint' is narrative the sources do not address.

era-1795.says: Wikipedia: the British Red Ensign was the unofficial flag c.1793-1816; a distinct Hawaiian flag first reached a foreign port in March 1817; early versions (1816-1845) varied in stripe count (nine stripes, 1:2 canton; Golovnin in 1818 saw seven); the eight-stripe design was specified in 1843 and first unfurled on 25 May 1845. Flags of the World's historical page: Hawaii flew the Union Jack from 1794 to 1816 and an early version of the present flag from 1816 to 1843; a quoted Polynesian newspaper of 31 May 1845 says the new national banner with eight stripes was unfurled on 25 May 1845, differing little from the former, which had seven; a contributor adds that the stripe count varied and was set at eight after 1843.
era-1795.open: The attribution to Kamehameha I is traditional and disputed (Wikipedia; a FOTW poster credits Captain Hunt for the 1845 design and others Captains Adams or Beckley). FOTW's chronology gives 20 May 1845, its newspaper quote 25 May. The meaning of eight stripes as eight islands appears only in FOTW's quoted newspaper and a contributor.

era-1206-1.says: This page's own caption calls the image a placeholder: «placeholder maroon field — pre-unification era, no flag survives».
era-1206-1.open: Whether a flag, banner or standard existed in this period was not checked. The colour shown is not evidence of one.

era-209bce.says: This page's own caption calls the image a placeholder: «placeholder — no banner survives from any pre-Chinggisid steppe empire».
era-209bce.open: Whether a flag, banner or standard existed in this period was not checked. The colour shown is not evidence of one.

era-1206.says: Wikipedia (Tug): a tug or sulde is a pole topped with horsetail hair of varying colours; the white banner was a peacetime symbol and the black one a wartime symbol, the original white banner disappeared early and the black survived as the repository of Genghis Khan's soul; a 15th-century Rashid al-Din manuscript shows white banners at his proclamation as Khagan. FOTW: chronicles describe white and black banners with nine tails, white sacred; it calls modern reconstructions of Genghis Khan's banners very doubtful.
era-1206.open: Neither source gives a fixed design or a date for the banner's adoption; the 1206 date comes only from an image file name, not the article text.

era-1240.says: Flags of the World (early Mongol flags): the 1375 Catalan Atlas shows a silver flag with an engrailed fly and two red charges, a crescent and a simplified tamga, over Sarai, Tana and Urgench, a variant of the 'Emperor of Sarai' flag in the Libro del conoscimiento that FOTW thinks may be one that really existed. Wikipedia (Catalan Atlas): the Golden Horde symbol resembles a tamgha, found on Golden Horde coinage until about Jani Beg, with no colours given. Wikipedia (Golden Horde): c. 1225/1242-1502; the name is first known from the History of Kazan of 1565. Second look: the Libro del conoscimiento (Markham translation) says the device of the Emperor of Sara (Uxbeco, crowned at Sara) is a white flag with a red sign, and that the king of Norgancio flies a white flag with the red sign of Uxbeco; this agrees in colours with the Atlas flag FOTW describes (silver with red charges). The Libro is described by Wikipedia as an armorial presented as an imaginary travelogue.
era-1240.open: Both the Libro (text) and the Atlas (map) are 14th-century European depictions of the khan of Sarai's flag and they are closely related works, so they are not independent proof that the Horde itself used the flag. The page's drawing now follows the Atlas flag; no source read says the khans' own banner looked like this.

era-1225.says: Flags of the World (early Mongol flags): the 1375 Catalan Atlas shows a white flag with a gold square in the centre, with an engrailed fly, over Chagatai cities (Khotan, Baldassia and others); FOTW warns that the flags may not reflect real use. Wikipedia (Catalan Atlas): cities in the Chagatai realm are shown with a Chagatai flag, with no colours described. Wikipedia (Chagatai Khanate): 1227-1347 as a whole, the western part to 1403 and Moghulistan to 1462. Second look: the 14th-century Libro del conoscimiento (Markham translation) gives a white flag with a gold pale to "the empire of Armalec", a name the translator glosses with a query as Bengal, so it cannot be tied to the Chagatai realm; no other Chagatai flag turned up. The Libro is described by Wikipedia as an armorial presented as an imaginary travelogue.
era-1225.open: The map depiction is documented, by FOTW only in colour, and no source read shows it was used by the Chagatai khans. The Libro text read does not name a Chagatai device. No specialist Mongol-flag reference beyond FOTW was found; the Reichert-published Kadoi article on the Timurid flag (cited by Wikipedia for the Atlas flags) is a 91 MB PDF on the publisher site and was not fetched.

era-1256.says: Flags of the World (early Mongol flags): the 1375 Catalan Atlas shows a golden flag with a red square in the centre over Ilkhanate cities (Kerman, Qeshm, Bukhara, Samarkand), remarking that it is in fact the flag of Persia from the Libro del conoscimiento, with a caveat on real use. Wikipedia (Catalan Atlas): the Ilkhanate flag appears on the ruler's realm and on a ship in the Indian Ocean, undescribed. Wikipedia (Ilkhanate): 1256-1335, with a remnant ended by Jani Beg's conquest of Tabriz in 1357. Second look: the Libro del conoscimiento (Markham translation) says the Emperor of Persia has for his device a yellow flag with a red square in the middle, and the translator's note names that emperor (Vnascayt) as Abu Said, Mongol sultan of Persia 1317-1335; this matches the golden-with-red-square flag FOTW describes on the Atlas. The Libro is described by Wikipedia as an armorial presented as an imaginary travelogue.
era-1256.open: Text and map agree on a yellow/gold flag with a red square for the ruler of Persia, but they are closely related 14th-century European works and neither shows the Ilkhans themselves flying it. Not attested for 1256-1335 as a whole.

era-1271.says: Wikipedia (Tug): a Japanese scroll reportedly shows a black banner on the Yuan fleet in the invasions of Japan of 1274 and 1281. Flags of the World (early Mongol flags): the 1375 Catalan Atlas flies a silver flag with three red crescents over the Grand Khan's cities, but FOTW adds that there seems to be no evidence the Grand Khan really used that design. Wikipedia (Yuan dynasty) dates the dynasty 1271-1368 and describes no flag. Second look: the Libro del conoscimiento (Markham translation) gives devices for the emperors of Persia and Sara but I found none for the Emperor of Cathay beyond a remark that people in Java carry his image on their flags. Wikipedia's Yuan article quotes the Yuan shi that Genghis Khan raised a nine-tailed white banner at his enthronement in 1206, which is before the Yuan.
era-1271.open: No source describes a red-and-gold court banner; the card's caption itself says its banner rests on no source. The crescent flag is a map depiction FOTW doubts, the black banner is a single reported scroll in Wikipedia, and the 1206 white banner is a Mongol Empire, not Yuan, record. The Chen Yuan article cited for the Yuan's choice of white (J. Song-Yuan Studies 44, 2014) is behind a paywall and Academia.edu returned 403 (not worked around).

era-14.says: Wikipedia gives separate end dates: Ilkhanate 1256-1335 (remnant ended 1357); Yuan 1271-1368 (Dadu fell 14 September 1368); Chagatai Khanate 1227-1347 as a whole, with a western part to 1403 and Moghulistan to 1462; Golden Horde to 1502 (the Great Horde by 1466, with the Kazan, Astrakhan and Crimean khanates as successors). Wikipedia (Tug) says tugs were later used in derived Turco-Mongol khanates.
era-14.open: The card is an openly stated placeholder (a plain gold card marked ABSORBED / DISSOLVED), and no source read describes a flag for the khanates' 14th-16th century ends or links gold to imperial authority. The dates are all Wikipedia, one publisher.

era-1370.says: This page's own caption calls the image a placeholder: «placeholder — no surviving Timurid national flag; Timur's own tamga (a trefoil of three rings) is attested on his tomb and coinage, not as a».
era-1370.open: Whether a flag, banner or standard existed in this period was not checked. The colour shown is not evidence of one.

era-1803.says: Wikipedia's Flags of the Mughal Empire does not discuss 1803-1857 and does not mention the East India Company. Its Bahadur Shah Zafar article says the empire had by the early 19th century been reduced to Delhi and its surroundings and the emperor was a titular ruler pensioned by the Company; its only flag mention is a caption for one of the many alams of the Mughal Empire. Flags of the World does not cover the period.
era-1803.open: No source read describes a Mughal flag, or Company colours, for the rump period. The card openly shows a label ('EIC / CROWN RULE') rather than a flag, so no flag is claimed; the 1803 start date is not given in the pages read.

era-1707.says: Wikipedia's Flags of the Mughal Empire calls the alam primarily moss green with a lion and sun, and captions an 1797 funeral of Asaf-ud-Daulah as showing the green Mughal flag raised higher than the Awadh flag; the article carries a needs-citations banner. Down To Earth says late-17th-century flags matched earlier descriptions (a radiant sun on a triangular flag). Flags of the World shows a lion with the sun on the imperial standard, undated and uncoloured.
era-1707.open: Neither publisher says whether any flag changed after Aurangzeb's death in 1707; the 1797 episode rests on Wikipedia alone, and the gold star on a rectangular field drawn on the card is not what either source describes.

era-1658.says: Wikipedia's Flags of the Mughal Empire calls the alam primarily moss green with a lion and sun and shows an illustration of Aurangzeb commanding his army with triangular green flags, a painting of his 1705 expedition with flags in the background, a green standard with a gold sun, and a seal of Aurangzeb. Down To Earth, quoting Robin Thomas, says that by the end of the 17th century the imperial flags matched the earlier descriptions of a radiant sun on a triangular flag. Flags of the World shows a lion with the sun on the imperial standard, undated.
era-1658.open: No source describes a flag specific to Aurangzeb's reign by name; the sources differ on whether the lion was still shown beside the sun, and only Wikipedia gives green. The card's gold sun-and-lion motif is therefore a reconstruction.

era-1628.says: Wikipedia: Padshahnama paintings of Shah Jahan's reign show scarlet pennons with green borders bearing a lion with a rising sun, and a green field with a couchant lion and rising sun; red and green standards at the 1631 Kandahar siege. Down To Earth (citing Padshahnama paintings of 1631 and 1655) describes scarlet pennants with green borders at the 1631 siege of Qandahar and standards with a green field in a 1655 painting, and says the lion-and-sun appears prominently on the imperial flag from Jahangir's time on. FOTW shows a lion with the sun on the imperial standard, without colours or dates.
era-1628.open: The sources describe more than one design (scarlet-with-green-border pennants and green-field standards), so no single fixed flag for the reign is established; the page's plain green alam is one of them.

era-1556.says: Wikipedia, citing the Ain-i-Akbari, says at least five alams were carried with Akbar, and cites Edward Terry (1655, at Jahangir's court) for a silk royal standard with a crouching lion partly shadowing the sun; it calls the alam primarily moss green. Down To Earth, quoting Robin Thomas, also relies on Terry for Jahangir and says Akbar-era flags carried only a radiant sun on a triangular flag. Flags of the World shows a lion with the sun on the imperial standard, undated and uncoloured.
era-1556.open: The sources disagree on Akbar's device (lion and sun traced to Timur per Wikipedia; only a radiant sun per Down To Earth), and no second publisher gives the colour green for either reign. The card's star on a rectangular field matches neither description.

era-1526.says: Wikipedia's Flags of the Mughal Empire says the principal imperial standard, the alam, was primarily moss green with a lion and sun, and that the Mughals traced its use back to Timur; for this period it shows only seals of Babur and Humayun. Flags of the World names Babur as founder without any date or flag detail. Down To Earth, citing Robin Thomas, dates the prominent lion-and-sun motif to Jahangir's time and says Akbar-era flags carried only a radiant sun on a triangular flag.
era-1526.open: No source read describes a flag of Babur or Humayun (1526-1556). The green alam here is a reconstruction from the empire's general standard; the star on a rectangular field drawn on the card matches no description (the sources give a lion and sun, or a radiant sun, on a triangular flag).

era-1000.says: This page's own caption calls the image a placeholder: «placeholder — no attested Norse or indigenous national banner».
era-1000.open: Whether a flag, banner or standard existed in this period was not checked. The colour shown is not evidence of one.

era-1949.says: Wikipedia: the Union Flag was readopted as the provincial flag in 1949 and stayed official until 1980, when the House of Assembly approved Christopher Pratt's design. FOTW's history page (citing Public Record Office papers): union with Canada took effect 31 March 1949 with no immediate effect on flags, the Revised Statutes of 1952 (chapter 272) retained the Red and Blue Ensigns and reaffirmed the Union Jack as the 'national flag', the ensigns were discontinued in 1965, and the Union Jack remained the provincial flag until the present flag was chosen by the House of Assembly on 28 May 1980, given royal assent on 6 June and first raised 24 June.
era-1949.open: The sources give slightly different 1980 dates (Wikipedia: approved 28 May, first flown 24 June; FOTW's main page: adoption 6 June, first raising 23 or 24 June) and the Canadian Red Ensign is not shown by either as the provincial flag; the end of the 1949 era at 1980 on this page is a design choice of the page.

era-1934.says: Wikipedia: the National Flag Act of 1931 made the Union Flag the national flag until 1949, with the Red Ensign for merchant ships and the Blue Ensign for government ships. FOTW's history page: the National Flag Act took effect 15 May 1931 and reduced the planned three national flags to one, the Union Jack; the legislature asked in 1933 for the constitution to be suspended and Commissioners took office in 1934, ending Dominion status; the Union Jack stayed the 'national flag' through the 1949 union and the 1952 statutes.
era-1934.open: Both sources date the Union Jack as national flag from 1931, not 1934; the 1934 start of this row is the start of the Commission of Government only, and the sources contradict the page's earlier statement that the Union Jack replaced the Red Ensign in 1934.

era-1907.says: Wikipedia: Newfoundland became a Dominion in 1907 without formally adopting an ensign; the Red and Blue Ensigns bearing the Great Seal were official from 1904 to 1931 and the Red Ensign was widely treated as the national flag. FOTW's history page: the 1904 badge (the allegorical scene from the colony's seal, approved 18 May 1904) appeared on the Governor's Union Jack and the government Blue Ensign, and was approved for the Red Ensign on 25 October 1918; from 1918 to 1965 Newfoundland flew the British Red Ensign with the badge on the fly as a merchant ensign.
era-1907.open: The sources differ on dates: Wikipedia has the Dominion from 1907, FOTW says Dominion status was granted in 1917; Wikipedia says the ensigns were official to 1931 while FOTW has the Red Ensign as a merchant ensign to 1965. Both place the national flag as the Union Jack from 1931, so this row's end at 1934 is not supported.

era-1870.says: Flags of the World (Newfoundland) documents a Governor's Union Jack and a government Blue Ensign with a crown and Terra Nova badge on a white disc from 1870 (the Admiralty agreed the substitution on 28 September 1870). Wikipedia says Parliament designated a Newfoundland civil ensign in 1904 and that a Red Ensign with a colonial badge was the civil ensign in the Victorian era.
era-1870.open: Only one publisher documents the 1870 Blue Ensign; Wikipedia's Red Ensign for the same years is not matched by FOTW, which dates the Red Ensign with the badge to 1918.

era-1610.says: Flags of the World documents a flag at Government House in 1862 (white with a red St George's cross) and nothing before it; the sources read do not cover 1610-1862.
era-1610.open: One publisher, one year: the 1862 flag is documented, and nothing is said of what flew from 1610 to 1862 or from 1862 to 1870. The drawing is a plain St George's cross; the Commons file for 1862-1870 was not used (it is 600 KB).

era-1299.says: This page's own caption calls the image a placeholder: «placeholder — Osman I's small frontier beylik, no fixed banner survives».
era-1299.open: Whether a flag, banner or standard existed in this period was not checked. The colour shown is not evidence of one.

era-1922.says: Flags of the World (Turkey): the flag in use since 1844 was adopted in law on 29 May 1936 without alteration, and nothing changed in the flag when the Ottoman Empire became the Republic; its Ottoman page ends the empire on 1 November 1922 with the sultanate eliminated and the republic proclaimed on 29 October 1923. Wikipedia's Flags of the Ottoman Empire dates the Turkish Flag Law to 29 May 1936 and lists a caliphate standard of Abdulmejid II (19 November 1922 - 3 March 1924). None describes a separate flag for 1922-23.
era-1922.open: The card is a text pointer to the Turkey page, not a flag; the sources read describe no distinct flag for this one-year span, only continuity of the 1844 design.

era-1844.says: Wikipedia: 1844 official adoption of the red flag with white crescent and five-pointed star (Tanzimat), after an eight-pointed-star flag 1793-1844; a footnote gives a rival claim of 1826 under Mahmud II. Flags of the World (Turkey): the basic form was established in 1793 under Selim III (green navy flags changed to red, white crescent and star added) and 'the five-pointed star dates from approximately 1844'; the 1936 Turkish law adopted the 1844 Ottoman design unaltered. Flags of the World (Ottoman Empire) flags its own 1793/1844 dates from Znamierowski as unevidenced and notes 1857 and 1905 charts show a five-pointed star. Flags of the World's 19th-century chart page gives no 1844 date and shows charts with six-pointed (Steenbergen 1862) and eight-pointed (Webster 1884) stars.
era-1844.open: Both sources date the five-pointed star to about 1844, but FOTW treats it as 'approximately' and unevidenced, Wikipedia has a rival 1826 claim, and a contributor recorded a seven-pointed star on one chart; the two sources may share one origin (Znamierowski). The 1922 end date and the claim that the flag is still Turkey's are covered under the 1922 row.

era-1793.says: Wikipedia: an 1793 decree required navy ships to fly a red flag with a white star and crescent; an eight-pointed-star flag was in use 1793-1844, before the five-pointed star. Flags of the World (Turkey): the basic form was established in 1793 under Selim III, with the five-pointed star from about 1844.
era-1793.open: Both publishers may draw on one origin (Znamierowski); FOTW's Ottoman page marks its 1793/1844 dates as unevidenced. The decree names a navy flag, and the sources do not say the same design flew on land. The eight-pointed star is hand-drawn.

era-1517.says: Wikipedia: Zulfiqar war flags were typical of the 16th and 17th centuries; a simple crescent flag is reported until 1780; the star and crescent is reported at Mohacs (1526) and Vienna (1683); two Ottoman naval flags of 1613 in Madrid are swallow-tailed, one green with a white crescent, one white with a red crescent; an 1793 decree set the navy's red flag with a white star and crescent, and 1844 adopted the national flag. Flags of the World agrees. Çetin (2021) adds museum evidence: a red silk banner dated 1683 (Metropolitan Museum / Khalili) with a Zulfikar and eight-pointed stars within crescents, and says crescent-and-star depictions exist from the 16th century, well before Selim III; Çetin (2021) cites Selânikî for the sultanic banners under Süleyman: one white, two red, one green, two green-and-red and one yellow-and-red, so several banners were in use at once.
era-1517.open: No source read calls a plain red single-crescent banner the empire's flag through 1517-1844. The documented flags are Zulfikar war flags, green and white naval flags, several concurrent sultanic banners in different colours, and by the 18th century crescent-and-star red flags. No land state flag for the whole period is described.

era-1453.says: Wikipedia says a simple crescent flag started to appear from 1453 (a Siege of Rhodes image of 1480 and a ship of 1487) and was reported until 1780, that Babinger thinks Mehmed 'possibly' took the star and crescent from the Byzantines, and that Selim I used a Zulfiqar flag in the 1510s. Flags of the World's Zulfikar page shows Selim I's standard. Çetin (2021) catalogues the Topkapı flag attributed to Selim I (1512-1520, inscribed on its finial), a 400x250 cm 'saltanat sancağı' of güvez-coloured silk with a gold Zulfikar and the Sura of Victory, and undated 'early Ottoman' flags of güvez silk with three gold crescents and of cream silk with one crescent.
era-1453.open: No source read calls a plain red banner the imperial banner of 1453-1517, and the surviving banners that Çetin ties to the period are described as güvez-coloured or cream silk with gold crescents or the Zulfikar, not red. The colour of Wikipedia's 1453-1780 crescent pictures is not given in the text. The card's red single-crescent flag is a stand-in.

era-1362.says: Wikipedia's Flags of the Ottoman Empire: pre-modern Ottoman armies used the horse-tail standard (tugh), war flags came into use by the 16th century, and the crescent had 14th-century associations with the Ottoman military. Flags of the World's 18th-century page shows the tugh (Tournefort, Picart); its Zulfikar page describes Barbarossa's green standard of the 16th century. Çetin (2021, peer-reviewed museum survey) says the single crescent can be traced to Osman Gazi and that each sultan from Osman Gazi had his own banners (citing Uzunçarşılı), but the Topkapı flags it lists are undated 'early Ottoman' pieces of güvez-coloured silk with three gold crescents and of cream silk with a crescent, none described as plain green.
era-1362.open: No source read describes a plain green battle standard for 1362-1453: the tugh is documented only in 18th-century images, the one green standard described is of the 16th century, and Çetin's early banners are güvez-coloured or cream, with crescents. The card's green stand-in is not confirmed.

era-2700bce.says: This page's own caption calls the image a placeholder: «placeholder — no attested banner; pre-vexillological ancient kingdom».
era-2700bce.open: Whether a flag, banner or standard existed in this period was not checked. The colour shown is not evidence of one.

era-633.says: Wikipedia (Battle of al-Qadisiyyah, 16-19 November 636): the Sasanian standard, the Derafsh-e Kaveyan, stood by the commander Rustam and was taken among the spoils; Wikipedia (Derafsh Kaviani) says its capture symbolised the Sasanian collapse. Wikipedia (Sasanian Empire) dates the fall to the Rashidun Caliphate to 651. Flags of the World (pre-Islamic flags) dates the loss to A.D. 637 in one footnote.
era-633.open: The card is a text panel marking the end of the Sasanian era and shows no flag. The only flag event in the sources is the loss of the derafsh at Qadisiyyah in 636-637, and no flag of the conquering side is described here.

era-224.says: Wikipedia: the derafsh was the official standard of the Sasanian Empire (224-651), bejewelled, with a star emblem; the lead image is an artist's rendition. FOTW: Sasanian use is 'purported', later Sasanian coins do not show it, and no image survives so all depictions are reconstructions; Qadisiyyah dated 636 or 637.
era-224.open: The page's 636 date is one of two dates given by FOTW; the apron legend is from the Shahnameh (10th century) and its antiquity is not established.

era-247bce.says: Wikipedia (Derafsh Kaviani): Shapur Shahbazi is quoted that the imperial standard of the Parthian Empire 'seems to have been' the Derafsh Kaviani, while Parthian texts do not mention it. Flags of the World (Sassanian Empire page): flag-like standards appear on coins of the fratarakas of Persis in the 3rd-2nd centuries BCE under Seleucid and Arsacid rule and vanish from coins by the end of the 2nd century BCE. Wikipedia (Parthian Empire) describes Parthian horse archers and a drachma showing a seated archer, but no standard or flag. Second look: the Encyclopaedia Iranica article 'Derafš' says the Arsacids used a flag with the image of the sun (citing Tertullian) and, as standards of units of 1,000 soldiers, silken banners bearing a dragon (citing Lucian), that eagle banners were used by the Parthians and Armenians, and that Persis rulers under Seleucid and Parthian overlordship used a saltire plaque banner on coins; its article on the pre-Islamic army says the Parthians carried various banners often ornamented with dragons; 'Flags i. Of Persia' says feudal magnates of the Parthian and Sasanian periods bore family devices on their standards (a dragon for the house of Rostam, a golden lion for Gōdarz).
era-247bce.open: These are banners reported from ancient writers through Iranica; none is an imperial flag of the Parthian state, no image of one survives in the sources read, and none is the bow-and-horse standard drawn on the card. The Derafsh Kaviani is tentatively linked to the Parthians by one scholar, and the Parthian drachma shows a seated archer, not a standard.

era-312bce.says: Wikipedia (Seleucid Empire, 312-63 BC): the horned horse, the elephant, the anchor and the goddesses Nike and Tyche were common Seleucid symbols, and its infobox shows a tetradrachm of Seleucus I with symbols of the monarchy. Wikipedia (Seleucus I Nicator): the anchor figures in the legend of his birth (an anchor ring, an anchor-shaped birthmark). Wikipedia (Derafsh Kaviani) and Flags of the World report a flag-like standard on coins of the Persis governors under Seleucid rule.
era-312bce.open: The anchor is attested as a Seleucid symbol, not as a banner; no source read says the Seleucids flew a flag, and a sun device is not described. The gold-disc-and-anchor drawing is a reconstruction. The Persis governors' standard is a local device of a subordinate dynasty.

era-334bce.says: Wikipedia (Achaemenid Empire): Alexander defeated the Persian armies at Granicus (334 BC), Issus and Gaugamela and annexed the empire in 330 BC. Wikipedia (Derafsh Kaviani) says some academics see the Derafsh Kaviani in a damaged part of the Alexander Mosaic; Xenophon gives a golden eagle as the Achaemenid standard. Flags of the World lists no flag of the conquest itself.
era-334bce.open: The card is a text panel and shows no flag. The sources describe no separate flag for the conquest years; Alexander's own banners are not covered by any source read.

era-550bce.says: Wikipedia (Khvarenah, Iconography): the winged emblem commonly known as the faravahar or Farr-e Kiyani, a bearded figure in a winged ring or an empty winged disk, is found in Achaemenid royal imagery from Darius I and is linked to Ahura Mazda, to fravahars or to royal glory, an identification that remains disputed. Wikipedia (Achaemenid Empire, infobox) shows the Standard of Cyrus the Great as a golden eagle on a shaft, a reconstruction based on a Persepolis tile and the Alexander Mosaic; Wikipedia (Derafsh Kaviani) cites Xenophon for a golden eagle standard, and Flags of the World quotes Preble for a golden eagle on a white flag.
era-550bce.open: The winged emblem is a royal relief motif, not said to be a flag; the standard the sources describe is a golden eagle, so the blue-field faravahar is the card's reconstruction and not a documented banner. The eagle accounts are secondhand (Xenophon, Preble).

era-753bce.says: This page's own caption calls the image a placeholder: «placeholder — the legendary Kingdom of Rome, no banner survives».
era-753bce.open: Whether a flag, banner or standard existed in this period was not checked. The colour shown is not evidence of one.

era-1000bce.says: This page's own caption calls the image a placeholder: «placeholder — scattered Iron Age hut villages, no polity or banner yet».
era-1000bce.open: Whether a flag, banner or standard existed in this period was not checked. The colour shown is not evidence of one.

era-1453.says: Wikipedia: Constantinople was captured by the Ottoman Empire on 29 May 1453 after a 53-day siege under Sultan Mehmed II, ending the Byzantine Empire. Flags of the World's Byzantine page: Michael VIII Palaiologos retook Constantinople in 1261 and his descendants held the throne until the city and the Empire fell to the Ottomans in 1453.
era-1453.open: This is a pointer card: the two sources date the event and the succession but describe no flag raised or lowered at the fall.

era-330.says: Flags of the World: 'The Byzantine Imperial flag is yellow with a black crowned double-headed eagle', 'the symbol of the Palaiologos' (1258-1453), first made by an emperor Komnenos, crowns added by the Palaiologoi (one for Nikaia, one for Constantinople after 1261), with the yellow-black the peacetime flag; the 14th-century Book of All Kingdoms shows Byzantine flags. Wikipedia: the double-headed eagle is not securely attested with the emperor before the 1301 chrysobull of Andronikos II (Soloviev c. 1288) and was used by the Palaiologan emperors for senior imperial family members; Pseudo-Kodinos (mid-14th c.) calls the tetragrammatic cross the customary imperial banner.
era-330.open: The two publishers agree on a Palaiologan double-headed eagle but differ on whether it was the flag (FOTW) or an emblem beside the cross banner (Wikipedia), and on its origin (Komnenos vs not before 1301). Neither covers 330-1261 or says the eagle descends from the aquila; the card is a later-form reconstruction.

era-395.says: Wikipedia's Western Roman Empire: after the death of Theodosius I on 17 January 395 the Western court under Honorius and the Eastern court under Arcadius were administered separately, and Romulus Augustulus was deposed by Odoacer on 4 September 476. Wikipedia's Byzantine flags and insignia article says the Eastern empire did not use heraldry in the Western sense and mentions emblems such as banners with the cross or the labarum, mostly for later centuries. Flags of the World's Roman Empire page covers vexilla, the labarum and legion flags without a flag for either half after 395.
era-395.open: The card is an openly invented split card (the caption says reconstructed); the sources read describe no standard or flag specific to the Western or Eastern court in 395-476, but that is silence, not a finding that none existed.

era-284.says: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Antiquities (J. Yates, 1875): after Constantine embraced Christianity 'a figure or emblem of Christ, woven in gold upon purple cloth' was substituted for the emperor's head on the standard, which 'was called labarum' (Prudentius, Nicephorus). Flags of the World: the emblem Constantine bore was the only recognised Christian emblem of his time, the Greek X and P, and the labarum was made of silk. Wikipedia (Labarum): Constantine's vision before the Milvian Bridge is dated 27 October 312 with differing accounts; little evidence for the labarum before c. 317; Wikipedia (Vexillum): Constantine replaced the spear point with the Chi-Rho.
era-284.open: Smith does not name the Chi-Rho; no source says the labarum replaced the older pagan legionary standards; the Tetrarchy (284-312) is not covered; the 312 vision is told differently by Lactantius and Eusebius. The card is a reconstruction.

era-27bce.says: Smith's Dictionary (J. Yates, 1875): 'In the second consulship of Marius, B.C. 104, the four quadrupeds were entirely laid aside as standards, the eagle being alone retained'; the eagle was of silver or bronze with expanded wings, and under later emperors it was carried with the legion. Wikipedia (Aquila): each legion carried one aquila; the Marius origin after 104 BC is Pliny's claim and disputed; bulls and wolves were also used by late Republican and early Imperial legions. Flags of the World mentions an aquila only as a modern re-enactment piece.
era-27bce.open: SPQR on the aquila is stated by none of the sources (Smith does not mention SPQR; Wikipedia's Vexillum doubts SPQR on army standards), so the card's caption detail is unsupported; no Imperial-era aquila survives.

era-509bce.says: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Antiquities (Yates, 1875): Marius in 104 BC kept the eagle alone as the standard, and the standards of the manipuli, the smaller divisions of the cohort, were called vexilla, borne by vexillarii. Wikipedia's Vexillum article: the legions began using the vexillum alongside other insignia during the Samnite Wars, a common vexillum displayed the aquila on a reddish backdrop, Marius made the aquila the sole legion symbol, and the only surviving vexillum is of the 3rd century AD. Flags of the World: the vexillum was a cloth on a crossbar and Suetonius records a blue ensign awarded to Marcus Agrippa.
era-509bce.open: The sources show the vexillum as a military standard of the Republican army, but not as a flag of the Roman state; no source dates a red vexillum, or an SPQR inscription, to 509-27 BC, and Flags of the World says SPQR was never used on flags in antiquity. The card's red field with a gold SPQR plaque is a stand-in.

era-1187.says: This page's own caption calls the image a placeholder: «placeholder — rival gusuku lords and, later, three separate kingdoms, no shared banner».
era-1187.open: Whether a flag, banner or standard existed in this period was not checked. The colour shown is not evidence of one.

era-1879.says: Wikipedia's Ryukyu Kingdom and Ryukyu Domain articles say Okinawa Prefecture was established in 1879. Wikipedia's Flag of Japan article says the sun disc flag was decreed the merchant flag and the navy flag in 1870 and became the de facto national flag, legally so in 1999; FOTW's Japan page says the flag became the national flag after the Meiji Restoration and was confirmed by the 1999 law. Wikipedia's Flag of Okinawa Prefecture adds that the prefectural emblem was adopted on 15 May 1972, when Okinawa returned to Japan, and the flag on 13 October 1972.
era-1879.open: Wikipedia says that during US rule (1945-1972) the US flag was the only national flag permitted to fly in Okinawa, so a continuous display of Japan's flag since 1879 is not true; no source read says when the Japanese flag began to fly in Okinawa after 1879.

era-1872.says: Wikipedia's Ryukyu Domain article says Japan created the domain in 1872 with Sho Tai as Domain King, abolished it in 1879 when Okinawa Prefecture was established, and captions the infobox image as the flag of the domain, the mon of the Second Sho family. FOTW's Ryukyu Dynasty page says its author could find no document or drawing of a Ryukyu national flag and could not confirm one with a researcher at the University of the Ryukyus, and notes ship flags and banners bearing the Sho three-comma family emblem, in various colours, from documents.
era-1872.open: Neither source says Japan's sun-disc flag flew over the domain; the sun-disc flag shown on the card is not confirmed. The Sho emblem banner is an emblem used by the royal house, and FOTW doubts a national flag existed; a white flag with a three-colour comma design is described as invented after 1945. The Okinawa prefectural education archive page on the Disposition of the Ryukyus confirms the domain of 1872-1879 but says nothing on flags (its certificate does not match its address, so it is not cited as a source).

era-1609.says: Wikipedia: the hidari mitsudomoe crest is called the first historical national symbol; Daisaku Kina (2012) found no contemporary source showing it used as a national flag, and ships bound for Satsuma after 1609 flew a banner with the Sho crest; a flag labelled 'flag of Ryukyu' from a ship drifting to Choshi in 1798 had a white field and black mitsudomoe. FOTW: no document or drawing of a national flag was found; a white flag with red, blue and yellow commas was probably invented after WWII; ship flags show the Sho three-comma emblem in both orientations.
era-1609.open: The sources do not say a flag was absent; they report none found. The red field shown here is not supported (sources describe white fields), so the drawing is a symbolic stand-in.

era-1429.says: Wikipedia: King Sho Toku adopted the hidari mitsudomoe in 1467 (a coffin inscribed with it and the year 1500 corroborates use); it does not describe any 1429 flag. Wikipedia and FOTW both report no document showing a national flag.
era-1429.open: The crest is dated after 1429 by the source, so it is not shown to be in use from the start of this era; the sources report no flag found rather than proving none existed.

era-1921-1.says: This page's own caption calls the image a placeholder: «placeholder maroon field — pre-republic era, no distinct territorial banner survives».
era-1921-1.open: Whether a flag, banner or standard existed in this period was not checked. The colour shown is not evidence of one.

era-200bce.says: This page's own caption calls the image a placeholder: «placeholder — no unified banner from any of the successive steppe polities».
era-200bce.open: Whether a flag, banner or standard existed in this period was not checked. The colour shown is not evidence of one.

era-1944.says: Wikipedia and Flags of the World agree that Tuva was absorbed by the USSR on 11 October 1944 and local flags and arms were abolished. Wikipedia says the Tuvan Autonomous Oblast (1944-1961) had no flag of its own, that the Tuvan ASSR (reformed 1961) used the RSFSR flag with a Russian inscription from 1962 and a Tuvan inscription from 1978, and that the Republic of Tuva adopted its own flag on 17 September 1992 (current design 2002). Flags of the World's Soviet-era page dates the ASSR (10 October 1961) flag to the law of 10 January 1962, the RSFSR flag with a gold Russian inscription, with the Tuvan inscription added on 10 November 1978.
era-1944.open: Neither source says a white-blue-red tricolour flew in Tuva in this period; the 1944-1954 flag shown by Wikipedia is the RSFSR flag. The Wikipedia and FOTW dates for the ASSR inscriptions differ slightly (1962/1971/1978/1990).

era-1943.says: Wikipedia's Flag of Tuva dates the last flag of the Tuvan People's Republic to 8 September 1943 to 11 October 1944, with the state's initials in Cyrillic after the change of script, and lists a possible variant with a hammer and sickle. Flags of the World (after Sokolov in the Flag Bulletin) says the constitution of 25 June 1941 set a red flag, 1:2, with the state initials in gold in the canton, that the Cyrillic letters came in on 8 September 1943 and the initials changed to 'TAP' by custom, not by law.
era-1943.open: The gold-on-red colouring comes from Flags of the World alone; the hammer-and-sickle motif named in the caption is only a 'possible variant' in Wikipedia, and neither source describes a blue canton. The page's caption wording needs to follow the sources, which give a red flag with the initials.

era-1921.says: Wikipedia's Flag of Tuva says that after independence was proclaimed on 14 August 1921 the republic used an unofficial flag of which there are several reconstructions, and that the first official flag (24 November 1926 to 18 October 1930) bore the name in Mongol script; later flags to 1941 were red with the state emblem. Flags of the World (after Sokolov and Lasmanis) says plain red flags were used in 1921, that the 1926 constitution set a red flag with the state arms in the centre, with revised arms in 1930, 1933 and 1941, and that a blue flag with a golden emblem for 1918-21 (Crampton) is doubted by contributors. Second look: the Russian specialist page Vexillographia.ru (after Tuvan historians, V. Sokolov in The Flag Bulletin XXII and the constitutions) says the first government flag, made in 1922 by the novice Tushpek-khuurak, has no surviving drawing and was presumably a red flag with the khorlo wheel; that a flag of the republic with the khorlo is visible in a newspaper masthead of July 1924, with reconstructions existing; that the Constitution of 24 November 1926 (articles 28-30) set a red rectangular flag with the state arms in the centre; that the Constitution of 18 October 1930 put a new arms at the centre of a red flag (no image found); and that in 1935 the arms became a horseman on a red flag with two versions. It also describes a party banner of the Tuvan People's Revolutionary Party (red, with a star, khorlo and a bull and plough) kept in the National Museum of Tuva, which is a party flag, not the state flag.
era-1921.open: No image of the 1921-1926 state flag survives beyond a newspaper masthead, so the card's drawing is a reconstruction, and the blue-and-yellow disc cannot be matched to any described design except as a loose stand-in for the state arms (a sky-blue field in a green wheel with gold edging in the 1926 description). The text read reaches 1943 only through red flags with changing arms in the centre.

era-1958.says: Wikipedia says the constitutions of 1946 and 1958 named the blue, white and red flag as the national emblem, quoting Article 2 of 1958: «the national emblem is the tricolour flag, blue, white, red»; that President Giscard d'Estaing introduced a lighter blue in 1974; and that on 13 July 2020 President Macron reverted the Élysée Palace to the darker hue without a statement. FOTW, citing the Société française de vexillologie, gives the same Article 2 wording for 1958, 1974 and 1976 for the lightening (Sache gives 1976), and 13 July 2020 for the darker blue, which it says was not officially announced and was mainly seen on state buildings.
era-1958.open: The sources date the lightening to 1974 or 1976. Neither names a shade, so the swatch colours are approximations. This is a start-year check only for the constitutional text; the flag itself dates from 1794.

era-1944.says: Wikipedia: the constitutions of 1946 and 1958 instituted the blue, white and red flag as the national emblem of the Republic (1958 art. 2: 'the national emblem is the tricolour flag, blue, white, red'). Flags of the World (Third Republic page): a tricolour that had been the last flown in Paris in 1940 was raised again on 19 August 1944; its Fourth Republic page shows the tricolour and gives no dated change in these years.
era-1944.open: No source read describes a Provisional Government flag distinct from the tricolour, and the Fourth Republic is covered only by the 1946 constitution reference; the abbreviation 'PFG' in FOTW's account is unexpanded.

era-1940.says: FOTW says the French State kept the tricolour (Stilling and Müller), that its only new flag was the head of state's standard, prescribed by a decree of 19 March 1942 as a tricolour with seven gold stars on the white stripe below a francisque (du Payrat and Blanc), and that Free France had to add a charge to the tricolour because Vichy kept it, the cross of Lorraine being prescribed as its emblem by a regulation of 5 June 1941 (Sache). Wikipedia's captions say Pétain used a standard with a francisque in the white stripe and the Free French a cross of Lorraine in the white stripe, and its Free France article says Vice-Admiral Muselier created the naval jack with a red cross of Lorraine by general order no. 2 of 3 July 1940 and that d'Argenlieu suggested the cross.
era-1940.open: The sources differ on when the cross of Lorraine was adopted (June 1940 or July 1940 for the jack, 5 June 1941 for the regulation) and on who proposed it (Muselier, d'Argenlieu). Neither describes the cross-of-Lorraine flags in enough detail to draw, and the image shows the plain tricolour. The star colour on Pétain's standard is gold in the decree and blue in a 1941 scout book.

era-1870.says: Wikipedia says the Comte de Chambord demanded a white flag as a condition of accepting the throne, rejected it when offered the throne in 1870, and that the tricolour was kept. FOTW says Chambord insisted on the white flag with fleurs-de-lis in the dispute of 1873, that compromise ideas were a tricolour with fleurs-de-lis or a white flag with a tricolour cravat, and that he held out.
era-1870.open: The sources differ on the year of the dispute (1870 or 1873). Neither gives a law fixing the flag under the Third Republic.

era-1852.says: Flags of the World (France: Second Empire): Louis-Napoleon was proclaimed Emperor as Napoleon III on 2 December 1852 and the national flag was the blue-white-red tricolour; its main France page says a regulation of 17 May 1853 officialised the 30:33:37 proportions for the ensign and that the dark navy blue was established at least from the Second Empire. Wikipedia (Flag of France): the tricolour has been France's national flag since 1830, the navy returned to 30:33:37 by a regulation of 17 May 1853, and the Third Republic followed the overthrow of Napoleon III.
era-1852.open: Wikipedia does not tie the 1853 regulation to the Second Empire in words, only by date; the imperial bee as an emblem is FOTW's alone.

era-1848.says: Wikipedia says the Second Republic adopted a tricolour variant for a few days, 24 February to 5 March 1848, and captions Philippoteaux's painting as depicting the rejection of the red flag in front of the city hall. FOTW says a decree of 7 March 1848 confirmed the tricolour ensign.
era-1848.open: Wikipedia does not describe the variant. The painting is cited as depicting Lamartine, not as a document.

era-1830.says: Wikipedia says Louis-Philippe restored the tricolour in 1830 and that it has been used since except in 1848. FOTW says the tricolour had been banned since 1815, reappeared during the July days of 1830, that on 30 July Lafayette gave Louis-Philippe a tricolour on the city hall balcony, that on 1 August 1830 his ordinance stated that the French nation resumes its colours, and that he used a fleur-de-lis coat of arms from 13 August 1830 to 16 February 1831 before dropping it.
era-1830.open: FOTW's July Monarchy page does not cover the cockade, military flags with the Gallic cock or 1848.

era-1814.says: FOTW says the white flag was restored as the national flag in 1814, which it had not been under the Ancien Régime (Sache). Wikipedia says the tricolour was replaced by the pre-revolutionary white naval flag in 1815–1830. FOTW says that on landing from Elba in 1815 Napoléon had the tricolour hoisted, that a decree of 9 March 1815 ordered the tricolour displayed on town halls, and that the Hundred Days ended at Waterloo on 18 June 1815.
era-1814.open: The sources differ on 1814 or 1815 for the white flag. FOTW's Restoration page gives no decree and does not cover the white cockade or royal standards. This page draws the plain white flag, without arms.

era-1804.says: Flags of the World (France: First Empire): Napoleon was proclaimed Emperor on 2 December 1804, the national flag during the First Empire (1804-1814 and the Hundred Days of 1815) was the blue-white-red tricolour, and the bee served as an imperial symbol. Wikipedia (Flag of France): the order was reversed to blue-white-red on 15 February 1794, 'under Napoleon I the proportions were changed to make the stripes' width equal', and the Bourbon restoration of 1815 replaced the tricolour with a white flag.
era-1804.open: Wikipedia gives no date for the change of proportions and does not mention eagle standards or bees; the 'imperial emblems beside it' rest on FOTW alone, and no decree confirming the flag was read.

era-1789.says: Wikipedia says the cockade was adopted in July 1789, Paris militia wearing blue and red with white added, that it became part of the National Guard uniform on 27 July 1789, that the Constituent Assembly approved a vertical red-white-blue tricolour on 24 October 1790, and that a resolution of 15 February 1794 reversed the order to blue-white-red. FOTW says the cockade existed by 12 July 1789, that the navy's jack and ensign of 1790 were the first vertical tricolours with red at the hoist, that a decree of 24 October 1790 became law on 31 October, that a decree of 26 June 1793 ordered tricolour flags on Paris public buildings, and that the decree of 15 February 1794 (27 Pluviôse, Year II) set blue at the hoist.
era-1789.open: Wikipedia says the attribution of the white is disputed, and FOTW calls the story of the king pinning the cockade a legend. The 1790 decree was about the flag generally, not only ships. The drawing shows the 1794 order.

era-1589.says: Wikipedia says the House of Bourbon ruled France in 1589–1792 and 1815–1848 and that the white Bourbon banner was used (image caption). FOTW says white was the royal and military colour, that the King's vessels carried plain white flags (Gay), and that a decree of 3 March 1781 prescribed the white flag on French consulates in the Levant, the first reported use of a white flag on land.
era-1589.open: FOTW says the white flag was a command flag and was not the national flag until 1814. Neither source describes a specific Bourbon royal standard.

era-987.says: Wikipedia says the red oriflamme, the banner of Saint Denis, was the royal banner under the Capetians; that the Valois arms of 1328 were blue with gold fleurs-de-lis bordered in red; that Charles V reduced the lilies to three about 1376; and that the blue field became the common standard of French armies in the Hundred Years' War. FOTW says the lilies first appear on Louis VIII's seal and on Philip II's banners (Gay), that Charles V reduced them to three in 1365, that a blue pendon with three gold fleurs-de-lis is described in 1350, and that in 1422 Charles VII adopted a white flag as his banner.
era-987.open: The date of the reduction to three lilies differs (1365 or about 1376). The oriflamme, which Wikipedia says was the royal banner under the Capetians, is not drawn, and the image shows the later blue banner for the whole span.

era-481.says: This page's own caption calls the image a placeholder: «placeholder maroon field — no flag documented for the Frankish kingdoms».
era-481.open: Whether a flag, banner or standard existed in this period was not checked. The colour shown is not evidence of one.

era-58bce.says: This page's own caption calls the image a placeholder: «placeholder maroon field — no flag documented for Gaul».
era-58bce.open: Whether a flag, banner or standard existed in this period was not checked. The colour shown is not evidence of one.

era-1898.says: Wikipedia and Flags of the World (Spain): the red-yellow-red flag with the crowned arms was the war ensign from 1785 and, by Royal Decree of 13 October 1843, the State and war flag and ensign. Flags of the World (War Ensign 1785-1931) shows a depiction of 1899; the US National Park Service says the red-and-gold flag replaced the Burgundian cross at sea in 1785 and as regimental colours in 1843, Charles III having adopted it as the naval ensign. Wikipedia adds that in the Bourbon years the Cross of Burgundy was still used with additions by individual military units. The National Park Service page says the red-and-gold flag became the naval ensign in 1785, was adopted by forts by 1793 and became the regimental colours in 1843.
era-1898.open: Three sources agree the red-yellow-red flag, not the Cross of Burgundy, was Spain's state and war flag in 1898, so the drawing is contradicted; no source read says the cross flew in the Spanish-American War. Wikipedia, Flags of the World and the National Park Service are three publishers; none documents the flag in the specific events of 1898 beyond its status as the state and war flag.

era-1808.says: Wikipedia (Flag of Spain): the red-yellow flag spread among people and volunteers from 1808 and became the colours of the Cortes de Cadiz; the red-yellow-red ensign dates from 1785. FOTW (War Ensign 1785-1931): the red-yellow-red ensign with crowned arms was the war ensign from the Royal Decree of 25 May 1785 and the state and war flag from 1843. FOTW (Kingdom of Spain 1808-1813), quoting a Spanish Navy page: during the Peninsular War white predominated but some corps used red and yellow flags popularised by Cadiz; Joseph Bonaparte's regime used a white flag with new arms.
era-1808.open: The sources confirm the red-yellow-red ensign for Spain in this period, not that it was flown in each rebel or loyalist territory; Joseph I's white flag of 1808-13 and the many local flags of the independence wars are not shown on the page, and the '1810-1825' label and the 1830s end are not covered.

era-1580.says: FOTW (Burgundy Cross Flag 1506-1785): the red Burgundy saltire raguly on white was Spain's ensign from 1506 to the 1670s, thereafter a jack until 1785, and the Spanish military flag from the 16th century to 1843. FOTW (1701-1785): Charles II and Philip V replaced it as ensign with royal arms on white. Wikipedia: Philip V's naval ensign was white with royal arms, the red-yellow-red ensign replaced it by 1785. NPS: the white flag with the red Burgundian saltire was flown by Spanish ships and fortresses across the New World until the 1785 ensign.
era-1580.open: The cross was the ensign only to the 1670s; for the rest of 1580-1808 the sources describe it as a jack and military flag, with royal arms on white and, from 1785, red-yellow-red as the ensign. FOTW also says it was never the official flag of the Empire, which was properly the royal standard. The gold medallion in the page's drawing is not supported.

era-1535.says: Wikipedia (Cross of Burgundy): the cross served as the flag of the viceroyalties, and New Spain's viceregal banner lasted to 24 August 1821. FOTW: the saltire was Spain's ensign from 1506 and its military flag in the 16th century, and a contributor calls it a military banner rather than the empire's official flag. NPS: this was the flag carried by ships and flown over the fortresses guarding Spain's New World possessions.
era-1535.open: No source gives the viceroyalties' founding dates (1535 for New Spain, 1542 for Peru) or says the cross was a viceroyalty's own flag in the 1535-1580s; FOTW says explicitly that it was never the official flag of the Empire, so 'naval and military ensign' is supported but 'imperial flag' is not.

era-1519.says: Wikipedia (Cross of Burgundy, Flag of Spain): from 1519 to 1556, under Charles V, various armies of his empire used the Cross of Burgundy over different fields, the earliest Spanish use being 1506. Flags of the World (Spain 1506-1700): it was 'the flag, if any was' carried by the conquistadors, and a military banner, never the official flag of the Spanish Empire. Flags of the World (Cortes): chroniclers (Tapia, Mendieta, Gomara) describe Cortes' flag as a red cross on white-and-blue flames with the motto 'In hoc signo', or royal-arms standards with a cross; the standard kept at Chapultepec is red with the Virgin Mary. Bernal Diaz del Castillo, a member of Cortes's expedition, says in his chronicle that Cortes in Cuba had standards and banners made, worked in gold, with the royal arms and a cross on each side and a Latin motto on following the sign of the Holy Cross. The U.S. National Park Service says Spanish naval ships flew the Burgundian cross from the early 1500s and that Charles I (1516-56) adopted it as the flag that came to represent Spain.
era-1519.open: The Cross of Burgundy is supported as a Spanish crown flag under Charles I, but the eyewitness account and the chroniclers quoted by Flags of the World describe Cortes's own banners differently (royal arms, a cross, a motto), so the drawing is contradicted for Cortes and unconfirmed for Pizarro, whose flag no source read describes.

era-1492.says: Flags of the World (15th Century Flags, after Calvo and Gravalos 1983): the Royal Standard of the Catholic Kings, 1492-1506, was a white flag with their arms, quarterly Castile-Leon and Aragon-Sicily, with St John's eagle as supporter; Columbus' logbook mentions the royal flag and two captains' ensigns, white with a green cross and the crowned letters F and Y. Wikipedia (Flag of Spain): a pennant of the Catholic Monarchs used until 1492, Aragonese and Castilian arms having merged in 1475 (citation needed).
era-1492.open: The sources describe a white flag with the Catholic Kings' arms; no image of the 1492 flag survives and FOTW notes landing scenes are later representations. Some authors cited by FOTW think the royal banner of Castile and Leon was carried instead; the page's earlier red-field drawing matches no source.

era-30bce.says: Wikipedia's article on Roman Egypt says Egypt was ruled as the imperial province of Aegyptus from its conquest by Roman forces in 30 BC to AD 642, and its Ptolemaic Kingdom article says the dynasty ruled until the death of Cleopatra VII in 30 BC. The World History Encyclopedia (Wasson) says Egypt became the property of Rome after Cleopatra VII's death in 30 BCE, ending the Ptolemaic dynasty. The flag articles originally read (Wikipedia's History of flags, FOTW's Egypt page) do not cover the annexation. Augustus's own record of his deeds (Res Gestae, chapter 27, Loeb translation) states that he added Egypt to the empire of the Roman people; the chapter gives no date.
era-30bce.open: The annexation is established, but no source read says anything about a flag or emblem for the event; the later Roman and Byzantine, Islamic and modern story on this page is carried by the Egypt page and was not checked here. Egypt's governance as the emperor's personal domain rather than an ordinary province is a nuance not covered.

era-305bce.says: A National Museums Liverpool catalogue record of a coin of Ptolemy I Soter (king of Egypt from about 305 or 306 BC) describes the obverse as a diademed head of Ptolemy I with aegis and the reverse as an eagle with closed wings standing on a thunderbolt; Wikipedia's Ptolemaic Kingdom article gives the dynasty's span as Ptolemy I until Cleopatra VII's death in 30 BC. Wikipedia's History of flags and FOTW's Egypt page say nothing of the period.
era-305bce.open: The diadem and the eagle on a thunderbolt are established on Ptolemaic coinage; their use on standards and the claim that Ptolemies kept pharaonic crowns and the uraeus in temple contexts are not established by the pages read. A search hit from National Museums Scotland returned a 403 and was not used.

era-664bce.says: Wikipedia's Late Period article: 664-332 BC, from the Saite 26th Dynasty to Alexander, including the First Achaemenid Period (525-404 BC, Egypt a Persian satrapy), the native 28th-30th Dynasties and the Second Achaemenid Period (343-332 BC), in which Persian emperors ruled as pharaoh; it does not mention a crown, banner or emblem. Wikipedia's Pschent article and the Egypt Exploration Society's resource describe the double crown as the emblem of unified rule but give no Late Period example. The Metropolitan Museum's record (34.2.1, via the AMICA library) of a Dynasty 30 statue of the falcon god Horus protecting King Nectanebo II says the god's double crown symbolises dominion over Upper and Lower Egypt; the small king wears a nemes headcloth and uraeus, not the double crown.
era-664bce.open: The double crown is documented as a symbol of dominion in Dynasty 30 (360-343 BCE) but on the god, not on the king, and no source read shows it for the Saite or Persian-ruled parts of 664-332 BCE or as a state emblem; no flag is documented for the period. The maroon field is the page's own.

era-1077bce.says: Wikipedia's Third Intermediate Period article gives c. 1077 to c. 664 BC (from Smendes to Tantamani) and describes a state that, after Osorkon II, had effectively split into two, with Libyan-descended (Meshwesh) 22nd Dynasty kings and later Nubian rulers; it names no emblem, banner or standard for any of these lines. Wikipedia's History of flags mentions Egyptian standards only for pre-dynastic nomes (Narmer Palette) and Diodorus's sacred-animal standards, and Flags of the World's Egypt page treats only modern flags and calls the attribution of colours to the ancients speculative. None of the three pages describes a flag or banner for this period.
era-1077bce.open: The card shows a blank frame and says no single flag is documented; our sources agree that none is described, but that is silence in three general pages, not proof that none existed. No Libyan or Kushite royal-emblem source (for example museum material on Shoshenq or Taharqa) was read.

era-1550bce.says: The Carnegie Museum of Natural History entry for a cobra (uraeus) head carved about 1345-1347 BCE at Akhenaten's Amarna (acquired from the Egypt Exploration Society in 1922) places it among Sun Disk (Aten) material. The Egypt Exploration Society's royal-crowns resource shows New Kingdom kings (Ahmose, Seti I, Ramesses II) in the Deshret and Khepresh crowns and describes the Wadjet cobra as shown on the forehead of kings. Wikipedia's Hedjet article pictures a New Kingdom royal statue head in the White Crown (1493-1482 BC). Together they show the cobra, sun disk and crowns as royal emblems of the New Kingdom.
era-1550bce.open: None of these sources says the uraeus or sun disk was a banner, flag or the single emblem of the New Kingdom state; the card's drawing is a reconstructed royal device, and the Carnegie piece is Amarna-specific (Akhenaten), not the whole 1550-1077 BCE span.

era-1650bce.says: Wikipedia's Second Intermediate Period article: Egypt divided into smaller dynasties between the Middle and New Kingdoms (dated there 1782-1550 BC, infobox 1700-1550); the Hyksos 15th Dynasty, said to be Canaanite or Amorite, ruled Lower Egypt from Avaris, while Theban dynasties held the south. The article names no emblem or banner for the Hyksos or the Theban kings. Wikipedia's History of flags and Flags of the World's Egypt page describe no flag for the period.
era-1650bce.open: The card presents a blank on purpose and our sources describe no emblem, but no Hyksos or Theban royal-emblem source was read, so this is silence rather than a finding. Wikipedia's start date (1782 or 1700 BC) differs from the card's c. 1650 BCE.

era-2055bce.says: Wikipedia's Pschent article: the double crown combined the White Hedjet of Upper Egypt and Red Deshret of Lower Egypt and represented the pharaoh's power over all unified Egypt; it was first worn by Djet of the First Dynasty and the Palermo Stone gives it to all First Dynasty 'and later' pharaohs, though no crown survives. The Egypt Exploration Society's resource says the double crown symbolises the unification of Lower and Upper Egypt under one ruler. Wikipedia's Hedjet article pictures a pair of Twelfth Dynasty (Middle Kingdom) statuettes of a king in the white and red crowns.
era-2055bce.open: No source read documents the double crown (rather than the white and red crowns worn separately) specifically for the Middle Kingdom, and it is not an emblem that begins then. The card's drawing is a reconstructed stand-in for a royal emblem, not a flag.

era-2181bce.says: Wikipedia's First Intermediate Period article (c. 2181-2055 BC): rule was roughly equally divided between a Heracleopolitan power base and a Theban one, with powerful provincial governors (nomarchs) such as those of Asyut and Ankhtifi of Hierakonpolis, and 'very little monumental evidence survives'. It describes no emblem or banner. Wikipedia's History of flags and Flags of the World's Egypt page describe no flag for the period.
era-2181bce.open: The card is an intentional blank and our sources describe no emblem, but that is silence, not a finding; no source on Heracleopolitan or Theban royal emblems was read.

era-2686bce.says: Livius.org: in the first dynasties the ruler's most important name was written in the serekh, and Fourth Dynasty kings stressed names in cartouches instead. Wikipedia's Serekh article: the serekh served as a royal crest, and the Horus name was the first of five royal titles in use by the Fifth Dynasty. The Egypt Exploration Society's resource describes the Hedjet and Deshret crowns generally; Wikipedia's Hedjet article places the white crown on the Narmer palette, on vases of Khasekhemwy (end of the Second Dynasty) and on a New Kingdom statue, with no crown surviving. The Egypt Museum site describes Cairo Museum JE 98943, a Fourth Dynasty limestone statue of Sneferu (c. 2600 BC) from Dahshur, showing the king in the White Hedjet crown, so the white crown as royal headgear is documented in the Old Kingdom.
era-2686bce.open: The white crown is shown on an Old Kingdom royal statue, but none of the sources read treats it, on its own, as an emblem of the kingdom or documents a flag for the period; kings of the era are also shown with other crowns and names in the serekh. The statue rests on a single compiled web page. The gold field and the 'monumental authority' wording are the page's own.

era-3100bce.says: Wikipedia's Serekh article: the serekh is a rectangular enclosure representing a palace facade, surmounted by (usually) the Horus falcon, indicating that the text inside is a royal name; it was the earliest convention for setting apart the royal name, predating the cartouche by four dynasties, and appears from the Gerzeh culture (c. 3400 BC). Livius.org (Lendering): in the first dynasties the ruler's most important name was written in the serekh, topped by a falcon thought to be Horus, e.g. on cups of Djer (Narmer's second successor) and an axe blade of Aha. Wikipedia's History of flags separately says the Narmer Palette is said to show the earliest standards.
era-3100bce.open: Neither source ties the serekh to Narmer's unification as a flag or banner; both treat it as a name-frame, so 'earliest royal identifying emblem' holds for the royal-name convention, and Wikipedia dates its first appearance (c. 3400 BC) before this row's 3100 BCE start. Livius says the falcon as Horus is likely but cannot be proved.

era-1975.says: Wikipedia (Flag of Sikkim): at present there is no official flag of Sikkim; the kingdom's flag lost official status in 1975 when Sikkim was admitted to India, and the Government of Sikkim can be represented by a banner with the state emblem on white. Wikipedia (List of Indian state flags): as of 2026 there are no officially recognised flags for Indian states, and the Constitution does not prohibit a state flag (Bommai, 1994). Flags of the World (Sikkim): the state flag is hardly seen and the Sikkim Democratic Front flag is the de facto flag. The Flag Code of India on the Ministry of Home Affairs site could not be read (HTTP 403, blocked; not worked around).
era-1975.open: No source read says that India's national flag is Sikkim's flag or describes it flying there; that rests on Sikkim being a state of India and on the absence of official state flags, and is not itself stated. The card's wording 'flag of the State of Sikkim' is not supported by the sources read.

era-1947.says: Wikipedia (Flag of Sikkim): a khorlo with gankyil on every flag of the kingdom from 1877 to 1975 and a simpler design with a solid red border from 1967; its Kingdom of Sikkim article shows a state flag (1967-1975) and a royal flag (1877-1975) for the kingdom. Flags of the World: c.1914-1962 a white field with a triple red, white and blue border and a red circular emblem (Carr 1961); 1962-1967 a red wheel with six motifs (Barraclough 1965); and a pre-merger flag of white with a red border and a yellow chakra (Barraclough).
era-1947.open: The drawing on this page is a reconstruction, as Wikipedia says of its images, and the two sources differ in detail on the emblem and colours. Neither gives dates for the Indian protectorate itself, or describes a maroon field or crossed dorje (which this page no longer claims).

era-1861.says: Wikipedia: the first Sikkimese flag was adopted in 1877, every flag of the kingdom bore a khorlo and gankyil, and its images of the 1877-1975 royal flag are reconstructions; its Kingdom of Sikkim article lists the royal flag as 1877-1975. Flags of the World: an 1877-c.1914 flag at 2:3 whose design is not described, and a c.1914-1962 flag, about 7:9, white with a triple border and red circular emblem (Carr 1961).
era-1861.open: There was no Sikkimese flag for 1861-1877 (Wikipedia has the Union Jack to 1877), so the flag is established for 1877-1947 only. The 1877-c.1914 design is described by neither source, and the maroon-and-gold banner is not supported. The British protectorate's dates are not given.

era-1642.says: Wikipedia (Flag of Sikkim): before 1877, under Nepalese-Bhutanese suzerainty and as a protectorate of Tibet, Nepalese, Bhutanese and Tibetan banners were flown in Sikkim until 1816, when Britain took control and the Union Jack flew until 1877, when the first Sikkimese flag was adopted. Wikipedia (Kingdom of Sikkim) shows flags only from the royal flag of 1877, and Flags of the World's Sikkim page begins with the 1877 flag. No further Sikkimese institutional or scholarly source on a Namgyal-era banner was reached in this pass.
era-1642.open: The card presents a maroon-and-gold crossed-dorje banner as the Namgyal dynasty's founding banner; no source read describes any Namgyal flag for 1642-1861, and the sources instead name foreign banners and the Union Jack. This is a gap in the sources read, not a finding that no Sikkimese banner existed.
